Question: How would you rate the musicianship of jazz legend Charlie Parker? Does his legacy stand up even today with so many talented people playing now?
Answer: You can tell the history of jazz in four words: Louis Armstrong, Charlie Parker. —Miles Davis Hi. Welcome to this answer. Please make yourself comfortable. We have some ground to cover. (Photo by William P. Gottlieb, source: [Portrait of Charlie Parker, Three Deuces, New York, N.Y., ca. Aug. 1947]) The Bare Minimum of Largely Unedifying Facts in the Case of Charles Parker Jr. Charlie Parker was born in Kansas City, Kansas, on August 29, 1920. His father Charles Sr was a dancer and singer and a serious alcoholic, and his mother Addie wouldn’t tolerate alcohol in the house. His parents separated, Charles Sr eventually becoming a chef on Pullman cars, which took him off around the country. Charles Jr began playing alto saxophone at the age of 11, but wasn’t very good at it. His mother bought him a new sax when he was 14, and he joined his high school band. In his mid-teens, he began to take music more seriously, and was taught the basics of improvisation by a local musician, trombonist Robert Simpson. Around this time, when he was first playing out as a musician, he got introduced to drugs. The same year, Parker proposed to his girlfriend, Rebecca Ruffin, and they were married. Again in 1936, on the way to a gig, he was in a car crash in which he broke three ribs. His effort to manage the pain may well have got him more dependent upon opioids. By 1937 he was addicted to heroin. At some point around this period, he adopted a regimen of practicing for several hours a day. He would sometimes vanish for days, because he was off practicing. His mother would go and find him and bring him home, he’d eat like a horse and then sleep for a couple of days, and then do it all over again. By 1937 he was working as a professional musician, actively seeking gigs. A residency in the Ozarks gave him ample practice time. In 1938 he joined Jay McShann’s band. In 1939 he went to New York City, where he worked for several months at several jobs, including dishwasher and washing cars. He was still practicing incessantly and playing at every opportunity he could find. His drug use slackened off, because he couldn’t afford them. All through his adult life, Parker alternated between being relatively clean, and using heroin. In 1940, he learned that his father had been stabbed to death. He returned to Kansas City for the funeral and rejoined Jay McShann’s band. While on tour with McShann he was introduced to Dizzy Gillespie, a trumpet player who was then with Cab Calloways’ orchestra. In 1942 Parker left McShann’s band and joined that of Earl Hines, a veteran pianist who’d played on many of Louis Armstrong’s classic early recordings. Here he played with Gillespie regularly for the first time: Gillespie had been fired from Calloway’s band after a misunderstanding that had led to a fight. In 1942, the American Federation of Musicians instituted a recording strike that would last until 1944. Parker left McShann’s band and started hanging out in New York with the group of musicians that centred around regular jam sessions in places like Minton’s Playhouse and Monroe’s Uptown House. (I wrote about this period in Alex Johnston's answer to What is Bebop in Jazz music?) The musicians at these sessions included Gillespie, pianist and composer Thelonious Monk, drummer Kenny Clarke, pianist Bud Powell, bassist Oscar Pettiford, and others. (Miles Davis joined the scene later on.) But these were not the only musicians who had been working towards taking jazz in a new direction, away from the riff-based swing that was then the dominant form of popular music in the Western world. Lots of other musicians had grown tired of swing and were pushing for something new. (This is amply documented in Gitler: see Sources.) It was into this situation that Parker arrived, having already made contact with Gillespie. He was almost immediately recognised by his peers as the dominant figure in the new music. From 1942 onwards, Parker, Gillespie and their colleagues made the first recordings of a new kind of jazz that would later be dubbed ‘bebop’, sometimes to the annoyance of the musicians themselves. Parker and Gillespie made many recordings together. In late 1946, Parker’s drug use became uncontrollable. He was asleep one night at the Civic Hotel when he accidentally set light to his mattress. He was arrested, beaten and jailed, then was checked into Camarillo State Hospital for six months. He got out in spring 1947, clean and healthy, and made dozens of recordings for the Savoy and Dial labels, with a band featuring Davis on trumpet and Max Roach on drums. For the next few years he continued to make the studio and live recordings which are the foundation of his legacy. He loved classical music, and made an album with a string section which was his most popular recording in his lifetime. He became tired of the limitations of three-minute recordings and song- and blues-based forms, and approached the modernist composer Edgard Varèse for music lessons. But he also went back to using drugs. When he wasn’t on drugs, he often drank to excess. At some point (I haven’t been able to find out when) he divorced his first wife Rebecca, married again (Doris) and divorced again, and then met his third and last partner Chan Richardson, with whom he had a daughter, Pree. Pree died in 1954 and Parker never got over her death. He attempted suicide twice and separated from Chan. In March 1955, he was at the apartment of his friend Nica de Koenigswarter, watching TV, when he had a heart attack and died. He was only 34 years old. The coroner who performed the autopsy had no idea of his birthdate, and estimated his age as being between 50 and 60. He is buried in Kansas City. For many years, his gravestone had the wrong date of death: March 23 instead of March 12. This was eventually fixed in 1992. However, the replacement gravestone bears an image of a tenor saxophone. Charlie Parker did not play the tenor sax. Not as his main instrument, anyway. His principal instrument was alto sax. Such were the fortunes of a jazz musician in the mid-20th century. Like so many lives of mid-20th century African-American jazz musicians, when you spell out the bare externals of Charlie Parker’s life like that, it’s mostly depressing. But what that story doesn’t tell you is what his impact was like on other people. What it was like to be around him. What people thought of him. You see, the opinions about Parker’s musicianship that truly matter, are not mine. What matters is the testimony of people who really knew his music, and understood from the inside what he was doing, and what made him different. Charlie Parker grew up in Kansas City. If we were to list only three cities in the USA which deserve to be regarded as true cradles of jazz, the first would be New Orleans, where jazz was created in the first place. The second would be New York City, where most great jazz musicians in the early/mid 20th century ended up coming to. The third would be Kansas City. In jazz terms, it was an astonishing combination of boot camp, battlefield and nursery. Stanley Crouch brilliantly describes Kansas City’s music scene in what I think is the best single book about Parker thus far for the general reader, Kansas City Lightning. Charlie Parker came out of Kansas City as one of those musicians who soaks up music more easily than other musicians do. When he was first living in New York in 1939, he attended a jam session at Dan Wall’s Chili House on Seventh Avenue and 140th Street, presided over by guitarist William ‘Biddy’ Fleet. Fleet noticed that Parker was interested in doing something unusual, and the thing that he really liked about Parker was that he didn’t need to go off and practice new ideas in privacy. He seemed to be able to absorb them instantly. His dexterity and the power of his playing became notorious. Many older sax players held their saxes at an angle in imitation of another of Parker’s influences, Lester Young, or otherwise posed while they played, or closed their eyes. Parker held his straight, and stared directly ahead while playing, and didn’t move, which earned him another nickname: Indian, after the wooden advertising figures used by tobacconists. During jam sessions among his friends, if things were getting competitive, someone would say ‘Go get Indian’, and Parker would be summoned from wherever he was practicing so that he could blow the interloper off the stage. His clean, aggressive tone makes his music stand out, especially on his many live recordings, where the rest of the band is sometimes a murky sound in the middle distance but he’s always there, in the foreground, his sax leaping up to the treble and then finding the most intricate and exploratory route down again. The jazz scholar Thomas Owens noted that Parker often accentuates the highest note in any phrase, and that’s one of the things that gives his playing that sense of soaring freedom, which in turn is why the nickname ‘Bird’ stuck to him. There are loads of stories about Parker’s negative personal habits: his tendency to pawn other people’s stuff so he could get money for drugs; his chronic lateness; his general unreliability as a human being; his greed (Miles Davis complains at length about this in his autobiography); his fatal susceptibility to his own appetites, which is maybe the same thing. There’s no getting around the fact that Parker as a human being was one of the legendary fuck-ups of jazz. The strange thing is that he’s not the kind of musician whose music was about how messed up he was. He’s not a Lester Young, or a Chet Baker, whose music seems to have functioned as a balm to their souls, a consolation for all the crap that they put up with. Parker’s tone is bright, aggressive and immensely confident. His music surges with life and power. It bucks you up. What was it like to be around that? The Testimonials It was one of the greatest uplifts of my life. Men like that just lift you up. It wouldn’t matter if they were playing with a washboard. They would still sound good. —Art Blakey, on the experience of playing with Charlie Parker It’s rare to get a genius on the scene. I guess not more than one will come along every quarter-century in any field you can think of. But Bird had all the necessary equipment. You could just follow the leader as far as Charlie Parker was concerned. —Kenny Clarke In my opinion, Bud (Powell) was a genius just like Bird. They were untouchable as far as their musicianship was concerned. They could do no wrong in anything they did, which was a hell of a mark for a young cat to try to achieve. —Sonny Rollins Bird used to come to Minton’s, and he was so great that everyone would leave the bandstand when he played. All the bad saxophone players showed him respect and let him have the bandstand. —Kenny Dorham The thing about Charlie Parker was that he was such a giant. He was so much better than everybody else. It’s not like there was this guy and that guy. There was everybody else, and there was Charlie. —Al Cohn [Parker] was always reading and learning. He was a very educated man. He could talk about—my car was goofing off and I said ‘Damn! I’m going to take this thing to the garage,’ and he said, ‘It ain’t nothin’ but such-and-such,’ and he got out there, and he went around the motor, and he fixed the damn thing! He knew all about the motor and what caused it to run and all that shit. He educated me to a lot of things because I’d go and keep him company. I know he’s over there by himself; he wasn’t interested in girls. Nothing they could do for him. He was outta sight. We used to sit up and listen to Firebird Suite and Rite of Spring. He hipped me to Stravinsky. ’Cause I wasn’t listening to that. I was listening to arrangers and bands. I wasn’t paying much attention to this real serious side of music, but he educated me to that fact and made me listen to it. And I got to learn Bartok and Wagner and all those guys. —Howard McGhee To me a Charlie Parker composition is a classic, it’s a work of art! —Freddie Hubbard Playing with Bird was an experience. Every night he would put something new in the tunes we played, like changing chords, playing different progressions. You never felt that you had to play the same thing you had played the night before. We used to wail! That’s what I dig. It was one of my greatest experiences; his mind was so fast. Other than playing the saxophone, Charlie was a very brilliant man. —Errol Garner Yard [Parker] was without a doubt my very favorite musician of all time. My favorite musician now is Dizzy. But Yard, I still hear things of his today that are so phenomenal I don’t believe it. […] In my estimation no-one has caught up with this man. —Carmen McRae You'll see that if Charlie Parker wanted to invoke plagiarism laws, he could sue almost anyone who's made a record in the last 10 years. If I were Bird, I've have all the best boppers in the country thrown into jail. —Lennie Tristano My uncle played me a Charlie Parker record when I was ten. I hated it—like hating your first cigarette, and then twenty years later you’re on twenty a day. —Derek Bailey I learned about improvising from Bean, Monk, Don Byas, Lucky Thompson and Bird. But Bird was such a great and inventive improviser that he would turn songs inside out. If you didn’t know music, you didn’t know where the fuck Bird was at when he was improvising. See, Bean, Don Byas, Lucky Thompson all had the same style: they would run their solos and then they would improvise. You could still hear the melody when they improvised. But when Bird played, it was totally another ball game, totally something else, something different every time. Among masters he was the master. —Miles Davis What did Charlie Parker do? He was no child prodigy. Bud Powell started piano lessons at five, and was playing in his brother William’s band at the age of 15. Parker’s early life, by contrast, has two famous moments of public humiliation. On one occasion, he went to a practice session of local musicians, at a time when he only knew how to play two songs, and not all of one of them: Fats Waller’s ‘Honeysuckle Rose’, and the first half of Hoagy Carmichael’s ‘Lazy River’ in F. The group started to play ‘Body and Soul’, and Parker was mortified, because he didn’t know it. He went off, determined to learn as many songs in as many keys as possible. Another time, around 1936, he attended one of Kansas City’s notoriously cutthroat jam sessions. Behind the drum kit at this session was one of the town’s top musicians: Count Basie’s drummer, Jo Jones. Parker started to play, but he lost track of the rhythm. Bass player Gene Ramey, who was there that night, observed that he was ahead of the rest of the band. Jo Jones had a way of signalling to a player that his time was up: he would hit the bell of his ride cymbal. He hit it, but Parker didn’t notice. He hit it again. People in the crowd were starting to say ‘Get this cat off of here.’ So Jones took his cymbal off its stand and dropped it on the floor. Everyone laughed, except 16-year-old Charlie Parker, who stopped playing and left the bandstand. He went back to stand with Ramey and others. Ramey advised him to ‘stop playing like you’re so anxious, because if you’re so anxious like that you’re sure to get ahead of them.’ ‘It’s all right,’ Parker said, keeping his face as impassive as possible to mask his frustration, and then he added, rather like the Terminator, ‘I’ll be back.’ More than one Parker biographer has noted that there was an element in his makeup of wanting to be never at a loss. His legendary practice regimen, which began some time in the mid-30s and ended around the time he properly hit the New York scene around 1942, was focused around learning as many things as possible in as many keys as possible, so that he could never be caught out again, the way he was at that practice session where he only knew one and a half songs. I’m not a sax player, so I don’t understand the arcane specifics of sax fingering, but whereas it’s relatively easy to transpose tunes on the guitar (shift your hand up and down the neck, bingo), it’s different with wind instruments. Parker formed his playing style so that he could never again get lost on his instrument, the way he did at those jam sessions as a teenager. When, in 1946, he recorded a version of ‘Lover Man’ while badly strung out and suffering from malnutrition, you can hear him playing in uncharacteristically short-breathed, broken phrases. It’s clearly the sound of a great musician in a very bad way. (It was later that night when the mattress-on-fire incident happened.) The recording was issued, and some people love it, but he was furious about it. It wasn’t his sound, the way he wanted to be heard. Inasmuch as he wanted always to be in full command of what he was doing, Charlie Parker was unlike John Coltrane. The jazz critic Ben Ratliff noted that Coltrane was always at his most creative at times when he expressed uncertainty about what he was doing, and where he was going. Coltrane was an obsessive student: he was always trying to move on and learn more. Parker, by contrast, hated not knowing what he was doing. He was about overcoming musical problems with apparently effortless mastery. He, too, was a student: in 1954 he told a novice player You see, once you stop wantin’ to learn things, you’re not alive anymore. But he didn’t like to play when he felt unsure of himself. He presented himself as one who, as they say, had authority. Parker did not single-handedly invent bebop. He worked and worked his way to a place where he could soak up new influences instantly, and transform them into something that was his own. It has been noted many times that a lot of musicians, when they improvise, use formulas: riffs and licks that they’ve practiced and which they insert where appropriate, rather than make up something totally new each time. Most musicians, especially in rock music, have maybe a dozen or so of these. The jazz scholar Thomas Owens estimated that Parker had about a hundred of them. Owens’ book Bebop: The Music and its Players is a survey of the music divided into different instruments, but Parker is the only musician to have a chapter to himself, ‘The Parker Style’. He came along when musicians like Gillespie, Monk and Clarke had been working their way towards something new. They had been reworking jazz from the ground up, harmonically and rhythmically: Gillespie with his close study of harmony, Monk with his extremely individual style of composition. Charlie Parker came along, took the music and, because he had already figured out so much of it by himself, showed them what could be done with it. Sax players before Parker used a wide variety of expressive effects, such as Ben Webster’s fondness for emphasising the sound of his own breath, or Johnny Hodges’ exceptionally wide vibrato and bent notes. Parker didn’t use these effects. He didn’t try to vocalise with his sax, or seduce the listener with sexy glissandi. He himself described what he was doing as: I’m looking for the pretty notes. He wanted his music to be expressive in terms of the notes he played, not so much how he played them. And I think this is fundamental to his importance as a musician, because it’s one reason why he was so influential. You can transcribe a Parker solo, and get down almost all the important musical information in the form of notation. Parker’s hard tone and brief vibrato is less important than his phrasing, his note choices, his sense of the blues, his incredible, dazzling sense of musical logic. But if you were to transcribe a Johnny Hodges solo, or a solo by Ben Webster, it’d be a lot harder to indicate with notation what’s so effective about it. The jazz scholar Gunther Schuller transcribed Louis Armstrong’s brilliant unaccompanied intro to ‘West End Blues’ in his essential book Early Jazz, but then added the caveat that his transcription was really only an attempt to convey what Armstrong had played. Parker’s approach changed the music that was played, more than it changed the way the music was played. He didn’t just find a new way of playing what was already there. Just as Shakespeare expanded the English language, Charlie Parker expanded the language of jazz. Owens: [L]ying beneath the surface of his improvisations is another factor that helps generate the sense of rightness in his music. Typically entire phrases, and even entire choruses and groupings of choruses, are goal-oriented: they arrive on a final note that lies at the end of a length stepwise descent. Parker, through his huge effort of striving to understand where the music could go next, mastered the new direction, and made it seem natural and inevitable. He helped give jazz a new life. In another answer, I wrote about the cultural legacy of jazz being the improvisational attitude, the wily, skilful presence of mind required to overcome difficulties that have been placed in your way. Jazz music specialises in this: creating a harmonic and rhythmic labyrinth from which the musician must heroically escape. How the musician escapes from it creates what we think of as the musician’s style. Miles Davis didn’t so much escape the labyrinth as act as if it wasn’t a problem. In his earliest years he tried to sound like a more virtuosic player, such as Dizzy Gillespie, one of the greatest musicians in jazz history. He later developed a more low-key, insouciant style that floats around the harmony, alluding to it but not chained to it. (In the legendary Plugged Nickel recordings, Miles and his band challenged themselves to do the exact opposite, and the result is amazing, but he didn’t stick with that approach for long.) Miles would go on to devise one labyrinth after another, and in each case saunter through them with the same inimitable, electrifying cool. Other players have different ways of getting out of the labyrinth. John Coltrane used every tool in the toolbox to blast his way out, even calling upon god to help him. His music is heroic in its determination, and it’s always relentlessly serious, and if we love it, it’s partly because we’re always rooting for him. Chet Baker lies on his bunk in his cell, mourning his plight, having failed to notice that his cell door is actually unlocked. Charles Mingus’ labyrinth is also his fortress, with himself standing on the battlements, heckling society through a megaphone. Parker surveyed the labyrinth, assessed its weaknesses, rebuilt it to make it more difficult to escape, and then gave that wide-eyed, radiant smirk of his, the one you can see in the picture at the top of this answer. Then he soared upwards into freedom. That’s why it makes so little sense to talk of his ‘musicianship’, as if he were like any other jazz musician that comes along, in any generation. It’s like talking about whether or not Rembrandt could paint people so that they looked like themselves. If there are curious readers of this answer who’ve never actually heard Charlie Parker play, well, props to you for getting this far. And you’re probably wondering what all the fuss is about. Rather than lament the shortness of his life and the sadness of his early death, you ought to be rewarded with a blast of his music at its most powerful and exhilarating. And given that Parker credited Ray Noble’s ‘Cherokee’ as the tune that prompted his great musical breakthrough, we should finish on the tune Parker wrote over the chord changes to ‘Cherokee’: ‘Ko-Ko’. Charlie Parker was born on August 29, 1920. I posted this answer on this site on August 29, 2020. One hundred years later, to the day. Happy birthday, sir. And thank you. (Charlie Parker in a photo booth, Kansas City, 1940.) And thank you, reader, for your time. Sources:

Question: Why do certain segments of the population believe having a woman President like Kamala Harris is in the nations best interest? Doesn't this make a country weaker, more vulnerable and less respected?
Answer: You would need to explain how having an experienced public servant like Harris as US president could make a country more vulnerable and less respected than it was under Donald Trump, during whose presidency the USA sank to a lack of international respect that was unprecedented in my lifetime. Trump’s followers think it was the other way around: that the USA was more respected when he was in power. But the fact that they think that, is one of the reasons why Trump made the USA during his presidency seem weak and contemptible: his supporters were the least well-informed, most bigoted, most shrill and demented group to have ever brought a president to office. And that was obvious to all observers, except the bigoted, shrill and demented ones in other countries that looked at Trump, and melted into puddles of worshipful goo. Other countries have had women premiers and have not lacked respect. I greatly dislike Margaret Thatcher and her legacy, but few thought that she made the UK look ‘weak’. Jacinta Ardern pissed off conservatives, but she made New Zealand look like a place that people could be proud to come from. Even now, in the UK, conservatives are keeping very, very quiet about the last fifteen years, and are bleating that the new PM Keir Starmer has made the UK into a ‘laughing stock’, because they don’t like him, and they do not want the topic of conversation to change back to the waffling liar Boris Johnson, or the idiot nonentity Liz Truss, the shortest-serving British prime minister by a very long distance, or the fumbling placeholder Rishi Sunak. (As a small measure of the way a small measure of political normality has returned to the UK, the tabloid newspapers no longer scream every day about the latest political scandal, or engage in furious whataboutism: instead, they’ve largely gone back to staple non-stories like ‘Look at these weirdos who eat cold baked beans’ or ‘Tragic last words of cancer dad.’) The thing about Harris is that, except in far-right-wing circles, she is not a standing joke, the way Trump is. If Trump were re-elected in November, international trust in the USA would go through the floor, because it would become clear that too many of its its citizens cannot be expected to understand what’s good for their country. Something that puzzles me is that, when the right believe that the wrong person in power, they squeal that the country is a ‘laughing stock’, and act as if they’re mortified by foreign opinion; but when they get their own person in power, and the country is a laughing stock, or at least despised and hated by intelligent people around the world, they think that a) they have the world’s respect, but also b) who cares about foreigners’ opinions anyway. I would say ‘it’s all just theatre’, except that that’s unfair to theatre.

Question: Why is there a left-handed advantage for beginners learning to play guitar left-handed that right-handed people will never understand?
Answer: There isn’t, so this question is invalid. Left-handed people have no special advantage that right-handed players don’t have. Everything depends on practice, not on handedness. There are people like myself who are ‘cross-dominant’, meaning we do some things with our left hand and some with our right hand. I write with my left hand, but play guitar right-handed. This is not uncommon among guitar players: David Byrne, Mark Knopfler, Gary Moore, Duane Allman and Robert Fripp are (or, in the case of Moore and Allman, were) cross-dominant the same way that I am. But there are also loads of great players who are uncomplicatedly right-handed and are superb players. Just as there are great left-handed players too. I don’t believe that there is a single natural advantage to any particular kind of handedness. It’s been said that Jimi Hendrix was able to get a different sound by playing guitar upside-down: big deal, a right-handed player could play a left-handed guitar upside down and theoretically get the same sound. So I don’t believe that the premise of this question is factual.

(Mr Lawrence’s writing on trans people consists of nothing but him mocking them as at best comical and at worst pathetic and awful.) What’s this got to do with ‘grooming’, you ask? I never tire of quoting the late, great Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, who observed in her masterpiece Epistemology of the Closet that: Many people have their richest mental/emotional involvement with sexual acts that they don’t do, or even don’t want to do. I think that this is true of homophobic and transphobic people, who tend to be irrationally fixated on things that they don’t do and don’t want to do, and who aren’t very willing to understand why they’re like that. I came out in middle life because I noticed the social phenomenon of younger people coming out, and that gave me confidence. (Thanks, Gen Z! You too, millennials! You guys rock!) But, to return to Sedgwick’s wise words from earlier, it is possible for people to have rich ‘mental/emotional involvement with sexual acts that they don’t do, or even don’t want to do’. Unfortunately, that rich involvement with acts that they don’t want to do can lead to some very nasty consequences for people who do want to do them. I spend a lot more time thinking about music, the guitar, language, politics, philosophy, my kids, my health and the finer points of stir-frying than I think about sexuality. But for some people, sexuality is so hugely important that it matters very much to them that it be policed and controlled. And those people think that we’re the problem. They are their own problem. Question: What are the best books or material to understand abstract art? My understanding is: It is something say a tree of which the essential nature is abstracted or obfuscated. Is the viewer to try to understand what the object was or enjoy?
Answer: I would say that that’s not a good understanding of abstract art. Abstract art is not meant to be a puzzle to figure out; it is not referential, in that there is not an object ‘behind’ it which the viewer is expected to recognise. Abstract art is more like music, in that it aims to convey meaning simply by structure and colour and the relationships between the elements in the picture, rather than by reference to actual objects. An extreme example of this would be something like Malevich’s 1918 painting Suprematist Composition: White on White, which is simply a white square inside a larger, slightly off-white square. ‘Suprematist’ has nothing to do with theories of racial superiority; it was just the name Malevich gave to his theories about an art that would be free from the compulsion to depict the visible world. White on White is itself a development of Malevich’s even more uncompromisingly minimalist Black Square, from 1915, which is… a black square. As you can see, the black paint has now cracked somewhat, so it’s no longer as purely black as it was. I don’t believe that that was intentional on Malevich’s part. There is no effort being made here to show a real object. It’s more about what staring at a black square does to you. Malevich would never be quite this extreme ever again: his later paintings (which are still very fine) depict figures. But later artists such as Mark Rothko (1903–1970) moved from earlier work that has some echoes of the outside world: Baptismal Scene, 1945 —to later work that was as abstract as it was religious in inspiration. Rust and Blue, 1953 Rothko associated particular colours with particular notions or states of mind. When someone once asked him if he’d paint a picture with ‘warm colours’, Rothko replied ‘Red, yellow, orange—aren’t those the colours of an inferno?’ There are plenty of books on abstract art. I recommend more or less anything published by the UK company Thames & Hudson, whose books on art history are pretty reliable. But in order to appreciate it, you should first rid yourself of the idea that the point is to figure out what object is being depicted. That’s not how abstract art works. Question: I’m writing a book but lately I’ve been having a block because I’ve been thinking that perhaps this book isn't entirely ~my~ creation but just an amalgam of my favorite books. How do I know if it’s really my voice and not that of other authors?
Answer: Your voice is that amalgam of your favourite books. This is why it really helps writers to have lots of favourite books. The more influences you have, the more they contribute to the general mix that constitutes your ‘voice’. The American novelist Kathy Acker (1947–1997) suffered from exactly your anxiety about ‘voice’, until she simply decided that it didn’t matter, and that her writing was obviously made up from different influences—whereupon she started writing books that couldn’t be mistaken for anyone else’s work. (Acker’s Blood and Guts in High School is one of my favourite American novels.) Kathy Acker, dressed down for a change. By abandoning the idea that she had to find something that was ‘really [her] voice’, she found her way of writing. (She would say that she found the whole concept of a writer finding their ‘voice’ to be ‘very big, very God-like’ and confusing.) This is a 20th century way of approaching the same sort of sensibility that prompted the young poet Arthur Rimbaud to say, in a letter to a friend, ‘Je est un autre’: I is an other. Other writers seem like they have ‘voices’ because we look at their work and it seems perfect and all of a piece. But secretly, they know where all that stuff is coming from. We are all made up of other things: other voices, other books, other people. What we have to do is be fine with that. Once we are fine with that, we relax, and we speak as ourselves. In the words of the great Pakistani Marxist poet Faiz Ahmed Faiz: Speak, your lips are free. Speak, it is your own tongue. Speak, it is your own body. Speak, your life is still yours. See how in the blacksmith's shop The flame burns wild, the iron glows red; The locks open their jaws, And every chain begins to break. Speak, this brief hour is long enough Before the death of body and tongue: Speak, 'cause the truth is not dead yet, Speak, speak, whatever you must speak. Whatever you must speak. So what if other voices are inside you? Your lips and your tongue and your body and your life are still yours.

Question: Should I watch Guy Ritchie's movie "The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare"?
Answer: There’s no ‘should’. Watch it if you want. I found it oddly inert. It is my basic belief that Henry Cavill can’t really act, but in this film, he did play the character as written: an unflappable British Chap, who strolls through the movie dealing out death to hapless German mooks with his silenced Sten gun, and quietly improvising on the fly when things don’t go according to plan. I found his character affable and entertaining. Trouble is, the film is basically an excuse to have all its protagonists be variants on that. The team consists of Cavill as the British Chap, then there’s an unflappable Irish Techie (the sailor of the team), and an unflappable Danish Killer, and another unflappable British Chap as the Planner. This one, when we first meet him, is attached by his nipples to a battery because he’s being tortured by the Narzies, but when our team almost effortlessly rescues him, shooting down his torturers as he watches with interest, he then politely and unflappably asks his rescuers to turn off the battery. Then there’s the Unflappable Black SOE Agent (Babs Olusanmokun) and the Unflappable Woman SOE Agent (Eiza Gonzàlez), who IMO is the person in the movie who really can’t act. I am normally the first person to come down hard on complaints that young attractive women can’t act, because the accusation often comes from mere sexism, but Gonzàlez is so wooden that they could have forced German sailors to walk the plank on her. To be fair, English isn’t her native language, and she does sing rather well, I’ll give her that, giving an interesting version of Brecht & Weill’s ‘Moritat’ (‘Mack the Knife’ to you), transposed into E minor to make it sound ominous. Then there’s Rory Kinnear, under a ton of unconvincing makeup, as Winston Churchill, of all people. Possibly the least interesting screen Churchill ever. The only point in the film where Cavill’s character betrays the slightest stress, concern or anxiety is towards the end, regarding a plot point (two characters needing to make a lucky escape under extreme conditions)… which is then simply glossed over, because they suddenly appear, their escape having been left undramatised. Watching this movie made me think idle thoughts about whether or not there’s been a decline in the British WW2 movie. British WW2 movies made during the war, such as The First of the Few, usually emphasised the importance of fighting. In the 50s, the focus shifted, making them films mostly about flawed men dealing with their demons. Ice Cold in Alex is a great example, but so I think is The Cruel Sea, in which some of the main characters are just rubbish, and a lot of them get killed. In the 60s, America was funding most of the war films (The Longest Day, The Bridge at Remagen) and so they’re heavily America-centric, and rely on spectacle and all-star casts. In The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare, although the plot is very loosely based on a real mission (Operation Postmaster), the movie is an excuse to peddle an image of perfectly calm, competent Britishness. With the Danish guy being sort of honorary British. When the team finds out, two thirds of the way through, that the ship they have trekked to Equatorial Africa to sink has been heavily armoured and is now unsinkable, it takes them about ten seconds of screen time to devise an alternative plan. In a desperate attempt to make them look like they have serious antagonists other than, you know, Nazi Germany, the film constructs Admiral Dudley Pound as a mean, obstructive bureaucrat, determined to stop them. This is not only unfair to Pound, but at this point in the war, Pound was suffering from hip degeneration, the pain of which kept him awake at night, which in turn gave him an unfortunate tendency to doze off in meetings. He would die of a brain tumour a year after the events in this movie, still grieving for his wife, who’d died a few months earlier. Needless to say, Operation Postmaster wasn’t exactly like this. There was an awful lot fewer dozy German soldiers being mowed down by Sten guns, and a lot more prisoner-taking and sneaking about. In short: just another Guy Ritchie movie. Neither a must-see nor an embarrassing shambles. A movie about 2024, not about 1942.

Question: What are the best examples of a really good design?
Answer: I’m sure someone’s already used this as an answer, but: The London Underground Map. A map of the London Underground from 1897. Not the subject of this answer. I think people forget, or don’t know, just how old the London Underground is. It’s one of the features of London which Londoners themselves routinely take for granted, because they use it all the time and it’s been there since long before living memory. Yet in the 160-odd years since the opening of the Metropolitan Railway in 1863, it’s had strikingly few major accidents, and during its prolonged construction, it’s had almost none. The Metropolitan Railway ran steam trains underground between Bishop’s Road in Paddington and Farringdon Street. One line, seven stations. Other lines quickly got built: the Metropolitan District Railway (soon known as simply the District), the City and South London Railway, the Waterloo and City, the Central London Railway. They were all in competition with each other and there was no central governing authority: the companies that built them were aiming to make money, not so much to provide a useful service. A map of the Underground from 1887, printed by someone who was evidently being paid by the Metropolitan District Railway to give that line more prominence than the others. By the end of the 19th century, London and its suburbs were criss-crossed with multiple underground railway lines, some ‘cut and cover’ sub-surface lines, others deep-level ‘tube’ lines. The suburbs themselves had in many cases grown up around the stations: Hammersmith had been mostly market garden territory until it got an Underground station, while places like Ruislip and Rayners Lane had been mostly farmland until the Underground provided an incentive for property developers to build houses. (Why did they build Underground lines out to the countryside in the first place, you ask, if nobody lived there except farmers? To carry agricultural freight such as milk and vegetables back into the city.) In order to make sense of this, maps were of course needed. But the earliest Underground maps, as you’ve seen above, were intricate and hard to read. In this 1908 map, we’ve finally started sensibly colour-coding the lines, and we can see all the different lines that existed at the period, and where they went. Mostly. Some of the outlying stations are too far away to fit onto the map, and station names are printed at weird angles so as to fit into the available space. The surface features have been ‘greyed out’, which makes the map more legible. It’s not great. But it’s better than the monstrous splodges above. Eventually, the organisational chaos of the Underground was brought under the regulation of the London Passenger Transport Board, better known as London Transport. But we’re jumping ahead slightly. By 1926, the network itself had got considerably more complicated. Here’s Frank Stingemore’s map from that year: Here, we see that we’re no longer trying to fit the map onto an actual map of London, because that’s just too confusing. But it’s very cramped in the middle, because it still shows the twists and turns of all the different lines, and it doesn’t have room for the outlying stations on the Bakerloo, Metropolitan and District lines. It’s a rather unhelpful compromise: it doesn’t show you where the stations are on the surface, and it’s difficult to follow the tangled lines to see how to get to where you want to go. Then, in 1931, Harry Beck, a technical draughtsman who’d recently lost his job at London Transport, had an idea. Beck’s great insight was that the map did not need to show you what the Underground network looked like. It only needed to show the network’s topology: what relationships the different lines and stations had to one another, regardless of how far apart different stations actually were, or how the tracks curved. The point of the map was to enable users of the Underground to figure out how to get where they wanted to go, so it didn’t matter if it bore very little resemblance to the relative locations of stations. Lines didn’t have to be curved the way they were in real life. As long as the relations between them were clear, you could use straight lines and only 45 and 90 degree angles. What he designed was not really a map. It was a diagram. (There is an urban legend that he based it on electrical circuit diagrams. He didn’t, but he did do a spoof version after someone pointed out the resemblance.) He submitted his design to London Transport. They turned it down for being ‘too revolutionary’. He tweaked it a bit, sent it back, and they accepted it, paying him a grand flat fee of £10. Harry Beck’s original map. London Transport was not sure if the map would take off. They initially distributed it as a folding handout, with the inscription A new design for an old map. We should welcome your comments. The map was snapped up. The initial print run was 750,000 copies but they almost immediately had to order another 100,000. All of a sudden, the network of lines made immediate sense. All that was necessary was to sacrifice geographical accuracy. Harry Beck’s map became the template for almost all subsequent versions of the Underground map. It has gone on being revised as new lines have been added, stations have been closed, and the geographical reach of the Underground has extended. There have been attempts to radically change the Tube map. None of them have taken off. For decades, Beck got no credit for this, and was quite bitter about it, but in 1997, he started being credited on each publication of the map. (Although this seems to no longer be the case.) In any case, to anyone with a more than passing interest in the Underground, he has a place of honour. This is the Underground in 2024, including the Overground, which will shortly be split up into separate lines (Lioness, Mildmay, Windrush, Weaver, Suffragette and Liberty) because it’s too big to be just one line. The Transport for London map today. The basic design principles of Harry Beck’s map are still used, over 90 years later. Harry Beck’s Underground map would go on to inspire similar maps of underground systems in other cities. In spite of half-hearted efforts to replace or tweak it, it remains one of the principal ways in which London is understood. Sources: Caroline Roope, The History of the London Underground Map, Pen & Sword Transport, 2022 Christian Wolmar, The Subterranean Railway, Atlantic Books, 2004

Question: Will you be doing the NaNoWriMo challenge this year 2024? And if not, will you be do something else instead?
Answer: No. Because I already tried it, and I learned the lesson that was mine to learn. Long before I did NaNoWriMo in 2013 or so, I had been a professional playwright. Between 1997 and 2006, nearly every play I wrote got produced. I wasn’t a particularly brilliant playwright, but I had my moments. However, I had very bad working practices. I couldn’t write unless I had an idea of something to write. The writing then became about executing the idea. Sometimes, when I was writing, ideas would begin to flow and I’d start writing really well. But at other times, when I had no ideas, I could spend entire days sitting at the keyboard and would end up with nothing. Eventually, immigration (and self-doubt) helped kill my playwriting career (Scotland in 2009 turned out to not want immigrant playwrights) and I stopped writing completely for a couple of years. Then I resumed, only this time, I was writing fiction. But, again, I could only write when I already had an idea of something to write. Then I heard about NaNoWriMo, and thought I’d try it. Characteristically, I didn’t get around to trying it until something like the 10th of November. The goal I set myself was to never again get up from a writing session with nothing, as I had been doing for years. I had a couple of chapters of a half-assed fantasy novel. One night, with everyone else in bed, I sat down at the computer with my half-assed novel document open, and no ideas. I stared at where I’d left off and thought, Well, I’ve got to do something. So I just started moving my fingers and making words. These turned into the next sentence. Then another sentence. Then another. Gradually, I picked up the story and it began to develop. Now that I was no longer trying to get it to go somewhere, it started to go somewhere. After a while, I looked up. It was an hour and a half later and I had two thousand words that hadn’t been there before. I went to bed feeling like I’d done something. The next night, I tried it again. And the next night. And it always worked, as long as I did it every night. I had realised what Flannery O’Connor called the power of habit in art. If you make a habit of writing, you can write something. By the end of November, I had 60,000 words. And the story had gone somewhere I liked but had never previously imagined. Ever since then, I have known (and have demonstrated to myself time and again) that I don’t need to have any ideas when I sit down to write. I just need time. When I start writing, the writing will happen, as long as I keep doing it. It was shortly after that that I began writing my Epic Fantasy Saga, which soon grew to a monstrous size (seriously, the word count is positively Proustian, at this point, and that’s not even including the pages and pages of world-building notes) and which demanded so much of my time and attention that it certainly contributed to the end of my marriage, which I still feel guilty about but, que sera sera. The half-assed fantasy novel never got finished, but I did incorporate much of it into the Saga because it was good stuff and there was a place where I needed it. I don’t need a special place to write, or a special pen, or a special room, or even a quiet room. In one of my former jobs, I used to regularly write a few hundred words at lunchtime in the local Pret a Manger. All because of the discipline that NaNoWriMo put on me. If I had to write a short novel in a month, on pain of death, I know I could do it. It probably wouldn’t be very good, but I could do it. So for that reason alone, I recommend it.

Question: In what books does Harold Bloom tell you the criteria for good literature? I want to be an author so I want to adopt the standards of the greatest literary critic?
Answer: That’s not how this works. It’s not how literary criticism works; it’s not how reading works; it’s not how writing works. Harold Bloom doesn’t know ‘the criteria for good literature’, although he behaves as though he does. Nor is he the ‘greatest literary critic’. The unfortunate truth is that this is a ton more difficult than you think. Correction: it’s a f**kton more difficult. There is not some list somewhere of the ‘criteria for good literature’ which you can learn and then tick off as you attempt to make your own writing comply with them. Writing is not a box-ticking exercise. You learn what great literature is by reading it, and reading about it, and thinking about it, and re-reading it, and thinking more about it, and reading more about it. Eventually, if you keep it up, you start developing internal standards that work for you. How do we know that there are not some universal standard criteria for good literature, which are—and this is the crucial bit—easily specified? Because there is no universal agreement about what those criteria might be. Good literature is diverse. Not all literature is good in the same way. I love the work of James Joyce. I also love the work of Franz Kafka. I have enough French and enough German to have looked at French and German translations of Joyce, and Kafka in the original German. The writer Gabriel Josipovici once observed (in his fascinating book about the Bible, The Book of God) that there is very little about Kafka’s work that gets irreparably lost in translation. If we read a good translation of his work, we’re getting a very good sense of what it’s like to read Kafka. This is much less true about Joyce, whose writing has a distinctly Irish flavour that even non-Irish English speakers sometimes don’t notice, or find baffling. I recently encountered an English reader who professed to not understand a phrase from Ulysses, that someone ‘let a bawl out of him’. A good deal of the specifically local flavour of Joyce has got lost in translations of his work. I also recently acquired the Penguin Book of Classical Arabic Literature, in which the editor confessed that much of classical Arabic poetry is made untranslatable by a feature of classical Arabic whereby you can write an entire poem using the same rhyme and it won’t get monotonous. The effect is impossible to reproduce in English. Why am I going on about this? Because if we decide that a criterion for good literature is something like Good literature vigorously exploits all the semantic, connotational and musical resources of the language, then we’re basically forced to admit that Kafka is not good literature, because he doesn’t do that. And that’s self-evidently absurd. Or it should be, to anyone who can perceive the genius of Kafka. But if we instead turn around and say Good literature is translatable without losing anything essential, then we’re chucking Joyce and classical Arabic literature and an enormous amount of other literature into the bin. (Gee, sorry, Mallarmé. And probably Shakespeare, too.) This is the mystery of literary quality: We all know that there exist standards of what constitutes ‘good literature’. We all carry them inside ourselves. But once we attempt to state them out loud, we make fools of ourselves. If we try to evade this problem and do it anyway, we end up uttering vaporous truisms. Like, ‘Good literature is human’. What does that even mean. I personally think that Harold Bloom uttered many a vaporous truism in the course of his unconscionably long and verbose career. But I’m more of a Barthes-time guy. A Frye cook. A Benjaminimalist. Judgements about literary quality acquire force insofar as they belong to wider arguments about individual works, considered from well-articulated perspectives. They are not a how-to checklist for making good writing.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Why did James Joyce not consider Kant a great thinker? And it true he disliked Goethe?
Answer: Thanks for the A2A, Lark Pill. On consulting Ellmann’s James Joyce, my main reference work, I can find no mention of Kant, so can’t help you on that one, sorry. With Goethe it was a bit more complicated. Joyce’s favourite writer was almost certainly Dante, and he once summed up the trio of Great European Writers, Goethe, Dante and Shakespeare, as ‘Gouty, Daunty and Shopkeeper’. On another occasion he scoffed at Goethe as a ‘boring functionary’. However, he acknowledged the influence of Goethe’s Faust on the more phantasmagorical bits of the ‘Circe’ episode in Ulysses, and said that Goethe’s depiction of the cynical Mephistopheles was an influence on the character of the endless denier, Buck Mulligan. Towards the end of his life, after he’d published Finnegans Wake and was considering writing something shorter and simpler (we’ll never know what, because he died without starting it), he was reading Goethe’s Conversations with Eckermann, one of the best German books. So, Joyce went back and forth with Goethe, even if his loyalty to Dante was constant.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Did Joe Biden really read Ulysses by Joyce a difficult novel?
Answer: He might have. I read Ulysses in my late teens/early 20s, and unlike Joe Biden, I wasn’t going to university at that point in my life. The difficulties of Ulysses are routinely overstated by people who either haven’t read it, or who unwillingly read it in college and were frustrated by it. I read an interesting New Yorker article on this topic which observed that although Biden likes to namecheck Joyce as a favourite writer of his, he seldom if ever actually quotes Joyce. He was apparently given a first edition of Ulysses: if so, lucky him. But if he had read it, I’d have thought that he might quote it a bit more often. The major American politician who evidently has read Ulysses is actually Pete Buttigieg, whose comments on it are unusually insightful—more insightful, I think, than the article itself. This should not come as a surprise to anyone who knows that his father Joseph Buttigieg wrote a book about Joyce’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man. The title of Buttigieg’s memoir Shortest Way Home is taken from a line in Ulysses: Curious she an only child, I an only child. So it returns. Think you’re escaping and run into yourself. Longest way round is the shortest way home. Buttigieg has observed that Ulysses is a profoundly democratic novel, in that it’s about an ordinary man having an ordinary day, and yet it finds in that day remarkable levels of depth and meaning. The New Yorker article indulged in a bit of inverted snobbery by saying that citing or admiring Joyce is a ‘snob’ thing to do, something you do to show that you’re part of an elite. But this ignores the fact that Joyce himself was not an elitist, certainly not in the sense that acquaintances like Eliot or Yeats were firmly, consciously elitist. The irony is that Eliot’s and Yeats’ profoundly conservative and elitist poetry is accessible to a lot of readers, whereas Joyce’s far more democratic art is talked about by cultural gatekeepers as if it can’t be appreciated without specialist training. (None of this should be taken to mean that I don’t consider Eliot or Yeats great poets. It’s just that I have no illusions about them.) Joyce once wrote in a letter to his brother Stanislaus, ‘Do you not find the search for heroics damn vulgar?’ What I think he meant is not that it’s bad to be heroic; he himself had had heroic pretensions as a young man. He meant the search for heroics, the need to have heroes in the first place, which he thought downgraded the value of ‘individual passion’ in people. In this he might have approved of the lines from Brecht’s Life of Galileo, in which a character exclaims ‘Unhappy the land that has no heroes!’ and Galileo replies ‘No. Unhappy the land where heroes are needed.’ Hero-worship is what Joyce regarded as ‘vulgar’, something beneath the dignity of people. The moments of heroism in Ulysses are small moments, such as in the ‘Cyclops’ episode, where Odysseus’ blinding of the Cyclops with a burning stake is enacted as Bloom arguing with the bigoted Citizen while holding a lit cigar in his hand, or later in the book when the drunk Stephen gets the attention of two British soldiers, and one of them, convinced that Stephen has insulted the king, punches him, knocking him to the ground, whereupon Bloom steps in. BLOOM: (Shoves them back, loudly.) Get back, stand back! PRIVATE COMPTON: (Tugging his comrade.) Here. Bugger off, Harry. Here’s the cops! (Two raincaped watch, tall, stand in the group.) FIRST WATCH: What’s wrong here? PRIVATE COMPTON: We were with this lady. And he insulted us. And assaulted my chum. (The retriever barks.) Who owns the bleeding tyke? CISSY CAFFREY: (With expectation.) Is he bleeding! A MAN: (Rising from his knees.) No. Gone off. He’ll come to all right. BLOOM: (Glances sharply at the man.) Leave him to me. I can easily... SECOND WATCH: Who are you? Do you know him? PRIVATE CARR: (Lurches towards the watch.) He insulted my lady friend. BLOOM: (Angrily.) You hit him without provocation. I’m a witness. Constable, take his regimental number. SECOND WATCH: I don’t want your instructions in the discharge of my duty. Bloom does this for someone he only met that day, and hardly knows. That’s heroism in Ulysses. So, I don’t know if Biden has read Ulysses, and I’m inclined to suspect he may only have read a couple of pages of Joyce, if that. Still, it’s no bad thing for politicians to talk about art and literature as if they valued those things, and in the case of Pete Buttigieg, the evidence suggests that he, at least, actively engages with the stuff.
