Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What is James Joyce's Dubliners about?
Answer: Lots of things. But principally, Dublin as a place which had, at the time, a particular range of effects on its inhabitants. Through which, Joyce made observations about people, which I think reflect his understanding of them, and his sympathy with them. James Joyce, aged c. 22 in 1904, around the time he began writing the stories in Dubliners. Photo taken by his friend C.P. Curran. Asked what he was thinking when this picture got taken, Joyce replied ‘I was wondering would he lend me five shillings.’ The popular image of James Joyce, among people who have an image of him at all, is of a perhaps fantastically virtuosic writer, who was more interested in messing around with language, than in telling us stories we can understand, about people that we can perceive as real people. I don’t agree with this, but I do know that, in my effort to persuade unconvinced readers that Joyce is not some boring classic, Dubliners is potentially an ace up my sleeve. If you’ll forgive the length of this answer, I aim to convince you that Joyce was not the word-juggler of purely academic interest that people who’ve had to read him but didn’t like him say he is, but a writer whose deepest concerns came out of human experience. Settle in. Get a beverage. We could be here for a while. But I will not be tracing some clever-clever argument. I’ll be presenting evidence. Dubliners, which was written between 1904 and 1907, and which didn’t get published until 1914, is very much about its time and place, but it’s not a ‘celebration’ of that time and place. It’s not the sort of book which makes you think the author wrote it in order to make the reader think Gosh, it sounds so wonderful—I wish I could have been there. I think some of Jane Austen’s work has that effect on some readers, and some of Henry James’ work, and some of Proust’s work. And that’s not a criticism, because I greatly admire those writers; just that those writers set their work in a world which some of their readers find very congenial to imagine, despite the implicit criticisms of that world in their work. However, Dubliners depicts Dublin in the late 19th/early 20th century as, mostly and unless you’re reasonably comfortably off, a cramped, dour, class-ridden, priest-ridden, poverty-stricken place, where most of the inhabitants are locked into financially strapped and emotionally starved existences. Men exploit women. Men bully other men further down the social scale, and those bullied men go on to bully their children. Socially ambitious women have to behave in ways that cause them to be perceived as pushy and unladylike. Emotionally and sexually needy women (which is to say, people in general who are women) are avoided as dangerous. Even when people are given a chance of freedom, they find it easier to stay in their captivity. There are next to no opportunities. Rather than go on blabbing about the book, let’s talk briefly about some of the individual stories, and see how these themes are illustrated in them. The Sisters. This, the first story in the book, is an excellent example of Joyce’s technique of implying dark secrets, without ever stating them outright. This was a technique he may have learned from Ibsen, who he was a fan of, and who, in plays like The Wild Duck, was a master of it. It’s told from the point of view of a young boy who has had a close and friendly relationship with an old priest, Father Flynn. At the very beginning of the story, Flynn is on his deathbed. The first hint we have that something about Flynn is little… off, is very early on, when a family friend, Cotter comes to the house to tell them that Flynn has died. The boy pretends to be unaffected by this news, and is annoyed when Cotter, on being told that the boy and Flynn were great friends, remarks I wouldn’t like children of mine to have too much to say to a man like that. The boy recalls his friendship with Flynn, and we learn that Flynn’s paralysis was a result of three strokes. Gradually, but very economically—this story is only seven pages long in my copy of the book—we get a picture of a priest who was increasingly infirm and incapable, and who had become incapable of carrying out his priestly duties, as a result of whatever weakness he had that cause the strokes in the first place. Joyce gets a lot of his effects in this story by means of aposiopesis: a rhetorical device in which people break off in the middle of sentences. Everyone around the boy wants to talk about Father Flynn, but none of them want to say in front of him exactly what’s on their minds. The story even ends on one, with Eliza recalling how Father Flynn was found alone in his confession box, awake and laughing to himself about something—but what, we’re never told. The result is that we’re obliged to infer that there is something about Flynn that nobody wants to discuss. One long-standing critical theory is that Flynn had syphilis, which would explain his trembling hands, his strokes and his increasing mental confusion. It would also explain something about Cotter’s distaste for him. But Joyce never says it in the text: it’s left there for us to put together. This is part of his method. An Encounter The first three stories in the book are all told from the perspective of children. ‘An Encounter’ is narrated by an unnamed schoolboy, obsessed with the Wild West, who decides to bunk off school for a day. He plans to do so with two friends, but one doesn’t show up, so he and the other one, Mahony, go wandering around the Dublin docklands, take a ride on the ferry across the Liffey, and end up chasing a cat into a field. (Note that where they are, at the base of Dublin’s harbour walls, is quite a long way away from other people.) Here, they sit down for a rest. A middle-aged man approaches them, sits down near them and begins talking to them. Most of ‘An Encounter’ is the boy’s account of what the man says to them: we get very little of the man’s actual dialogue. The boy describes him to us as having a ‘good accent’, meaning he sounds middle-class, but his suit is rather shabby, implying that he’s been on hard times. He starts out by reminscining about his schooldays as being the happiest days of his life, and then talks about the books he loved to read. The boy pretends to have read them. The man goes on to ask them if they have ‘sweethearts’, and opines that Every boy has a little sweetheart. He starts talking about young girls and their soft hair, and after a while he gets up and walks to the other end of the field. At this point, Mahony exclaims with surprise, I say! Look what he’s doing! The boy says nothing. Mahony says I say! … He’s the queer old josser! This was a period when ‘queer’ mostly meant ‘odd’, but by this time it also referred to sexuality. ‘Josser’ is old Dublin slang for an old or superannuated person. The boy tells Mahony that if the man asks their names, Mahony should give his as ‘Murphy’ and he will give his own name as ‘Smith’. Presently the man comes back, and so does the cat, which Mahony proceeds to chase around the field. The boy is now left alone with the man, who calls Mahony a ‘rough boy’, and asks the boy if Mahony is whipped at their school. The boy remains silent, and the man starts talking about the need to whip boys who talk to girls. He described to me how he would whip such a boy as if he were unfolding some elaborate mystery. Joyce has the boy tell us, with rather precocious sarcasm, He seemed to have forgotten his recent liberalism. When the man pauses in his monologue, the boy stands up, pretends to tie his shoelace and shouts Murphy! He walks away from the man, afraid that the man is going to grab him, and Mahony finally runs up to him so that they can leave together. ‘An Encounter’ has been described as a ‘homophobic’ story, written at a time when Joyce was less understanding about homosexuality than he later became. But, as a queer man, I have to disagree. I read it as being about a sexual predator, told from the point of view of the kid he’s using as prey. Joyce has the boy describe the man’s tone, when talking about his sexual fantasies, as that of someone who is hoping to be understood (his voice, as he led me monotonously through the mystery, grew almost affectionate and seemed to plead with me that I should understand him.) This does address the obvious desperate need in the man for some kind of human connection. But the fact remains that it’s a grown man talking to a schoolboy. A man should not be talking to a boy about how much he’d like to whip boys for sexual misconduct. A man talking to another man about his fantasies, and the two of them role-playing it between each other—that’s a different situation. But it’s not the one here. This is, as far as I’m concerned, a story about exploitation. Araby A slight but still intriguing story about another boy who’s got more than a crush on a schoolfriend’s sister. A charity bazaar is being held (a kind of one-off marketplace), and ‘Mangan’s sister’, as she is only ever referred to, dearly wants to go to it, but she can’t because her school is having a retreat to a convent. The narrator tells her that he will go, and get her something. Having promised to do this, he’s then kept waiting by his uncle, who is supposed to give him some spending money, but who comes home late, and then has his dinner, before finally getting around to handing the boy the cash. The result is that, by the time the boy gets there at 9.50pm, the bazaar is mostly closed, he has to spend half his money on the admission fee, and there’s nothing for him to buy to give as a love offering to Mangan’s sister. ‘Araby’ is really about the promise of a better life, playing with imagery of the exotic east, perfumes and jewels, but bringing it all down in the end to a mostly empty, darkened hall, with a few tired and bored stallholders waiting to close everything down and get the hell out of there, and a frustrated and angry boy cursing himself for his ‘vanity’ at pretending he could get Mangan’s sister some delightful bauble. Another example of Joyce’s precise use of locations: the boy and Mangan’s sister live in North Richmond Street, on Dublin’s north side, which was then very much the poorer part of Dublin, but the bazaar is in the Royal Dublin Society buildings on the prosperous south side district of Ballsbridge, underlining how he’s spent all his money on what was basically a pointless sojourn to a richer part of the city. Eveline One of the shortest stories. Eveline is a young woman who will be leaving Ireland to start a new life in Buenos Aires with her fiancé Frank, but at the last minute, as they are just about to get on the ship, she can’t do it. ‘Eveline’ is about promises made and loyalties kept or broken. It contains one of the most memorable and enigmatic images in Joyce’s work: Eveline’s memory of her late mother, who in her last illness became delirious and kept repeating the phrase Derevaun Seraun! There are many interpretations, in the literary scholarship world, of what this might mean, most of them wildly different from each other, except that every commentator everyone agrees that it sounds vaguely like Irish. I’ve seen it interpreted as Irish for ‘the end of pleasure is pain’, ‘little sea anemone’, ‘must go, must come back’, ‘death is very near’ and ‘worms are the only end’. Obviously, all of these can’t be right. All we know for sure is that Joyce placed, at the heart of this story, Eveline’s memory of her dying mother saying this unintelligible phrase ‘constantly with foolish insistence’. And, whatever effect it has on her, ultimately she does not board the ship with Frank. I don’t want to describe every story in the book, because you should discover them for yourself. But before I get to the last parts of this answer, I can’t resist talking about two of the more grim ones. Counterparts is about a guy named Farrington, a worker in a law firm, really a mere document-copier (a data entry clerk, if you like), who finds his job exceptionally boring, and hates his boss, a shrill-voiced, obnoxious Ulsterman named Mr. Alleyne, who bullies and demeans him. Farrington is a medium-functioning alcoholic with some rage issues. He lives only for the point in the day when he can finally meet his friends in the pub. He spends most of the day looking forward to having a drink. In fact, at one point late in the afternoon, with a lot of important work still to do, he slips out and has a quick beer around the corner, making it even more difficult for him to finish his work by 5.30. Later still, Alleyne chews him out viciously in front of a woman client for not delivering some documents he was supposed to deliver, and Farrington makes an unexpectedly quick-witted snark that drives Alleyne into a shrieking rage. Having spent the day wondering how he can get an advance on his pay cheque, and realising that he’s not going to get one, Farrington decides to pawn his pocket watch, which he does, getting a considerable sum of money for it: six shillings, about a quarter of his weekly wage. He takes this to the pub, where he meets some friends, and over the course of the evening they go to various places and he buys a lot of drinks, and he tells the story of his snarky remark, which his friends then retell to each new arrival, to his great satisfaction. This compensates him, somewhat, for the humiliations of his working day. However, the evening ends up in further humiliation and disappointment, and late that night, his six shillings all gone, and not even pleasantly buzzed after all those whiskies, Farrington returns to the family home, to find that the kitchen fire is almost out, his wife is at the chapel, and his young son—who should be in bed asleep by now, but who has stayed up to wait for his father—hasn’t cooked his dinner, as he was supposed to. Farrington proceeds to beat the crap out of his son with a walking stick, while his terrified son begs him not to: I’ll say a Hail Mary for you.... I’ll say a Hail Mary for you, pa, if you don’t beat me.... I’ll say a Hail Mary... An interesting side-note: in the first part of the story, the part set in the office, Farrington is referred to in the narration only as ‘the man’. In the middle part, when he’s in the pub with his friends, he is referred to as ‘Farrington’. In the final part, when he goes home to his dark house and flies into a rage because he has no dinner, he’s again referred to merely as ‘the man’. As if only among his friends is he really himself. And that isn’t much. Left to his own resources, he’s a blundering, angry, violent shadow of a man. Two Gallants is about two guys with little money, wandering the streets. Lenehan is a clever and loquacious sort who tends to hang around his friends in bars, hoping to be bought a drink. Corley fancies himself as a ladies’ man, but he’s the kind of guy who, having courted young women, spent money on them and been disappointed, now only courts young women who will spend money on him. We can tell that they are planning something, but we don’t know what, except that Corley has his eye on a young woman who he’ll be meeting later. They part, arranging to meet after Corley’s appointment with his new girl, and much of the story is Lenehan walking the streets, wishing he had a better life—which, to him, means a wife who would do everything for him, and would also have more money than he does. He buys himself some dinner, and Joyce, who wrote some of the most memorable meals in fiction, gives him one of the cheapest and least satisfying-sounding dinners ever: a bottle of ginger beer and a plate of green peas with vinegar, because it’s all Lenehan can afford. Finally, after Lenehan has spent hours in more aimless mooching (he can’t afford to go to the pub), he meets Corley, who has concluded his tryst with the serving girl, and eagerly asks him Did it come off? Corley opens his closed fist and reveals a golden coin: so, either a sovereign (worth 20 shillings) or a half sovereign (worth 10 shillings). The implication, of course, is that Corley has either managed to wheedle this money out of the girl (who works as a servant), or that she’s stolen it and given it to him. In return for the attentions of a handsome lech, who’s only in it for a quick feel and some cash. (Lenehan and Corley both reappear in Joyce’s second novel Ulysses, Lenehan in several episodes. Lenehan plays an important role in fuelling an anti-Semitic rumour about the principal character Leopold Bloom, when he becomes convinced that Bloom has won a considerable amount of money on the horses. Corley in Ulysses is still out of a job, and indeed borrows money off the other principal character, Stephen.) I will resist the temptation to talk about most of my other favourite stores in the book, such as ‘A Mother’, ‘A Painful Case’ or the great ‘Ivy Day in the Committee Room’, in which the political paralysis of early 20th century Ireland is condensed into a mere 15 pages. Because we have to talk about the final story. Having finished writing the book, or so he thought, and having tried to get it published, and failed to do so, Joyce began to wonder if perhaps it wasn’t too relentlessly negative. He’d been living outside Ireland for nearly three years, at that point, and his initial mood of disgust with his home country had mellowed slightly. He wrote to his brother Stanislaus, saying that he felt like paying tribute to some of Ireland’s better qualities, such as hospitality, and respect for art and culture. This, plus some personal details in Joyce’s own life, was the inspiration for the last and by far the longest story in the book, ‘The Dead’. The story of ‘The Dead’ is very simple. Gabriel Conroy, a thirtysomething educated Irishman, attends a late dinner party in early January, still just about the Christmas season, with his wife, Gretta. The dinner is held by Kate and Julia Morkan, two of Gabriel’s aunts, and their unmarried niece Mary Jane, who lives with them. The ‘Misses Morkan’ are highly active as music teachers in Dublin society, so it’s a big party, with lots of people. At the party, Gabriel gets off to a rather awkward start. The Morkans’ serving girl Lily takes his coat and scarf and he makes cordial chit-chat with her. When he learns that she’s no longer in school, he makes a would-be jovial remark about how they’d soon see her stepping out with her young man, only for Lily to bitterly say The men that is now is only all palaver and what they can get out of you. Disconcerted by this, Gabriel does his best to seem like not one of those men by giving her a lavish tip. Then, during the dancing bit of the party, he has a conversation with an old friend, Molly Ivors, who’s an intellectual like him but who, unlike him, is big into the whole Celtic Revival thing, and she mocks Gabriel for not taking his holidays in the west of Ireland, and for writing articles for an English newspaper. Gabriel is nettled by this, but Molly leaves the party before the food gets served. Dinner arrives (it’s one of Joyce’s feasts), and Gabriel helpfully carves the goose for everyone before serving himself. Then, after the food, he gives a speech, which it’s implied is something he does every year. In it, he pays tribute to the Irish tradition of hospitality, and gets some implied digs in at Molly Ivors for not living up to it by leaving the party early. He warmly thanks and compliments his hostesses, and the dinner ends with a chorus of ‘For they are Jolly Gay Fellows’, which is a variation on the more traditional lyrics that for obvious reasons doesn’t get sung much anymore. Gabriel’s speech is a great example of Joyce’s genius for pastiche. Although sincere and heartfelt, it’s slightly pompous: the sort of thing that you think Gabriel would write. It also introduces the theme of death, which haunts the story throughout, but will really kick in later. At the end of the party, everyone goes off in various horse-drawn cabs and Gabriel feels pretty pleased with how the evening has gone. He sees Gretta on the landing, listening to one of the guests singing a traditional Irish song, ‘The Lass of Aughrim’. He and Gretta return to the hotel room they’ve booked so as to have a night to themselves for a change, and he’s looking forward to some passionate nookie. But Gretta seems sad, and eventually she bursts into tears and tells him that the song she heard has reminded her of a young man she knew in her home region of Galway, in the west, Michael Furey, who was in love with her, but who died. He used to sing that same song, which Gabriel himself doesn’t know. This stirs up a lot of Gabriel’s latent jealousy, but once he realises just how much of an impact the young man had on Gretta, he simply asks her about him, and when she gives in to a fit of weeping, he feels like it’s not his place to muscle in and tell her to buck up, so he withdraws and sits by the window. Gretta falls asleep, and Gabriel thinks at first about the fact that he’s clearly not, as he had previously believed, the most important person in his wife’s life. Not that she doesn’t love him, but she doesn’t love him like Michael Furey loved her. Then he thinks about the role of death in everyone’s life, and reflects that one day, he and everyone he knows will be only a memory. The snow that has been falling all through the story becomes the final motif. ‘The Dead’ is as perfect as short stories get. T.S. Eliot thought it actually perfect. It also fulfils its role as the final story in the book, bringing all its themes together, and capping them with more human warmth, comedy and passion than any of the previous ones. (Not that there are no other lighter moments in the book: ‘Grace’ is a subtle masterpiece of satire, and ‘Ivy Day in the Committe Room’ has some very funny depictions of the once-fiercely patriotic political workers arguing in defence of King Edward VII.) The other stories are sometimes hardly more than sketches, but ‘The Dead’ is a symphony. More than one commentator has noted that if Lily, the Morkans’ serving girl, isn’t the servant girl in ‘Two Gallants’ who Corley gets a gold coin out of, she might almost be: The men that is now is only all palaver and what they can get out of you. The characters in ‘The Dead’ are of a slightly higher social class than many of the characters in the rest of the book, and Gabriel is far more educated and articulate than most, but Molly Ivors’ mockery of him for not being more interested in his own country has a good point. Gabriel is, to some extent, like any clever, literary-minded, would-be cosmopolitan middle-class person with literary ambitions: he’s like Joyce himself without genius. Which brings us to the way that Dubliners is not merely a collection of made-up tales about people being randomly mean, even if the sociocultural situation they live in prevents them from being more free. Every story draws on Joyce’s personal experience. ‘Counterparts’ was based on people he knew; his own father John Joyce lost jobs because of his alcoholism. ‘An Encounter’ was inspired by something that had actually happened to Joyce as a schoolboy. ‘Ivy Day in the Committee Room’ was inspired by an afternoon Joyce’s brother Stanislaus had spent with their father in an election commmittee. Lenehan in ‘Two Gallants’ was based on Michael Hart, a friend of Joyce’s father, and Corley was essentially a representation in fiction of someone of that name. (When Joyce met the real Corley on a trip back to Dublin years later, and told him that he’d appeared in one of Joyce’s stories, Corley was delighted.) ‘The Dead’ itself was inspired by the fact that, before he met his wife Nora, she had been in love with a young man named Michael Feeney, who’d died of typhoid and pneumonia, and indeed another young man who’d been in love with her had also died. (This had earned her a certain reputation among her friends as a ‘man-killer’, even though she’d had nothing to do with it.) Nora Joyce, née Barnacle Joyce had reeled, as a young man, when he first realised that the great love of his life had actually had a life before him. He was used to thinking of himself as the brilliant, superior Dublin intellectual who knew everything, and Nora as the simple Galway girl who would look up to him, and be moulded by him. But he’d realised that he was wrong; she had depths, and had had experiences, that he’d no clue about, and had never come close to having. And he got over it. He learned to see her more clearly, and in doing so, he gained new respect for her, and he became more able to take the raw facts of his life and turn them into art—which was what he had wanted to do all along. Dubliners was James Joyce’s first masterpiece, the book where he took apparently trivial or unpromising events from life, and by means of his craftsmanship, transformed them into great art. Having done that, he never wrote short stories of that kind ever again. Dubliners is sometimes talked about as Joyce’s early work, or a sort of apprentice piece. I think it’s more than that. It is the first chapter in the giant, four-book work that Joyce spent his life writing: Dubliners, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Ulysses, Finnegans Wake. If this answer has made you more curious to read that first chapter, then my work here is done. Thanks for reading.

Question: In fiction, what was one of the most ridiculous ways a world was destroyed?
Answer: A classic example has to be planet Earth in Douglas Adams’ The Hitch-Hiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, which is to be demolished by galactic bureaucrats to make way for a hyperspace bypass. When the people on Earth protest, the bureaucrats point out that all the paperwork on the case has been on display ‘in your local planning office in Alpha Centauri for fifty of your Earth years, so you’ve had plenty of time to lodge any formal complaint, and it’s far too late to start making a fuss about it now.’ When the increasingly panic-stricken people of Earth further protest that they’ve never been to Alpha Centauri, the head bureaucrat lambasts them for ‘not taking an interest in local affairs’ and orders the planet to be destroyed. To add irony, one of the Earth’s few survivors only escapes because he happened to be protesting the demolition of his own house by the local council to make way for a bypass, instead of being at work as he normally would have been, so a friend who happened to be an alien hitch-hiker found him outside the house in question, and was able to rescue him, hitching a ride for both of them on one of the bureaucrats’ spaceships.

Question: Can Led Zeppelin be considered a punk band?
Answer: Ah, one of my least favourite structures of a Quora question: Can [something] be considered as [something else that it does not resemble in any way]? I agree with everyone who says that Led Zeppelin were in no way a punk band. The trouble here is that we have no way of knowing what you think constitutes ‘punk’, Jeannie Jimski, but I think it’s a good faith question and you certainly have some interesting ones (I definitely plan to answer Why aren't the Yardbirds more popular?, because it’s right down my alley). Punk isn’t just a musical thing. It’s also a way of being a band, a way of playing music, an attitude towards the music industry. It’s not a simple or pure thing, although it sort of wishes it were: you can be a punk band and be on a major label. I think punk had ‘compromise’ built into itself from the outset, but that’s OK, because it also had ‘resentment’ and ‘aggression’ built into itself, which are two useful things to have when you feel compromised. Ever get the feeling you’ve been cheated? —John Lydon at the Sex Pistols’ original final concert, Winterland Ballroom, San Francisco, 14 January 1978 Led Zeppelin, as observers including our OP know, grew out of the Yardbirds. The band’s prime mover was Jimmy Page, a seasoned session musician, who had tasted fame with the Yardbirds and had a plan to make it very, very big, as long as he could get the right guys. Jimmy Page was not, like most punks, a music business outsider. By the time he was in a position to get Led Zeppelin together, in 1968, he was a showbusiness veteran. He’d first appeared on British television eleven years earlier, as a 13-year-old skiffle musician: Just for context, this was April 1957. John Lennon and Paul McCartney would not have their fateful encounter at Woolton Fete until 6 July, three months later. Page’s early music career was crippled by his chronic ill health. He kept getting glandular fever. By 1963, he had committed himself to the less strenuous lifestyle of a session musician, although he couldn’t read music. He earned his money by being a nimble and imaginative stylist, at a time when British popular music didn’t have a lot of guitarists like that. He played on many classic 60s recordings by British bands. I’ve heard that he played the rhythm guitar on the Kinks’ ‘You Really Got Me’, although Dave Davies played the guitar solo: if so, Page has the more credit, because the riff in ‘You Really Got Me’ is the entire fucking song. His Beatles connection was that he played some guitar on the incidental music for A Hard Day’s Night, so presumably that’s him twanging away on at least some of those tracks, although I have heard that it was the legendary Vic Flick who played the guitar part on the instrumental version of ‘This Boy’ that accompanies Ringo wandering around London (Vic Flick is most famous for his rendition of the James Bond theme in the early Bond movies.) … Aaaanyway, all this is to show that Jimmy Page was a seasoned music-biz insider by the time he put Led Zeppelin together. So… not a punk, then. The recorded evidence shows that Led Zeppelin started out with a lot of musical ideas, but rather fewer lyrical ones. I am hardly the last person to accuse Led Zeppelin of stealing songwriting credit from black musicians. I even wrote an answer about it, which compared Led Zeppelin album labels from different years, showing how their early pressings denied due credit to songwriters but, after the musicians had successfully taken the band to court, later pressings gave the original writers due credit. However, it’s often said that they simply ‘ripped off black music’, and that’s not the case. Led Zeppelin did not simply play Willie Dixon or Howlin’ Wolf songs louder. They radically reshaped the music into something else. It’s just that, while Page was directing the creation of the new music, Plant—who was supposed to be off writing new lyrics—could seldom be bothered to, at least on the first couple of albums, and ended up singing the original lyrics to the blues songs that Page had completely recomposed, which is what landed them in court years later. However, once Plant started taking his songwriting responsibilities more seriously, he began to write the sort of preposterous but effective nonsense that is one of the reasons why we love Led Zeppelin today. ‘Immigrant Song’: We come from the land of the ice and snow From the midnight sun where the hot springs flow The hammer of the gods Will drive our ships to new lands To fight the horde, sing and cry Valhalla, I am coming ‘The Battle of Evermore’: The Queen of Light took her bow And then she turned to go The Prince of Peace embraced the gloom And walked the night alone Oh, dance in the dark of night Sing to the morning light The dark Lord rides in force tonight And time will tell us all Oh, throw down your plow and hoe Rest not to lock your homes Side by side we wait the might Of the darkest of them all ‘Over the Hills and Far Away’: Many have I loved, and many times been bitten Many times I've gazed along the open road Many times I've lied and many times I've listened Many times I've wondered how much there is to know Many dreams come true, and some have silver linings I live for my dream and a pocketful of gold This is… not punk. As Led Zeppelin became bigger, they became ever more remote from their fans. At one point, they were renting their own airliner: As the Seventies wore on, Zeppelin struggled to remain creative. Their last unequivocally decent album, Presence, came out in early 1976, when punk was really getting going: the Ramones’ first album was out within weeks, and the Sex Pistols’ ‘Anarchy in the UK’ was out in November. Unlike The Who’s Pete Townshend, Led Zeppelin had little sympathy with punk. (Townshend himself had little sympathy with Led Zeppelin, liking them personally but detesting their music.) Their last proper album, In Through the Out Door, was a sign of how lost they had become. Coda was a collection of odds-and-sods, including ‘Wearing and Tearing’, the band’s ‘take on’ or ‘response to’ punk. To my ears, ‘Wearing and Tearing’ is just unconvincing. It sounds like Led Zeppelin anxiously trying to show that they’re still hip, but compared to real punk tracks like the Pistols’ magisterial ‘Holidays in the Sun’, or even post-punk like the Clash’s effortlessly swinging ‘Train in Vain’, it’s fussy and fiddly. Led Zeppelin in their prime were never this desperate to prove anything. They just bulldozed ahead. No, Led Zeppelin were not punk. They represented one of the things that punk had no time for.

Question: Rachel Maddow said that the Lord of the Rings is a far right and alt-right white supremacy story. Is she an idiot, and why do people even watch MSNBC?
Answer: Actually, what Rachel Maddow said was that there are some far right and alt-right people who love The Lord of the Rings, a book which she herself appears not to have read. And she’s correct. She mentioned Peter Thiel, a big donor to J.D. Vance, who said in 2009 that he thinks that ‘freedom and democracy are not compatible’ and who named six of his companies after things in Lord of the Rings. In 2016, Thiel donated $1.25m to Trump’s campaign. In 2020 he donated another quarter of a million to Trump’s re-election campaign. By 2023, Trump’s increasing willingness to get into bed with totalitarian Christian nationalists seemed to have put off the right-libertarian Thiel, because he was said to have ‘lost interest in politics’ and would not be donating any more money to Trump or anybody else. Oh, to be so rich that you can just decide not to be affected by whoever runs the country. However, he absolutely pumped money into Vance’s senate campaign ($15 million) so maybe he was merely bullshitting us. The fact is, LOTR is popular with right-wing and alt-right people. It’s also popular with other people, but there remains something in its DNA that has an appeal for those who long for a world which is ruled by just, wise and handsome white people from the north and west, while the grubby, nasty people from the south and east are kept in their place. I’m guessing that Peter Thiel identifies with the Noldorin. Look, don’t blame me for pointing this out. It’s in the book. I’m not saying that Tolkien himself was a white supremacist; he was disgusted by Nazism. But products of the imagination can draw on a wider range of things than one’s personal opinions, and can be picked up and appreciated by people who think very differently from the people that created them. It’s true that LOTR is one of the codifiers in fantasy literature of the north/west=good/fair, south/east=bad/dark tropes, but as other people have pointed out, the ‘west’ in Tolkien is ultimately a multicultural society, with humans and dwarves and hobbits and ents, etc. living in more or less harmony. Then again, Mordor is also multicultural, although obviously there’s a lot of top-down pressure to wear black. (Imagine the messages from Mordor HR: Hi all, just a reminder that green and brown are not approved uniform colours. One or two people have been seen on patrol wearing pale blue trim on their cloaks. Please make sure that your work gear conforms to the attached style sheet. Also, it’s Ogbúrg’s birthday on Tuesday, so please reply to this with greetings for the card.) So, Rachel Maddow was not wrong to point out that LOTR has a lot of very dubious fans, but that’s not the same as saying that the story itself is a far-right-wing story. Whether it is one or not is a different question, but she didn’t claim that it is one: she merely correctly pointed out that some very right-wing people love it.

Question: If white supremacists truly believe they are supreme over other races, then why don't they just shut up and enjoy their fantasy instead of showing how insecure they are by always ranting about people who never even think about them?
Answer: Because white supremacism is not about contentedly feeling like you are superior to other ‘races’. It is not a sort of inner religious conviction; not a mere belief, or a warm cuddly feeling inside. It is, at its weakest, a series of discursive practices. At its strongest, it is a programme of genocide. What this means is that the white supremacist is not a white supremacist by simply thinking that they and folks like them are better than others. They practice white supremacism by continuously and aggressively asserting their superiority to people they regard as inferior. Only by doing that do they hope to bring about a situation in which most people agree that they are superior, simply because they’ve had it dunned into them that white people are superior, or else because of specious arguments, dank memes, racist claims repeated ad nauseam, etc. White supremacists continually harp on a select few, non-trivial themes in ‘Western culture’: that that culture is superior to other cultures by virtue of (choose the reasons you want.) The usual reasons are that ‘our’ culture is civilised, rational, law-abiding, righteous, and sometimes also ‘pure’ or ‘authentic’, but ‘their’ culture is uncivilised, irrational, chaotic, evil and also strangely unreal, and not part of natural human society. (We have seen certain rhetorical tropes applied by the Germans, and others, to the Jews in the early and mid-20th century, and then reapplied all over again by, well, others in the late 20th and early 21st century, to the Palestinians: that they are unreal, and therefore less than human, and therefore undeserving of the kind of consideration that we owe to people like ‘us’.) White supremacism lives not as something that people casually think about other people. It lives as a thing that people do to other people, by trying to change the way we talk about them. It seeks to put people outside the in-group: as we used to say in Ireland, with some retrospective irony, ‘beyond the pale’. (The ‘pale’ didn’t refer to skin colour, but to the part of Ireland that was directly controlled by England in the late middle ages. I grew up right on the historical southern border of it.) If you can control the discourse, you are perhaps more than halfway to controlling the situation. White supremacists, with their fondness for neat but false distinctions, and simple but dishonest tropes, have more of a knack for controlling the discourse than those of us who prefer nuance, complexity and things that take explaining. This is why they tend to win the wars of words. And this is why they must be defeated by other means.

Question: What should we believe, scientific evidence about our universe or the Bible's description of creation?
Answer: Look, believe whatever the hell you want to believe, as long as you accept the consequences. Just bear in mind that the universe in general behaves as though the scientific account of how it works is correct, not as if the Bible’s description of creation is correct. We have not had any verifiable encounters with the Deity in recorded history. The only accounts of these are religious accounts, which in most cases can be dated to long after the events themselves are supposed to have happened. So, believe in the Bible if you want, but while it’s in my opinion inaccurate to dismiss the Bible as a silly fairy tale or a conscious effort at deception—because it weighs too heavily upon our culture to be dismissed so easily—know that there is no evidence that almost any of the things in the Bible happened, other than that the Bible says they happened. The universe conforms far better to scientists’ accounts of it, than the Bible’s account. When the Bible is true and interesting, it’s because it’s—sometimes inadvertently, to be sure—true and interesting about people and what goes on in their heads. Not about how Moses hit the sea with a stick and the water made a canyon, or that a carpenter in Galilee could turn up again a couple of days after he’d died from crucifixion. That stuff just doesn’t happen in real life. That ought to be a clue.

Question: What's the most overrated band of all time?
Answer: Well, the answer should be obvious. Yet I predict that this will be one of the least popular answers I will ever write. No, not ? and the Mysterians. It’s The Beatles. Now, before you blow your tops and stab the downvote button, let me explain. Because, unless you are already familiar with my opinions on the Beatles, it’s almost certainly not what you think. I have written (checks profile) 877 answers on this site about the Beatles. In these answers, I have consistently argued that they: In other words, it’s not like I don’t admire the Beatles. And it’s not like I don’t think that they made great music. And it’s not like I don’t like their music. I absolutely love most of it. You’re not going to get me saying the kind of things about the Beatles, that some people answering this question have said about other groups, e.g. that the Sex Pistols just weren’t that good, or that Bob Dylan is pretentious and hard to understand, or blah blah blah. I love the Pistols. And Dylan. I’m not here to knock the Beatles. No no no. I’m here to knock their fans. Some of them, at any rate. The more abandoned, uncritical, worshipful, supine ones. The ones who fall at the feet of the Beatles, but never really think about them. You see, I think this question is not about the bands. It’s about what ‘overrated’ means. My perception is that the Beatles are consistently overrated, over and over again, by people who talk about them as if they could do no wrong, and they could supply every kind of music a person needs, and they influenced everyone who came after them, and they invented heavy metal and blah blah blah. All I want to do is help us to see the Beatles clearly. Because there is a lot that they couldn’t and didn’t do. They were not instrumental virtuosos. They could play the music that they played very well, but in the Get Back documentary, George Harrison, the one who was arguably most committed to being a good player, frankly admitted that he couldn’t do what his mate Eric Clapton could do, fluently improvise for minutes on end. Ringo Starr was a highly musical and meticulous drummer, but he couldn’t play with the power of John Bonham or the flash of Keith Moon. He had more sense than to try to play like them, and it’s not like the band’s songs would have been improved if he could play like that. Except. Talking of those drummers, the Beatles were rubbish at sounding heavy. This wouldn’t have mattered at all if they hadn’t tried to, but they did, in songs like ‘Helter Skelter’ and the rejected ‘That Means A Lot’. In some cases, later remixes have brought out some of the latent heaviness of these songs. But ‘Helter Skelter’, while great fun to play, is a bit of a chore to listen to. But really, I’m not talking about the Beatles’ own limitations (which they were wise enough to not try too often to transcend) so much as the sheer mountain of crap that is talked about them. For example, the Beatles are constantly used by listeners of a certain type as a stick to beat today’s popular music. This doesn’t make any more sense than complaining that the Beatles were nothing compared to, say, Duke Ellington. We don’t compare musicians of successive generations like that—and we’re now two or three generations removed from the Beatles. So, saying that Taylor Swift, or even Justin Bieber, is nothing compared to the Beatles, is irrelevant and stupid. The Beatles blazed the trail: we compare them to other musicians of their own generation who didn’t blaze a trail (e.g. Herman’s Hermits), or who blazed a different trail of their own (e.g. the Rolling Stones). (Do not attempt to claim in the comments that Herman’s Hermits were better than I think they are.) This is one of the things I mean by ‘overrating’ the Beatles: using their privileged place in history to scorn later musicians who didn’t have a similar opportunity to make history on the same scale. Today’s musicians make history in their own way, and their music has its own validity. Anyone today who is trying to be a creative musician, in however meagre a way, is contributing more to music than the slickest Beatles cover band. Because music has to keep developing, or it drowns in the increasingly cantankerous nostalgia of its fans. I mean, look at what happened to rock music: a once sprawling and experimental and eclectic music is now defined by its most vocal fans as ‘people with guitars who sound like my favourite bands from the 60s/70s/80s.’ Meanwhile, rock bands in distant lands go on bearing the flame of innovation and experiment that bands in the Anglosphere have all but dropped. But ageing rock fans go on listening to the same few dozen albums over and over and over again. And bitching that there isn’t another dozen albums like that. The hell with those people. For another thing: while we’re talking about ‘opportunities to make history’, let’s contextualise the Beatles’ reception, which is a fancy way of saying that we should remember the conditions in which the band earned their early fame. The early 60s, in the UK and especially the USA, were not exactly prime conditions for popular musicians who weren’t smart, weren’t presentable and, to be blunt, weren’t white. Now, to their credit, the Beatles themselves were as apparently unprejudiced as it was possible for a band in those days to be. They refused to play to segregated audiences. They constantly praised the black musicians who had inspired them: the Shirelles, Arthur Alexander, Larry Williams, Little Richard and others. The only guest musician who ever got a full joint credit on a Beatles recording was Billy Preston, a black musician. (A couple of session musicians were namechecked on Revolver but that was a one-off.) But there can be no doubt that part of the appeal of the Beatles, for some of their audiences, especially in the USA, was that they fed back the influence of black American music into their own music, but at least they weren’t themselves black. If we are to believe some people, innovation is a supreme value in post-WW2 popular music. If that were really the case, Ike Turner should be valued far higher than Elvis. Yet he isn’t. And it’s not just because he was a mean man and a bad husband. It’s because Elvis was ‘acceptable’, in a very specific way that Ike Turner was not. The Beatles were as anti-racist as any band, back in the 60s. Yet there are white supremacists out there who love them, and prize them as ‘white culture’. It’s amazing how people can choose to not hear what they don’t want to hear. The Beatles cult began in the 60s, swelled, became a global phenomenon, and slowly waned in the 70s, only to be kicked off again by Lennon’s murder. It then became a very Lennon-specific thing in the 80s, with the rest of the band’s contributions being ignored or downplayed. But in the 90s, with the combination of the rise of Britpop and the Beatles’ organisation’s careful curatorship of its own legacy with the Anthology series and CDs, it was revived, and revised, and it’s never quite gone down again since then. (That was when I seriously got into them.) The Beatles are now safely classic and respectable. Two of them are dead, and the other two are beloved grandfathers of popular music. But as their time recedes into the past of our parents and grandparents, their strangeness and their individuality gets lost. They risk becoming an icon which, if we don’t pay reverence to it, we don’t get taken seriously. I personally am under no illusions about how, if I want to write something that will get a lot of upvotes, a heartwarming and familiar story about the Beatles, told in a new way, is a safe way to do it: 1,500+ upvotes in 42 days. Not that I wrote that answer in a cynical attempt to be more popular. I wrote it as a stylistic exercise. And because I like the story. But it really doesn’t tell anyone familiar with the story anything that they didn’t already know. It’s just that Beatles fans tend to be like hobbits. They like to be told things they already know, in a neat, readable and entertaining way. The Beatles couldn’t do everything. There are things they did which few other people did, but there are things they didn’t do, and that’s fine. But that means that we shouldn’t praise them as if they had done it. They didn’t ‘invent prog-rock’. They didn’t ‘invent heavy metal’. They tinkered with many styles, and they suggested or implied directions that other bands went in, but that’s not the same thing. If we talked less crap about the Beatles, they would not be so overrated, and we could come to a more sensible appreciation of them. But we have to wade through miles of empty adulation before we get to anything like an interesting insight into their work. And we live in dark times. There are other, active musicians who better deserve our attention. We have to move on. We need to stop talking crap about the Beatles. Thanks for reading. Question: Does listening to rap that has a few violent lyrics all the time make you aggressive?
Answer: No, no more than listening to country music that has a few maudlin lyrics makes you more soft-hearted. Rap does not have more mysterious magical powers to change its listeners’ behaviour than any other form of music whatever. We do not become more aggressive by listening to rap with a few violent lyrics. Just as we do not become more convinced of the immortality of the soul by listening to gospel, and we do not become more fearful of a vengeful God by listening to Bach’s cantatas, and we do not suddenly believe in the existence of hell, because we listen to AC/DC. What happens is that people who like rap are drawn to rap; people who like gospel are drawn to gospel; and people who like Bach are drawn to Bach, and sometimes, mysteriously, these are all the same person. (Me. I’m talking about me, in case you’re wondering. But there are others like me.) But this idea that rap magically does something to its listeners, usually making them worse (because the unspoken implication is that they’re bad to begin with), lingers on, mostly in the minds of ignorant racists, but also in people who are merely poorly informed. Along with this, I think, there is often an unspoken implication: We superior folk should stop these people from listening to rap because it’s making them violent. They need to be educated into being more the sort of people that we want them to be, i.e. people who shut up about themselves and their insignificant problems, and stay in the background until we require their services. The idea that people have the right to artistically express themselves as they see fit, is not one that these people are willing to entertain. I’m not saying that the OP thinks this. I don’t think he does. He may simply be wondering if listening to rap is bad for him. (Or good for him.) People will make the art that enables them to feel like they have said something, even if we try to stop them from doing so. And, anyone who can’t hear a comparable longing for deliverance in Mos Def’s Black on Both Sides and Kendrick Lamar’s ‘Alright’, and Bach’s Mein Gott, wie lang, ach lange? BWV 155, hasn’t bothered to listen to them.

Question: What do you think about jazz hop (combination of old instrumental jazz tunes and modern hip hop beats with or without chorus)?
Answer: It was quite pleasant in the 1990s, but it’s very old hat now. I assume you’re thinking about things like US3’s ‘Cantaloop (Flip Fantasia)’. Cute but not very interesting. Contemporary hip-hop and contemporary jazz have been fertilising each other for decades. The drummers in jazz have been influenced by the new rhythmic approaches in hip-hop. Modern jazz pianists like Jason Moran and Robert Glasper and Vijay Iyer have been doing things with hip-hop rhythms for years. Kendrick Lamar regularly gets jazz musicians to play on his albums. Glasper played on To Pimp a Butterfly. A Tribe Called Quest got Ron Carter to play on The Low End Theory in 1991: thirty-four years ago, for goodness’ sake. So, US3 looping a Herbie Hancock piano figure over a simple beat is child’s play, by comparison. Here’s Glasper from 2007’s In My Element, performing a tribute to the hip-hop producer J Dilla, who’d died the previous year: 2007, people. Seventeen years ago. The more I learn about hip-hop, the more I realise how little people of roughly my age and background have actually listened to it, and how unaware they tend to be of what has been going on in it since the 1980s. Which does go some distance towards explaining the abysmal quality of at least one of the other answers to this question.

Question: What is a heartwarming story you have heard?
Answer: In 1907, in the city of Trieste, in what is now Italy but was then the Austro-Hungarian Empire, there lived a man named Ettore Schmitz. He was born in 1861, into a Jewish family, and grew up speaking the Triestine dialect, with Italian as his second language. But his father was German-speaking and cultured, so he could read in Italian, French and German. His first job was as a bank clerk. He had ambitions as a writer. While working at the bank, he wrote short stories and plays, the latter of which he sometimes didn’t finish. He wrote a novel, Una Vita (A Life), which was published in 1892. It sank without trace. Undeterred, or at least only partly deterred, he wrote another one, Senilità, which was published in 1898. It got equally bad reviews and sold not at all. He was intelligent, sensitive, dryly funny, self-effacing, and rather lacking in confidence. He loved literature and writing, but in Trieste, he was far from the centres of Italian literary activity, and he had few to no contacts in the literary world. By the time he was forty, his literary career was apparently over. But he had a happy marriage, to an intelligent and interesting woman (Livia), and they had a daughter, and that consoled him. He was an atheist, but in order to marry Livia, who was a Catholic, he’d converted to Catholicism. He took a position as senior manager in an industrial paint company founded by his father-in-law. They specialised in an anti-corrosion paint used on naval warships, which meant that Ettore Schmitz occasionally had to travel overseas. In his mid-forties, he was resigned to obscurity. By the 1900s, the paint company was opening a branch in Britain, and Ettore Schmitz decided that he needed English lessons. He found an English teacher, an eccentric young Irishman who had moved to Trieste with his wife only a few years earlier, and who was now teaching part-time at the Berlitz school, and giving private lessons. Schmitz liked the young man, who was clearly very intelligent and startlingly well-read, and they struck up a friendship. The Irishman in his turn appreciated Schmitz’s wit, modesty and kindliness. In the English lessons, the Irishman used to occasionally read his own stories to his pupils. Impressed with the young man’s work, Schmitz mentioned in passing that he had published a couple of novels himself, years earlier. He admitted that nobody had liked them, and that I could come to only one conclusion: that I was not a writer. The Irishman had a look at the copies of the novels, and took them home with him. The Irishman and his wife had a young baby, and another on the way. Various members of his family from Ireland were staying with them, including his younger brother. Schmitz has given me these two novels of his to read, the Irishman said to his brother. I wonder what kind of thing it is. When they next met, the Irishman said to Schmitz Do you realise that you are a neglected writer? There are passages in Senilità that Anatole France could not have improved. Anatole France was, at the time, one of the most eminent living men of letters in Europe. (He would go on to win the Nobel in 1921.) The Irishman admired the coolness and insight of the books, but he also liked the specifically Triestine flavour of them. They were rooted in a time and place, just like his own writings were, but they still had the power to speak to a wider readership. Schmitz was startled and pleased, and grateful to his teacher for such encouragement. He began to think that maybe he should go back to writing. In return, the Irishman gave Schmitz the manuscript of three chapters of his own novel: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, by James Joyce. Schmitz read them, and wrote Joyce a letter, telling him that it was clearly very good indeed, but he had a couple of queries about a few passages where he thought Joyce was writing about stuff that didn’t really matter. Joyce took these criticisms on board, although the book did not get finished until 1914, and wasn’t published in full until 1916. Joyce remained in Trieste until 1915, in the course of which time he began writing his second and most famous novel, Ulysses. One of the principal characters of that novel, Leopold Bloom, is Jewish, and Joyce used Schmitz as one of his models for Bloom, not only adopting Schmitz’s curiosity, kindness and literary ambitions but also questioning him about Judaism, which Schmitz good-humouredly put up with, even though he wasn’t that interested in his own Judaism. Ettore Schmitz—or, to use his pen-name, Italo Svevo—remained friends with James Joyce for the rest of his life. When Schmitz finally wrote his third and greatest novel, La coscienza di Zeno, it was the early 20s. Joyce was, by then, one of the most famous writers in the world. Schmitz sent Joyce a copy, saying in a covering letter that he was worrying that he was making a fool of himself at the age of 60. Joyce read it, wrote Schmitz a letter of fulsome praise (Why worry? You must know that it is by far your best book), and promised to do all he could to boost it, as well as advising Schmitz on who else to send copies to, including T.S. Eliot. He wrote to friends and colleagues, telling them about the book, and asking them to say nice things about it. The French critic Valery Larbaud, who had worked on the first French translation of Ulysses and who respected Joyce’s judgement, read the book, greatly admired it, and said so in print. Larbaud’s influence helped spread the fame of the novel to Italy, where the young Eugenio Montale read it and admired it. Ettore Schmitz died in 1928, from injuries sustained in a car accident. Zeno’s Conscience is about a character who structures his life around his attempts to give up smoking. While he was terminally ill, Schmitz asked one of his visitors for a cigarette. On being denied one, he commented That really would have been the last one. Italo Svevo is now regarded as one of the most eminent 20th century Italian novelists. Plaque at the base of a bronze statue of Italo Svevo, outside the Museum of Natural History, in Trieste. The inscription says ‘Life is neither bad nor good, but it is original.’

Question: News: What are the most notable news stories proven false but never thoroughly publicly acknowledged as false?
Answer: Warning: contains descriptions of violence. I have one that is reproduced over and over again, and there is always much hand-wringing and shocked disbelief, and sad words at human depravity. And the trouble is that, at the core of it, there is a true story about a real crime: a brutal murder, in which a young woman was killed, for no reason, by a sick man whose motives are completely opaque to us. But, around that murder, a narrative has been created that purports to tell us something harsh and sobering about our collective humanity. And that narrative is entirely based on the first and most well-known news story about the murder. I’m going to tell this story in two ways: first recounting the version of it that usually gets told, based on that news story, because it’s the version that people seem to want to believe, and the version which has gone into popular culture. Then, a somewhat different version. If you hadn’t already guessed, this is about the murder of Kitty Genovese. Kitty Genovese in 1956, eight years before her death. Catherine ‘Kitty’ Genovese was born into an Italian-American family in Brooklyn, NYC in 1935. In her school years, she was considered to be ‘sunny’ and ‘self-assured’. In 1954, the family moved to New Canaan, Connecticut after her grandmother witnessed a murder. Later the same year, Kitty got married, but the marriage was swiftly annulled because, one way or the other, it became evident that Kitty was a lesbian. She found work as a bartender in NYC, and in 1961 was arrested for bookmaking. This is why the most frequently reproduced photo of her is her police mugshot: By 1964, she was managing a bar and sharing an apartment in Kew Gardens, Queens, with her girlfriend, Mary Ann Zielonko. In the small hours of the morning of 13 March 1964, she came home from her shift and parked her car in a lot some 100 feet from the door to her apartment. Unknown to her, she was being watched by a man named Winston Moseley, who was sitting in his own car down the street. As she walked towards her door, Moseley got out and came towards her, holding a knife. She saw him, because she started running towards her door. He caught up with her and stabbed her twice in the back. She screamed ‘Oh my god, he stabbed me! Help me!’ Lights in neighbouring buildings began to go on. A man called from the window of his apartment, ‘Leave that girl alone!’ Moseley ran off. While he was gone, Genovese moved around to the back of her building. Nobody came to her aid. After about ten minutes, Moseley returned and attacked her again, stabbing her a third time, fatally wounding her. It was 3.35 am. Thirty-eight people in the vicinity saw or heard the attacks take place, mostly from the windows of their own apartments, or from a bus that went past while the first attack was happening. None of them did anything to stop them. Only at 3.50 am did anyone call the police. By that time there were a couple of people in the street. A New York Times reporter, Martin Gansberg, interviewed some of the witnesses: “We went to the window to see what was happening,” he said, “but the light from our bedroom made it difficult to see the street.” The wife, still apprehensive, added: “I put out the light and we were able to see better.” Asked why they hadn't called the police, she shrugged and replied: “I don't know.” A man peeked out from a slight opening in the doorway to his apartment and rattled off an account of the killer's second attack. Why hadn't he called the police at the time? “I was tired,” he said without emotion. “I went back to bed.” The story appeared in the Times on March 27, with the headline ‘37 Who Saw Murder Didn't Call the Police; Apathy at Stabbing of Queens Woman Shocks Inspector’. This was the opening paragraph of Gansberg’s article: For more than half an hour 38 respectable, law‐abiding citizens in Queens watched a killer stalk and stab a woman in three separate attacks in Kew Gardens. In 1988, the writer Harlan Ellison wrote about the story in a magazine article, in which he said that Kitty Genovese’s murder was: witnessed by thirty-eight neighbors, not one of whom made the slightest effort to save her, to scream at the killer, or even to call the police. Ellison also claimed to have read reports that said that one man turned up his radio, so as to drown out the sound of her screams. The story is also partly fictionalised in Alan Moore’s great comic Watchmen, as further evidence of the inhumanity of people. It’s one of the incidents that pushes the bitter and angry Walter Kovacs over the edge into full-blown violent vigilantism, as Rorschach. (Kovacs is a garment worker who was making a special dress that Genovese ordered; when she doesn’t collect it, because she’s been killed, he remakes the fabric into his mask.) Every so often, someone posts something on this site, telling this story all over again. The murder of Kitty Genovese is horrific enough in itself. But I think what makes people react to this story so strongly is the thirty-eight people who knew that this was taking place—either because they saw it happening, or heard it happening—and did nothing, and who didn’t know, or wouldn’t admit to, why they did nothing. Because we all know the reason, right? They did nothing because they just didn’t care. Or, the bystander effect. Or, the diffusion of responsibility. And this says something about the fundamental callousness and inhumanity of people. Now, there is a problem with this story as I’ve told it above, which is this. It didn’t happen. The above account of it is wrong, in some very important respects, and the ways in which it is wrong ought to make us think rather differently about human nature than the way it’s normally told does. Everything in the above account really happened up until the point that Winston Moseley stabbed Kitty Genovese for the first time. That much is not in dispute. What happened then was that some people in neighbouring buildings heard her cries. Or, more accurately, some people heard someone in the street, screaming. One man, Robert Mozer, heard what was being screamed, and he went to his window and shouted ‘Let that girl alone!’ By this point, some people were looking out of their windows at what was happening in the street. Only one witness actually saw Genovese being stabbed, at this point. Alerted by the shout, Moseley broke off his attack and moved away from her. Genovese, seriously injured, moved from the front to the back of the building. Moseley was seen going back to his car and driving away. Ten minutes later, with nothing having happened in the meantime, people had gone back to their own concerns. Moseley returned and searched the area. He found Genovese behind the building, lying in a hallway. She already had a punctured lung from the first attack, and would not have been able to call for help. She couldn’t get inside because a door was locked. Moseley proceeded to stab her multiple times and rape her, wounding her on her hands as she tried to defend herself. Only one witness saw or heard anything of this attack, at the time. Moseley then stole $49 from her and ran off. Nobody who saw the first attack could have seen or heard anything of the second one. It was on the other side of the building, off the street, and indeed, inside the building. Shortly after Moseley had left, Genovese’s elderly neighbour and friend Sophia Farrar found her in the hallway and held her, whispering ‘Help is on the way.’ An ambulance arrived at 4.15 am but Genovese died on the way to the hospital. This was before New York City had implemented the 911 emergency call system, so there is no clear or complete log of what calls were made to the police or when they were made. Later, one witness reported that his father, having witnessed the initial attack, called the police to say that a woman had been seen getting ‘beat up’ but ‘got up and was staggering around’. Of the people who had heard or seen anything at all: To put it simply, most of the people who ‘witnessed’ the murder of Kitty Genovese, did not realise that they were witnessing a murder. They thought maybe it was a lovers’ quarrel, or a random shout in the street, or a fight which quickly ended. Of those who thought it was something more serious, at least two of them called the police, but records are scanty because of the absence of call logs. Immediately after the story was published, a WNBC police reporter, Danny Meehan, who was aware of what the investigation had uncovered about the attack, noticed that the story contained inconsistencies. He contacted Martin Gansberg, and asked him why the article did not reveal that most of the witnesses had not even realised that a murder was taking place. Gansberg replied, It would have ruined the story. Meehan did not want to wreck his career by revealing what Gansberg had told him. He passed his notes on to a colleague, Gabe Pressman, who also taught journalism. Some of Pressman’s students contacted the Times’ metropolitan editor, Abe Rosenthal, to question him about why he had allowed the story to go through when it was grossly inaccurate. Rosenthal got angry, and gave Pressman a furious phone call, telling him not to question editorial decisions. And so the story lived on, unchallenged, for decades. Only in 2016 did the New York Times add a note to the online version of this story: This is, of course, a public acknowledgement that the story is significantly inaccurate. Funny, though, that people who want to retell the story, tend to leave it out. What did not happen at Kew Gardens that night was For more than half an hour 38 respectable, law‐abiding citizens in Queens watched a killer stalk and stab a woman in three separate attacks. At least one witness directly intervened, Robert Mozer, and he had no reason to suppose that his intervention hadn’t succeeded in frightening off the attacker, because he didn’t know that the attacker came back a few minutes later. Another witness, Sophia Farrar, held Kitty Genovese in her arms and tried to reassure her that help was on the way. Which, by then, it was. Too late, but it was on its way. Harlan Ellison did not help, 24 years later, by repeating the original story word-for-word, and apparently making up the detail about the guy turning up the radio to drown out Genovese’s screams. (Which she hadn’t been able to make, because of her punctured lung.) Alan Moore did not help by having Dave Gibbons include, in Watchmen, a couple of panels depicting Genovese’s neighbours silently observing the murder going on down below. Since then, it has gone into psychology textbooks as an example of the ‘bystander effect’. It is a story that will not die. No matter how often we repeat the facts. People want to believe that dozens of people watched Kitty Genovese get killed, and did nothing. To my mind, there is a vast gulf between ‘hearing something dodgy going on in the street which seems to be over quite quickly’ and ‘casually witnessing a murder for half an hour and not lifting a finger to help the victim’. There is an appetite for stories that tell us how terrible we are. To me, the murder of Kitty Genovese tells us only how terrible her murderer was. (He later confessed to two other murders, and he never showed any evidence of contrition, eventually dying in prison in 2016 at the age of 81.) What has happened to this story is that Kitty Genovese’s murder has been hijacked by people who want to tell a supposedly even more shocking tale about general human callousness. Why they do this, especially if they know that the details about the onlookers aren’t true, I’m not sure. (I can hear Samuel Johnson in my ear, saying In ostentation of their sagacity, vindication of their crimes, or gratification of their malice.) But while the truth may be messy and unsatisfying, it’s still true. The moral people want to draw from this story cannot be drawn from what actually happened that night. The people who realised what was going on did not fail to bother to do anything. Should the people who didn’t realise what was going on, and thought it was no big deal, have investigated further? I leave that question open. RIP, Kitty Genovese. You should have had a long and happy life, and been remembered for that. Not for the thirty-eight imaginary people who supposedly watched you die.

Question: What are the different sounds an electric guitar can make?
Answer: More than most people think. Including most electric guitar players. The electric guitar is notable for being perhaps the instrument with a wider dynamic range than any other—meaning that it can be anything from next-to-silent (especially if it’s a hollow-body electric played with the volume turned down) to shrieking walls of raging sonic fury. This, in itself, makes it unlike e.g. the acoustic guitar, which can only be so loud, unless you amplify it, and even then, you can’t really get the sort of sonic mayhem on an acoustic that you can get on an electric. Unless you’re Sir Richard Bishop. But it also makes the electric guitar unlike wind instruments like the saxophone, or brass instruments like the trumpet, which are incredibly difficult to play very, very quietly, whereas guitars are easy to play quietly, because the guitar—at least, the acoustic guitar—is a fundamentally quiet instrument. Y’see, there is a basic conceptual difference between the solid-body electric, like this: and the hollow-body electric, like this: And the difference is this that the traditional design of the hollow-body electric is basically that of an acoustic guitar with, essentially, a prosthetic, in the form of the pickups and electronics. But the solid-body electric guitar goes beyond that, in that it doesn’t sound at all interesting or usable until it’s plugged in. (I have had people attempt to argue in comments that you can play a solid-body electric unplugged and it’s still a viable instrument, but… no. It’s not.) (Semi-hollow electrics, like this: Are, in my view, closer to solid-bodies than to their hollow-bodied second cousins like the above.) The solid-body electric is much further away from this: than this is: Why? Because the solid-body it relies entirely on its electronics to make a usable sound, via the amplifier. And what this means, for the purpose of answering this question about the different sounds an electric guitar can make, is that the electric guitar, be it like this: or like this: —needs to be regarded as a sound source. What do I mean by that? I mean two things: And once you start thinking of the signal coming from the guitar as being something that is potentially manipulable in all sorts of ways, you realise that there is potentially a huge variety of sounds that you can get the electric guitar to make. There’s a reason I keep bringing up hollow-body electrics. Very simply, it’s that hollow-body electrics offer the creative guitarist rather more possibilities, in terms of making a wide variety of noises, than solid-bodies. Yes, with solid-bodies, you can play clean, you can play fuzz, you can get all sorts of variations within that particular range of timbres. But what you can’t do is get the body of the instrument itself to produce a wide range of interesting sounds. With hollow-bodies, you can play them acoustically. If you tap on them, they will resonate: a Les Paul or a Telecaster won’t, to anything like the same extent. You can mic them up and then blend the acoustic sound with the sound of the pickups. Try doing that with a solid-body like the Ibanez above, and see how far you get. Don’t get me wrong, I love my Strat and my Tele and my Les Paul, but apart from being pretty rubbish as sources of natural sound, they also don’t sound great below a certain volume. The louder they are, the better they tend to sound. The hollow-body electric, though, can deliver all the pure pickup signal you want for you to mess around with, but it also has a whole bunch of other timbres as well. With any electric, given the signal from the pickup, you’re not confined to the same ADSR (attack, decay, sustain, release) envelope that you’re confined to with acoustic instruments. You can use all sorts of devices to make it fade in, swell, change pitch, sustain indefinitely: there’s no limit. Hell, you don’t even have to play the strings. If you know how to work your effects, you can play noise at different pitches, if you so desire. If you have a synth, you can be a string section, or a flute, or a brass instrument, or at least a pleasingly fake approximation of same. My synth pedal gives me the ability to sound like one of those sonar units from naval warfare movies: psssshhhhh… psssshhhhh… psssshhhh… That’s not the only thing it does, and it’s not all that useful in itself, but I’m sure I could find other things I could do with that noise, if I wanted to hook other effects into the chain after the synth. You can use pitch-shifting effects to play in registers way outside the guitar’s normal range. I’m not talking about using them to whoop up briefly into another octave for effect, like Tom Morello: I’m talking about deliberately trying to play one to two octaves higher or lower than normal, and adjusting your playing style, or not, to account for your new range and timbre. But with the sound turned down, if you happen to be playing a hollow-body, you can also do a lot of other effects too: percussive ones, acoustic ones (try playing an acoustic guitar with an eBow: it’s worth trying). What I’m saying is that the electric guitar enables you to be an entire orchestra, plus a sound effects unit from the local radio station. And of course, you can still play guitar. Every so often, probably more often than not, I just plug in and play without anything else, just to remind myself that I like the sound of this instrument. At the moment, I’m experimenting with ways to play traditional Irish slow airs on electric guitar, with as little kitschy vibrato/fake drama and as little glamorous fuzz or effects as possible. Just to see if the electric guitar, played simply, can get that plain, direct, lonesome feel that the uilleann pipes seem to be able to get with almost no effort. It’s not easy. I haven’t even gone into the ways that other players have used the electric guitar to make different kinds of noise: with string, felt, sandpaper, powerdrills, golf balls, radios, violin bows (I didn’t mention the eBow because I took that for granted), crocodile clips, half-full plastic bottles, drumsticks, paint tin lids, false bridges, extra pickups, extra strings, et cetera. I’ve been playing with all these things since I was a teenager, thanks to reading about people like Fred Frith, Hans Reichel, Peter Cusack, Davey Williams, Derek Bailey, Keith Rowe and others when I was young and impressionable. The electric guitar is an extraordinarily versatile instrument. But some types are more versatile than others. In general, solid-body, high-output, metal-optimised racehorses are not that versatile. But enterprising and creative players can pull a wide variety of sounds from them. As someone who, when playing with others, is obliged to be more open and experimental than most guitar players get to be, one of the things I value most about the electric guitar—besides the regular tones you can get from it—is its ability to imitate anything from skritchings on the forest floor to full nuclear Armageddon. You just have to start thinking of it as a sound source. And free yourself from the idea that you’ve gotta always be playing notes. Further reading: Derek Bailey, Improvisation: Its Nature and Practice in Music Bart Hopkin & Yuri Landman, Nice Noise (book about preparing and modifying guitars) Brian Olewnick, Keith Rowe: The Room Extended Ben Watson, Derek Bailey and the Story of Free Improvisation (useful but frustratingly non-technical) Davey Williams, Solo Gig
