Question: If I wanted to play every genre of music on my Squire Telecaster Deluxe that already has 2 humbuckers, would I need to switch one of them out for a single coil?
Answer: [sigh] No. You’re looking at this completely the wrong way. You are being a slave to your instrument. You can play, or attempt to play, literally every genre of music in the world on your Squier Telecaster Deluxe, as-is, without modifying it in any way. (I have always mildly wanted to own a Telecaster Deluxe, btw. Just saying. Not enough to actually buy one, but I like the idea.) A Squier Telecaster Deluxe. Squier’s budget version of Fender’s cover version of the Gibson Les Paul. Your challenge, if you choose to accept it, is to play all those genres of music on your Squier Telecaster Deluxe, and to find a way to make them all sound good. To put it another way, this is not an instrument problem. This is a you problem. If you change one of the pickups to a single-coil, what you have is no longer a Telecaster Deluxe. If you are a creative musician, you find a way of playing the music on the guitar that you have. What you don’t do is change one of the pickups because Oh dear, guitarists in the genre I’m playing in don’t typically use guitars like this one.

Question: I’ve been playing guitar for two months. Is it too early to get my own electric guitar as a 17th birthday present? I’m scared that I will quit playing just a few weeks afterwards and lose interest.
Answer: If you suspect you’ll probably stop playing a few weeks later, and if this is based on your observation of your own previous behaviour, probably better not get a guitar, eh? At least, not yet. Personally, when I got my first guitar at the age of about 16–17, you couldn’t tear it out of my hands. Indeed, I still own and play it, 36-odd years later: Admittedly it has had some… tweaks, since 1987. Don’t waste a birthday present on something you’re not sure you really want. I’m never giving this thing up; it’s like an extra limb, at this point. But if you’re not sure that you love playing, go for something you know will make you enduringly happy.

Question: If you could create a soundtrack for a specific moment in history, which historical event would you choose, and what kind of music would you compose for it?
Answer: Thanks for the ASA, Michelle John. However, I wouldn’t. The reason is that soundtrack music is not, in my view, designed to accompany historical events, but to accompany video (TV/film) narratives. In narratives, there is artistic intention at work. The makers of the narrative want to tell a particular story, and they want to use music to enhance the effect of that story. But with historical events, the situation is completely different. Historical events exist in all their chaotic and bewildering multiplicity and complexity. Until we decide to fit them into a narrative. Then, they become interpretation of the historical event. If we slap a soundtrack over it, we instantly fit an interpretation on the event which rules out competing interpretations of the same event. Yeah, interpretations of the same event can be contradictory, and it’s certainly possible to wilfully or accidentally misinterpret a historical event in such a way that you read it as something that it was not (*cough* the causes of the American Civil War *cough*). But I think it would a very particular kind of poor taste to suggest that historical events, in all their multifold causes and determinations and effects, could in any way by enhanced or made more understandable by putting a soundtrack on it. However, let’s think of a possible counter-example. Has anyone ever used music to comment on, or underline, a historical event, in such a way as I’m describing, and it’s actually been moving, powerful or otherwise artistically effective? Well, yes, they have, I think, although it’s a bit of a special case. Yes, Jimi Hendrix’s performance of ‘The Star-Spangled Banner’ at the Woodstock Festival in 1969. I wrote one of my better answers analysing that very performance: Rather than get into the details of Hendrix’s performance, which I went into in that other answer, I’d like to argue why this performance, for all its grandeur and power, does not in fact counter my basic argument. Hendrix had his own reasons for performing the tune. He was a patriotic American, an ex-soldier (not a very good soldier, but he’d completed paratrooper training) and he claimed to like the melody. However, generations of listeners since 1969 have heard Hendrix’s performance as a soundtrack to the ongoing war in Vietnam, what with Hendrix’s use of his guitar to simulate machine gun and artillery fire and explosions. And the use of these sound effects in a performance of the US national anthem can’t help but make us feel like Hendrix’s performance is, as it were, throwing blood on the flag: calling into question the good intentions of the US in Vietnam, at the same time as lamenting the war’s victims. At least, I think it’s really hard to hear the Hendrix ‘Star-Spangled Banner’ as triumphalist, in any way. I don’t think General Westmoreland would have been exactly delighted. Or President Nixon. But if that performance struck a chord with the more awake members of the audience in 1969, I argue that it’s because it probably fitted, and underlined, and sonically illustrated their existing conception of the war as being a bad thing. The typical Woodstock attendee had likely already made up their mind about whether the war was worth fighting or not, and insofar as they had determined that it wasn’t, they were somewhat in advance of much mainstream opinion at the time. What Hendrix did was put their feelings about it to music. Which he did memorably. What he did not do is play the tune as if the USA were winning a just war with ease. So, in my view, soundtrack music is appropriate for narratives, not for messy reality. Narratives are good. We need them. But they’re still narratives. Which is why I wouldn’t do what this question asks—unless my audience and I were following the same narrative. And, whatever Hendrix’s personal opinions were—at this moment, he was brilliantly in touch with his audience.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Would it be best for a left-handed guitarists to play right-handed if they use a strumming technique but better to play left-handed if they play finger style using classical, blues, or flamenco style?
Answer: I don’t know if it’s a question of having to make a decision about it. I write with my left hand. The first time I picked up a guitar, it felt comfortable playing it right-handed. I’ve tried flipping it over, and when I try to play left-handed, I play like I played the first time I ever picked one up. When I play right-handed, I play like I’ve been playing for 35 years. Your handedness on the guitar is not something you get to choose, is what I’m saying. I can’t play the guitar left-handed, even though I do a lot of other things left-handed. I’ve never experienced my handedness as an obstacle on the guitar; I do quite a lot of hybrid picking, for example, but not all the time. But that means that my right-hand finger are sometimes doing a lot of work. In any case, when I’m using regular picking, especially on really fast passages, my left-hand fretting technique is not the one I’m focusing on: I’m focusing on moving the pick in a clean and regular way and syncing both hands with each other. Everything you have to do on the instrument is a skill that you have to learn. I don’t think handedness has anything do with it. When you try to play the instrument, you very quickly find out which way feels ‘natural’, and then you go with that one. … Also, do any guitar players really tell themselves Well, I won’t ever be playing fingerstyle, ever, only strumming, so it doesn’t matter if I use my dominant hand for fretting? Cause that’s just weird.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Were the early invented electric guitars capable of producing the sounds and techniques we heard from Hendrix era?
Answer: No. For one thing, they were almost all hollow, which meant that by the time you’ve turned them up loud enough to get distortion, you’ve got scads of uncontrollable feedback. (Ask me how I know. I play a Casino.) Next, it’s not just the guitars, it’s also the amps. Advances in amplifier design—in making the bigger, more powerful, much louder amps required to produce Hendrix-like walls of noise—didn’t happen until early rock musicians, mostly in the UK, were pushing for them. Jim Marshall was an English drummer who owned an instrument shop in London, who had diversified into selling guitars and amps. His clients wanted more powerful amps, so Marshall and his assistants started Marshall Amplification and began designing and building them. Their very first product was a game-changer: the Marshall JTM 45. It wasn’t just that Marshall’s amps were louder. They were also designed to be overdriven. The JTM 45 was the basis for the Marshall 1961 and 1962 combos: the hugely influential ‘Bluesbreaker’ amp. Marshall’s amps were intended to be used by players who wanted huge sounds and rich tone and lots of cool harmonics when the amps were overdriven. This, as much as the existence of solid-body guitars, is the technology that made it possible for Hendrix to turn his Stratocaster—an instrument which had been designed with country guitarists in mind—into a firestorm. My Marshall AVT 20.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What do you think of the album Naked City by John Zorn?
Answer: Great album. I have loved it almost since it came out. Naked City, the band that came of this album. L to r: Wayne Horvitz (keys), John Zorn (sax, composer), Joey Baron (drums), Bill Frisell (guitar), Fred Frith (bass). Various factors conspired to make me listen to that album. I was already a fan of Fred Frith, an English guitarist/composer who was recruited by bandleader/composer John Zorn because Frith could a) play bass and b) was a really good sight-reader. I knew about John Zorn from reading about him in The Wire magazine in the late 80s, and from the album Spillane, which I’d acquired in my late teens and loved, and which was basically the only Zorn album you could get in Dublin in the late 80s. Also, I’d read that the album was a cross between jazz, soundtrack music, other kinds of music and punk, and the idea of a fusion between jazz and punk rock was basically the fusion I’d been dreaming of in my head since I first started playing guitar. It turned out that Naked City were not, in fact, the band of my dreams, but I still really enjoyed them. I forget how I first heard this album, except that I know I had a cassette of it by about 1991, because some friends and I used it liberally as soundtrack to some early theatre things we were doing back then. So many things to enjoy. That’s not all there is, of course, because what with all the bursts of ridiculous hardcore there are 26 tracks on this album. But it’ll do for now. Naked City would go on to make other fine recordings, including ‘Metaltov’ from Radio, which as ‘Metal Tov’, as played by Zorn’s Electric Masada, would become one of my favourite tracks ever and one which still defies my efforts to transcribe it. They also made Leng Tch’e, half an hour of shrieking noise that I’ve listened to precisely once, and with some of the most horrific cover art ever used. I think in the end I prefer Zorn when he’s being either less wacky, like with Masada, who I sometimes think I could listen to every day, or more wacky, doing weird sound experiments like Songs from the Hermetic Theater. But the album he caused to be made of Pat Metheny playing his tunes, Tap: Book of Angels Volume 20, was really great. Thanks for the A2A, John Kramer.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What's the last great TV show that you watched and why?
Answer: This one: We Are Lady Parts, a British comedy-drama about Lady Parts, a punk band composed of Muslim women. The first season came out in 2021 and the second season only came out a few weeks ago. Above: Momtaz (manager), Bisma (bass and vocals), Amina (lead guitar and vocals), Ayesha (drums), Saira (vocals, rhythm guitar, bandleader). We Are Lady Parts was created by writer/director Nida Manzoor, herself a Muslim woman: I can’t believe I hadn’t really heard of this show until someone mentioned it in a comment on one of my answers a couple of weeks ago, and then, in my dazed way, I went: What? A show about… Muslim women punks? This I must see. The brilliant thing about the show, apart from the quality of the writing and acting and production, and the thing about it which is the most utterly well-known cliché about it, but which I must nevertheless repeat here, is that the members of Lady Parts are not presented as punks who are rebelling against the fact that they are Muslims. They are, precisely, and in their very different ways, Muslim punks: they are Muslim women who find that punk rock offers them a way of being Muslim women that suits them. Just as the rest of us, who have been or still identify as punks, find that ‘punk’ is a way of being whatever else we might be. ‘Punk’ is an identity, or maybe a way of doing things, that can be shared among people from otherwise quite different backgrounds. (I, for one, feel that ‘punk’ is a big part of who I am.) This show probably sounds to some readers like ‘So woke it hurts’. Probably just a lot of earnest posturing and no jokes, right? However, when we first meet Lady Parts, they are rehearsing their song ‘Ain’t No One Gonna Honour Kill My Sister But Me’. Punk rock, y’all. We Are Lady Parts is simply one of the most brilliant and forward-looking shows on TV at the moment, in the way that it effortlessly evades the assumptions that viewers like me feel tempted to make about it. Over and over again, whenever I’ve thought I’ve known where it was going, it’s smacked me back in my seat, and then rewarded me with a great moment. In season 1, the main POV character is Amina, a rather meek biochemistry postgrad who teaches guitar to local kids and who the band decides to recruit as their lead guitarist, because Saira, their actual guitarist, can’t play solos, and Amina is a much better player. Amina’s main problem with this, other than the fact that she is far from convinced that playing music in public is halal, is that her performance anxiety is so great that, whenever she is confronted with the prospect of playing guitar in public, she tends to vomit and/or lose control of her bowels. Much of the subplots in the first season are about her learning to get over her performance anxiety. This is a show with musical numbers, many of which are among the high points. There are many, but one is when Amina, early in season 2, having gained confidence, decides that she’s got a song in her, which she decides to show to the rest of the band, even though it’s basically about standing up to a colleague at work about a fairly minor issue. I love the idea of a soaring punk rock song about replying to emails within working hours. Also, that’s them playing. And singing. Well, certainly singing. The actors learned to play their instruments for the show, at least enough that their movements exactly match what we’re hearing. I haven’t been able to find out exactly the extent to which they’re really playing what’s on the soundtrack—the sources are frustratingly ambiguous about that—but Anjana Vasan as Amina might as well be playing that guitar solo. Juliette Motamed (Ayesha, the drummer) plays keyboards in real life. We Are Lady Parts starts as a sitcom but becomes darker and more serious in season 2, as the band struggles with becoming more famous. It’s still very funny, though. There’s a great sequence in season 2 when, having decided that they must earn some cash by playing a wedding gig, the band dresses up in suits and shades and gets a slo-mo power walk moment that’s absolutely, consciously Reservoir Dogs: Taz, the band’s devoted manager, is almost never seen without her niqab: her actor Lucie Shorthouse has said She doesn’t owe anyone her face. In the only scene where she isn’t wearing it, we see only parts of her face, never all of it. She becomes a very important character in season 2. It also has a streak of surrealism, or medium awareness, which is quite fun. Amina is prone to imagining scenarios which we see dramatised: in one of them, she and the guy she kinda likes, Ahsan, are imagined as terribly British people in a 1940s movie like Brief Encounter, having very clipped and brittle chit-chat. In another, when going on yet another blind date with yet another unsatisfactory guy, she imagines herself on a game show with her date, who then (in her imagination) turns to her and asks (perhaps influenced by knowing that she plays in a band, and is therefore a Loose Woman) if she gives blow jobs. In real life, Amina comes back to herself in the cafe with her date, and asks him to repeat what he just said. Do you give blow jobs? he says. Fuck this, she mutters, and walks out. At another point, we hear about a legendary Muslima punk, Sister Squire, who Amina has never heard of. The other characters describe her and her only hit, and we see a clip of the video, in which Sister Squire is singing with male dancers throwing bananas at the camera. We cut back to reality, and a banana comes from offscreen and bounces off Amina’s head, making her give a puzzled ‘Ow.’ (Sister Squire is played by Meera Syal, a much-loved figure in British culture, being a playwright, actor, comedian, journalist and general legend.) Also, what other TV comedy features a country and western song about Malala Yousafzai, with a cameo by Malala herself: It’s such a good show that, having finished it last night, reckon I’ll watch it all over again. You can thank me later.

Question: How do I create chords without learning music theory?
Answer: You don’t ‘create’ chords. All the chords have already been created. Every way of voicing them has already been done. You learn how notes in scales are linked together to form chords. This can be done with very little effort. But it involves learning some music theory. Otherwise you’re like the head chef in the kitchen, trying to tell the cooks what to cook, without knowing the names for the foods, or the names of the methods of cooking them. ‘Take the red meat out of the fridge thing, no not that one, the other one, with the bone… no, not the bone in the middle, the bone on the edge… no, not that red meat, are you blind? Right, that one. Question: What can I make with flour, eggs, salt, water and olive oil?
Answer: You can make a simple flatbread with the flour, salt, water and olive oil, and you can fry the eggs and dip the flatbread into it. Here’s a simple flatbread recipe which I’ve made, so I can assure you that it works: Make the dough, then fry the flatbreads and keep them warm while you fry a couple of eggs in very hot olive oil. I suggest searingly hot olive oil, for sixty seconds each, so they’re crispy on the outside but still have liquid yolks. It would be nice to have some raw vegetables with this, or salad, but when we’re poor, we’re poor, and the contrast between the crispy/doughy flatbread and the fried eggs is very pleasant. A few leaves, if possible a squeeze of lemon or some vinegar, and some cheap wine, would make this into a feast.

Question: How do you start formulating answers in high words, or in general using high language?
Answer: Why, Miss, by ceaseless Hours of Application at the Craft of Writing, incessant Study of the Mother Tongue, and the pursuit of Conversation with such Wits and Sages as are willing to associate with my poor Person, quaffing Beverages where convenient. Much has Man learned, many of the Heavenly Ones has he named, said the German poet, since We have been a Conversation. Alas, his Wits broke soon after, from a Surfeit of Hegelianism. But his Spirit lives on, and I believe the Tourist Shops of Tübingen do a brisk Trade in Environmentally Amiable T-Shirts, emblazoned with Images of his Countenance. Rather than trust the Mechanick Artlessness of the Chat-GPT (I believe it was Mr. Beauclerk who wittily claimed the Ackronym to stand for Gullible Person’s Twaddlemaker), I rely on my Brain, my Knowledge (such as it is) of the Language, and the Powers of my Will to speak Truth garb’d in Noble Words. —When, that is, I can be ars’d to. At other times, Miss, I own that I blether. I rely on my Friends to nudge me, when I seem to have forgot the Difference. I am, Miss, your most obedient Servant, Alex. Johnston

Question: What can you use instead of rolling paper?
Answer: The great Russian literary theorist Mikhail Bakhtin (1895–1975) was a heavy smoker. When he was living in Moscow in straitened circumstances during WW2, he got around the shortage of cigarette papers by using the pages of the only manuscript he had of an unpublished monograph on Goethe. Bit by bit, he smoked the whole thing. This is not advisable, because you end up inhaling extra harmful chemicals from paper that wasn’t intended to be smoked. But Bakhtin was a hardy soul, who scarcely grumbled when he lost a leg from osteomyelitis at the age of 43.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What are the benefits of playing and memorising music by J. S. Bach?
Answer: Besides being a wonderful composer, Bach is a great teacher. His approach as a composer was strikingly rational, systematic and thorough. For all that his ultimate inspiration seems to have been 17th century Lutheran theology, when it came to music, he liked to demonstrate shape and pattern and transformation. Learning some of the cello suites, and/or the violin sonatas and partitas, and some of the keyboard works, gives you a boot camp in traditional Western harmony which is made the more enjoyable by the fact that those works are already masterpieces. I can’t play much Bach on the piano (I’m more of a one-handed piano player) but I have figured out some of it on the guitar and bass. It’s always been worth it. Playing any music which, like Bach’s, is incredibly well-made, makes you better acquainted with what well-made music is like: it raises your standards as a listener and as a musician. Just as habitually playing music which is lazily put together, or lacking in shape and structure, habituates you to thinking that shape and structure aren’t really necessary. That is a bad habit to form. Playing and memorising Bach won’t teach you to improvise, or to play modern popular music. But it will give your ear a terrific workout, and when you play his instrumental music in such a way that you respect its dance rhythms, you’ll also get a great kick out of them.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Why does my brain come up with these awesome technical level melodies, and riffs when I mindlessly play guitar (like when I’m doodling)? For a fact, I know I'm bad at playing guitar.
Answer: You mean ‘noodling’, rather than doodling? I think all or most of us guitarists have some sort of badly imagined, out-of-focus ‘dream music’ in our heads when we’re playing, which represents (but isn’t really) what we would like to be able to play, but can’t. I say ‘isn’t really’ because we can’t usually imagine it in detail: we can’t audiate it, meaning we couldn’t say for sure what the actual notes are, or how to play them. It’s just a kind of idealisation of how we would like to be able to play. And we work towards it, but never quite reach it. I remember when I was a teenager and was listening to 40s bebop and 80s alternative rock with equal enthusiasm, and used to fantasise about a kind of music that would have elements of both of them: something which would be as harmonically sophisticated and as varying in moods and feel as the jazz I loved, but was also as energetic and as viscerally exciting as the rock music I loved. Years later, after decades of practising and studying scales, and listening to jazz and other musics, and trying to play them, and working on my technique by doggedly learning other people’s flashy guitar parts, I’m a little bit closer to being able to play what teenage me couldn’t quite hear. But only a little bit closer. Bill Frisell (above), who is a world-class musician, once had a dream, recounted in Philip Watson’s biography of him, Beautiful Dreamer. In the dream, Frisell encountered a group of strange hooded monk-like people, one of whom said to him We’d like you to hear what real music sounds like. They proceeded to play him some music which consisted of all the music he’d ever heard, played at the same time, but put together in such a way that it all made a kind of beautiful sense to him. He has said that that dream is what keeps him going as a musician. He has never succeeded in realising that music in real life, although sometimes he’s come close. So perhaps we’re all dreamers. I, for one, would be quite depressed if I realised that my dreams had shrunk to the point that I could play without effort whatever I wanted to play.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Why didn’t Thin Lizzy get big?
Answer: Ah. By far my favourite band from my own country. Well, them and the Bothy Band, anyway. Please excuse if I ramble on about them a bit before directly addressing the question. Arguably the most ‘iconic’ lineup of Thin Lizzy, c. 1977: l to r, Scott Gorham (g, backing v), Brian Robertson (g, backing v), Brian Downey (d) and Phil Lynott (b and lead v). Thin Lizzy were a wonderfully odd hard rock band. I think that, in the end, their wonderful oddness might have worked against them, in that they were always a vehicle for their chief songwriter: Philip Lynott, above, Ireland’s most famous black celebrity. Lynott was the son of an Irish woman, Philomena Lynott, and a Ghanaian man, Cecil Parris. He was born in England in 1949, and spent the first few years of his life there, but was then sent to live with his grandparents in Crumlin in Dublin. To give you an idea of what Crumlin was like at the time, on the classic Irish version of a Monopoly board, Crumlin is in the same space as (in the US version) Mediterranean Avenue, or on the UK version, Old Kent Road. Lynott began as a singer, and was taught to play bass guitar by a rather lesser Irish rock legend, Brendan ‘Brush’ Shiels. He was never a technically brilliant bass player, but he was good enough to come up with some memorable lines. His real skill was songwriting. Thin Lizzy took three or four albums to hit their stride, but even on the first two, Thin Lizzy and Shades of a Blue Orphanage, he was writing quirky, intimate songs that had more to do with folk-rock than anything else. And I think that that was part of the reason why Thin Lizzy never became as big as they might have become. Because, romantic that he was, he kept on writing whatever he wanted, rather than trying to make the band sound consistently one thing rather than another. The first Lizzy song that makes everyone go ‘Thin Lizzy!’ is actually their cover version of the traditional song ‘Whiskey in the Jar’, with its catchy guitar riff and Lynott’s hoarse, Jameson-soaked vocal. But I think the first Lizzy song that’s truly and inimitably theirs is ‘The Rocker’, from Vagabonds of the Western World, with its clanging guitar intro: a classic, pounding, balls-to-the-wall, end-of-gig song. If Thin Lizzy had consistently put out whole albums of songs like ‘The Rocker’, they might have acquired an audience that valued them for that kind of music. But their next album, Nightlife, was hardly that kind of album: it was soulful, funky and rather romantic. The title track shamelessly stole the refrain from Willie Nelson’s ‘Night Life’: The night life ain’t no good life, but it’s my life. It contained one of the band’s most searing ballads: ‘Still In Love With You’. Now that it's all over Woman, there's something I think you should know Baby, baby, think it over Just one time before you go Call on me, baby If there's anything I can do for you Call on me, baby Help me see it through Perhaps only Phil Lynott would write a song in which the singer tells his ex-lover to call him if there’s anything he can do for her. (Yes, I agree it’s maybe undercut by the next lines in which he asks her for help. But still, it’s a thoughtful moment.) At this point it was 1974, and Thin Lizzy were four albums in, and still didn’t sound like they had the kind of solid identity that other rock bands of the period had generally achieved by their second or third albums. By the time of their next album, Fighting, they arguably still hadn’t got it. Geoff Barton, an English music journalist and a founder of the heavy metal magazine Kerrang!, reviewed it in Sounds magazine and complained that Thin Lizzy’s music lacked energy and aggression. A little later, he was at a Lizzy concert and Phil Lynott launched into a rant about music journalists. Barton wondered if he’d touched a nerve, but at the end of the rant, Lynott smiled and said ‘But no matter what, this next song is for Geoff Barton: “Still In Love With You”.’ Barton was both flattered and humbled. By late 1975, Thin Lizzy’s label, Vertigo, was a bit peeved that the band wasn’t selling more records. The pressure was on to have a major hit. The result was Jailbreak, which had at least five great songs on it. Lynott had finally digested the influences of people like Van Morrison in a song like ‘Running Back’, which is not about American football but is a kind of song he would write over and over again: the I would love to get back together with you, if you’re at all interested song. Henry Rollins once praised it as having the kind of emotional generosity that he never had, saying that while Phil Lynott’s attitude was You left me… but I’d come running back, his own was You left me… but I’d come running back to stab you in the head! Twenty years later, Rollins was still full of admiration for them. Jailbreak was the only Lizzy album to go gold in the USA. But in the ensuing US tour, Lynott came down with hepatitis, and the remaining dates had to be cancelled. While recuperating, Lynott began writing songs for the next album, Johnny the Fox. Again, he was in no rush to write more songs like ‘Jailbreak’ or ‘The Boys Are Back In Town’: the track ‘Johnny the Foxy Meets Jimmy the Weed’ was written under the influence of one of his favourite funk tracks, ‘For the Love of Money’ by the O’Jays. Then there was ‘Don’t Believe A Word’, which was originally written as another ballad like ‘Still In Love With You’, but ended up being remade as a hard rock shuffle. They ended up playing it as a ballad anyway, which I think improved it as it put the spotlight on the lyrics, among Lynott’s most unsparing: Don't believe me if I tell you Not a word of this is true Don't believe me if I tell you Especially if I tell you I'm in love with you Don't believe me if I tell you That I wrote this song for you There just might be Some other silly pretty girl I'm singing to Don't believe a word For words are so easily spoken And your heart is just like that promise Made to be broken Lynott and guitarist Brian Robertson tended to clash with each other, and things came to a head when Robertson tried to stop a fight from breaking out in a Glasgow bar and his hand got badly cut by a bottle, preventing him from playing for several months. As a result, a planned US tour had to be cancelled. The next album, Bad Reputation, was made mostly without him, and included another classic, ‘Dancing in the Moonlight (It’s Caught Me In Its Spotlight)’—yet another Thin Lizzy song that wasn’t aggressive cock-rock, but a romantic mid-tempo number about coming home in an ecstatic mood from a great date with your girlfriend. Robertson stuck around for the ensuing tour, which yielded one of the all-time great live albums, Live & Dangerous, certainly the album I would point anyone at who wanted to know what the fuss is about Thin Lizzy, even if it’s heavily weighted towards the hard rock stuff rather than the more reflective songs. But then Robertson was out, and Gary Moore, who’d played with them before, joined for long enough to make an entire album: 1979’s Black Rose: A Rock Legend, my favourite Lizzy album on account of its majestic title track, ‘Róisín Dubh (Black Rose): A Rock Legend’, which manages to be genuinely epic in its use of Celtic mythology— Pray tell me the story of young Cú Chulainn How his eyes were dark his expression sullen And how he'd fight and always won And how they cried when he was fallen Oh tell me the story of the queen of this land And how her sons died at her own hand And how fools obey commands Oh tell me the legends of long ago —and tongue-in-cheek in its punning references to Lynott’s culture heroes: My Roisin Dubh is my one and only true love It was a joy that Joyce brought to me While William Butler waits And Oscar, he's going Wilde Ah sure, Brendan where have you Behan? Looking for a girl with green eyes My dark Rosaleen is my only colleen That Georgie knows Best For those who’ve never heard of George Best, he was probably Ireland’s most famous footballer, a fabulously gifted player whose sex, drugs and booze lifestyle wrecked his career. (There is a probably apocryphal story of a young waiter delivering room service to Best’s hotel room, and finding him in bed with two naked women, surrounded by mounds of cash and bottles of champagne, with lines of cocaine on the bedside table. On seeing all this, the waiter bursts out Oh Georgie, where did it all go wrong?!) But by this point, Lynott was starting to do a lot of substances. He even wrote a good song about his own substance abuse, ‘Got To Give It Up’, but by Chinatown in 1980 he was writing ‘Sugar Blues’, which is for my money the best song ever written about what it feels like to be on cocaine. (There’s definitely something coke-fuelled about Brian Downey’s absurdly fast drum fills.) The title track, though, is a bunch of clichés strung together with a liberal splash of Yellow Peril nonsense. Guitarist Scott Gorham said later that it was during the making of Chinatown that he realised that the band wasn’t getting any bigger. It could have been a time for them to have a second wind. Punk had happened, the New Wave of British Heavy Metal was under way, and Thin Lizzy slotted rather neatly into it. Except that Lynott’s songs weren’t as good as they used to be. On 1981’s Renegade, the opening song ‘Angel of Death’ was the band’s most convincing attempt yet to sound metal, except that he’d forgotten to write a melody for the verses. The lyrics were a load of tosh inspired by a documentary he’d seen about Nostradamus. I have a soft spot for Renegade’s title track because it was one of the first bass lines I ever learned to play, but that’s about the best thing I can say about it. (The vocal on the studio version is awful; the live version on Life is better.) By Thunder and Lightning, the last album, in 1983, the band had gone full metal, yea, even unto the risible cover image of a gloved fist emerging from some gravel while lightning strikes Phil’s bass in the distance. Still, there are some good songs, but on listening to ‘The Sun Goes Down’, the band’s last single, it’s hard not to hear it as a kind of farewell: There is a demon among us Whose soul belongs in hell Sent here to redeem us She knows it all to well He comes and goes, he comes and goes She knows it all too well But when all is said and done The sun goes down Lynott released two solo albums, but died in 1986 from complications of drug and alcohol abuse. A version of Thin Lizzy, featuring their longest-serving guitarist Scott Gorham, continues to occasionally perform their music. In the end, Thin Lizzy didn’t make it bigger than they did because of a number of factors. One is that it took them a long time to find a sound that was really theirs. Maybe four or five albums. There are good tracks on all their early albums, but not many that you can point to and say ‘Nobody else except Thin Lizzy could have made that’. Whereas, although ‘Cowboy Song’ on Jailbreak isn’t much more than a bunch of Western movie tropes slung together, it’s cheerful and bouncy and nobody else could have done it. Another is that they always mixed up genres on their albums, and not all fans like that, especially hard rock fans, who tend to want hard rock, not thoughtful songs about what a bad boyfriend you’ve been. Another is that, for one reason or another, they cancelled or postponed tours more than most bands. Another is that they found it hard to maintain a consistent lineup. Eric Bell was the guitarist on the first three albums, then he left and Scott Gorham and Brian Robertson joined, and that was the lineup that rose to their peak of fame, but Robertson found the fame too much pressure and he drank, and he ended up leaving. Then Gary Moore came and went (one album), and Snowy White (two albums), and finally John Sykes, but then they broke up. Another is that Phil Lynott did too many drugs and drank too much, and it ended up wrecking his voice. The deterioration from Black Rose to Thunder and Lightning is audible, and it was only four years. And, ultimately, Phil Lynott was too much himself as a writer. As we’ve seen, he wasn’t exactly disciplined about making sure that the band had a consistent sound. He followed his wayward muse. He didn’t just write a song for his mum (‘Philomena’, from Nightlife), he wrote one for his grandmother (‘Sarah’, from Shades of a Blue Orphanage). Take that, Neil Peart! Squeeze that lemon till its juice runs down your leg, Robert Plant! Apart from a brief period between about 1976 and 1978, the more Thin Lizzy tried to be any one sort of band, the less interesting and imaginative they tended to be. They played with the usual lyrical tropes of hard rock and metal—rockers, warriors, vagabonds, cowboys, killers, apocalypse—but almost always with their tongue firmly in their cheek. They were a little too grown-up to believe in all that stuff, at least not with the kind of naive sincerity with which Ozzy Osbourne sang Geezer Butler’s lyrics. Lynott was his own worst enemy, but he knew it, and he had the honesty to sing about it. And he always had a certain sympathy for the despised and disregarded, which was evident in his introduction to ‘Got To Give It Up’, from their final live album, Life: We'll be back just after this message. We have heard that there are people, here, in the Leisureland... that have consumed large quantities... of alcohol. And on behalf of the management, this is frowned upon, as alcohol... is dangerous. It has also been brought to our attention, that there are those... out there... and on the stage, [dropping his voice to a deep bass] that have indulged in sex. This is also frowned upon, as sex can damage your health. So for all those people in bad health... Welcome. Thanks for reading.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: As a religious person, if you were lost in a cold place at night and only had a copy of your holy book, would you use it to start a fire?
Answer: I am not a religious person, but I am interested in religion, and in my Unpublished Fantasy Saga (TM) I have a character who is intensely religious and belongs to a religion who treat their holy book with Islam-like reverence. Copies of the book itself are rare and precious, and have many, many pages, and he’s a scholar of just one part of it, because the book is so long and complex and so partially indecipherable that nobody is an authority on all of it. His own study copy is enormous. He’s a rather puny character but at one point, he’s in a tense situation with a female character who’s well-disposed towards him and two other guys who are extremely malevolent (they’ve already been extremely brutal to our unfortunate scholar, from which the woman character extricated him). A fifth character enters, and tries to take charge and defuse the situation, but then one of the bad guys, feeling like his chance of doing mean things is slipping away, lunges towards the female character. So, on impulse, our very tense and keyed-up scholar literally throws his book at the guy. It knocks the villain down and, unluckily for the villain, he lands in such a way that the boot stand by the fireplace pierces his skull and fatally injures him. Things get worse before they get better, but the main consequence for our scholar is that pages of his Book are now covered in blood and bits of brain, and partially charred. Much of his character development from there is his coming to terms with the fact that, nominally a guardian of the holy book, when it came to a crisis he used it as a weapon to defend someone who is not a member of his religion. I wanted to write a character who, from the outside, is gaining something (a broader sense of human worth—people of his religion do tend to regard everyone else as being stupider and more sinful than them) but who experiences it as, among other things, a falling-off from his previously exalted position. He liked feeling as though he was part of a special people, but boring old human empathy made him instinctively try to protect someone who his religion had told him wasn’t worth protecting. … Also I liked taking literally the metaphor ‘threw the book at him’.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Is there a word or a phrase to describe someone that force themselves to watch or listen to boring pretentious films or music?
Answer: Do you know anyone who does that? I mean, people who force themselves to watch films or listen to music which they themselves consider boring or pretentious? Or just people who force themselves to watch films or listen to music which you consider boring or pretentious? Because if it’s the latter, has it occurred to you that maybe they don’t find it boring or pretentious, but… actually like it? Another answer just says ‘Critic’, and it’s true that critics, unlike the rest of us, are sometimes obliged to endure films and music that they don’t like. I did slightly know a film reviewer, some years ago, who seemed to specialise in the most forbidding kind of obscure arthouse cinema. He would frequently praise such films by saying something like In this film, [X] does not indulge in the cheap satisfactions of Hollywood conventions of narrative ‘pace’, but continually and bracingly challenges the lazy viewer’s patience by static shots of up to ten minutes and a refusal to pander to audience expectations, which from context usually meant This film has no story. I actually like a lot of so-called ‘arthouse’ cinema, but I never understood the tactic of praising a film by saying, in essence, This film is plotless, frustrating and impenetrable but, see, that’s actually what’s good about it. In the meantime: is this a question about people you know, or is it a question about films and music you don’t like?

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Do any restaurants serve food named after famous people? Has anyone ever had something named after them by their favorite place to eat?
Answer: The Savoy Grill in London still serves a variant on Omelette Arnold Bennett. Arnold Bennett (1867–1931) was an English writer whose excellent Wikipedia article happens to be today’s featured article. I’ve never actually read him, partly because one of his biggest fans, the English academic John Carey, is in my opinion one of the most cloth-brained chowderheads to rise to a major Oxbridge professorship. But Arnold Bennett liked to dine at the Savoy (he made a ton of money from writing, and was commendably generous with it), and the head chef once made him a bespoke omelette with smoked haddock and a cheese sauce. Bennett liked it so much that he used to ask it to be made for him, and it ended up being named after him. I’ve made it for myself. It’s not hard to make, astonishingly rich and surprisingly cheap, but you don’t want to do anything afterwards except go to bed. And not engage in strenuous exercise. Anyway, the Savoy will do you a Soufflé Arnold Bennett, which is a bit classier.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Which ancient civilization are you most interested in, and what about it fascinates you the most?
Answer: Rome. It used to be classical Greece. I studied classical Greek briefly in college, because like a lot of people I fell rather in love with the idea of it being the ‘cradle’ of this and the ‘birthplace’ of that. I read the Iliad in translation, and then limped through it using a facing-page translation. In Greek class I discovered the verbal genius of Aristophanes, who I still think is goddamn hilarious. But over time, Greece came to seem stranger and stranger. I mean, the Athenians ‘created’ ‘democracy’, but it only applied to a few people. So… was it ‘democracy’? They invented drama, but it was a semi-religious civic ritual, rather than ‘art’ as we presently understand it. They invented Western philosophy, except that I found it quite hard to see what was good about their philosophy, compared to… well, later Western philosophy. (I’ve since mellowed a bit about that, but I still reach for Wittgenstein or Williams or Nietzsche, or even Rousseau, sooner than I reach for Plato.) I got interested in Sparta, again because of an idea of Sparta, but on reading serious academic histories of Sparta I realised that the ‘real’ Sparta is almost inaccessible, behind the giant mass of contemporary commentary about the place, written by non-Spartans with ideological axes to grind. Basically all history consists of texts about history, and so historiography involves the interpretation of texts, but the texts about Sparta are of such questionable facticity that you end up doing what people have always done to Sparta over the centuries: projecting onto it what you want it to be like. I still love Aristophanes. He seems tons more sophisticated than he ought to be. But Homer no longer does it for me—and it could be that I’m missing something, but still, I have moved on. With Rome, I had fewer preconceptions. I first got into it via poetry: Catullus, to be precise, Rome’s first great, sexy, cheeky lyric poet. Then, some history books. Then, more poetry: first Horace, then Ovid, and culminating in my very late, mid-life discovery of Virgil, whose Aeneid quickly became my favourite Latin classic and one of my favourite books, ever. It seems to me that, if or when we compare ourselves to the Greeks, we flatter ourselves, because we tend to see in them the things we admire, and we shout down the voices that remind us that, e.g., Athenian women are almost invisible, or that Socrates was a friend to the closest thing the Greeks had to fascist bully-boys. But with Rome, the faults are all hanging out on display. Roman society appears to us more like a mirror, with its corruption and its assassinations and its lobbyists and its infighting. The poets are almost always in somebody’s pocket, and part of the fun is in seeing how they dealt with that, like Horace’s habit of cautiously complimenting his patron Maecenas while insisting that he’s nobody’s puppet, or Virgil writing for Augustus a national epic that ends with its virtuous, dutiful hero losing his shit in a fit of rage, and stabbing a vanquished, pleading enemy to death. Catullus pines after his elusive mistress, and threatens to face-f**k people who diss him (cf. XVI, Pedicabo ego vos et irrumabo), but when he writes a violently libellous poem about Julius Caesar (LVII, Pulcre convenit improbis cinaedis), Caesar gets angry until Catullus basically says Ah, yeah, sorry about that, whereupon Caesar calms down and invites him to dinner. The Romans are nearly always a very modern combination of grandeur, silliness, sordid realism, high talk, sometimes noble intentions, and low morals. I was reading Scullard’s From the Gracchi to Nero the other night, and a guy like Sulla seems to me recognisable in a way that Greek public figures kind of don’t. Sulla emerges as a general under Marius; is (per Scullard, anyway) the first figure in Roman history to seize power by force, in 82 BC; becomes dictator, kills a bunch of people, and then passes a bunch of reforms that are intended to make it harder for anyone like him to seize power in the future. And, having done this, rather than bask in his power, he retires to the country, where he dies less than two years later. Sulla’s abrupt retirement baffled the man who would most famously emulate him a little over 30 years later: Julius Caesar, whose career is the great hinge around which Roman history turns. Unless that’s Augustus. Well, it was one of them, anyway. I admit that I’m not into Latin poetry because I’m fascinated by Rome. I’m fascinated by Rome—all the backstabbing and the regime changes and the triumvirates and the pax Romana—because I’m into Latin poetry, most of the best of which came out of years of social unrest and civil war. It’s as if the Romans needed to be really troubled in order to properly sing. Virgil is, for me, the most thoughtful, the least garrulous, the most ambiguous, and the one whose works will I think endure longest. Horace I kick back with; Catullus I chuckle with; Ovid I sit up and look studious in case I miss anything. Juvenal I can’t be bothered with, cranky old snob that he was. But Virgil just works for me, on some level. He’s the least personal: no bitching about his mistress (if he even liked women; we don’t know), no glimpses of his private life. All his personal feelings are sublimated into the work, with its careful attention to existing conventions. But that’s the mystery of his poetry: how the hidden dramatist in him could so convincingly inhabit Dido and Turnus and Juno and Aeneas, etc., and know exactly what they would be doing as they said the things he has them say. An essay by Wendell Clausen points out that the Homeric epics are about a very traditional kind of hero: a hero whose fulfilment is found in martial prowess, or sheer competence and guile. It’s where Achilles gets his glory, and Odysseus gets our admiration. But Aeneas, in the Aeneid, does not get nearly as much of a kick out of being Aeneas, as Achilles gets out of being Achilles, or Odysseus gets out of being Odysseus. Unlike them, Aeneas is constantly torn between what he wants to do, and what he feels he has to do. Achilles wants to be the biggest badass out there. Odysseus wants to get home. They both succeed. Aeneas, by contrast, spends most of his book wishing he were doing almost anything else. He would like to have his dead wife back, and his dead father, and for Troy to still be a place where he could live, and he’d like to shack up with Dido, and he’d like to be able to see his father some more times, and… … But he can’t. He knows what he has to do, which is find a new home for the Trojans. And, every time his sense of duty conflicts with what he wants, he ends up giving up what he would like to do, and doing what he knows he has to do. In this, he is much more like us, than like those Greek heroes whose opportunities conveniently dovetailed with their desires. And that’s why the Iliad, for all its violence, is I think ultimately joyful, and the Odyssey, for all that Odysseus loses on his journey, is ultimately about the satisfaction of coming home. Achilles blazes like a star, and he will die young—but look at the figure he cut in the meantime. But the Aeneid is not like that. Virgil is the great poet of loss. Of distances; of things that have gone that we won’t get back. (His landscape painting is some of the best ever.) And the Aeneid is a poem about, among other things, what it costs us to make something worth making. C.S. Lewis pointed out that the Greeks weren’t really that interested in how things came to be what they are, whereas the Romans were obsessed by it. And the Aeneid pulls off the extraordinary feat of making a relatively brief period (from Aeneas leaving the smoking remains of Troy, to coming to Latium and conquering it) seem like a huge era of time. It fascinates me that, even at the very birth of the Roman Empire, it was being imagined by its greatest poet as something that was arguably not worth the trouble it took to create. Maybe that’s why Borges recognised in Virgil a poet who is, par excellence, a trusted friend: Of all the poets of the earth, there is no other who has been listened to with such love. Which is maybe why Dante chose him as the guy to guide his avatar through Hell. Of all poets, Virgil’s the guy who won’t bullshit you. So, whereas there are other poets I love more, and other civilisations I am more fascinated by, still, of the Greek and Latin classical ones, I am most fascinated by Rome. Because I am so fond of its greatest poet. Modern bust of Virgil, from 1930 or so.

Question: Out of all the conquests in human history, European colonization always seems to receive the most criticism. Was there anything uniquely bad about European imperialism, or is it simply a matter of scale and/or recency?
Answer: It’s because, if we are Europeans, and we wish to criticise colonialism, it is morally imperative that we criticise our own, before we criticise anyone else’s. I find it depressing that this basic lesson in ethics needs to be taught to, presumably, an adult, but there you go.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What do you think are some of Taylor Swift's best lyrics or what songs would you recommend to a person new to her? A Google search didn't produce impressive results or songs that struck me as particularly poetic. Looking to discover her best work.
Answer: I think you’re looking for something that maybe isn’t there. Taylor Swift, because I’m not sure people know what she looks like. Taylor Swift is, in my opinion, a fine songwriter, capable of writing great songs. But: a poet? I’m not sure. You want poetry? Real, in-your-face, glittering, 24-carat poetry? Rap contains some great poetry. Leonard Cohen was a poet. Bob Dylan is a poet. Patti Smith and Nick Cave and Joni Mitchell and Tim Buckley have some great poetry in their songs. Hell, Jim Morrison had some great poetry in his songs. Taylor Swift is not, in my view, much like the above. Her great strength is storytelling. Her best songs tend to have a story to them, and it’s the story that’s compelling and moving. Bob Dylan can write something like this: Louise, she's all right, she's just near She's delicate and seems like the mirror But she just makes it all too concise and too clear That Johanna's not here The ghost of electricity howls in the bones of her face Where these visions of Johanna have now taken my place I don’t know what ‘Visions of Johanna’ is ‘about’, exactly, but it works on me the way poetry works; it defies simple interpretation and creates a mood or a frame of mind. But a line like The ghost of electricity howls in the bones of her face is clearly not meant to be a line from a horror story; it’s poetry. What Taylor Swift does is use words to create a narrative situation that we can understand and sympathise with, which she does in, e.g., the opening verse of ‘We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together’: I remember when we broke up the first time Saying, ‘This is it, I've had enough,’ 'cause like We hadn't seen each other in a month When you said you needed space (What?) Then you come around again and say ‘Baby, I miss you and I swear I'm gonna change, trust me’ Remember how that lasted for a day? I say ‘I hate you’, we break up, you call me, ‘I love you’. In print this is rather banal, but in the context of the song and its original production, it has a kind of elegance and wit. The melody is very simple, a rather lilting major key ditty, but it’s broken up by the way she sings it. In the original, the interjection ‘What?’ is a spoken word, which is said in exactly the same tone that it would have been uttered by the singer if her boyfriend had said, after a month, that he ‘needed space’: Taylor Swift: [outraged] What?! Similarly, the ‘I love you’ is also spoken word, but it’s said with a kind of swooning release, as if she’s completely forgiven him all his shenanigans and is already back in bed with him. I don’t think that ‘We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together’ is her deepest or most moving song, by any means, but it does what it does very neatly. And it’s actually funny. It reserves its biggest impact for the chorus, which is the narrator boiling over with rage and drawing a line: that’s it, we are never getting back together, you hear me, dummy? And yet I think we also doubt her, what with her line about You go talk to your friends, talk to my friends, talk to me, which is her leaving the lines of communication open. The song works as a defiant screw-you to an unsatisfactory boyfriend, suitable to be sung loudly by groups of young women after a few drinks. And why not? That is a perfectly dignified kind of song to write. Everyone needs songs. And it doesn’t try to be anything more than that. Taylor Swift’s lyrics make me think of a remark T.S. Eliot made about Ben Jonson’s poetry: … [Y]ou can hardly pick out a line of Jonson’s poetry and say confidently that it is great poetry; but there are many extended passages to which you cannot deny that honour. The trouble is that, in order to understand the passage, you need to know the narrative. Perhaps my favourite of her albums, folklore from 2020, contains these lines, from the song ‘Cardigan’: I knew I'd curse you for the longest time Chasing shadows in the grocery line I knew you'd miss me once the thrill expired And you'd be standing in my front porch light And I knew you'd come back to me You'd come back to me And you'd come back to me And you'd come back And when I felt like I was an old cardigan under someone's bed You put me on and said I was your favorite This song, and these lines, make a great deal more sense when we learn that the narrator of this song is the subject of another song on the same album, ‘Betty’, which is sung from the point of view of the ‘you’ in ‘Cardigan’, and who it turns out was Betty’s teenage boyfriend, who cheated on her and regretted it: But if I just showed up at your party Would you have me? Would you want me? Would you tell me to go fuck myself Or lead me to the garden? In the garden would you trust me If I told you it was just a summer thing? I'm only seventeen I don't know anything but I know I miss you And we know that this is the case, because of a mention in the last line: I'm only seventeen I don't know anything But I know I miss you Standing in your cardigan Kissing in my car again Stopped at a streetlight, you know I miss you When the one song is considered in relation to the other song, they echo off each other, and the result is, in my view, Taylor Swift’s sort of poetry. I know quite a lot of her songs, and very few of them fascinate me with their enigma, as maybe Dylan’s songs do (and I am not a great Dylan fan, btw). But they have their own eloquence, and they are not cheap, or pretentious, or dishonest, like the lyrics of some songs by musicians who I like more than her. (I am on record as a King Crimson fan, but King Crimson have some of the worst lyrics I have ever had to sit through.) I think she writes best when she’s writing little short stories in song form. Her songs about herself don’t grab me as much as her songs about other people. I would not be at all surprised if she turns to fiction as she gets older. I think she’s got the chops for it.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: When creating an evil character on the road to redemption, how evil can you make them at the start?
Answer: I don’t think it’s a question of ‘how evil’, which makes it sound like there’s a sort of measuring jug for evil: If your character has more than 750ml of evil, they can’t go on the road to redemption. Suggest reducing the quantity of evil, possibly by pouring some of it into your world-building. I think it’s more a question of ‘what sort of evil can they be?’ To explain what I mean, consider that characters can only go on the ‘road to redemption’ if they at least kinda sorta want to. Otherwise they would just stand at the beginning of the road and go Nuh-uh. I’m fine as I am, thanks. So, it follows that a character can only be redeemed if they know they are evil. A character who does evil things, but thinks that they are the good guy, is hardly going to be seeking redemption for their acts, since they don’t believe they’ve done anything wrong. Likewise, a character who is wholly selfish, lazy, callous and malicious, but thinks that they are awesome, cool, decisive and principled, first needs to learn that they aren’t any of those latter things. For a character to seek redemption, they must first know shame. They have to have a functioning sense of right and wrong, and they have to know that they’ve strayed off the path. They can have done some seriously evil stuff, but if they realise that they shouldn’t have done it, then there is at least theoretically some hope that they might achieve redemption. Now, some readers may feel that there are certain acts that are so heinous, that any character who commits them may never be forgiven, no matter how contrite they become, or what good deeds they perform in order to make amends for their bad ones. And that’s a matter for the reader. I wouldn’t argue with that. I had a seriously compromised character in my novel who had done something so bad that one of my readers adamantly refused to give a shit about him thereafter. Since I needed the reader to find that character not wholly despicable, I changed the story so that the character didn’t do the bad thing himself; he just did nothing while somebody else did it within earshot of him, and when he did finally make up his mind to intervene, which he could have done at any time, it was very much a ‘too little, too late’ type of deal. I think this made him slightly more interesting: selfish and lazy, a creature of bad habits, rather than a monster who would then have to do a complete turnaround, and spend the rest of the story vainly battering his head against the reader’s refusal to care about him. On a related note, the literary effect of confessions, and the way they work on a reader, is I think very interesting. I refer curious readers to the final chapter of Paul de Man’s Allegories of Reading, which contains a lucid and brilliant discussion of Rousseau’s use of confessional tropes in the Confessions, written by someone who had excellent personal reasons for not wanting to own up to his own major flaws.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Can you explain the difference between single coil and humbucker pickups on a guitar? Which type of pickup is generally considered to have a better sound, and why?
Answer: Sure. The humbucker was invented to solve an engineering problem. First, you need to understand how pickups work. This is a typical single-coil pickup, from a Fender Telecaster: There’s more going on here than meets the eye. The pickup, FYI, is the slanted black doodad on the right with the metal circles embedded in it. (The rest of what you see here is the bridge plate, with the bridge saddles; ignore that.) Those metal circles are actually short, rod-shaped magnets, known as pole pieces. All you can see is the top of them. Inside the plastic casing, those metal rods are wrapped around with copper wire: thousands of turns of it, which is known as the coil. The ends of the coil are attached to the jack socket, which is a sort of metal clamp that goes through a hole elsewhere in the guitar. The pickup works because of electromagnetic induction. When you pluck a string, the string vibrates. The string itself has a steel core, and is vibrating inside a magnetic field created by the pole piece. When the string vibrates, because it’s steel, the magnetic field changes slightly, which, because of electromagnetic induction, creates a very small current in the coil. This current flows through the wire of the coil and, therefore, through the jack socket. When a guitar cable is plugged into the socket, the current flows through the cable (let’s leave wireless units out for now, eh) and through the amplifier. The amplifier uses mains electricity to make the current much more powerful—so powerful that it can drive a speaker cone, and convert that current into sound, which is the sound of the electric guitar. The above pickup has six pole pieces, and only one coil. So, it’s called a single-coil pickup. There is just one problem with single-coil pickups, which is that they’re prone to interference. Any other electromagnetic activity in the vicinity, including the very fact of your amplifier being on, will create hum: a steady, low-level, electronic purr coming out of the speaker. The louder you turn up the volume, the louder the hum. So, in the 1950s, an engineer at the Gibson guitar company, Seth Lover, set out to create a guitar pickup that didn’t hum. The basic principle had been used in other devices, but nobody had successfully implemented it in a guitar pickup. This was the result: The humbucker, so called because it ‘bucks’ the hum. Well, actually, that’s a descendant of the original pickup: it’s an Epiphone Probucker 3, fitted to an Epiphone Les Paul. It was designed to emulate the sound of Lover’s original pickup. There are slots in the pole pieces so that you can use a screwdriver to manually adjust their height, which I have done. Beneath the metal cover is a second set of non-adjustable pole pieces, wound with a second coil, which is wired in series with the first one (which you can see here), but out of phase with it. Each coil is in contact with the same bar magnet, but each one is in contact with opposite poles of the magnet. The result is a pickup which does not hum, or at least, not nearly as much as the other one does. So much for the how-does-it-work. What’s the difference in terms of sound? Well, single-coil pickups are very simple. It should be clear from the above that it’s not that the pickup gives you ‘the natural sound of the guitar’: it’s all electronics. The ‘natural sound’ of the Telecaster is a faint, weedy twanging noise: it only sounds like an electric guitar when it’s being amplified. But single-coil pickups typically have more higher harmonics, and sound more ‘crisp’ and sparkly. Humbuckers, because of the way they are made, have fewer higher harmonics, and sound less ‘crisp’ and more bassy and ‘rounded’. But their differences become more pronounced when you fiddle with the amplification. If you increase the gain in the amplifier enough, you will overdrive it, which will cause it to clip: the waveform of the signal will literally ‘flatten out’ at its peaks and troughs, creating distortion. There are no specifically technical terms for the particular ways in which the signal from single-coil pickups distort, compared to the signal from humbuckers, but I would liken it to the difference between ‘screaming’ and ‘roaring’. The former tends to have more higher harmonics and overtones, the latter tends to sound ‘fatter’ and the more mid-range frequencies are emphasised. Now to address your question: which type of pickup is generally considered to have a better sound, and why? I can only echo the consensus of anyone who knows even as little as I know: Neither. It’s purely a matter of aesthetic preference for one type of guitar sound over another. Pickups and amplification are by far the most important factors in electric guitar tone, far more than the kind of material the guitar is made of, or whether you use gold-plated jacks, or what you use to pluck the strings with. There are considerations to do with the kind of music you’re playing. Most metal guitarists prefer guitars with humbuckers, because humbuckers tend to give you a ‘heavier’ tone. But not all. Ritchie Blackmore, formerly of Deep Purple, favoured a Fender Stratocaster with single-coils for most of his time with that band. And you can get a pickup which is designed to emulate the unusually fat and humbucker-ish tone of his Stratocaster: That’s it on the left: the Seymour Duncan SSL-4. Look at the size of the pole pieces compared to the regular-syle Strat pickup on the right. The SSL-4 has more than twice the output: 13.4k Ohms, compared to the 6.5k of the other one. The difference is very, very audible. But it still sounds like a single-coil pickup, just a lot louder and more aggressive. Just to confuse things, there’s also a single-coil pickup that looks a bit like a humbucker: the P-90. The P-90 is one of the oldest types of pickup still being made, having been designed as long ago as 1946. (Here, it’s affixed to an Epiphone Casino.) It’s got more mid-range than a typical Fender single-coil, but is more sharp than a humbucker—and it isn’t a humbucker. It can be quite noisy. But those of us who love the sound of P-90s, love them because of their unique squanky tone. To sum up: You should know now why there are single-coils and humbuckers, and you should also know why neither is better than the other. It all depends on what you want.

Question: If you could have only 3 guitar pedals, what would you choose and why?
Answer: Hmm. I used to believe that, the more pedals you had at your disposal, the better. In this, I was a follower of the late and indisputably great Robert Quine, a guitarist who had an immense collection of obscure fuzzboxes. The rock critic Lester Bangs, who was a friend of Quine, recalled that Quine used to ring him up and say You have to hear this new box I’ve got, it makes the most offensive noise… Quine was a wonderful player, who made indispensable contributions to recordings by Richard Hell and the Voidoids, Lou Reed, John Zorn and Matthew Sweet. But his love of obscure fuzzboxes, while it worked for him, is not necessarily practical for lesser mortals. For one thing, it’s not very practical to own loads of different pedals and cart them about, on the off-chance that one of them might come in useful. And also, over time, I’ve just come to prefer using fewer pedals. In any case, over nearly 40 years playing, I’ve amassed a small collection. At the moment, I have (in roughly chronological order of acquisition): If you break these down into categories, there are really only five types of pedal here: The Zoom does all of these things and more, but at the price of sucking out your tone. So, while it’s useful if you don’t care that you sound completely digitalised, and sometimes I’m fine with that, nevertheless, if you do want to keep something of your tone, we can rule it out. I’ve often been tempted to chuck it, but I hold onto it because sometimes its cheap digital allure still appeals to me. The following is not my account of the three pedals that I think all guitarists need, or any nonsense like that. Not at all. Each to their own. If you love flangers and choruses, good for you. This is just about what I feel like I need. And, since I tend to schlep my gear around town by myself, and I don’t drive, I have an interest in minimising how much gear I need to schlep. I don’t use a lot of delay or looping, so the loop station and the delay pedal are hardly close to my heart. So they can go. I do, however, want to extend the range of my guitar way beyond its ‘natural’ range, so the Whammy stays. I don’t really use it for whammy effects, but to play well outside the possible range of the instrument. I love the Whammy. I understand its peculiar timbral ins and outs. Definitely one of my favourite pedals of all time. And since most of my guitars don’t have actual whammies installed, it’s all the more useful. Next, I have a lot of fuzzes and overdrives, and I used to have more. I sold my ProCo Rat, and my old Big Muff PI, and my Boss OD-3, and I gave away my ancient Digitech PDS 1550. If I’m honest, the only one I really adore is the Green Russian Big Muff. Small as it is, it sounds huge, it’s dark, and it fulfils all my fuzz needs. And for reasons which will become apparent, I don’t really need an overdrive. I like the sound of the compressor, as a special effect. But I don’t need it. And since three of my guitars are single-coil-equipped (Strat, Tele, Casino), and it makes them even noisier, that makes it even less essential. So that leaves the tone controls. I don’t play a lot of crazy wah-wah stuff. I like the wah-wah, but having long since got the funky wah-wah moves out of my system, I find myself more and more using it in one random position where it sounds cool. And it’s big, and it’s really heavy. So that just leaves the graphic EQ. Possibly the single most useful pedal I own. I only got it recently. Graphic EQs are absurdly simple. All they do is raise or lower particular frequency bands in your signal. Like all simple and powerful things, they are immensely more useful than they appear to be. This simple pedal not only allows me to completely change the tone of my guitar, it also functions as an overdrive. I’m not sure that even people who know how to properly use a graphic EQ, understand just how ridiculously versatile it is. I’ve seen tons of videos in which guitarists tentatively shift individual faders upwards, and then go Oh yeah, this is handy for shaping your tone. You can do so much more insane shit than that. Not only can you boost individual frequency bands, you can also cut them, making your guitar sound like no guitar that has ever lived. And you can bring up the mids, and not bring up everything else, so it sounds like a wah-wah in a stationary position. And, not content with that, you can also set the faders to neutral and also bring up the overall level, so it works like an overdrive. Also, try putting a fuzzbox in front of this thing and then sculpting the resulting tone with the faders. All of a sudden you have clean tone/clean tone with EQ/fuzztone/fuzztone with EQ. I’m not endorsing any product, but this particular EQ pedal works on frequency bands that are both above and below the natural range of the guitar—which works great for me, with my pitchshifter. So, if I could have only three guitar pedals, it’s easy: the Digitech Whammy, the Green Russian Big Muff, and the Joyo Band Controller. Between them, they do everything that I need pedals to do.
