Question: Do composers need to know sight reading or read music? What is the difference between those skills and how do you train them?
Answer: If composers want their music to be playable by people who can read music, then they should learn how to write it down. Otherwise, if a time should come when their music has to be read by musicians who expect to be reading it, the composer will have to pay someone else to write it down for them. If they don’t want or expect their music to be playable by musicians who prefer to read, or who only read, not play by ear, then they don’t need to write it down. Sight-reading is a type of high-level score reading where you can pretty much play a piece of written music at sight, without having heard it first or practised it. It’s not a skill that a composer needs to have. I’ve said this before but I’ll say it again because it still amazes me that people don’t get this: score reading is a skill, and like all skills, it has levels. Learning to read scores doesn’t mean you go from a.) wondering what all the squiggly lines mean, to b.) can literally play anything put in front of you immediately. It is not a binary state: non-reader/perfect sight-reader. There are many intermediate levels, and the level you’re at should be the level you need to be at: maybe slightly ahead of the level you need to be at. I’m very good at using a score to help me to figure out bits of music that my ear can’t figure out, but if you were to put a work for guitar by Villa-Lobos in front of me, I couldn’t play it—because I’m not interested in that music, and I don’t play classical guitar. (I could, however, tell from what it looked like, roughly what it would sound like.) Finally: how do you learn to read scores? There is no ‘how’. You just learn it. You get a book to tell you what the little squiggly lines mean, then you listen to a ton of music while following the score, until you can tell from what’s coming up on the page what’s going to happen next. And you know you’re getting OK at it when you can hum or sing or play what’s on the page, while it’s happening, and you get it right. It’s really not that hard. It just requires lots of practice.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Can schizophrenics speak foreign languages?
Answer: Yes, and there’s a remarkable example of a person with schizophrenia learning multiple languages, and using them with remarkable flair. This is the strange story of Louis Wolfson. Louis Wolfson was born in New York City in 1931. He was diagnosed with schizophrenia very early in life. He was given electro-convulsive therapy on multiple occasions. His parents divorced when he was four or five, and his father adopted a rather casual lifestyle, devoted mostly to hanging around in bars and cafés, smoking cigars and jawing away to his acquaintances. When he was prevailed upon to pay some sort of child support for his son, he coughed up three dollars a week. (For comparison, the average weekly salary of an office worker in NYC in the late 30s was just under $31.) Little Louis spent a good amount of his childhood in and out of mental hospitals, in between which he would return to the cramped apartment in the Bronx which he shared with his mother. At some point in his childhood or adolescence, Wolfson developed an acute horror of, and revulsion towards, the English language. Since this was his native language, this naturally made things somewhat difficult for him. The solution that he devised was as extraordinary as it was radical. He took to studying foreign languages obsessively: mostly French, German, Hebrew and Russian but also others. Here, he explains why (referring to himself in the third person): However, as it was hardly possible to not hear his native language, he tried to develop methods of converting these words (especially those he found the most tiresome) into foreign words, almost instantaneously, every time they had penetrated his consciousness in spite of his efforts to not perceive them. Note the word convert. He learned multiple foreign languages, not so that he could merely translate any English he heard or encountered into those languages. That wasn’t enough. In order to deal with the hostile and painful presence of English, he not only had to translate English word into these languages, he had to do so in such a way that the result sounded as much as possible like the original English word, so that he could tell himself that he had ‘converted’ the original English by successfully hiding it behind both the meanings and the sounds of foreign words. The first example he gives of this is the word tree, which bothered him enough that he ended up using the Russian дерево, derevo, which was acceptable to him insofar as the ‘r’ after ‘t’ was similar enough to the ‘r’ after the initial ‘d’. The French arbre was too unlike the original word. The above quote from Wolfson is not what he wrote. It’s my translation of what he wrote. This is because, when he wrote a book about his life, and his efforts to deal with the constant presence of his hated ‘langue maternelle’ in New York City, he wrote it in French: Le Schizo et les langues, ‘The Schizophrenic and languages’. The sentence ‘Don’t trip over the wire’ was transformed by Wolfson, using the German Tu’nicht, the first four letters of the French trébucher, the German über, the Hebrew èth hé and the German Zwirn, into Tu’nicht tréb über èth hé Zwirn. Wolfson submitted Le Schizo et les Langues to the distinguished French firm Gallimard around 1961. It wasn’t published until 1970, when it carried a foreword by the French philosopher Gilles Deleuze. I first learned about Wolfson’s book and his life in a fascinating 1974 essay by the late Paul Auster. Auster noted that, in a way, the book can never be translated into English, at least not in full: it would amount to a kind of injury to its author to do so. Auster talked about Wolfson’s vivid writing, and his skill at rendering what New York City could be like in the early 70s. In the book, Wolfson recounts in French conversations he’d had with his parents in English, in which his French seems to accurately render the flavour of their New York Jewish English. At one point, the father, who Louis finds annoying, is trying to discourage his son from learning foreign languages. Louis is sitting next to him on a park bench with his fingers in his ears, trying to block out the sounds of the city. His father he tells him to take his fingers out of his ears, because he’s giving him useful advice. Louis irritably replies Parle donc! Je t’écoute déjà!, or in my reconstruction of what he may actually have said, So talk! I’m listening to you already! Pages and pages of the book are devoted to Louis’ linguistic strategies, his ways of keeping English at bay. I found a Lacanian comment on his work, to the effect that we can’t really tell if his writing is ‘really’ French, or New York English translated into French. Louis’ mother appears in the book as a sort of comic monster, refusing to take seriously her own son’s mental health problems and refusing to speak to him in anything other than English. She buys herself a beautiful but expensive electric organ, and then has a fit about how expensive it is and declines to accept delivery of it. She takes it in the end, and then drives her son up the wall by obsessively blasting out popular songs on it. (It doesn’t take the genius of Freud to realise that the term ‘mother tongue’ is a heavily loaded one, in this case.) At one point, as Auster notes, Wolfson spends several pages struggling to find a way to cope with the lyrics of the song ‘Good Night Ladies’. (He eventually settles on the Russian люди, ‘lyudi’, for ‘people’, and then has to spend some pages justifying his decision to change ‘ladies’ to people’.) He wrote about his eating disorder (he had a horror of ingesting larvae and maggots, so he would only eat tinned food); he articulated his irrational fears of Jewish and black people, in spite of being, as far as I can tell, Jewish himself; he wrote about his uncertain and awkward encounters with prostitutes. Le Schizo et les langues is not a maudlin or morbid book. Neither is it at all a happy one. A few years after the book came out, Wolfson’s mother died. He had a tough life after that, with periods of homelessness. He wrote a second book, mostly about his relationship with his mother at the end of her life, Ma mère, musicienne, est morte de maladie maligne mardi à minuit au milieu du mois de mai mille977 au mouroir Memorial à Manhattan, which was published in 1984. And then, in a last bizarre twist in this story, Louis Wolfson’s luck twisted and turned once again. In 2003, he won the lottery, and became a millionaire. He went to live in Puerto Rico, where he lost most of the money he’d won, by (as far as I can tell) a combination of poor investment decisions, bad advice, and the 2008 financial crisis. At the time of writing, he still lives in Puerto Rico. Le Schizo et les Langues is still in print, and a new edition of his second book came out in 2011. In 2020, he was the subject of a documentary, Sqizo, by Italian filmmaker Duccio Fabbri. Merci pour lire. Sources: Paul Auster, ‘New York Babel’, in The Art of Hunger and other essays, Faber & Faber, https://academicworks.cuny.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2617&context=gc_etds (An MA thesis about Wolfson’s writing, useful and perceptive) Louis Wolfson, Le Schizo et les langues, Editions Gallimard, 1970

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What did George Orwell mean in the book 1984 when the character said, "Men are infinitely malleable"? How might this apply to current political life?
Answer: George Orwell didn’t say it. Well, not exactly. He had O’Brien, the chief villain in Nineteen Eighty-Four, say it in the context of a chapter where O’Brien is overseeing the torture of the book’s protagonist, Winston Smith: We control life, Winston, at all its levels. You are imagining that there is something called human nature which will be outraged by what we do and will turn against us. But we create human nature. Men are infinitely malleable. Or perhaps you have returned to your old idea that the proletarians or the slaves will arise and overthrow us. Put it out of your mind. They are helpless, like the animals. Humanity is the Party. The others are outside--irrelevant. Richard Burton as O’Brien and John Hurt as Winston in the movie of Nineteen Eighty-Four. This is part of Orwell’s theme about how the Party controls reality itself, by having supposedly total control over the perception of reality. O’Brien can torture Winston into seeing five fingers when he holds up four, so he concludes, with sublime complacency, that therefore the Party is eternal and all-powerful and can do anything, and can never be stopped. And millions of the book’s less intelligent readers have been gaslit by O’Brien into accepting his vision—because Orwell never suggests an alternative point of view, although, weirdly, he does imply in the afterword that the Party was somehow defeated, without bothering to specify how. In real life, people being tortured do not, as a result of the torture, routinely accept complete lies as a result of the extinction of their selfhood. Partly because, unlike in the book, most torture is not done simply in order to destroy the victim’s sense of self. Most torture is done to extract information. People being tortured will tell their torturers whatever they think will make the torturer stop torturing them. If that means making shit up, they will do it. Torture is an extraordinarily inefficient and stupid way of getting information. Some people in real life have suffered horrendous torture, more intimately horrible than whatever it is that’s being done to Winston in 1984 (because have you ever noticed that we’re never told what O’Brien’s torture machine actually does?), and not only have they not been broken as people, but they’ve survived, and told the tale in sober detail, and have gone on to lead their lives. Not without trauma and depression and suffering, sure. But they have been more resourceful, and more brave, and have had more integrity, than Orwell, in Nineteen Eighty-Four ever suggested humans were capable of. And before you think I’m saying that torture is therefore not that bad: no. Be under no illusions about that. It’s fucking awful. Many people die under torture, and some people never recover from it. But Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four presents torture as the Party’s 100% efficient way of turning people into zombies. And in that respect, Orwell was full of shit. Because torture is not that effective a tool for controlling people. It’s merely brutal. Let me give you a real life example. And before we go any further, I would just point out that most of my answers are leavened by some sort of good humour. This one is not. I have to seriously warn you, before you read any further, that the following answer contains descriptions of real-life torture. That is a portrait of Dr Sheila Cassidy, made in 1982. Sheila Cassidy is an English doctor, who went to work in Chile in the early 1970s. By her own account, she was a working doctor who was tired of working for the National Health Service in the UK. She knew little about politics, she had intermittent feelings of being strongly drawn to a religious life (she was a practising Catholic), and she thought that Chile, which then was under the socialist government of Salvador Allende, sounded like it’d be more interesting. She had only been working there for a couple of years when the Allende government was overthrown by a right-wing military coup, led by General Augusto Pinochet. Pinochet’s coup had the full approval of (and some support from) the US government. The Nixon administration was gravely concerned that Allende’s government might spread socialism to the region. While the violence was still ongoing, Dr Cassidy gave medical care to an opponent of the Pinochet regime, Nelson Gutierrez, who’d been shot in the leg by Chilean security forces. As a result, she was arrested by the Chilean secret police, and taken to a detention centre, where she was tortured for information. The particular form of torture that Sheila Cassidy was subjected to is called the parrilla. Parrilla is a Spanish word for ‘grill’. The parrilla is simply the metal frame of a bed, with straps attached to it. The blindfolded victim is made to undress completely, and then strapped to the parrilla. The parrilla is then connected, at the will of the torturer, to the mains electricity supply, adminstering strong electric shocks to the victim’s entire body. I would like to point out, at this juncture, that one American user on this site, Jake McMahon, has cited Pinochet as a good example of a benevolent dictator. When Dr Cassidy was brought into the room with the parrilla, and was first ordered to undress, she was understandably reluctant. She told her captors that if it became known that they had tortured a British citizen, it would cause an international incident. They said, Our reputation abroad is already so bad that it does not matter. She then told them that her father was an Air-Vice-Marshal in the Royal Air Force. They were not impressed. In a last-ditch attempt to appeal to their religious sensibilities, she then told them (truthfully) that she was training to be a nun. They inquired, Are you one now? She admitted that she wasn’t one yet. They told her one more time to get undressed and lie down on the parrilla, which she did. They strapped her to it, and duly administered electric shocks to her body. Under torture, she was asked who had helped her to treat enemies of the regime. She decided to lie, and made up names and addresses. After they had tortured her, they dressed her, took her out in a car to the addresses she’d given them, and quickly established that she had given false information. So they took her back to the detention centre and tortured her again, but worse, and this time she felt she had no option but to tell them the truth—except that she told them as little as possible, and in some cases, she couldn’t remember people’s names or addresses. This second time around, because she had lied the first time, her torturers didn’t believe her. The third time around, they did eventually get some information out of her, but one of the questions they kept returning to was Why did you treat Gutierrez? He was sick. I am a doctor, she replied. One of them said in an irritable tone, But if I had a wounded leg, you wouldn’t treat me. Of course I would, she said. There was a long pause, and the man said slowly I believe you would. Eventually, her torture ended, and after signing documents which falsely stated that she hadn’t been tortured and had been well treated, and promising not to tell anyone what had happened to her, she was released from custody and returned to the UK. Before she left, one of her fellow prisoners told her that ‘since she had known me her opinion of Catholics had fallen even lower than it had been before.’ The prisoner explained that this was because of Cassidy’s decision to not speak about her experiences. Dr Cassidy greatly respected the woman who told her this, so this hit her hard. She decided that she would renege on her promises, because she owed it to all the inmates of her former prison camp to speak out on their behalf. On returning to the UK, she not only gave detailed testimony about what had happened to her and others, but wrote a book about it, Audacity to Believe, which I have, and where this account is taken from. Dr Cassidy did not become a Winston Smith: a broken shell of a human being, whose sense of herself was destroyed. She did become a nun, but she left holy orders soon after, having realised that she wasn’t cut out for it. She went back to medical practice, and became a respected authority on hospice care. She is now 87, and still lives in Plymouth, where she practised as a doctor for many years. She has written more books about her faith, including her 2010 book Confessions of a Lapsed Catholic, in which she said that she no longer took communion, and was strongly opposed to both the church’s anti-celibacy stance and its refusal to allow woman to become priests. I say all this not to diminish the power of torture to traumatise people. Sheila Cassidy would be the first person to admit that she still suffers from the after-effects of what was done to her in Chile. I say it to show up Orwell’s failure. O’Brien thinks that the Party’s torture cells can remake people into whatever the Party wants them to be. Hollow mouthpieces, who are mere robots for the Party. O’Brien thinks he is all-fucking-powerful. And Orwell nowhere gave the impression that he thought that O’Brien might be wrong. Orwell seems to have agreed with O’Brien that ‘men are infinitely malleable.’ In Nineteen Eighty-Four, he hands the victory to O’Brien. But then, inexplicably, he implies, in the afterword, that O’Brien and Ingsoc lost after all. But he never got around to telling us how they lost. It’s as if Orwell watched the newsreels of all those communists giving public ‘confessions’ in the Soviet purges of the 1930s, and it never occurred to him that they might have been lying; saying whatever they had to say in order to end their ordeals. He seems to have really believed that they had become faithful party drones—or at least, he wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four as if they had. George Orwell never experienced torture. Instead, he got spooked by accounts of it, and wrote a horror story about how torture destroys people, without any alternative outcome being even imaginable. Sheila Cassidy, unlike George Orwell, lived through torture, and told the truth about it, and has gone on to lead a distinguished life as a respected doctor. And she gave full credit, in her book, to others who had gone before her, and who inspired her: Gladys Díaz, for example. (Don’t follow up that link if you don’t want to read more descriptions of torture.) History shows that people are not ‘infinitely malleable’. But somewhere along the line, Orwell lost what faith in people he had ever had. Once, in Spain in the 1930s, he had known how strong people could be. But somewhere along the line, he forgot that. And he tried to warn people by writing a book about it. Instead of giving them a sober and intelligent warning, he merely frightened the bejesus out of them. He painted a picture of absolute power, with no possibility of resistance. And, while he was doing so, he attributed the abuse of this power to the side that he claimed to be on. I’ve been reading Orwell since I was ten years old. I would bet that I’ve read more of his work than most people who’ve read this answer. He is a bad judge of people, and an unreliable guide in dark times. Thanks for reading. Source: Sheila Cassidy, Audacity to Believe, Darton, Longman & Todd, 2011 George Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four, sourced at https://gutenberg.net.au/ebooks01/0100021.txt

Question: What movie, songs or books do you enjoy that were not produced in your country?
Answer: Well, most of them, because this is my country: It’s off the north-west corner of Europe: Most movies, songs and books were not produced in my country. That said, my country has produced some damn fine books, from the ancient epic Táin Bó Cúailnge and some very good lyric poetry in the head-bustingly difficult language of Old Irish, down to the fiction and poetry of the modern day, in both English and Irish. My favourite writer is an Irish writer, James Joyce. We also have a glorious and extremely enviable body of traditional music, and an IMO rather less enviable body of popular music, which I’m less keen on. There are a couple of exceptions. But I’m not that into our popular music. And we have a few pretty good movies. Not that many. (Fwiw, I think the greatest Irish movie is Neil Jordan’s 1997 The Butcher Boy.) But basically, if we want to watch most good movies, or listen to most really good songs, or read most really good books, we have to read stuff made elsewhere. We are obliged, by virtue of being natives of a small country on the edge of a major continent, to become cosmopolitan. If, that is, we don’t want to be narrow-minded and parochial. And I don’t.

Question: How do I learn to write comedy?
Answer: To get started, you learn the ways that other people write comedy, and you adopt the methods that suit you. And you do this by abstracting from their work the basic techniques that they use, and analysing them to see how they work, and then making them work for you. However, techniques will only take you so far. To write great comedy, it’s not enough to follow a method. You need to put something of yourself into it, and push it to somewhere that nobody else would have pushed it. For an example, let us look at a classic comedy sketch that’s not so old that we can’t learn from it: Key and Peele’s ‘Soul Food’, from about 12 years ago. The following analysis is serious, but I know it’s also somewhat ridiculous. ‘Soul Food’ makes use of a technique that you could call the escalating variation. It only really has one basic joke, which we’ll get to in a moment. But that basic joke is the seed for the other jokes in the sketch, as Key and Peele use their own playful imaginations to top each sub-joke as it comes up. The sketch begins with Key and Peele playing two white-collar black guys in a soul food restaurant, ‘Mama Sugarback’s’. We can see from how they dress and how they talk that these guys are middle-class: Peele’s opening line is So glad that we could bring this project to this neighborhood. Key agrees, It’s so rich in history. This suggests that they themselves are not from around here, but are basically tourists in a place to which they feel a connection, even if it’s slightly removed from them. Let’s see what happens next. Peele: I grew up in a neighborhood like this. Key: Oh, yeah, I grew up in a neighborhood exactly like this. So already, there’s a slight sense of power-play going on: each of them is keen to show the other how ‘authentic’ he is, how in tune he is with a restaurant like the one they’re both sitting in. There is a slighly uncomfortable pause, which I think is meant to convey that these two are work partners, but maybe not close friends—after all, if they were, they would probably both know where the other had grown up. The owner/maitresse d’ (who, for reasons of space, I will call M.D.) arrives. M.D.: All right, welcome to Mama Sugarback’s—y’all ready to order? Peele: [beaming, drops into more downhome voice] Yeaaahh. Can I have a chicken-fried steak with gravy and a cola. So, immediately, Peele has code-switched slightly—changing his way of talking from his earlier standard English to something a bit more… relaxed. Key: I will have the baked beef short ribs with collard greens, and throw down some o’ that cornbread. Key has immediately escalated the situation, not only by ordering something slightly less bland than chicken-fried steak and a cola, but talking in an even more vernacular way. At this point, Peele gives him a sidelong look: There’s an awareness that a challenge is being made. And Peele is going to answer it: M.D.: All right then. Peele: You know what? Hold up a second. I’m also gonna have some o’ them collard greens and cornbread as well, but hook a brother up with some o’ them [deepening his voice and grinning] hot links. M.D.: Okay. Peele: Alriiight. Not content to merely change his order, Peele adds to it, giving this encounter the atmosphere of a potlatch, in which whoever orders the most food/spends the most money is the winner. But that’s not quite where this sketch is going. Key: [chuckles] You know what? Why am I trying to front. Scratch all o’ that. Gimme some okra, and some fried red snapper, and, girl, you know I want some chitlins. [smirks at Peele] M.D.: All right then. [she starts to go] Peele: Y’all got ham hocks? M.D.: Of course. Peele: [icily staring at Key] Well, that’s what I want. I want a plate o’ ham hocks, deep-fried, blackened, and served on a bed of mustard greens. Now, I may be a novice when it comes to cooking and serving soul food, but while the ham hock is, as George Ramos points out, a soul food staple, nevertheless the deep-fried ham hock is a thing from Filipino cuisine, and this order shows that Peele is now making up stuff because he thinks it’s more authentic-sounding than what he previously ordered. (Also, he wants a plate of ham hocks?) To me, blackened ham-hock does not sound good. But that’s not the point of what these guys are doing. Key: Pig feet! I want some pig feet, and four pounds of grits! See how we’re constantly escalating to less and less pleasant-sounding food? I actually like pig feet, and grits, but four pounds of grits is ridiculous. Key: Oh, oh, and you know what else? Give me a little Dixie cup full of lard! Again, this is so skilfully written that it’s not yet completely absurd (I’ve been in a Polish restaurant in Krakow which did have bowls of lard on the table for you to smear on your bread), but the sadistic, or possibly masochistic, glee with which Key orders this is fantastic. But Peele is about to take us over the top. Peele: [slaps the table] I just remembered what I wanted. A bowl of mosquitoes. None o’ them tiny ones, either, give me them biiig motherf***ers you find down at the swamp. Key: [turning to her, making a prayerful gesture] Could you please hook a brother up with a rusty bucket full of fish heads, wrapped in razor wire. At this point, we reverse cut to M.D., whose expression is… unfathomable. But just at this moment, Peele initiates what looks like the final conflict: Peele: Donkey teeth! M.D.: Donkey teeth? Peele: [glaring at Key] Straight. Out. A donkey’s mouth. You know what, f*** it. Any animal tooth will do. I want you to stick it in some honey glaze, fry it with fatback and serve it in an old tin coffee can. Key: Forget everything I said up to this point right now. Bring me some dandelion greens, a cow face, and a dog hip. Wrap that whole mess in an old Ebony magazine and serve it to me in a shoe box. Peele: Okay, I want a platter o’ stork ankles, an old cellar door, a possum spine—and a human foot. Key: [silent, shaken] M.D.: [leans down] You want a human foot. Peele: Mm-hm. M.D.: [pause] I got just one question for y’all. [They look at her, and at each other, and seem embarrassed at how out-of control the situation has got. They stop staring at each other.] And at this point, we are certain that she is about to call them all out on their nonsense, and maybe throw them out of her restaurant. Possible alternative ending: they shamefacedly ask for their original orders. However. This is the point where the sketch stops using the technique, and goes into a new place, which lifts it onto a new level. This is the kind of thing that you can’t learn how to do. Behold: M.D.: [cheerily] … You want gravy on that cellar door? Peele: Oh, definitely. Key: Oh yeah, you got to put gravy on there, yeah. [She notes the order on her pad] Peele: What’s a cellar door without gravy. Key: It’s not food. [Laughs] And we fade to black. When we return, Key is munching his cow face wrapped in a copy of Ebony, and Peele is biting down on his cellar door with a human foot on it. Peele: … Mmm. Key: [nods thoughtfully] It’s really good. [gags. So does Peele.] So, the basic premise here is, obviously, about the two male characters’ competing need to seem more authentic than the other, which pushes them to order food that’s ever more inedible, but also more redolent of poverty and suffering. On that level, it works as a sort of extended joke about how things like pigs’ feet are an acquired taste. What I think makes it both funny and a great sketch is the tension between not just the increasing awfulness of the history implied by the things that they feel compelled to order, and the fact that anyone would actually order a ‘dog hip’ or a ‘stork ankle’ in a restaurant, and not only does the restaurant actually serve those things, but the customers attempt to eat them. Anyone else writing this sketch would I think have ended it with M.D. telling the two of them to get out and stop wasting her time, but only Key and Peele would have had her actually take their ridiculous order and serve it. Key and Peele liked this technique of escalating variation, and they used it elsewhere in the sketch ‘Loco Gangsters’, where the hapless Carlito (Peele), intimidated by the ‘loco’ reputation of new gang member Eduardo, attempts to demonstrate to his fellow gangsters that he’s the more ‘loco’ one because, for example, every time he goes to the frozen yoghurt place he gets a new loyalty card, instead of filling up his existing one, causing his friend (played by Key) to respond Carlito, that's just being cavalier with your finances instead of collecting your free dessert. That's not loco, that's just like...financially irresponsible. Carlito finds more and more bizarre and harmful ways to demonstrate his loco-ness, culminating in him spinning his loaded gun around his finger, and then dropping it, causing Eduardo to be shot in the head. Carlito asks Now I’m the most loco in the gang? And is told that he is, if only by process of elimination. Which is then topped by Eduardo springing to his feet and revealing that he caught the bullet in his teeth. Another use of it is the sketch ‘Is This Country Song Racist?’, in which Peele visits his new neighbour Key, who shows him his basement and his guitar collection, and then proceeds to sing some of his own country songs: Well, I’m just a good old American boy With a heart that’s red, white and true I’m dreamin’ of the girl with the red hair and freckles And her eyes like the skies of blue. ‘Country music,’ Peele says, smiling. Key explains that he grew up in Texas, and continues: Keep her safe from the homies in the wrong side of town Where they’re smokin’ the reefer and actin’ like clowns Keep that pretty white dress from getting dirty and brown Cause that’s the American way. Peele mildly observes that the song is ‘pretty racist’, but Key replies that that’s just what country music is like, and adds there are all kinds of homies, White homies, Asian homies… Peele demurs, but Key sings another song with the immortal couplet: The only dark I like is when I turn off the lights The only hood I love is pointy and white … And it just gets worse from there. Until it doesn’t. There are lots of techniques for writing comedy. The escalating variation is as old as literature itself, but in comedy alone it was also used in the legendary ‘Four Yorkshiremen’ sketch that lovers of vintage British comedy may be aware of (Monty Python did it at the Hollywood Bowl). Key and Peele don’t use this technique all the time. But when they did use it, they used it to push things beyond where we thought they would go. Really good comedy writers go beyond techniques, and use comedy to illuminate something about ourselves. So, learn the techniques, but don’t use them as a safety net. Play with them.

Question: What are good ways to make broccoli tasty while keeping its vitamins?
Answer: Allow me to present my recipe for pasta with broccoli and pancetta. This came about because I was very aware that I wasn’t eating enough vegetables, and I wanted a dish where broccoli would be the main ingredient but yet would not be the dominant one, with its heavy, worthy green-ness. Instead it would be the ripe, fresh, healthy backdrop to something more fun. This recipe lives or dies by the quality of the pancetta. It’s no good getting that super-thin-sliced stuff. That lacks the requisite texture and, tbh, I’m not sure what it’s good for. The teeny-weeny diced stuff is also cut up too small, in my opinion. In Edinburgh we have a really good but rather expensive Italian deli, Valvona & Crolla, where the excellent pancetta affumicatta comes in what they consider thin but I call thick slices, about 4mm thick, and is frankly the only thing they sell that I can regularly afford. So: you need pancetta, broccoli, garlic, crushed dried chilli flakes, pasta of your choice (I like chifferi for this dish because the little tubes hold the sauce), a fresh lemon and a chunk of parmesan. Cut the pancetta into pieces. I get about 5–6 pieces from one slice. Let them crisp up in a hot sauté pan, yielding that delicious pancetta fat. A little olive oil wouldn’t hurt. When they’re crispy-chewy, remove and set aside. (Tip for extra flavour: let them rest in the bowl you’re going to serve this in, so any melty fat they exude as they cool will be mopped up by your food. Don’t tell anyone I told you to do that.) Leave the fat in the sauté pan. That’s gold. Boil water for pasta. Cook pasta. When it’s almost al dente, drain but reserve pasta water. Fry sliced garlic in the pancetta fat/oil for a few seconds, then add chilli flakes and cut-up raw broccoli. Let the broccoli change colour in places to dark green, then add a glug of pasta water and cover the pan until broccoli is barely cooked, mostly in steam. I like the broccoli to have plenty of bite, not to be mushy. It keeps its vitamins and also contrasts better with the pancetta that way. Toss pasta in pan with broccoli and let it finish cooking, put the pancetta back in to warm up, and grate parmesan over. Add more pasta water if needed to tie it together. Toss it all together so parmesan melts a bit into sauce, then serve in a bowl with freshly ground black pepper, generous squeezes of lemon and more grated parmesan if desired. Obviously, with the pancetta and parmesan there are less high-sodium dishes in the world, but the clash between the virtuous broccoli and the rakish pancetta is what this is all about. When very hungry, I have bulked this up by adding sliced onion at the sauté stage and cooked cannellini beans at the broccoli-cooking stage, and if you want to go low-carb you could omit the pasta. In which case it also works as a sumptuous side dish. But I prefer it as a main meal.

Question: I'm trying to understand the difference between Ambient and New Age music. Can you make some examples that highlight the difference?
Answer: Actually, no, because there are no hard-and-fast differences, other than how they’re marketed. Don’t get hung up on the labels we slap on music. The music is what matters. The earliest examples of ‘ambient music’ in the modern era had a certain art-rock cachet, because they were often made by art-rock hero Brian Eno, but, honestly, what’s the meaningful difference, in purely musical terms, between something like Fripp and Eno’s Evening Star (respectable ambient music) and Patrick O’Hearn’s 1985 Ancient Dreams (New Age music)? Not a hell of a lot, in my view, except that the latter has rather more musical events per minute. Eno’s later Apollo: Atmospheres and Soundtracks is rather more uneasy listening, but I note that he’s not exactly continued to mine that vein. Eno’s classic 1975 album Another Green World is one of his most praised albums, but most of it sounds pretty New Age-y to me. And I really like that album. Understand that I’m not coming from a place where I despise ambient or new age music. Neither am I a huge fan of either, but I’m not here to praise or dispraise. Just to say that both of them are forms of music which tend to adopt pleasingly predictable harmonic progressions and occasionally non-Western rhythms and timbres, with the aim of providing pleasantly soothing music that works both as background music, and as music to listen to which doesn’t make too demanding claims on your attention. If I were being cynical, I would say that ‘ambient music’ is what a certain kind of rather snobbish music fan calls this music when they want to listen to it, and ‘New Age music’ is what those same people call almost identical music when they think it shouldn’t be listened to.

Question: Has any band become a one-hit wonder with a song that was completely different from their usual style?
Answer: Yes. The Canadian pop-punk group Len (aka LEN) made most of their music as, well, pop-punk: But by far their biggest and indeed only real hit was this trashy, sun-kissed, one-off, dance-pop slab of incomprehensible nonsense: I’ve always enjoyed the fact that the band spent most of the video’s $100k budget on booze, so much of it that they managed to break the elevator in the Daytona Beach hotel they were staying in, when trying to bring all that booze up to their rooms. Len are still sort-of around: their last single, from 2011, was a love song to their home city of Toronto, a place I’m rather fond of too (although J’t’suis toujours fidèle, Montréal, tabarnak.)

Question: Do you have any critique/critiques of Marxism?
Answer: Sure. Marx predicted that capitalism would not be able to reform itself and appease the disgruntled proletariat. It turned out that capitalism could do that, by (albeit very reluctantly) introducing health and safety regulations, increasing the basic rates of wages and creating social welfare safety nets. That said, once these were established, they remained in place for many years but capitalism is now relentlessly chipping away at them, and some right-wing capitalists would like them to be abolished, reintroducing child labour, lowering wages and resisting the merest hint of social welfare. Another thing Marx didn’t predict was that capitalism would further resist regulation by outsourcing low-wage jobs to poorer developing countries, where the population is more desperate for work and has less money and leisure time to organise itself into resistance. The proletariat is no longer in the slums of the cities of developed countries, but in slums on different continents. Edit: Luís D Oliveira points out that Lenin did foresee this, in his 1917 book Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism. Relevant quotes can be provided if requested. End of edit. Edit 2: Judson Parker points out that even Marx predicted outsourcing, 50 years before Lenin did! So truly did Marx have de Krystal Bol. End of edit. Meanwhile, the relatively middle-class people in the developed world get distracted from the problems and crimes of capitalism by shiny baubles such as racism, and are persuaded to demonise immigrants, rather than change the unfair system that is the reason why people want to immigrate to their countries in the first place. In some countries, child labour never went away—but it’s okay, because they’re not our children, you see. Marx was alert to racism, and quickly perceived the racist rhetoric of the Confederacy for what it was. He didn’t foresee the extent to which capitalism could utilise historical racism by weaponising it against the class struggle. I recently got a little selection of Marx’s writings on economics, published by Pelican in the 1960s. It’s a useful book with a rather patronising introduction, explaining that Marx obviously got a lot of things wrong, but it’s still important to read him because so many people take him seriously. Then it says this: ‘The capitalist nations of the West have not seen a polarization of the population into a small group of extraordinarily wealthy capitalists facing an enormous mass of enslaved helots.’ Maybe not in 1961, buddy. Give them sixty years. ‘Shared among all major elements of the population’. That wasn’t even true in 1961. (Also: ‘major’?) These passages have not aged well, especially in the last 25 years. Marx remains relevant, but the author of this introduction was out of date even as he was writing.

Question: What is TDS? Who coined it?
Answer: Trump Derangement Syndrome was actually formed as an adaptation of BDS, Bush Derangement Syndrome, which was coined in 2003 by the Conservative pundit Charles Krauthammer, to describe what he considered to be the hysterical overreaction to the behaviour of then-president George W. Bush. It was intended to be a way of suggesting that people who hated Bush were being illogical, and were emotion- rather than reason-driven. Trump never creates new things, he just makes existing things worse, so Trump Derangement Syndrome was adopted by his followers (possibly starting with a columnist for American Spectator) to suggest the same thing about people who even slightly dislike Trump. Bad as Bush was, Trump is a new low in incompetence, cruelty and lack of respect for law and order, so the term has been co-opted by people who dislike Trump to characterise the belief among Trump’s followers that he is fit for public office.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What is the meaning of arts and its importance?
Answer: Of all the ways that humans have devised to model the world, and our relationship to it, art is the most playful, even when it’s at its most formally rigorous. Perhaps that’s because, of all our models of the world, art is the least arrogant. Unlike both religion and science, it does not demand, for reasons of its own, that we accept it. It offers itself up as a gift. We can take it or leave it. That’s why it’s important. That’s why it’s valuable.

Question: Why is Hollywood not making a new WW2 movie on the great German battleship Bismarck with modern technologies?
Answer: While I agree with Rodra Hascaryo's answer (namely, that you couldn’t do it without CGI, and so it would probably look fake), I think that there’s more to it than that. Bismarck. For a mighty killing machine, damn, she was elegant. I think that the deeper problem with a movie about the Bismarck is that it’s not easy to tell exactly what story within the pursuit of the Bismarck is the one that’s worth telling. Because, like it or not, movies tend to live and die according to whether or not their stories tell a tale that the audience wants to be told. What is the story of the Bismarck? It seems to me that there are quite a few of them. The problem with telling a story about the Bismarck itself is that its operational career was extremely brief. And, to be blunt, it’s not a very interesting story. If you make the story about the ship itself and its crew, so that they are the focus, then it’s a story about its sole mission. A mission in which it goes into the Atlantic to sink Allied shipping; is quickly detected; gets into a battle with Royal Navy ships, in which it rather flukily sinks a British battleship, Hood, in a long-range naval battle; then it gets attacked by aircraft, is crippled, heavily damaged, and eventually scuttles itself. Most of its crew goes down with it. And they’re not even the good guys. I mean… big deal. Its executive officer ordered it to be sunk, which sinking happened while it was still taking damage that it didn’t even need to take, because it was going down anyway. Is that a tragedy about misplaced bravery in a terrible cause? If so, not a very clear-cut one. A big ship, with a fearsome reputation, has a career in which it notably fails to live up to its promise—not because of failure on the part of the ship or the crew, but because it was no longer an age for battleships, and so the whole idea of a ship like the Bismarck being an all-powerful threat to shipping was no longer, as it turned out, very credible. (Its sister ship, Tirpitz, never even got to go into a battle at all, before being ingloriously sunk.) That’s not a story which can be told with sole reference to the ship itself. It needs a bigger canvas and a wider perspective, because only on that scale does it make sense. A potentially more interesting story is to tell it from the point of view of its pursuers, which was basically the approach taken in the 1960 movie Sink the Bismarck! But still, the pursuers don’t get to take full credit for the sinking of the ship. If there is any one person, or small group of people, who ought to be at least a major focus in this angle on the story, it’s the crew of the Fairey Swordfish that launched the torpedo that permanently jammed the Bismarck’s left rudder, rendering it unmanoeuvrable, and therefore fatally vulnerable—except that they can hardly have been witnesses of the whole action, so their point of view is necessarily limited. Another issue, here, is that no US vessels were involved in the pursuit of the Bismarck, so there’s no American angle that could guarantee at least some US audience. It seems to me that no one movie can be made that encompasses the potential breadth of the story of the sinking of the Bismarck. The ship’s crew performed with skill and bravery. But Bismarck and its victim Hood were a type of ship that didn’t have a role anymore, in the era of carriers and torpedo bombers. You could do some spectacular explosions with CGI, sure—but the most spectacular explosion in the whole saga is the catastrophic destruction of Hood, which is fairly early in the tale. Bismarck itself gets battered into committing an undignified seppuku. It doesn’t get to go down in a blaze of glory. Maybe we’re talking about a miniseries. But I doubt that the economies of TV production would run to making that kind of show, with this huge amount of effects shots, for a story which is ultimately about a ship being sunk. The more we focus on the ship itself and its crew, the more downer a story it is; the more we focus on the effort to sink it, the less glamorous is the appeal of the great, sleek battleship, because it becomes merely the antagonist. It would take a better writer than myself to think of a way to tell the story of the sinking of the Bismarck in TV or film form, and make it really worthwhile as drama. In the meantime, I think history and non-fiction are the way to go. The late Ludovic Kennedy’s 1974 book Pursuit: The Chase and Sinking of the Bismarck is a gripping read (Kennedy was a Scottish journalist and broadcaster who, as a Naval officer in WW2, took part in the Battle of the Denmark Strait and witnessed the final battle), and while in its vividness and snappy pace, it cries out to be dramatised, I think the expenses would not ultimately be worth it. Younger audiences in particular aren’t exactly begging for WW2 stories to be told.

Question: Who are your favorite lesser known Jazz musicians?
Answer: This is a chance to make good on a sort-of promise I made. I could have written about a variety of people, but for a combination of reasons, I’ll keep it to this one. To serious jazz fans, he’s a revered and even beloved figure: to casual listeners, probably not much more than a songwriting credit. Ladies, gentlemen and non-binary friends, Mr Billy Strayhorn. If you vaguely like jazz, but have never heard of Billy Strayhorn, I hope you’ve at least heard of his great friend, patron and employer, Duke Ellington: Duke Ellington: suave? Moi? In order to grasp the stature of Billy Strayhorn, we first have to grasp the stature of Duke Ellington. Ellington came to fame in the late 1920s as one of the foremost bandleaders in jazz—which is a little like saying that Ludwig van Beethoven came to fame in the 1800s as one of the foremost writers of music. Ellington was not just one of many good bandleaders in jazz. He was the greatest of them all. Edward Kennedy Ellington was born in 1898, and grew up in Washington DC. His father worked as a butler—he occasionally helped cater events at the White House—and later worked at the US Navy Yard, making blueprints. Both of his parents had parents who were former slaves. Most jazz musicians with nicknames got them as adults, but Ellington got his as a child: the other kids called him ‘Duke’ because he carried himself like a natural aristocrat. Ellington formed his first band in 1917. Between then and 1939, his band became probably the most admired outfit in jazz, largely as a result of Ellington’s compositions and arrangements. His compositions were incomparably more innovative and sophisticated than those of his peers, many of whom weren’t particularly distinguished as composers. Ellington’s daring and creativity as a jazz composer in the 20s and 30s were simply unrivalled. But, much as I would like to spend 500 words raving about Duke’s music, he’s only tangentially the subject of this answer. Most bandleaders in the big band era (which is what we’re talking about) hired and fired bandmembers at will. Ellington preferred not to. He liked to keep his bandmembers for years, because he wrote music specifically for those guys to play, and he couldn’t do that if they kept coming and going. He wanted his band to be his instrument: something that could instantly respond without him having to explain things endlessly. In return, he kept them on-side by giving them special features, and bespoke compositions, and occasionally doing them big favours, such as buying them a house. The fact that he managed to do this for several decades, speaks to his genius as a bandleader. Alto sax player Johnny Hodges joined the band in 1928, left in 1951, came back in 1955, and stayed until his death in 1970. Trumpeter Cootie Williams joined in 1929, left in 1940, came back in 1962 and stayed until Ellington’s death in 1974. Clarinetist Jimmy Hamilton joined in 1943 and stayed until 1968. Baritone sax player Harry Carney joined in 1927, and never left. So we’ll fast forward through Ellington’s career as a bandleader until we get to the late 1930s. By 1939, the Ellington band was reaching the height of its power and fame. But there often comes a point in the second act of a musician’s career when they need a bit of a jolt: something to get them excited all over again, some new injection of information or enthusiasm. The Ellington band had been to Europe, and had played there to rapturous audiences. The English composer and critic Constant Lambert (father of future Who manager Kit Lambert) compared him favourably to Ravel and Stravinsky. But Ellington’s beloved mother had died in 1935, and his father in 1937, and his finances were tight. Then, after a gig in Pittsburgh in 1938, Ellington met Billy Strayhorn. Strayhorn was born in 1915. At the time he met Ellington, Ellington was 39 and he was 23. Strayhorn was a precocious kid. He studied classical music for a while at the Pittsburgh Music Institute, and wrote an entire musical in his teens. Among his earliest songs is ‘Lush Life’, an extraordinarily sophisticated song about ennui and decadence from someone who wasn’t even old enough to get served alcohol when he wrote it. But that was Strayhorn’s style. A melancholy haunts all but his most cheerful tunes. His classical training is in all his music, in its elegant construction and rather European attitude to harmony, and maybe in a certain world-weariness. Strayhorn would have liked to be a classical composer, but as a young black man, that route was pretty much barred to him, so he took up jazz. In his first meeting with Ellington, he said that he’d show Duke how Duke had played one of his tunes. He sat down at the piano and proceeded to play, note for note, what Duke had played. Now, he said, this is how I would have played it. And he played it slightly differently, lengthening a phrase here, varying the rhythm there. Ellington, who had been lying back staring at the ceiling (he’d been having his hair conked), sat up and looked interested. He let Strayhorn play and sing a couple of his own songs. He was impressed with this short, bespectacled, obviously gifted, exceedingly polite young man. He told Strayhorn he’d send for him when the band returned to its home base of New York City. He gave Strayhorn detailed instructions about what subway to take to get his apartment. The instructions began with the phrase, ‘Take the A train’. Strayhorn waited for Ellington to send for him, but Ellington never did. Finally, the band was playing in Newark in January 1939, and Strayhorn showed up backstage. Ellington installed Strayhon in his apartment, and informed his son Mercer and sister Ruth, who also lived there, that Strayhorn was going to live with them and be the band’s new lyricist. Socially adept as he was, Strayhorn immediately hit it off with Ruth Ellington, who was about his own age, and who fondly remembered long intellectual conversations with him at the breakfast table. Mercer Ellington was a little more wary. In 1940, ASCAP, the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers, raised its licensing fees for broadcasting. Ellington was a member of ASCAP, and now he couldn’t play his tunes live on the radio because the radio stations wouldn’t pay the licensing fees. Ellington turned to Strayhorn and Mercer, both of whom were members of ASCAP’s rival BMI, and told them that if they were going to be able to play on the radio, the band would need an entirely new book of tunes, and because neither Mercer nor Strayhorn were with ASCAP, they would have to write them. Strayhorn and Mercer got to work in a frenzy of writing, fuelled by cartons of cigarettes and a gallon of blackberry wine. At one point, Mercer retrieved a discarded Strayhorn tune from a wastebasket and said What’s this? Oh, Strayhorn said, that’s an old thing I was working on, but it’s too much like Fletcher Henderson. That tune was ‘Take the “A” Train’, which became Ellington’s signature tune for the rest of the band’s career. And here’s the original recording: I don’t know about you, dear reader, but for me, ‘Take the “A” Train’ is the quintessential swing track: the perfect combination of sass, danceable rhythms, catchy tunes and effortless sophistication. It’s intricate yet simple: that C#, the third-last note in the second phrase, is genius. Ellington used to hang on that note in later performances, because nearly everyone used to get it wrong, singing or playing D natural instead of C#. Ellington recorded constantly, building up an immense back catalogue of tracks which he called ‘the vault’ to assure himself that he could always be issuing recordings. In 1952, he revisited ‘Take the “A” Train for one of his earliest vinyl albums, Ellington Uptown, and expanded it to a mini-suite with a cunningly constructed build-up before the iconic piano intro, and a memorable vocal from singer Helen Roché, featuring some great scat singing. I’m not sure that I don’t prefer this to the original. When Strayhorn recorded the tune himself, he played it as a reflective, medium-tempo ballad. Strayhorn became Ellington’s co-composer, musical secretary, arranger, and general compositional sidekick. Besides writing several of the band’s most famous tunes himself, such as the subtle and impressionistic ‘Chelsea Bridge’ and the lilting ‘Rain Check’, Strayhorn co-wrote many tunes for which Ellington took sole credit—for example, ‘Satin Doll’. Strayhorn’s nickname for Ellington was ‘the Monster’, and while he eventually grew impatient with the extent to which his own talents were always in Ellington’s shadow, he clearly valued Ellington’s friendship and stayed loyal to him. He travelled with the band, who affectionately nicknamed him ‘Swee’Pea’ after Popeye’s adopted baby son, because of Strayhorn’s shortness. Strayhorn was as out a gay man as it was possible to be in those days—namely, to his friends and acquaintances (and Ellington and the band), but not to anyone else. He had a passionate friendship with singer Lena Horne, who adored him and wanted to marry him. Billy Strayhorn and Lena Horne. He met his longterm partner Aaron Bridgers through Mercer Ellington, who was friends with both of them. He was a strong supporter of civil rights, and was a friend of Martin Luther King Jr. Strayhorn stayed with the Ellington organisation through its roaring success in the 1940s. He quit briefly in the early 50s, but came back. At Ellington’s spectacular second-wind gig at the 1956 Newport Jazz Festival, Strayhorn was there, doggedly composing two-thirds of the Festival Suite Ellington had promised to write but hadn’t got around to. (It was ultimately upstaged by Paul Gonsalves’ epic performance in the band’s show-stopping rendition of ‘Diminuendo in Blue/Crescendo in Blue’, but that’s another story.) He got co-composer credit on Ellington’s great Shakespeare album Such Sweet Thunder, the crackling soundtrack to Preminger’s Anatomy of a Murder and the surprisingly effective version of the Nutcracker Suite. He made a few albums as leader: The Peaceful Side from 1961 is definitely worth a listen. In 1964, Strayhorn was diagnosed with oesophageal cancer. He had to have his oesophagus removed, and a gastrostomy implanted, so that he could feed himself by pouring his (liquefied) meals directly into his stomach. Over the years he had become quite a drinker, so he decided that this also included his martinis. In 1967, Strayhorn died. Ellington’s friend Arthur Logan phoned him to commiserate, and asked Ellington if he was going to be all right. Fuck, no, I’m not going to be all right, Ellington replied. Nothing is all right now. Strayhorn was composing to the last. His final tune, ‘Blood Count’, with a title inspired by his medical troubles, was a dark lament, with winding, torturous (and tortuous) lines. Ellington’s and Strayhorn’s relationship was possibly the most important friendship in Ellington’s life. They were a strange pair—the ebullient, robustly heterosexual, ever-hungry, charmingly vain Duke, and the quiet, gay, fastidious, studious Strayhorn—but in account after account of Ellington’s offstage behaviour, Strayhorn is always in the background, working on music, arranging Ellington’s tunes or suggesting how to proceed when Ellington got stuck. Richard O. Boyer’s classic 1943 New Yorker profile ‘The Hot Bach’ has some amusing moments where a sleepy Strayhorn is summoned from his bed on the band’s train, just because Ellington at midnight has suddenly had an idea of how to revise a work in progress, and he wants Strayhorn’s opinion. In his generally fulsome 1973 memoir Music is my Mistress, Ellington paid generous compliments to Strayhorn’s memory: Billy Strayhorn was always the most unselfish, the most patient, and the most imperturbable, no matter how dark the day. I am indebted to him for much of my courage since 1939. He was my listener, my most dependable appraiser, and as a critic he would be the most clinical, but his background—both classical and modern—was an accessory to his own good taste and understanding, so what came back to me was in perfect balance. In music, as you develop a theme or musical idea, there are many points at which direction must be decided, and any time I was in the throes of debate with myself, harmonically or melodically, I would turn to Billy Strayhorn. We would talk, and then the whole world would come into focus. The steady hand of his good judgement pointed to the clear way that was most fitting for us. He was not, as he was often referred to by many, my alter ego. Billy Strayhorn was my right arm, my left arm, all the eyes in the back of my head, my brainwaves in his head, and his in mine. Three months after Strayhorn’s death, the Ellington band went into the studio to record a tribute album of his compositions, entitled … And His Mother Called Him Bill. The result is one of Ellington’s greatest late albums. At the end of the session, the band was packing up and Ellington started playing one of Strayhorn’s most yearning tunes, ‘Lotus Blossom’. Perhaps he knew he was being recorded; the rest of the band apparently didn’t. But as he went on, they seemed to have noticed, because they stopped talking and moving stuff around, and listened, as Ellington played a forlorn, wordless lament for his collaborator. Perhaps the band decided that they couldn’t release a take with so much background noise, but at any rate, they recorded it again, with a shiveringly melancholy sax part by Harry Carney, and delicate bass from Aaron Bell. Strayhorn’s music lives on. The great sax player Joe Henderson won a Grammy for his magnificent 1992 album Lush Life: The Music of Billy Strayhorn. To anyone delving into the music of Duke Ellington, the music of Billy Strayhorn is more than a fabulous bonus disc that comes with it: it’s an integral part of the whole thing. He was a sublime composer, a gifted musician and one of the lesser-celebrated jewels of jazz. This answer is a small contribution towards two things that are happening right now, June 2024: African-American Musician Appreciation Month, and Pride Month. And I would like, if I may, to dedicate it to Toni Skinner and Robert Strickland, who gave their support to the idea of it being written in the first place. Thanks, guys. Writing this rekindled my affection for Strayhorn’s music. Sources: Duke Ellington, Music is my Mistress, W.H. Allen, 1973 Mercer Ellington with Stanley Dance, Duke Ellington in Person, Hutchinson, 1978 David Hajdu, Lush Life: A Biography of Billy Strayhorn, Granta, 1996 Stuart Nicholson, A Portrait of Duke Ellington, Pan, 1999 Walter Van De Leur, ‘“Seldom seen, but always heard”: Billy Strayhorn and Duke Ellington’ in Edward Green (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Duke Ellington, Cambridge, 2014 The Duke Ellington Reader, ed. Mark Tucker, Oxford University Press, 1993

Question: Guitars: What are the key differences between a Fender Stratocaster and Fender Telecaster? How can I tell the difference by only looking at them?
Answer: Well, they look different, for a start. One rather obvious giveaway is that the Telecaster has the word ‘Telecaster’ on the headstock, while the Stratocaster has the word ‘Stratocaster’ in the same place. While we’re looking at the headstock, consider another difference: the shape of the headstock. The Telecaster headstock is rounded on its lower edge, while the Stratocaster headstock has a pointy bit:: Next: the neck. The Telecaster neck is slightly wider, because the strings are placed further apart. Next: the bodies. The Telecaster body curves slightly inwards at the top of where the neck meets the body: But the Stratocaster body has a cutaway in the same place: Now, have I ever made use of this cutaway? Not very often, tbh. The Stratocaster body is contoured to fit the player’s body: The Telecaster body is famously not: Although more high-end Teles are contoured. (This is not a high-end Tele.) Stratocasters generally come with a vibrato unit, by which the bridge is connected to a solid block of metal which is attached at one part by screws to the guitar, and at the other end by springs, so that it can rock back and forth. This is variously referred to as the ‘whammy’ or ‘tremelo’ unit, although the latter term is incorrect. Telecasters don’t generally have this, unless one has been retrofitted. The strings pass over the bridge and through the back of the guitar body, and are held in place by metal cups. The bridge does not move. Finally, they sound different, on account of having differently designed pickups, and different configurations of pickup. Stratocasters generally have three pickups, bridge, middle and neck, and a switch enables you to select one of five possible positions: bridge, bridge & middle, middle, middle & neck, and neck. There are some models of Strat that only have two pickups but the basic model has three. Telecasters generally have two pickups, neck and bridge, and a three-way selector switch which enables you to use the bridge, the neck, or both of them together. However, adding a video to this answer which would demonstrate the sound of them would only be helpful about the sound of me, playing my Strat and my Tele (both of them modified), through my amp. And would be a lot of work, which I wouldn’t get paid for.

Question: Why was the music that was remembered as "60s music" i.e (Hendrix, CCR, Led Zepplin, The Rolling Stones) not actually top the charts during the 1960s?
Answer: That’s not actually true. Hendrix’s Are You Experienced? got to no. 2 on the UK album charts. Axis: Bold as Love, its follow-up, got to no. 5. Electric Ladyland reached no 1. on the US album charts and no. 6 on the UK album charts. Hendrix had three top 10 UK singles off his first album alone; ‘Hey Joe’, ‘Purple Haze’ and ‘The Wind Cries Mary’: of these, ‘Purple Haze’ got to no. 3. I can’t be bothered to look up the statistics for CCR because I don’t like them. If you mean Why didn’t everything these bands release get to no. 1?, that’s a stupid question. That doesn’t happen to anyone.

Question: Which type of art allows for the most thorough expression of creativity, painting, sculpture, writing, or film?
Answer: Sorry to be blunt, but it’s a foolish question. None of these kinds of art ‘allow’ for any more creativity anymore than any other. Creativity is unique to each individual, both in the degree of it and in the form it takes. If people want to be good at a kind of art, let them be lucky enough to find out early on what they’re best at doing, so that they can put in the necessary practice. If I were to try to make a sculpture, I would end up with a mess, because my particular configuration of measly talents is such that I’m far better at working with words. And I’m similarly untalented at painting. I’m just not that good at making things that look nice. Or even basically presentable. I can edit video, and do the mechanical things necessary to cut a piece of video together (adjusting sound levels etc.), but it’s not my forte. Other people excel at making pictures: Feifei Wang, for example. That woman can draw. I can only look on her pictures and marvel, because I can’t do that. But I can paint with words a lot better than I can paint with paint. And I’m fine with that. We don’t compare, say, Michelangelo with Dante and say Well, sculpture let Michelangelo be more creative than Dante because it’s more blah blah blah. Incidentally, Michelangelo was also a poet, whereas Dante was not a visual artist—but Dante did leave us with an unforgettable vision of the afterlife, sculpted out of words. So I don’t think the question makes sense. I’m not even sure what ‘expression of creativity’ is supposed to mean. I long ago stopped thinking about art as a form of expression. That’s a dilettante’s attitude. Art is about Making Stuff.

Question: What is a novel that you were disappointed with the film adaptation and how would you imagine a better adaptation of it be like?
Answer: One I can think of is Vladimir Nabokov’s The Luzhin Defense. It was Nabokov’s third novel, written in Russian and first published in Berlin in 1930, and later translated by him and Michael Scammell into English, and published in translation in 1964. It was also Nabokov’s first truly brilliant novel. Its predecessor, King Queen Knave, was a tiresome murder story, and his first novel, Mary, was forgettable. The Luzhin Defense was the first novel in which Nabokov combined his verbal and structural brilliance with a core of genuine emotion and feeling. It’s about a chess master, Aleksandr Luzhin, who as a lonely and awkward child picks up chess at an early age, and quickly becomes brilliant at it. (Nabokov was himself a pretty good chess player.) Luzhin grows up using chess as both a sword and shield: a means to make his way in the world, and also a way of holding the world at a distance. He is afraid of people and their complications, and chess enables him to be a person who amounts to something. In his awkward, shambling but rather endearing way, he manages to become romantically involved (as Wikipedia puts it) with a young woman. They become engaged. He competes in tournaments, but when he plays against an Italian grandmaster, Turati, his game falls to pieces. He has a complete mental breakdown. He slowly recovers, but his fiancée is advised that if he goes back to playing chess, he might have a relapse. He gradually reassembles himself, but then, bit by bit, he starts perceiving life as a grand chess game, seeing patterns of the board in ordinary situations, and feeling more and more embattled. It all ends tragically, but Nabokov’s genius managed to convey Luzhin’s chess-themed paranoia—such as that the courtyard below the bathroom window of his apartment has a floor that has alternate black and white tiles, a detail which becomes terrifyingly vivid in the book’s last pages. Anyway, in 2000, the book was adapted into a movie of the same name, directed by Marleen Gorris and starring John Turturro and Emily Watson. I watched that film. It sucks. Peter Henry’s screenplay, and Marleen Gorris’ direction, completely failed to bring out what was unique and brilliant about the book: its weaving of Luzhin’s complete obsession with chess into the prose itself, and into the structure of his delusions. It was a movie about a sad, lumpen guy with serious mental health issues, who’s good at chess, and the woman who for plot reasons falls in love with him. And they changed the ending to a more-or-less happy one. Also, the chess games in the movie feature illegal moves. I don’t actually care about that, but to make a movie about a supposedly brilliant chess player in which players win with illegal moves… that’s a pretty basic failure. I like John Turturro, but he’s boring in this movie because it’s a poorly-written part. I have never really liked Emily Watson, but that’s just me. I don’t think you can make a good movie out of The Luzhin Defense. I think the best thing about it is its prose, and that would inevitably get lost in adaptation. However, I think somebody could make a great graphic novel out of it. Something like Paul Karasik and David Mazzucchelli’s City of Glass, a brilliant adaptation of Paul Auster’s novella from The New York Trilogy. A page from City of Glass. I see all kinds of possibilities for weaving in visual references to chess in a graphic novel, which could look really cheesy on film but which could be done in visual art in a much more organic and effective way. You wouldn’t have to lose so much of Nabokov’s prose. I don’t think I could write the adaptation myself (I have some experience of adapting classics) but I’d like to see somebody else do it.

Question: If a language doesn’t have a word for something, can we say that thing doesn’t exist in that language?
Answer: We can not. The reason is that although there may not be a word for a thing in that language, it is still possible for that language to express the concept that the word represents. For example, the first non-English language I was taught was Irish. Irish is notorious for there being no words in the language that equate to ‘yes’ and ‘no’. (It’s not the only language with no words for ‘yes’ or ‘no’, but people who don’t know this about it still tend to react with surprise.) However, a lesser-known fact about Irish is that there is no Irish word for ‘have’. There is literally no Irish verb that expresses the concepts of ownership or possession. But this doesn’t mean that you can’t express those concepts in Irish. You just do it a different way. Actually, you do it the way I did in this answer. Above, I could have written Irish doesn’t have a word for ‘have’. Instead, I wrote There is no Irish word for ‘have’, which means the same thing but doesn’t use that verb. If you want to say in Irish that you ‘have’ something, you say it’s ‘at’ you. I have a bicycle in Irish is Tá rothar agam, literally ‘It-is-that bicycle at-me.’ There are also possessive pronouns: ‘my bicycle’ is mo rothar. (Don’t even get me started on the forainmneacha: Irish prepositional pronouns.) As you see, it’s perfectly possible to express ownership in Irish. You just don’t use a verb meaning ‘have’ in order to do so, because there isn’t one. Likewise, Mandarin doesn’t have different forms of verbs to express tenses. Even Irish has them: chuaigh mé is ‘I went’, rachaidh mé is ‘I will go’. (‘I go’ is, confusingly, Téim.) But in Mandarin, there’s just 去, ‘go’. There’s no equivalent form for ‘went’. This doesn’t mean that Mandarin has no way of expressing time, and so therefore time doesn’t exist for Chinese people. It just means that Mandarin conveys the time of an action differently from how English and Irish do. It does it by using words to indicate when an action takes place. Languages are surprisingly resourceful. If a thing has to be said, people will find a way for it to be said it in their language.

Question: Why do people think that Germans and Austriams are the greatest classical music composers even though classical music as well as its instruments were invented by Italians in Italy?
Answer: Lotta nonsense to unpack in this question. ‘Classical music’ wasn’t ‘invented’ anywhere in particular. It mostly evolved from previous music, with occasional nudges from composers of particular genius. Polyphonic vocal church music, for instance, very much got started in France, in the choir of Notre Dame cathedral in the 12th and 13th centuries. The first all-round composer in the Western tradition, the first one to write with equal brilliance for voices and solo instruments and instrumental ensembles, was from England: William Byrd. We shouldn’t ignore the amazing achievements of Dutch and Flemish composers during the Renaissance: Ockeghem, Obrecht, Josquin des Prez. But even if it were true that the Italians ‘invented’ classical music, that has absolutely nothing to do with how good they were at it. The only truly ‘invented’ form of classical music is the opera, and that was indeed invented by Italian composers, partly based on their notions of how classical Greek drama probably worked. The first opera that we know of was Peri’s Dafne, from around 1597, and the first opera that we know that has actually survived is his Euridice from a few years later. However, Euridice ain’t much good. The first great opera composer was also Italian: Monteverdi, whose L’Orfeo is still in the repertoire, and well worth hearing. But that doesn’t mean that later composers from other countries didn’t write great operas. Eighty years after L’Orfeo, the Englishman Purcell wrote Dido and Aeneas, which is another masterpiece. Are we going to write off the operas of Handel, and Mozart, and Wagner, simply because Italians wrote the first operas? No, we are not. Italian composers played a major role in developing the symphony as a musical form, but it was an Austrian, Joseph Haydn, who played the biggest role in making it the musical form that everyone had to have a go at. Then he did it again, for the string quartet. How? Because he wrote so many masterpieces in those forms. I can’t actually think of a single major Italian symphonist—certainly not on Haydn’s level, which is admittedly a very high one. So this was a stupid question.
