Question: Did George Harrison's answer to George Martin "Well, for starters, I don't like your tie", save the Beatles from being rejected? I get the feeling that Martin wasn't very impressed with the band but their sense of humor won him over.
Answer: Put yourself in George Martin’s position. It’s June 1962. You’re the head of a fairly small but reasonably profitable label, which is a small branch on the giant corporate tree that is EMI. You’ve kept control of the label by your willingness to do anything: obscure classical music, folk music, original cast recordings of shows, skiffle (when skiffle was A Thing, which was a few years ago now), but mostly comedy and novelty records. You are recognised as imaginative, and a good earner, but hardly a major player. You’re in your mid-thirties. You could be forgiven for thinking that this is as good as it will ever get. You’re the guy who produced Peter Sellers’ records. Peter Sellers. The film star. Then these four sullen Herberts from Liverpool show up to record something. Nobody is entirely sure if it’s a demo, or an attempt at a first single. You’ve met their manager, who seems smart and engaging, but is also clearly rather infatuated with them. You’ve already heard their actual demo, which is rubbish, but for complicated office politics reasons to do with music publishing, there is pressure upon you to find something worthwhile about these boys. Your boss has found out that your marriage is over, and you’re having an affair with your secretary Judy, and he doesn’t like that. So you have to play nice. And part of playing nice is that you’ve agreed to let the ‘Beattles’, as you thought they were called until a few days ago, record something. You’re so not interested in this session that you aren’t even there at the start of it. You delegate it to Ron Richards, your assistant. You slope off to the canteen for a cup of tea, leaving Ron in charge: no need to subject yourself to this. You know how it’s going to go. Halfway through your tea, tape operator Chris Neal comes in and comes over to you. Chris says, Ron said to ask you to come and have a listen to this song. So you go back to the studio, and they play this bog-simple ditty: Love, love me do. You know I love you. Plee-ee-ee-eeease… love me do-o. Well, he’s right. It’s not exactly ‘Body and Soul’. But it’s also… odd. It’s got harmonica: you like harmonica, Sonny Terry and Brownie McGhee, that kind of thing. And this is that kind of harmonica. Not a hit song, though. Plus, they’re making a mess of the vocals, because the rhythm guitarist is having to sing and play harmonica at the same time. So you tell the bass guitarist to sing the title line. He looks worried. But also: guitar bands that sing? What’s that? And who’s in charge? They all look the same. Who’s the boss? And their gear is in awful shape: Ken Townsend has clearly rigged up some sort of impromptu bass amp for the bass guitarist, whose actual amp, ragged and crappy-looking, is lurking unused in a corner. So afterwards, you bring them up the stairs into the control room, and you play their stuff back to them, and you give them The Talk, to let them know what they’re going to need to do to shape up. And as you do so, you overhear yourself lecturing them, and it occurs to you that this must be a bit boring, and now they’re staring back at you, stone-faced. So you ask them if there’s anything they don’t like. And for a moment, nobody says anything, but then the youngest and scrawniest one, the ‘lead guitarist’, who’s hardly Bert Weedon, drawls Yeah. I don’t like your tie. And you think You cheeky git!, because you’re rather proud of your taste in ties, but his timing is so good that you can’t help but chuckle. And then they all perk up and start wisecracking, and it turns out they’re all comedians. Well, except for the drummer, the handsome one with the quiff. He doesn’t talk. Ever. Not much of a drummer, either. Twenty minutes later, they’re on their way out the door, and you and Norman the engineer have had a bloody good laugh, and you think, Well… if nothing else, they’d be fun to work with. I’ll need to get a proper drummer for them in the studio, though. So you tell Ron to find them a song that they can have a hit with. Because clearly, their own songs aren’t good enough. It’s a little over eighteen months later. Early February 1964. You’re in bed, with Judy, asleep. Your divorce still hasn’t happened, because your estranged wife doesn’t want to have a divorce yet. She has the care of your two kids. Anyway, that’s another issue. In the immediate term, the Beatles are now very, very, very big. Like, huge. And their latest single, ‘I Want To Hold Your Hand’, has been rocketing up the Billboard Hot 100. It’s been over a year of sheer madness. Like nothing you, or anyone else, has ever seen before. Starting in early 1963 and snowballing since then. Everyone wants the Beatles to go to the USA. But they have refused to do so until they have a US No. 1. It’s annoying, but they’ve played things pretty well so far, so we are indulging them. You only just fell asleep. But you’re woken up by the phone ringing. You answer it. It’s Brian Epstein, now a trusted friend and colleague. What is it? you say. We’re number one in the States, he says. That’s it: the four Herberts from Liverpool are now the biggest thing in show business. You don’t even know what to say. You’re grinning all over your face. That’s terrific, you finally manage. Fancy a drink-up? Brian says, and you can hear him grinning down the phone. Not half, you say, and you put down the phone and go and wake Judy up. The two of you get dressed, and pop around to Brian’s place, and party all night. Because, in defiance of every opinion you had of them in June 1962, the Beatles have reached the top. Sources: The Beatles, The Beatles Anthology, (DVD), Apple, 2003 Mark Lewisohn, The Beatles: All These Years - Tune In, Little, Brown, 2013

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Were all the British lords bad or were there some good ones? If there were good ones, what were their names and what charitable works did they do?
Answer: Allow me to present you with this rocking-ass dude: Anthony Ashley-Cooper, the 7th Earl of Shaftesbury. He was born in 1801. He grew up with absolutely zero experience of parental love. Even when he was an adult, he disliked his parents. However, he didn’t grow up with zero experience of being loved and cared for. The family housekeeper, Maria Millis, was kind and generous to him. As were her sisters, apparently. His early school years were unhappy. He hated his first school. At Harrow public school he witnessed the funeral of a pauper, and the generally shambolic crappiness of it made him realise that his own problems were pretty minor by comparison. He was, by his teen years, a devout Christian (partly thanks to the housekeeper), and it was partly his Christianity that made him absolutely devoted to the idea of improving the conditions of the poor and underprivileged. After college (Oxford), he ran for Parliament. He was elected as the Tory MP for Woodstock, in Oxfordshire. (Town’s still there, constituency was abolished in 1918.) He’d hardly been an MP for a year when, in his mid-twenties, he was appointed to the Select Committee on Pauper Lunatics in the County of Middlesex and on Lunatic Asylums. Lunatic asylums in early 19th century Britain were horrendous places. In one asylum that the committee heard evidence about, in Bethnal Green, inmates were chained up in their cells at weekends and left to shit and piss in their bedding, then they’d be unchained on Monday morning and hosed down with freezing water. There was one towel for 160 people, and no soap. The Committee recommended sweeping reforms of the system, and Ashley-Cooper made his maiden speech in the Commons in support of it. It passed. Over the next few decades, he was a tireless advocate for the better treatment of asylum inmates. But that wasn’t his greatest achievement. In 1833, when he was in his early 30s, he introduced the Ten Hours Act 1833. This stipulated that children working in the cotton or woollen industries had to be nine years old or older, because up until that point, they didn’t have to be. It said that nobody under the age of 18 should have to work more than ten hours per day, or eight on a Saturday. And it had other stipulations. It was a major reform of child labour law. However, the Whig government changed ‘18’ to ‘13’ because, you know, the free market. Over the next several years, Ashley-Cooper pushed for more reforms of child labour. He wrote to the prime minister, Robert Peel, to urge support for a new Factory Act, which would introduce more humane working conditions. Peel said no. A Ten Hours Act resembling his original proposal was finally passed in 1847. In 1842, he introduced the Mines and Collieries Act 1842, which outlawed employers from making women and children work underground in coal mines. He spent thirty-five years pushing legislation after legislation to regulate the barbaric chimney sweeping industry, in which boy chimney sweeps suffered from diseases and burns, caused by their appalling working conditions. He started in 1840, and only in 1875 did the government pass his Chimney Sweepers Act 1875, which required that sweeps be registered with the police, and licensed. It killed the employment of children as chimney sweeps. He also pushed for education reform, and he created legislation whereby lodging houses became subject to inspection by local authorities. This was the kind of thing that earned him his nickname of the Poor Man’s Earl. Yes, he was a paternalistic One Nation Tory, but at a time of rapacious and unregulated capitalism, he did the best he could to regulate it, and reduce the harm it caused. That said, in Capital Vol. 1, Karl Marx mentions him in two quite different contexts. He quotes Shaftesbury’s meticulous statistics on working hours, but also sardonically points out that Shaftesbury, as a philanthropist, worked for the better conditions of the labourers on his land, but also, as a landowner, pocketed a large part of their wages in the form of rent. Still, this is Britain we’re talking about. When Shaftesbury died in 1885, his funeral procession was lined with working people who waited to see his coffin as it passed by. He did other things, too. He was a strong supporter of Zionism, and he was also heavily opposed to the opium trade, one of the nastier aspects of British colonialism. On the whole, and bearing Marx’s comments in mind, I think Lord Shaftesbury was a lord who spent his long career mostly trying to do right by people. In case it looks like I cribbed most of this answer from Wikipedia (which, admittedly, was remarkably helpful), I first heard of him when I was collecting stamps in my misspent childhood. I had the set that included this one, from 1976: Lord Shaftesbury. Not the worst toff who’s ever lived.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Did the Beatles create such three part harmonies as "That Boy"? The block harmonies seem to pat. I recently heard a guy who trains Beatle tribute bands state that the three part harmonies were composed by George Martin and taught to the Beatles.
Answer: I know of no evidence that George Martin wrote the Beatles’ harmonies for them. It’s ‘This Boy’, by the way, not ‘That Boy’. The three-part harmony on ‘This Boy’ is actually pretty simple compared to the three-part harmony on 1965’s ‘Yes It Is’, the B-side to ‘Ticket To Ride’. There’s nothing in ‘This Boy’ that couldn’t have been figured out by the guys who did the harmonies on ‘Please Please Me’. ‘Yes It Is’ is a good deal more complicated because it’s a more harmonically complicated song In any case, the Beatles were doing three-part harmony long before they met George Martin. Their Decca demo recordings shows them doing three-part harmony on ‘Searchin’’ in January 1962: they wouldn’t even meet Martin until 6 June of that year. Finally, devising three- or even four-part harmony is pretty damn basic, as musical skills go. My school garage band did a version of the Housemartins’ a cappella version of the Isley Brothers’ ‘Caravan of Love’, which we used to do to entertain our classmates before the teacher came in, and we didn’t even have thousands of hours of boot camp in Hamburg nightclubs to tell us how to do it. (I sang the bass part.) The idea that the Beatles would have needed George Martin to show them how to do the harmony on ‘This Boy’ is ludicrous, frankly.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: How does Frank Zappa play guitar like that?
Answer: Now, that is a good question. If I answer it, it’s because, as a guitar player myself, I’ve paid some attention to Zappa’s guitar playing. In order to understand how Zappa ended up playing the way he did, we need to look briefly at his early development. Frank Zappa, counter-cultural rock legend. Zappa began as a blues player. Well, actually, he began as a drummer in his high school marching band. As part of his drum tuition, he probably learned some basic score reading skills. As a teenager, he loved blues and doo-wop and built a serious record collection. A little later he became interested in modern classical music, after reading an article about a local record shop that had sold an album of works by the French composer Edgard Varèse. He improved his reading skills by checking out scores from the library, and started composing his own music onto paper. This made him unusual as one of the few rock musicians who could read and write music before he’d learned the guitar. When he was 16 or 17, he got his first guitar, and started by copying his favourite blues players: Guitar Slim, Johnny ‘Guitar’ Watson, Clarence ‘Gatemouth’ Brown. From this, we can tell that Zappa’s preference was for more aggressive players, and also for guys who were soloists, not so much supporting guitarists. Not, therefore, brilliant sidemen like Hubert Sumlin or Willie Johnson or Jimmy Rogers, or the more versatile, flowing, jazz-inspired style of B.B. King (although both B.B. and Gatemouth shared a common influence in T-Bone Walker), and certainly not the acoustic blues of the Delta. From the beginning, Zappa liked guitarists with a certain… attack. From Brown and Watson, he might also have been impressed by their non-purist attitude to genres: Brown was interested in country and zydeco, and Watson made a great album of cocktail piano early in his career, I Cried For You. Anyway, in the late 50s and early 60s, Zappa struggled to make a living as a working musician, playing mostly guitar and occasionally drums in lounge bands (where he learned a mostly healthy contempt for bad jazz), and writing and producing songs. At some point, he became a great admirer of Wes Montgomery, who as far as I know he never attempted to emulate as a player. Zappa said that what he liked about Wes’ playing was that he puts his personality, something about him as a person, into playing, and I don't detect "watch me show off now" – there is none of that syndrome. Putting himself into his own playing was something that took Zappa his entire life to do. One of the interesting things about Zappa’s playing is that he developed into a great guitarist in public, and did so basically in mid-career. He was arguably one of two lead guitarists on the first Mothers of Invention album, Freak Out!, and he wasn’t dramatically better than the other one, Elliott Ingber. Zappa’s early leads, on the first Mothers of Invention albums, are very much the sort of thing you’d expect to hear from someone who’d developed as outlined above. They are basically sped-up pentatonic minor blues licks, played with lots of attack. Zappa used a fairly clean tone at the time: his main guitar at that point was a Gibson ES-5 Switchmaster, so he probably couldn’t turn it up very loud without feedback issues. In 1967, the Mothers of Invention got a five-month residency at the Garrick Theater in NYC. It was here that Zappa first met Jimi Hendrix, who can hardly have failed to influence him. Zappa reportedly introduced Hendrix to the wah-wah pedal. Gail Zappa, his widow, compared the Garrick period to the Beatles’ time in Hamburg. It was when Zappa realised in full what he could get away with on stage. By the late 60s, Zappa was writing quite complex and interesting music (and had largely switched to a Les Paul goldtop with P-90s), but it wasn’t yet informing his guitar playing. By the time of Uncle Meat, In 1968, he was starting to play solos in a style that was more like his way of writing melodies. He had incorporated more modes into his playing (he once mentioned that he used the Mixolydian a lot), but when he was really going for it, he still tended to use blues and pentatonic scales. He cleverly dealt with any monotony in his actual playing by continually coming up with new contexts to put it in. On Hot Rats he put his playing front and centre, perhaps as a deliberate gesture towards guitar hero status. If so, it worked: that album has a ton of fans, although I’m not one of them, except for the sublime ‘Peaches En Regalia’. In his 1971 movie 200 Motels, he was playing with his live band and the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, and he played up the timbral contrasts between the two ensembles for all they were worth. The segues from the splendid ‘Semi-Fraudulent/Direct-From-Hollywood Overture’ into the filthy ‘Mystery Roach’, and from the arch Schoenberg parody ‘A Nun Suit Painted on Some Old Boxes’ into ‘Magic Fingers’, are great moments of Zappa jolting the listener with brutal contrasts of styles. Fortunately, because 200 Motels was conceived as a movie as well as an album, we have some footage of Zappa actually playing: From this, we can tell a few things about Zappa’s playing at this period, or at least, in this song: Also, whoever edited this may have been on crack. But that’s another story. In 1971, Zappa had a rather mixed year. The 200 Motels thing went sour when the Royal Albert Hall cancelled a Zappa gig at the last minute, on the grounds that his music and lyrics weren’t the kind of thing that they wanted. Zappa was outraged, as he’d offered them choices between original lyrics and safer, less potentially offensive alternatives, but they’d ignored him. A gig in Montreux Casino in Switzerland went pear-shaped when fire broke out. (Yes, Deep Purple wrote a song about it.) Nobody was hurt, but the band’s equipment was destroyed. Days later, he was playing at the Rainbow Theatre in London, using rented gear. His guitar that night was a ‘stock Telecaster with chubby strings’. A live recording from that evening (which ended up as part of ‘King Kong’ on You Can’t Do That On Stage Anymore, Vol. 3) shows Zappa struggling to adapt his style to a guitar whose strings he couldn’t bend. It was one of the few times that his attention to jazz guitar came out: he plays a lot of rather pretty chordal stuff. But his struggles that night were cut short when a fan got it into his head that Zappa was flirting with his (the fan’s) girlfriend. The fan invaded the stage, and shoved Zappa off it, causing him to fall several feet into the concrete orchestra pit. Zappa came out with a crushed larnynx, which permanently lowered the pitch of his voice, and various injuries, including one leg that healed shorter than the other. He was in a wheelchair for months. In order to make up for not being able to tour, Zappa wrote a bunch of music around this time. He’d already been writing a lot of music, but the process of detaching himself from the notion and the personnel of the Mothers of Invention opened him up to collaborating with/employing a wider variety of musicians. Especially jazz musicians. I think the evidence shows that this made him a more resourceful and imaginative guitar player. One general thing I would say about Zappa’s guitar playing: he was seldom a man for tasteful restraint. ‘Less is more’ was not really a trademark of his. In the early 70s, Zappa’s band toured with the Mahavishnu Orchestra, and Zappa and John McLaughlin had some… interesting things to say about each other. John McLaughlin in the early 70s. Only a man devoted to serving god with his music would play such an enormous guitar. (Unless he’s Rick Nielsen.) Zappa professed to be impressed by McLaughlin’s formidable technique, but phrased it as very faint praise indeed: A person would be a moron not to appreciate McLaughlin's technique. The guy has certainly found out how to operate a guitar as if it were a machine gun. But I'm not always enthusiastic about the lines I hear or the ways in which they're used. […] I think anybody who can play that fast is just wonderful. And I'm sure 90% of teenage America would agree, since the whole trend in the business has been "faster is better". A few years later, Zappa was more generous, calling McLaughlin ‘a great guitar player’. McLaughlin was more diplomatic, showering praise on Zappa as a great bandleader and composer, but also someone who played, in those days, 10 to 15-minute guitar solos, ‘when maybe they should have been about two to three minutes.’ There is something in that. Not all of Zappa’s longest solos have the pleasing shape of his short to medium-length ones. I’m not always up for yet another ten minutes of ‘The Torture Never Stops’, but on the other hand, ‘Yo’ Mama’, off Sheik Yerbouti, is a genuinely epic solo, made more epic by some skilful overdubbage of keyboards to bring out its structure. However, after Zappa had toured with Mahavishnu, he began to be more exploratory in his use of different scales, and more single-minded about ‘making up a melody on the spot’ in his solos. I’m not saying that McLaughlin’s criticisms of Zappa’s style ‘got to’ Zappa. He may never even have read them. But his playing in the later 70s takes leaps in harmonic and rhythmic complexity. Here is Zappa playing his tune ‘Black Napkins’ on the Mike Douglas Show, in 1976. The first thing I note here is the increased sophistication of the harmonic backdrop he’s playing against. Despite his admiration for Wes Montgomery, Zappa didn’t like playing against busy harmonic backdrops, like mainstream jazz players do. He valued contrast and drama, and when you hear a really technically able guitar player such as Tal Farlow playing bebop, it can sometimes sound less like imaginative music and more like athletics: Is he going to negotiate that chord change? Oh yes. Good job, Tal. (That’s my personal opinion, anyway. I’ve said lots of times that I’m not into an awful lot of mainstream jazz guitar.) So, ‘Black Napkins’ has basically two chords, C#min7 and Dmaj7, and it rocks back and forth between them, giving Zappa plenty of scope to execute all kinds of intricate arabesques and rhythmic things. But note also how the mood of this is different: more sophisticated, more jazzy, more… grown-up. ‘Black Napkins’ is a rather dreamy, impressionistic piece of music, certainly by Zappa’s standards, and he plays an appropriately serene melody before going off into one of his solos. Tonight, I watched the DVD Does Humour Belong in Music?, a recording of an NYC concert from 1984. I notice that Zappa played with the ring and little finger of his right hand touching the guitar, and the pick apparently held between his thumb and his index and middle finger—a very odd way to hold a pick. He also usually played over the end of the neck, which is quite unusual, but it enabled him to do a particular kind of string-tapping he liked, when he’d touch the string to the fret with the pick and pull it off then put it back, very rapidly for several notes. He sometimes called this iirc the ‘Hungarian bagpipe’ technique. In the early 80s, Zappa hired Steve Vai in his band after employing him as a music transcriber, and Vai, plus his own son Dweezil, seem to have opened Zappa’s ears to developments in metal because the 80s feature some of Zappa’s most outrageously hard-rock solos. The solo in the title track of Them or Us starts out with howling feedback, romps all over the fretboard (I think that at one point he’s soloing in one of Messiaen’s modes of limited transposition), and only devolves from there, ending up as comically over-the-top filth and sleaze, with Zappa gleefully divebombing on his inebriated-sounding guitar, which he then samples and plays back in delirious loops of fuzzy noise. That’s a Zappa who has fully learned the lessons of Hendrix, yet he doesn’t sound like a Hendrix copyist. As we have seen, Zappa started out playing blues, but over the years he developed a highly eclectic approach to scales. Besides the Mixolydian mode, he was very fond of the Lydian, which is basically a major scale with the fourth degree raised a half step. It’s maybe not a coincidence that the Lydian is what you get if you start the Mixolydian on the seventh degree instead of the tonic (i.e., Lydian C is enharmonic to Mixolydian D). Any player with some decent soloing skills who gets the Lydian mode under their fingers can soon begin to sound like Zappa in playing ‘out’ mode. I’ve also heard him use the harmonic major, which is like the major scale but with a diminished sixth: so, in C, that would be C, D, E, F, G, Ab, B, C. The minor third between the sixth and the seventh degrees is what gives it its peculiarly salty flavour. We have to talk about Zappa’s approach to rhythm as a player. He began as a drummer, and his rhythmic sense as a composer was always pretty free and resourceful, but as a guitarist, he started out rather hemmed-in by blues clichés, before becoming more and more free as he got older. The definitive resource on this is the Frank Zappa Guitar Book, which contains transcriptions of some of his solos. Opening it at random, I find in ‘Soup ’n Old Clothes’ that, in a song that’s a D minor 4/4 with a 12/8 shuffle feel, Zappa starts out by playing a quick lick that takes him to a long extended note, then after another flourish he plays, in measures 5–7, a phrase that Vai transcribes as (partly) triplets nested within triplets, then a triplet nested within a sextuplet, then two triplets nested within a quintuplet, then another quintuplet, and then five more triplets. It’s between about 0:16 and 0:20 in the video. The effect of this is that the rhythm of his phrasing is constantly pulling and pushing against the beats. It’s like the way people talk, rather than like regular musical phrasing. This goes with Zappa’s remark in an interview that his solos are ‘speech-influenced, rhythmically.’ Zappa took this interest in nested polyrhythms and made of it his most infamously tricky composition, ‘The Black Page #2’, which I wrote about elsewhere. Anyone who wants to play like Zappa needs to break away from playing in regular fourth- and eighth- and sixteenth-notes. Zappa claimed to be literally unable to play like that, which is why he hired people like Warren Cucurullo and Steve Vai, who could. Zappa had a very remarkable ear. Everyone who knew him, said so. The great mastering engineer Bob Ludwig was once mastering a Zappa album (Sheik Yerbouti) when Zappa asked him to slightly bring down a particular frequency band in a certain passage on a bass track, for a few seconds. Ludwig accidentally used the wrong switch on the desk, and although he chose the right passage, and adjusted it in the right direction by the right amount for the right duration, he used the wrong shape of bandwidth: sharp, rather than the medium Zappa had asked for. The distinction would be completely inaudible to most listeners. Zappa, who had his back to Ludwig and hadn’t seen what he’d done, commented that that didn’t sound quite right. Ludwig realised his mistake, and that incident made him regard Zappa as one of the few people he’d worked with who was a genuine master of sound. One of the things Zappa did when he was playing live in a venue was use fairly small amps, and close-mike them. In soundchecks, he would find out what notes on the fretboard were most likely to yield good-sounding feedback in the space he happened to be working in, and make a note of them, sometimes using a parametric equalizer to emphasise them, so that he knew he could rely on them in performance. How he did this in an empty venue when he knew that its acoustic properties would change once it had people in it, I don’t know, but his son Dweezil testifies that he was brilliant at it. I’ve been watching a lot of Zappa-related stuff lately, and gave another spin to Alex Winter’s documentary, which was much better than I remembered it as being. One thing I noticed is that the emotional content of his playing got deeper and broader, as he grew older and possibly wiser. The young Zappa was playing like a mischievous scamp, well into his early 30s. By his late 30s, he was playing things like the yearningly melancholy ‘Watermelon in Easter Hay’, which I’ve also written about. I’ve said it before, but people who think that Zappa’s music is all relentless snark and no heart have never paid attention to his greatest guitar playing, where he wears his heart non-referentially on his sleeve. The quieter tracks on Shut Up ’n’ Play Yer Guitar, like ‘Stucco Homes’ and ‘Canard du Jour’, are meditative and thoughtful. ‘Canard du Jour’ had Zappa nodding to his Greek ancestors, with him playing an electric bouzouki. Zappa was always interested in traditional musics of the world (I touched on this here), and I wish he’d lived to finish the project he was working on that involved the Chieftains, one of the greatest Irish traditional ensembles. However, I’ve saved one of my favourite Zappa solos until last. The solo is ‘Ship Ahoy’ from 1976 or so, which in fact was the coda to a much longer improvisation: Zappa saved just this bit. There are lots of things I like about this. The texture of this music: the sharp, jagged tone of his Strat against the silence, underscored by only very discreet bass guitar, a little keyboard, and some mostly very subtle drumming from Terry Bozzio, who carefully follows Zappa until by the climax he’s drumming up a storm, and then brings it down when Zappa does too. Zappa is using an Oberheim voltage-controlled filter that lets higher frequencies through when he picks harder, but rolls the treble back when he picks softer, which gives his tone an almost living quality. But mostly, I think it’s the sense of musical construction in this solo. Zappa starts it off playing almost entirely on just one note, for the whole first seven seconds, working the harmonics of it (he may have done this by brushing his finger up and down the open D string so that it brings up the string’s harmonics in passing, the filter emphasising or de-emphasising them as he did so) and wringing every timbral variant out of it that he can get, and only gradually does he stray away from it, scurrying up and down the blues scale. And at 1:09 it becomes clear that the previous 69 seconds have been the intro, because Roy Estrada’s bass comes in underneath, playing a one-note drone. (Whether Estrada actually came in at that point or whether Zappa created the effect by fading him in during editing, I don’t know, but it’s very effective.) This states the basic idea of the solo. At 1:28 or so, Andre Lewis’ keyboard enters, establishing the basic harmony: Dm7. At 2:19, Zappa brings it down to basics again, coaxing tiny little squeaks and yelps from the guitar, but then he builds it up, and at 2:47 he plays a fanfare-like Cmajor-Dmajor chord change, which he repeats a few times. At 2:49 he plays a Mixolydian figure that introduces a toccata-like section, with some of his most extravagant playing, an outburst of notes that contrast with the claustrophobic mood of the rest of the solo. At 3:48, as if he feels like that’s enough of that kind of soul-baring, he goes back to the ominous, hanging-on-one-note thing. He plays around with the harmony (kind of a development section), and at 4:20 he does a very Hendrixoid thing, pushing down the whammy bar of his Strat as he repeatedly plays a note, so that the pitch drops in a sort of atonal drawl (ah-wa-da-wa-da-wa-da…). At 4:47, he and the bass fall into a brief funk groove which then falls away, and all that’s left is the wisps of organ and the sniffs and coughs and squeaks of the guitar, and then Bozzio brings the whole thing to an end with a brisk crack on his snare. In this answer, I’ve tried to offer a few tips on Zappa’s playing, gleaned from watching and listening to him play over the years. This may only have been of interest to other players who like Zappa’s playing. It could have been longer. Still, I think it’s a start. If I keep tinkering with it, it’ll just get worse. Thanks for reading, and thanks for the A2A, John Kramer. Sources Lots of things, but for books, Ben Watson’s Frank Zappa: The Negative Dialectics of Poodle Play; Zappa and Peter Occhiogrosso’s The Real Frank Zappa Book; Ralph Denyer’s The Guitar Handbook; The Frank Zappa Guitar Book; Ted Gioia’s Delta Blues. Bob Ludwig’s anecdote about Zappa’s ear is from the John Zorn edited anthology Arcana IV: Musicians on Music from 2009. Video: Alex Winter’s 2020 documentary Zappa, with wonderful interviews with people who’d known him; Thorsten Schütte’s 2016 Eat That Question: Frank Zappa In His Own Words, a treasure trove of interviews with Zappa himself; the official Zappa films/videos 200 Motels, The Dub Room Special and Does Humor Belong in Music? Audio: Of course, Zappa’s own sprawling discography. Internet: the website Zappa Wiki Jawaka was very helpful.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: When you’re sad, what’s your favorite restaurant to go to?
Answer: It no longer exists. But I recreate it myself, in my kitchen. It was a pizza restaurant on Goldhawk Road in Shepherd’s Bush, London, near the former site of the Bush Theatre. It was called The Hat Shop, because on the outside, it looked like a hat shop, but when you went inside, it was a pizza restaurant. It was a kind of joke about speakeasies. This is roughly where The Hat Shop was: I think Liz Cafe might be the actual site. Anyway, Shepherd’s Bush was also the location of the BBC Television Theatre, now a music venue, the Shepherd’s Bush Empire. My mum, who worked in the BBC in the 1960s, had an old friend and work colleague who’d been a floor manager in the Television Theatre for years, and who in retirement lived in a block of flats around the corner, who was a sort of godmother of mine (not really, because I was never christened). She would occasionally send me gifts of cash. One of these gifts of cash formed the basis for my purchase of my first proper musical instrument, a bass guitar, so I’ll always remember Joan Marsden fondly for that. And for her formidable collection of fluffy toy bears. Joan was seriously agoraphobic and hated leaving her flat, but when my mum and my brother and I visited her in the 80s, she would consent to take us to lunch. A few times, she took us to The Hat Shop, because she thought it was funny (and, looking back, perhaps because its blacked-out interior calmed her agoraphobia.) Everyone else would order pizza, but at the time, I was a very picky teenager and I didn’t like pizza or any other Italian food. (I’ve since learned to love them.) Instead, the first time I was there, I ordered the one thing on the menu that looked good to me: spare ribs and a baked potato. I had never had spare ribs before, and I loved them. Years later, I’ve found that whenever I feel sad and I want something comforting for dinner, I will make myself spare ribs and a baked potato, with spinach on the side. The only drawback is that it requires the spare ribs to be coated in rub and put in the fridge overnight. But I find that even the act of buying the ribs and making the rub and coating them and fridgeing them helps to cheer me up, because I know I’ve got spare ribs to look forward to, the following night. So, yeah. A restaurant that no longer exists is my favourite restaurant to go to in my memory, because it gave me my one comfort meal.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Why is metal music becoming boring to me as I'm learning more blues and jazzy stuff on the guitar?
Answer: Okay, a small personal note before I get going on this. Because I think I know where you’re coming from. And I know where you might be going. I have never pretended to be a huge metal fan. I liked some of it as a kid, but I liked other music too, and as I’ve grown older, I have less and less need to listen to metal, or metal-like music. I don’t think it’s a disparagement of metal to say that it can play a really important role in a person’s development, but it’s also the sort of music a person can grow out of. I think metal makes more sense when you’re young, stroppy, uncertain, dealing with feelings of aggression, and generally want to assert yourself in some loud and explosive way. Metal is really, really good when you feel like that. But jazz and blues are… a little bit more nuanced. I’m currently coming to the end of Ted Gioia’s magisterial book Delta Blues, basically a history of the blues of the Mississippi Delta told mostly through studies of some of its most eminent musicians: Charley Patton, Son House, Skip James, Robert Johnson, Muddy Waters, John Lee Hooker, Howlin’ Wolf, B.B. King. Gioia also gives excellent space to less famous figures you’ve never heard of. I’ll always be grateful that he drew my attention to such almost forgotten but memorable people like Mattie May Thomas, whose entire recorded legacy is four scalding tracks recorded in a prison camp, or Geeshie Wiley, whose ‘Last Kind Words Blues’ is an extraordinarily original blues song in terms of its structure, or the brilliant pianist and singer Louise Johnson. But the blues runs through a lot of emotional range, from the spectral art songs of Skip James, through the robust self-assertion of Muddy Waters, to the soulful mastery of B.B. King. And then there’s later blues still, such as the grown-up songwriting of Robert Cray, and there’s Gary Clark Jr in the 21st century, bringing the blues together with rock and rap and reggae. That’s a music you could spend your whole life in, and not feel like your needs as a music fan and as a human being weren’t being catered for. I’m just not sure that metal is so… emotionally available. If what you want is to blast out your angst and surplus feelings with maximum drama and volume, it’s good for that. If not… then not. At least, whenever I hope that metal’s going to be less predictable, it never is. It’s great at the thing that it does, but it’s not so good at doing anything else. (Hard rock, now, that’s another matter. Probably my favourite hard rock band is Thin Lizzy, who really could give you balls-to-the-wall rockers and soulful ballads and good-time funk, and make you laugh. But I doubt that metal fans would consider them metal.) And jazz? I mean, there are jazz musicians who can provide that sort of diversity of mood in a single career. Miles Davis is only the most obvious example. But my hero Bud Powell could also play frenetic high-intensity bebop, and also play a ballad so slowly and simply that it could break your heart (check out his version of ‘It Never Entered My Mind’). So if you feel that metal’s becoming more boring to you as you learn new stuff, it could be that metal no longer reaches the parts of you that jazz and blues reach. You wouldn’t be the first person who’s felt that way.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Even if a new work of fiction is a derivative of tropes that came before, how does that new work still manage to captivate a portion of the everyday audience?
Answer: Why wouldn’t it captivate them? The question seems to assume that readers only want to read things that are 100% unfamiliar. Actually, many readers want the same kind of thing over and over again, and there’s no shame in that—unless that reader professes to believe that anything a bit more outré or experimental or difficult is, therefore, ‘pretentious’ and ‘self-indulgent’ and contemptible. It’s mostly the recombination of existing tropes that makes the new fiction different and interesting and fresh. I say ‘mostly’ because, although new tropes do get invented from time to time, it’s far more common for writers to put their own twists on existing ones. When a writer does this enough, one of the effects is that the writer strikes us as being ‘original’, because they ring enough changes on existing tropes that they come across as having a ‘voice’ that consists of the peculiar combination of all their influences, or precursors. The Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges described this in his essay ‘Kafka and his Precursors’, in which he noted various pieces of writing that predated the work of Kafka but all of which resembled his work, even though they didn’t resemble each other. Borges’ argument was that these writers were, as a result, precursors of Kafka, but that that only became evident after Kafka had written—so, in effect, Kafka created his own precursors. Borges also took the idea of literary originality to its ultimate extreme in his story ‘Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote’, in which the titular character, an early 20th century French writer, resolves to write Miguel de Cervantes’ 17th century novel Don Quixote. As in, literally write it, word-for-word: not copy it out, but recreate it himself so that his version is identical to the original, which he’d read as a kid and so he at least knew how it went, rather like the way a novelist vaguely knows the book they plan to write. Menard first attempts to do this by trying to live Cervantes’ life (learning Early Modern Spanish, fighting against the Ottomans, etc.) but eventually decides that it would be better to write it from his own experiences. Against all the odds, and after numerous rewrites, he succeeds in writing a couple of chapters of Don Quixote himself. This is where Borges introduces his twist: he argues that Menard’s Don Quixote is more interesting than the original, in spite of being verbally identical to it. The point is that we read Don Quixote very differently if we think it was written by a 20th century Frenchman, rather than a 16/17th century Spaniard. A passage written by Cervantes means one thing; the same passage written by someone with an entirely different history can hardly be read in the same way. If this seems hard to understand, consider the opening of the Sermon on the Mount, from the Bible: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted. Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled. Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God. Now, imagine if this were said not by Jesus, but by a convicted murderer on death row. Doesn’t mean quite the same thing, does it? The art of writing is as much an art of rewriting and re-contextualising, as it is an art of writing things no-one has written before.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What's your review of the movie Poor Things?
Answer: I thought it was great. Like some viewers, I was already familiar with Alasdair Gray’s novel, having read it when it came out in paperback. Unlike perhaps many of the people who both knew the novel and liked Gray’s work, I thoroughly approved of what they did in the adaptation—basically, stripped out almost all the Scottishness and also the unreliable narrator elements, neither of which I thought were the best things about the novel in the first place. The only Lanthimos movie I’d already seen was The Favourite, which I thought was excellent. So I was looking forward to this, and I ended up watching it immediately after finishing Barbie, its mighty box office/award-season rival. First things first: if the Oscar had to go to either Margot Robbie or Emma Stone, it should have gone, and indeed did go, to Emma Stone. If there is one overriding reason to watch this movie, it’s not the costume or set design or the model shots or the general look of it. It’s Emma Stone’s performance as a woman growing up with zero sense of shame. I mean, there are all kinds of amusing things she does with her body to suggest the infantile brain inside the body of a grown woman, but for me, she cruises into the superlatives once her character, Bella, is aware and articulate enough to talk about what she wants and doesn't want, and likes and doesn’t like, with the bluntness of a small child but the precision of a Vulcan science officer. It’s things like the way she learns from her rakish-but-ultimately-inadequate lover Duncan (Mark Ruffalo) how to eat a Pastel de Nata, a custard-filled Portuguese pastry. He instructs her how it must be not be nibbled, but ‘inhaled with gusto, like life itself’, and manages to fold one with some delicacy into his mouth. Bella then stuffs an entire one into her own mouth, with the kind of ungainly relish not seen since Bill Murray in Groundhog Day consumed an entire cream cake, and immediately announces through a mouthful of pastry ‘Incredible. Who made these? We need more.’ He tells her that one is enough, but later, she goes walking around Lisbon by herself and proceeds to bolt down several more, whereupon she throws up, and then stares down at her own sick with a quizzical air of I see. Well, that happened. Or when she’s at dinner with Duncan and some strangers and starts casually discussing Duncan’s penis, because another guest made a coy allusion to her own husband’s one. ‘Duncan’s can sometimes be salty,’ Bella matter-of-factly informs her fellow diners. At another table, a baby starts crying. Bella looks around and announces ‘I must go punch that baby,’ gets up and starts stomping over to the unfortunate infant. And don’t even get me started on the dance scene, which starts off like it’s going to be endearingly but embarrassingly awkward, and then turns into pure awesome. I don’t quite know where Emma Stone reached to find this performance, but watching the film, I thought Yes, this is what someone would be like if they were truly not worried about other people thinking mean things about them. At one point, finding herself in Paris with Duncan and no money (she intended to give all Duncan’s money to poor people in Alexandria, but naively entrusted it to two dock workers to do it for her, the implication being that they kept it), she finds she can earn money as a sex worker. Having already had lots of good sex with Duncan, she decides that the sex here wasn’t so bad, so she asks the madame for a job ‘in your musty-smelling house of good-time fornication.’ Cue Bella having sex with multiple clients, including one guy who brings his teenage sons along to watch, as part of their education. The slightly awkward smile Stone gives them while he’s banging away on top of her has to be seen to be believed: Don’t worry, I’m sure your father won’t be too much longer. Bella is simply too much for Duncan, who can’t cope with her lack of patience with his latent concern for the rules of polite society (which he imagined he was flouting by running off with her in the first place.) Just as she is too much for her far more callous and unpleasant sort-of husband Alfie (it’s complicated), who turns up in the last twenty minutes, evidently determined to rob her of a happy ending. This was a marriage of many talents: Gray’s humane and amiable interest in innocence and experience, Lanthimos’ genius for stories about characters who are at odds with the rest of the world, and Stone’s what-the-hell, maximum-overdrive commitment to a character that required her actor to abandon all vanity. I mean yeah, everyone else is good, too. Willem Dafoe is as funny as he’s ever been as Bella’s ‘creator’, Godwin Baxter, calmly telling the horrifying stories of all his father’s hideous experiments on him. Ramy Youssef is as genuinely nice a Nice Guy as you’ll see in a movie: Max isn’t being nice to get a reward, he really is like that. Mark Ruffalo is glorious as poor Duncan, driven steadily mad by Bella’s imperturbability to his nonsense. And great as ever to see Kathryn Hunter as the heavily tattooed Madame Swiney, whose ruthlessness comes out when she sweetly informs another sex worker, Toinette, that because she complained about working conditions, she’s not getting paid for her next client. And even the great Hanna Schygulla, star of many classic Fassbinder movies, pops up as a sweet old lady on an ocean liner, who gives Bella some words of wisdom which annoy Duncan so much that he tries in vain to throw her into the sea. (Oh, Duncan. Just stop already.) But Emma Stone ruled this movie. One of my favourite performances of the decade. Poor Things is great. I liked Barbie, but this is so much more down my dark Victorian alley.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Can you recommend a few must-listen audiobooks?
Answer: James Joyce’s Ulysses, read by Jim Norton and Marcella Riordan. Jim Norton is a veteran Irish actor who some viewers of British/Irish TV comedy will remember as the fearsome Bishop Brennan from the 90s sitcom Father Ted. He won a Tony award in 2008 for his performance in Conor McPherson’s play The Seafarer on Broadway. He’s quite old now, but he recorded Ulysses in 1994, and his intelligence, skill and humour are a perfect way to help Ulysses slip down easily, without having the terrifying bulk of the yet-to-be-read pages still in one hand. Joyce was a musician, not a visual kind of writer, and his work always gains by being read aloud. If you’ve been wondering how to get into this book and are put off by its size and reputation, have a listen to Jim Norton reading it. There is another audiobook of Ulysses, read by the late great Donal Donnelly, who I had the honour to share a stage with in 1996. (His most visible role was probably Archbishop Gilday in The Godfather Part III, where he got shot by Al Neri and fell down a staircase.) A lovely man and a fine actor, but his reading of Ulysses is a little bit hammy for my taste. Jim Norton makes it sound natural, like a regular storybook.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Is bass easier than guitar?
Answer: I don’t think it’s a sensible question. Almost everyone will say Yes, it’s easier to get good at bass when you’re starting out. I’m not so sure. I think can be as easy to get basically presentable when you’re starting out on bass as it is to be basically presentable on guitar, depending on what kind of music you’re playing. If you’re playing indie rock, guitar is probably fractionally more difficult, but still easy. If you’re playing soul and R&B, bass is almost certainly more difficult. A pretty average guitarist can quickly learn to play Motown guitar parts, but Chuck Rainey himself admitted that James Jamerson’s part on the Four Tops’ ‘Bernadette’ has been known to cause him some problems. Anything else and it depends on the music. I’ve seen rock and metal bands where the guitar definitely involved a lot of showing off and the bass merely plodded along, but on the other hand, if you want to play John Myung’s or Steve Harris’ bass lines, you’re going to need to put in hundreds of hours. In jazz or jazz-rock, I don’t think it even makes sense to talk of either one being easier. I do think that a good bass player makes more difference to the general quality of the music than a good guitar player. There’s something dispiriting about a good guitar player in front of a mediocre rhythm section, but if the rhythm section is cooking, who cares? At least there’s a groove going on. But that good bass player only becomes good by putting in the hard work of learning what to play, and when to play it. And rhythmic styles change over time. Rhythm is perhaps the most important single factor in popular music: if you can’t get the rhythm right, it all sounds shit. I’m reading Dan Charnas’ excellent book Dilla Time, which among other things outlines how rhythms in popular music have changed since the 90s, becoming less on-the-nose and in-the-pocket, more edgy and unpredictable (or rather, predictable but in an entirely new way). If, like me, you grew up listening to James Brown and thinking you had it sorted, you need to keep up. So I would say, it depends entirely on what you want to play. And I would add, finally, that if all you want to do is show off, that’s a hell of a lot easier to do on the guitar.

Question: What’s the most recent show one has binge watched?
Answer: Extraordinary. I started it last week and finished it the other night. Well, it’s only two seasons (so far) and they have only eight episodes each. l to r… Look, I’ll explain later. Minor spoiler ahead (episode 1 only): Extraordinary is a TV comedy (more of a ‘dramatic comedy’), created by a Northern Irish screenwriter, Emma Moran. She began writing it while studying for her MA in screenwriting at Manchester University. It’s set in a world in which everyone has a superpower. Except one person. That person is Jen (above, on the right, played by Irish actor Máiréad Tyers), a 25-year-old worker in a costume shop in London. Her stepfather Ian can sense other people’s emotions, and her mum Mary is at least theoretically capable of controlling any technology, but only if she knows how it works. (At the beginning of the show she can’t even work her own phone, but she gets better.) Jen’s flatmate Carrie (second from right) can channel the spirits of the dead. She works for a legal firm, where she helps to sort out problematic wills by channelling dead people, who explain through her who they really want to leave their stuff to. Carrie’s boyfriend Kash (Bilal Hasna, lying on the back of the sofa) can turn back time. A bit. He can rewind a few minutes into the past, but this turns out to be less useful than it appears. And then there’s Jen’s dad, Martin (voiced by Ardal O’Hanlon, who was Father Dougal in Father Ted a long, long time ago), who’s kind and wise and who she has heartfelt phone chats with. … Except that, in episode one, Jen is in the middle of one of these phone chats when she comes back to her flat and opens Carrie’s bedroom door—and we see that Carrie is on the phone talking to her in Martin’s voice, because Martin is one of the dead people she routinely channels. Naturally, Jen knows that her father is dead; whenever Jen really needs to talk to him, Carrie channels him for her, as a special service for her friend. At the start of the show, Jen is being interviewed for a job, and the interviewer asks her how her journey was. Jen replies in full detail and at length, mentioning in passing that she’s sitting oddly because she’s worried that her tampon is falling out. Having done so, she looks startled, and the interviewer makes it clear that her superpower is that she can get people to tell the truth. Having not got the job, Jen returns to her own job at the costume store, where her manager Ange is a chain-smoking, no-nonsense fiftysomething whose superpower is that she has the body of an eleven-year-old girl. Ange (she shows up at about 0:53). In an early episode, Jen goes on a date with a rather nerdy guy named Gordon, whose superpower is that he can make other people have instant orgasms just by touching them. He discovered this when he was playing football with his previously estranged dad and they shook hands afterwards, with rather embarrassing consequences. The date ends very badly, because Gordon absolutely refuses to use his power to enhance sex, instead putting on gloves, which neutralise it, ‘so that I can feel like I did it myself.’ Then the stray cat that Jen adopted touches its paw to his face while he’s asleep, which in turn leads the cat to be named Jizzlord. (Later, Carrie, who’s upset that her boyfriend is neglecting her in favour of his rubbish vigilante group, goes to see Gordon and persuades him to give her just one orgasm by touching his fingertip to hers. In the end, she decides not to go through with it, and when he says he feels useless, she tells him that he has a great gift, and he should use it. After she’s left his flat, there’s a knock on the door, and he answers it to a rather sketchy middle-aged woman in a grubby tank top smoking a cigarette. You the cum man? she says. Yes. Yes, I am, he says, and opens his door to let her in.) All of this works because, first, the writing is really fun. Everyone has a superpower but they only have the one, and sometimes they’re rather useless. One man has the power to ‘change anything into a PDF’. What, not just Word documents? he’s asked. Anything, he says ominously. Jen goes to a dentist whose superpower is that people generate their own background music around her, so when Jen goes to see her, the background music becomes ominous, atonal and creepy, like a horror film. The dentist looks mildly exasperated. Not surprisingly, anyone who’s got a conventional superpower like flight or super-speed is a smug dick about it. But also, the performances are great. Máiréad Tyers reminds me of basically everyone I went to school with—well, the likeable ones, anyway. But Jen is a complex character, rather selfish and impatient and with major issues that need sorting out, and the show is partly about how she does that. Carrie’s actress, Sofia Oxenham, is remarkable: when she’s channelling people, the only change in her physical appearance is that she gets glowing blue eyes, but otherwise she physically becomes whoever she’s channelling before your eyes, whether it’s a grumpy old man, or a horribly misogynistic country singer, or a batshit crazy Hollywood starlet from the 30s, or Ardal O’Hanlon, or even Adolf Hitler, who she channels when Jen’s feeling gloomy, so that the flatmates can all taunt him. And the stories have a genuine arc. Jen wants to develop her own superpower and can’t understand why she doesn’t have one yet. Carrie is, at the start, a weak-willed doormat who exists only to oblige others. Kash is a manchild who needs to stop sponging off her. And the guy sitting on the floor in the photo is actually the cat, Jizzlord, who is a man who turned into a cat three years ago, for initially unexplained reasons, and has spent so long as one that he’s forgotten his previous life. (Who he was is part of the story of season 2.) Finally, Jen’s mum Mary is played by the great Siobhan McSweeney, who was the wonderfully sarcastic head nun Sister Michael in Derry Girls a few years ago. Here, she’s playing someone completely different but no less memorable. Fine show. Season 2 ends on a massive cliffhanger, which will hopefully be explained if there is a season 3.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Who’s your favorite band from Manchester?
Answer: That’s very easy. Amplifier, a sort of prog-metal band. I’m not even sure which members are depicted above, except that I know that the guy second from the right is Sel Balamir, the guitarist, lead singer and main songwriter. One of the bald guys on the left is drummer Matt Brobin; I’m not sure which. Right now, the lineup seems to be Balamir and Brobin and nobody else. My older brother told me about this band because he thought I’d like them. He is the metal fan of either of us. I duly bought their 2005 EP The Astronaut Dismantles HAL, and swiftly fell in love with the lead track, ‘Continuum’: I am honestly not a big fan of this genre of music, but I utterly fell in love with this song. I think partly because it’s a song about music itself, but also because of the unforced ease and power and naturalness of the songwriting and performing. To me, it’s a perfect unity. It just works. It also had something to do with Balamir’s faintly Ozzy-esque voice: he has that slight edge of emotional detachment, coupled with full commitment, that Ozzy has, like he’s not quite of this world, but he’s determined to understand it as well as he can. Plus there’s the awesome bit whenever he goes ‘JUST LISTEN!’ And at 5:30, the song just deconstructs itself and goes into a whole new thing. Culminating, at 7:06, with the extraordinary ‘Que sera sera’ bit, which rounds it off and brings the whole song to a close. I listened to this song obsessively, almost every day between 2013 and 2015 or so. I’m not sure why. It just spoke to me. Possibly because it took almost exactly as long to listen to, as it took me to walk to work, at the time. The whole EP is a blinder. My brother later gave me their 2010 album The Octopus, a sprawling concept album about something or other—I couldn’t be bothered to figure out what, but I loved the sound of it. I have to admit that, since then, I’ve only intermittently kept up with them. But everything I’ve listened to since then has confirmed me that this is one of the most underrated bands in the UK. Certainly many orders of magnitude better than literally every other band from Manchester that I have ever listened to. Without exception. Yes, you know who I mean. I would consign them all to the memory hole, as long as I get to keep ‘Continuum’. Don’t try to be cute in the comments. This is literally the only Manchester band that I have ever liked.

Question: What do Americans hate the most about America?
Answer: Allow me to present the testimony of one eminent American. Frank Zappa. The documentary Eat That Question: Frank Zappa In His Own Words features an interview with Zappa from I think the late 70s or early 80s, in which he says the following (my transcription but you’re welcome to look it up): The thing that sets the Americans apart from the rest of the cultures in the world is, we’re so fucking stupid. This country’s been around for a couple of hundred years and we think we’re hot shit. And— and we don’t even realise that the other countries have thousands of years of history and culture. And they’re proud of it. And when we deal, on an international level, with, uh, foreign policy and stuff like that, we try to go in and say ‘Oh, big American, strong country’ and all that stuff, they must laugh up their sleeves at us, because we are nothing. We’re culturally nothing. We mean nothing. We’re only interested in the bottom line. Y’know… every other country has their own art, their own music, their own theater, their own drama, their folk dances, folk songs, folk lore. It means something to them, they’re proud of it and that’s their ethnic heritage. We have Levi’s, we have designer jeans, we have hamburgers, we have Coca-Cola, we have REO Speedwagon, we have Journey, we have this one and we have that one and then we go out there and we say ‘Yeah, but we also have neutron bombs and poison gas, so maybe that makes up for it.’ I mean… it’s really kinda sad, when you evaluate it that way. And I think that a country that doesn't do something to sustain its culture, whatever it is, doesn’t invest in it, doesn’t keep it happening, isn’t proud of it… maybe they just shouldn’t exist. Because it’s the culture, the beautiful things that society produces, those are the things that should survive for thousands of years. Not the designer jeans.

Question: When women say "I'm indignant" is what they feel indignity? Such words were made up by men to describe male emotions. Indignity is derived from dignitas: The face or standing of men in Roman society. Should we coin seperate words for female feelings?
Answer: Hey, Alper Kaan Bilir. I feel like we have to have a little chat. You see, words are not the same as the things they are the word for. Most people already know that. Therefore, words for emotions are not the same as the emotions themselves. This means, in turn, that the emotions are not inextricably linked to the etymology of the words we use for them. The inanity of your question becomes a lot clearer when we consider that different languages have different words for things. With different origins. One of the Irish words for ‘indignant’ is feargach, which is related to fearg, the Irish word for ‘angry’. Now, the Irish word fear means ‘man’. But fearg has nothing to do with fear. It’s descended from an Old Irish word, ferg, meaning ‘anger’, which in turn comes from Proto-Celtic *wergā, which is ultimately descended from the Proto-Indo-European root *werg-, meaning ‘make’. Nothing to do with the ‘standing of men in Roman society’ blah blah blah. Once again, repeat after me: Words are not the things that they stand for. Or, to put it more simply for your benefit: The word ‘indignant’ is not an emotion.

Question: Why did John and Paul prevent George from adding more songs to their albums?
Answer: They did so by a very underhand method: they wrote a lot more good songs than he did. Lennon and McCartney started writing songs in their teens; they had been trying to write songs since before they even met each other. Harrison didn’t start writing them until the Beatles were already beginning to be famous, several years later. As a result, he had a lot less practice than they did. By the time the band became famous, L & McC had evolved a writing practice that was occasionally the two of them together, head-to-head, co-writing as they went, but more often one of them writing the bones of a song and the other one helping him to finish it. As time went by, they almost entirely stopped completely co-writing, but they kept the ‘one starts a song then the other one helps him finish it’ method to the end of the Beatles’ career. Harrison just had Harrison. As a result, not all of his songs are, to put it tactfully, all that great. Especially not the early ones. By the time he was writing anything indisputably fresh, original and 100% effective—which in my view was ‘Taxman’ on Revolver, a unique fusion of British beat music and Stax-style R&B (with a little added flavour of Indian music, courtesy of McCartney’s guitar solo)—it was already 1966, and the other two were at the peak of their powers. Under the circumstances, they weren’t exactly in the mood to hold their own songs back, so that he could get sub-standard ditties like ‘Only a Northern Song’ or ‘Blue Jay Way’ onto an album. (Yes, I know those songs have their fans, but I don’t know why.) They had enough songs between them that there was precious little space on albums as it was. Revolver is the first Beatles album to have more than two George songs, and all his songs deserve to be on that album because he was finally finding his voice as a songwriter. Let’s not forget that ‘Only a Northern Song’ was his first attempt at writing a song for Sgt Pepper, and it was rejected because it was thought to be not good enough, which indeed, it isn’t. The rejection forced him to up his game, and he came up with the brilliant ‘Within You Without You’, one of the most original songs the band ever did. The next time they tried to make an album, circumstances were such that all of the three regularly songwriting Beatles were determined to get as many songs on it as they possibly could, and the result is the should-it-have-been-a-single-album White Album. (For the record, I think the White Album’s imperfections are part of what’s worthwhile about it.) … And before you know it, it’s 1969 and he’s finally writing songs that are easily as good as anything by the other two. But by then, the band was starting to break up. If George had wanted to get more songs on Beatles albums, yes, it could be argued (as Lennon did to McCartney in the ‘secret interview’ scene from Get Back) that the other two should have encouraged him more. But also, he should have written more good songs.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: You have to choose one religion. Which do you choose?
Answer: Ahh… one of the ones they practiced in ancient Greece, I think. Or Rome. Not a huge amount of difference. They didn’t have one single religion in ancient Greece, but a bunch of related religious practices. It’s more a question of observing the practices and doing the rites, not so much about actually believing in anything. I certainly wouldn’t choose one of the big three monotheisms: Judaism, Christianity or Islam. My reason is that I’m wary of the whole idea that God is fundamentally just, which I agree with George Steiner in The Death of Tragedy was one of the great contributions of Judaism to Western religion, and which can therefore be seen in Christianity and Islam too, insofar as they inherited the basic concept. I recognise that the idea of a just God lies behind the appeal of all three of these religions, and of course I believe that justice is (on the whole) a good thing. But, see, I don’t think that humans are very good at handling the idea of a divine being who is omnipotent, and also the source of both justice and mercy. Oh, and also infallible. I think that bitter experience has shown that, once people start thinking God is just, they start thinking So therefore God’s side is the side with justice on it. So then, they start to think, Well, I’m on God’s side, so my side must be the side with justice on it. And then they start acting like their own side is the saved, and everyone else’s is the damned. And then they start to think that, insofar as they’ve been victorious thus far, it must be because God favours them. And then they start to think they’re always justified. And then you have people who end up committing horrendous atrocities, because they think that God is on their side, and therefore it’s okay. I prefer justice to be something that has nothing to do with god. Just as I prefer ethics to have nothing to do with religion. Religion always messes up the discussion. But the question is about what religion you’d take if you had to have one. If I have to have one, I want one which doesn’t flatter me. The Greek gods, and their Roman adaptations, were more capricious than YHWH. They favoured you until they didn’t. Maybe you annoyed them, or perhaps they wanted to pay back some score against somebody else, possibly a human or a rival god. And then you were screwed. In Vergil’s Aeneid, my favourite work of classical literature, Juno torments the Trojans and puts them through hell, simply because a Trojan prince, Paris, didn’t pick her in a beauty contest. She only lays off in the last pages of the last book, because her husband Jupiter basically says Oh stop it, you’ve had your fun. Her price for stopping is that the Trojans will become the Romans and be great, etc. etc., but they must lose their name and identity, and adopt those of the people they’re currently defeating in battle, the Latiums. The misfortunes of the Trojans happen not because of Juno dealing out justice, but Juno being spiteful. The wheel turns. What was once high up gets cast down. Justice has little to do with it. All you can do is hope that the gods will, someday, get around to favouring you once again. Out of their bottomless caprice. This is not a very healthy attitude in general, because it tends to encourage a rather toxic kind of stoicism, rather than working to fix injustices. But as religious attitudes go, I think it’s less likely to lead to the believer getting a swollen head, and thinking that God is always on their side, and that they will earn their reward for believing, one way or another. Other cultures have been more healthily sceptical of the whole idea. The great Chinese epic Romance of the Three Kingdoms has the unforgettable opening lines: Empires arise from chaos and empires collapse back into chaos. This we have known since time began. It is ὕβρις to believe otherwise.

Question: Why do LGBTQ people make their orientation their sole identity and personality?
Answer: This is a stupid question, Clark El, and if you’d stopped to think for a second you’d have come up with the answer. It’s because you don’t know any LGBTQ people, or the ones you do know you don’t like, and so don’t care to know better, and therefore the only time you encounter us is when we’re talking about LGBTQ issues which you’d prefer not to know about. Or when you’re seeing us in the news doing something LGBTQ-related. I am queer and that fact makes up about 10% of who I am. The rest of me is consumed by being a father, a worker, a citizen, a writer, a musician, a home cook, a middle-aged white guy, etc. I am not currently dating anyone or looking to date anyone, or seeking casual hookups with anyone. I go on being attracted to men and women because I just am. It takes up next to none of my time. The real question is, why do you make hating people who you imagine to be entirely unlike you your sole identity and personality? That is, when you aren’t posting dick pics or fantasising about topless Indian girls.

Question: Why do people say Labour and Tories offer nothing to Scotland and are in fact English puppet parties and not really Scottish at all?
Answer: Because neither Labour nor the Tories have demonstrated the slightest interest in specifically Scottish issues or values. The Conservative party in Scotland is a joke. Its only vaguely competent leader in recent years has been Ruth Davidson, and the toxic and provincial atmosphere of Scottish political discourse, in which the most trivial problems are inflated to maximum drama, and the animosities on the independence issue, which have become ludicrously hateful on the anti-independence side, have driven out politicians with normal intelligence and sensibilities, like Davidson, who might have preferred a calmer conversation. In the next election, Labour in Scotland may well get some rebound votes from floating voters who are simply bored with the SNP being in power. The SNP itself has struggled with the damned-if-you-do, damned-if-you-don’t nature of Scottish politics: it has failed to broadcast its successes, which have been multiple but not as big and dramatic as the ones people expected of it, such as the independence issue itself, because after the referendum that has been blocked at every conceivable turn; but if it had broadcast its successes, it would have been screamed at for wasting public money on doing so, whether it had done so or not. As an Irishman living in Scotland who is pro-Scottish independence, I am increasingly of the opinion that Scotland is nowhere near ready for independence. It deserves it, and should have it, but the Scottish public is divided into those who want it, who are on the whole humane and intelligent but who lack the ability to persuade the rest, and those who don’t want it, who tend to be either enslaved to the idea of their own Britishness, or who don’t want to abandon the time-honoured Scottish habit of moaning about things that they can’t actually bear to get rid of. In Ireland, back in the day, we knew what to do. I don’t think that the Scottish people, on the whole, have the cojones to do it.

Question: Were there any artists before or during Bach and Beethoven’s time who were underappreciated and/or ahead of their time in terms of their writing and producing?
Answer: Bach and Beethoven didn’t have a ‘time’. Bach died twenty years before Beethoven was born. That’s quite a long time in terms of the music history of the period. Neither of them were ‘producers’, as recording technology had not yet been invented. I think I know what you’re wondering about, but no, there are no wiggy geniuses from the period 1685–1827 (Bach’s birth-Beethoven’s death) who sound like they came from 100 years later and who, as a result, were spurned by the editors of Rotating Megalith, the music industry journal of 18th century London. You would need to calibrate this question so that it makes sense in terms of the music of the period in question.

Question: If the works of Beethoven disappeared, like the works on the Beatles in the file 'Yesterday', would the person that reintroduced them be held in the same regard? Or would their work be considered dated and uninspired?
Answer: This is unanswerable, for exactly the same reason that the movie Yesterday doesn’t work. Here’s my review of that movie: The gist of the review is that the movie took the Beatles’ music out of history, but it failed to remove every trace of the Beatles’ influence from history, and the result was that the entire history of popular music in the alternate history presented in the movie is almost exactly the same as it is in our universe, except that the Beatles didn’t make their music. Which therefore prompts the question, why, in this alternate version of history, did music after the period in which the Beatles didn’t exist, change in exactly the same way that it did in the true history in which the Beatles did exist? The result was a nonsensical conception of music history, in which music behaved as if the Beatles had existed, except that they hadn’t existed. Which makes no sense. Likewise, if you remove Beethoven’s music from music history, but you don’t touch the subsequent history of music to reflect that he never happened—which job of unknitting Beethoven’s influence from music would be a gargantuan and impossible task—you’ve not really removed Beethoven’s music from history. You would be left with a version of music history in which an inexplicable phenomenon occurred between the late 18th and early 19th century, which caused music to change course in many important ways, among them the collapse of the traditional patronage system, and composers like Brahms feeling like they had to live up to a standard that… had never actually existed. So what we’re left with is a nonsensical question that we can’t answer. This is where alternate histories cease to be interesting and become silly. So there’s no sensible answer to this question. It’s just stupid, because it’s based on an idiotic premise—namely, that erasing a highly important musician from history will not have massive knock-on effects on the subsequent history of the music.

Question: What key experiences at the Cooper School of Art and the Art Institute of Pittsburgh shaped Nash’s artistic journey and his choice to work with clay?
Answer: Well, Jay-Ar Pangilinan, I don’t know who ‘Nash’ was, or what his experiences at the Cooper School of Art and the Art Institute of Pittsburgh were, but I’m guessing that his failed experiments to work with parmesan foam as a medium tell their own story. And then there was the incident with the Turkish language DVD of Caddyshack 2, the park ranger and the hand-cranked coffee mill, which permanently put him off the post-Impressionists, as it would anyone. And then his 27-second marriage to Deborah alienated him from the art establishment of the day, many of whom were at the reception and had spent a lot of money on gifts, most of which Nash kept and then pawned. But ultimately, his choice to work with Clay was influenced by Clay’s long, reaching jab, his extremely fast combinations, his unrivalled ability to defeat his opponents mentally, and of course Clay’s brilliant use of forced perspective in his frescoes for the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua, which gave maximum dramatic effect to his compositions. The Clay/Nash partnership was rewarding for both men, although Nash broke off relations when Clay converted to the Nation of Islam and changed his name to Muhammad Do Your Own Homework.
