Question: How do I write a character’s physical description without it feeling unnatural and clunky? I’m able to describe their hair and body relatively easily because my writing puts emphasis on small movements and fidgeting, but I can’t describe faces.
Answer: Well, here’s Thomas Wolfe to show you how not to do it. Case Study #1: Thomas Wolfe Thanks, Thomas. The problem with the above is— Case Study #1a because he wouldn’t shut up: Thomas Wolfe FFS, Thomas Wolfe, enough with the face-describing! The problems with the above are manifold. (It goes on for two more pages.) One is that Wolfe is determined to tell you what the person looked like, and so the story grinds to a standstill while he does that. Another is that he is determined to emphasise how this character’s inner soul is reflected in her face, perhaps by way of justifying why he’d described it in the first place. But he’s just telling us this stuff. You know when people say ‘Show, don’t tell’? Thomas Wolfe was an incorrigible teller of stuff. The other problem is specific to Wolfe himself: the reason why he was determined to tell you what his characters looked like is that they were based on people he knew—family members, friends, neighbours—and he was heroically but idiotically determined to render them in fiction with as much completeness and detail as he possibly could. Please tell us that you’re not also describing what a character’s face looks like, as if it directly reflects their innermost soul. I would echo Rachel Neumeier’s question in her fine answer: Why do you want to write a character’s physical description? Why do we need to know what they look like at all? What’s it got to do with the story? If I think of classic novels that I admire, like Kafka’s The Trial, or Melville’s Moby-Dick, in neither of those novels do I ever find out what the protagonist looks like. Why? Because it’s completely irrelevant to the story that Melville wants to tell. But that doesn’t mean that a character’s physical appearance is always completely irrelevant. Case Study #2: Naguib Mahfouz In the great Egyptian novelist Naguib Mahfouz’s 1956 novel Palace Walk, the first volume of his Cairo Trilogy, the physical appearance of the two principal characters, Ahmad Abd Al-Jawad and his wife Amina, is sketched fairly quickly but in detail in the first few pages. The book opens with Amina waiting for her husband to come home after a night on the town, and she is described as looking slender and still beautiful, whereas he is extremely well-groomed and also very overweight—because he doesn’t need to bother to keep in shape, since he has an extremely obedient and, indeed, subservient wife, who gets up every night at midnight, and waits up for him to come home around 1am, so that she can tend to his needs (i.e. take his socks off, among other things) and make sure he goes to bed in comfort. This is because Amina’s submission to her husband is one of the themes of Palace Walk, and indeed the trilogy as a whole. He is a complacent and immensely confident philanderer, whereas she lives as though he is her faithful and wonderful husband, and her role is to treat him as though he’s perfect. She overlooks things like the obvious evidence that he’s been drinking wine all night, which is frowned upon for someone who claims to be as good a Muslim as he is, because she thinks he’s flawless. So, in terms of Mahfouz’s artistic intentions, it makes sense for us to know that Amina is portrayed as someone who, under other circumstances, wouldn’t need to be content with such a patriarchal asshole as Ahmad, but she is anyway—and that’s one of the things that drives the story. Physical appearance should be worth mentioning if it matters to the story. Is the story set in a world where visible ethnic differences matter? Is it about sexual attraction? Then physical appearance may well play an important role, and could be worth mentioning. There could be other cases. Is a character well-known for having an unusual appearance? Then it’s worth mentioning. But if the story is mostly about what goes on inside the characters, and their physical appearance isn’t really that relevant… why mention it? If a character is a bit out of physical shape, there’s no need to point this out in advance. In the Irish novelist Emma Donoghue’s second novel Hood, the protagonist and narrator, Cara, is supposed to be rather on the large side, but the only way we know this is that she talks about how she habitually sweats and chafes, and gets red in the face, whenever she has to do even minimal exercise, plus (iirc) a couple of casual remarks by her deceased lover. She never actually tells us what she looks like. (Donoghue went on to write the award-winning novel Room, which was later made into a 2015 movie of the same name, for which Brie Larson won the Best Actress Oscar, and Donoghue was nominated for the Oscar for her own screenplay.) In the end, we always return to the same question: What do you want to do? Do you feel it’s absolutely necessary to tell the reader what characters look like? If so, why? What’s so important about their appearance that you have to describe them to us? Because, as I hope I’ve shown, some of the greatest writers ever have not been bothered to describe what their characters look like. So, does this really need to be a problem? Free yourself from the need to describe what your characters look like. You might find it liberating.

Question: What do you think of the Quora group "It's Ok to Be White" for people who are proud of being white?
Answer: For a long time, I was missing something about the idea of being ‘proud to be white’, and I myself missed it for a long time. It’s that it’s not really about the mere colour of one’s skin. It’s about ‘whiteness’. In the following answer, when I talk about white people, I will use the second person plural, because I am a white person. ‘Whiteness’ is not so much a skin colour as an ideology. It involves a lot of assumptions about history and society, and I think part of being proud of one’s ‘whiteness’ entails accepting all or at least many of these assumptions. White people who do not embrace them tend to be regarded by those who do as ‘self-hating’, or by the real hardcore whiteness fans as ‘race traitors’. And yet, you do not need to be a white person to embrace ‘whiteness’. There are plenty of white people who will accept people of colour as, at best, temporary camp followers, if they are willing to espouse the ‘whiteness’ thing. One way to start considering ‘whiteness’ is to think of sentiments, or propositions, or ideas, that we don’t associate with it. Here are some things that you don’t tend to hear from ‘whiteness’ fans: You do, however, tend to hear this kind of thing: Every single one of these statements can be, and has been, comprehensively refuted, or at the very least dismissed as a hopelessly ignorant and bigoted misrepresentation of a far more complex reality. For example, white people who claim that white people have had a superior civilisation tend to be completely ignorant of other civilisations, and of the conditions in which civilisations arise in the first place, and of the vital exchanges between civilisations that have occurred all along. But, I’d like to touch on three themes in particular. Let’s leave aside, for now, the vast question of what ‘civilisations’ are, and how much they transfer learning and experience between each other, and how much so-called ‘Western civilisation’ owes to other civilisations, who discovered things and had ideas that made later things and ideas even possible. Not to mention all the resources that ‘Western civilisation’ took from the lands and peoples it conquered, and then how we used those resources to feed and fuel and enrich ourselves. It’s a little difficult to see why, if we white people today are entitled to be proud of the positive things that previous generations of white people have unquestionably achieved, we must also however forget about the negative effects our forebears had upon the world, on the grounds that it was a long time ago and we didn’t do it ourselves. (The idea that we had the best intentions can be easily refuted with a quick skim of the documentary evidence.) Because we do think like that: If we still enjoy any of the benefits of our ancestors’ greed and exploitive nature—maybe through inherited wealth or property, or social and legal systems that were created to benefit us—we don’t get to pretend that we’re not still implicated in the exploitation. However, it can also be argued that that’s not a very profitable line of argument. Why? Because it makes the conversation about whether or not white people ought to be ‘proud’ of being white, or not. And that problem is the same problem that ‘whiteness’ fans always rally around, whenever it comes to discussions about race, racism, inequality and justice. What many, many white people tend to do, whenever those discussions get into areas that we aren’t personally comfortable with, is that we switch the entire conversation away from talk about inequality and justice and systems and repair. And instead, we make the whole conversation about our own hurt feelings. Because god forbid white people should feel the least bit uncomfortable talking about these matters. This is why some white people become connoisseurs of minor injustices against white people: because the least slight against a white person that can be shown to issue from prejudice is so vastly more heinous than whatever happens to anyone else, that all efforts to help other people must come to a halt until all prejudice against white people is eradicated from the face of the earth. Only when we white people feel safe and comfortable, can we get around to taking anyone else’s problems seriously. Why? Because until then, someone, somewhere, is thinking mean thoughts about us. And, given our immeasurably and unquestionably superior contribution to the world, that is simply unacceptable to us. I think the space ‘It’s OK to be White’ is populated by people who cannot stand the idea that someone, somewhere, doesn’t automatically admire them for being white. And the reason why they’re like that is that they subscribe to ‘whiteness’, and consider themselves intrinsically more admirable than other people, because of the false history they have chosen to believe in, and the unpleasant facts that they prefer to ignore. White people who dislike the idea of white supremacism tend to conceptualise it as white people violently suppressing people of colour, by means of trained dogs, fire hoses, truncheons and worse things. And since they don’t personally call for those things to be used, or at least they don’t do so out loud, they therefore think Well, I’m not white supremacist. I’m not racist. I’m simply looking at the facts. But white supremacism is, among other things, the conviction that white people deserve to have more power than others, and that people of colour do not deserve to have as much power, because they’re not as important: they’re only ‘minorities’. White supremacism means ignoring people when they speak. It means applying double standards to public officials: ignoring the felonies of mediocre white men, but calling Kamala Harris a ‘slut who slept her way to the top’. It means relentlessly minimising other people’s achievements. It means denying other people’s histories. It means constantly raising the same topics over and over again, to ensure that the conversation is only ever about what’s wrong with black people and why it’s their fault, never connected to anything we did. It is the tone taken by people who simply assume that it’s their god-given right to be in charge. And that’s what I think of ‘It’s OK to be white’. I think it’s a space for people who believe that it’s their god-given right to be in charge. And that’s white supremacism.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What is your review of The Office (U.S. TV series)?
Answer: The main cast of The Office, US version, season 3, except for the black-haired woman at the back on the left, a minor supporting character who doesn’t really belong in this photo but I guess she was there on the day. I have a theory about the US version of The Office, which I think illuminates both versions, but which also might illuminate: It’s rather elaborate, though, so if you’re in a hurry, please bookmark this for reading later. Otherwise, get a beverage and take a seat. Let’s grab this thing and shake it until we get some results. … That’s what she said. One of the things that more recent American sitcoms have liked to do is show the characters growing. A situation is set up, things go wrong, there are amusing complications and after 24 or so minutes it winds up with what the creators of Seinfeld mocked as ‘hugging and learning’. I myself think Seinfeld is about as funny as watching a family pet get hit by a car, but they made a good point about the way sitcoms have to reset between episodes. If characters grow and learn too much, they will no longer be foolish enough to get into the situations where they can be funny. For the sitcom to be funny, Basil Fawlty cannot learn to stop being a fawning snob; Father Ted Crilly can never priest up and take his job seriously; Ross in Friends can never quite lose the stick up his butt. Seinfeld itself deferred its characters from learning anything for so long that the only way they could finally end the show was to send the characters to prison. Both versions of The Office, however, featured personal growth in their characters. In the UK version, Dawn learned the self-confidence to dump Lee and find Tim. Gareth became a semi-decent manager. And David Brent met a woman who liked him, and finally acquired the balls to tell Chris Finch to fuck off—my favourite moment in the UK version. Perhaps only Tim didn’t grow, but only because he started out relatively mature. The US version, however, took the idea of ‘growth’ and hugely expanded and elaborated on it. Which made it more ambitious and, I think, ultimately more impressive than the UK version. Which brings me to my theory. My theory about the US version of The Office is that it works, on one level, as a spiritual epic about the development of personhood from infancy to maturity. Now, I’m sure that this will hardly come as a surprise. Obviously, Michael Scott develops enormously from his beginning in season 1 to his end in season 7. He begins as an utterly self-absorbed manchild, with poor relationships with other people and a weak but malicious sense of humour, which switches itself off whenever he feels like people are laughing at him, rather than at his crappy jokes. However, by the end, he is in a happy and secure marriage with someone who loves him, and indeed they have children, of whom he is so proud that he owns two phones, just to hold all the pictures of them. (This was before cloud storage really took off.) But, you see, my theory is that The Office is not primarily about the development of Michael’s soul. It’s also about the development of Dwight’s. Obviously, Michael is the biggest manchild in the office: the character who most desperately needs to grow up. But Dwight, at least in the first two seasons, is his loyal lieutenant. What does it say about you when you’re so loyal to such an idiot? I think it says that you have so much more to unlearn. For much of the show, Michael oscillates between childish self-absorption and selfishness, and an almost palpable and rather endearing adoration of, or at least startling empathy for, his employees. But, while Michael in season 2’s ‘Christmas Party’ is mostly a whiny, selfish idiot, in the following episode, ‘Booze Cruise’, he yaws between his worst and his best. He takes the staff on a booze cruise, where Jim is crushed that Pam’s fiancé Roy finally sets a date for their wedding. Jim admits to Michael that he’s dejected about this, but Michael, who himself has been humiliated over the captain of their vessel putting him in his place, is surprisingly encouraging: Michael: Yep. Well, Pam is cute. Jim: Yeah. She's really funny, and she's warm. And she's just... well, anyway. Michael: Well, if you like her so much, don't give up. Jim: She's engaged. Michael: BFD. Engaged ain't married. Jim: Huh. Michael: Never, ever, ever give up. In the episode ‘Email Surveillance’, Michael muses on his relationship with his staff: There's always a distance between a boss and the employees. It is just nature's rule. It's intimidation mostly, it's the awareness that they are not me. I do think that I am very approachable, as one of the guys. But the whole point of that episode is that Michael spends it completely failing to realise that his employees are not him. He can’t perceive boundaries. Michael Scott in season 1 craves something or other, but we’re not sure what. By season 2, his character comes into more focus, and we can see that what he really wants is, like all children, to be loved. But the story as a whole puts Michael in the position of a father to the family of his employees. Which is a role Michael has to grow into, because he is comically unfit for it. He wants all the power and love that a benevolent father might get, but for the longest time he can’t give it back, because he’s obsessed with his need to be given it first. However, not all of his employees realise this: only the relatively grown-up ones, such as Jim and Pam. Dwight does not realise it. So, as long as Michael doesn’t grow up, Dwight can’t. In an early episode, Dwight, who as usual is trying to make some wrongheaded point according to his arcane private code, asks Ryan what Michael’s greatest fear is. ‘Loneliness,’ Ryan astutely replies. ‘Maybe women.’ ‘Wrong,’ says Dwight, his eyes gleaming with triumph. ‘Michael Scott isn’t afraid of anything. Also, I would have accepted “snakes”.’ Dwight will pay, elsewhere, for not understanding his ‘father’ better. The responsible children: Jim and Pam Jim and Pam are uneasy in that they know, on some level, that they are mere subordinate players in the drama of Michael’s personal development, and are eager for him to grow up so that they can get the hell out of there. Both of them know Michael’s habits extraordinarily well, because he’s as predictable as an infant. If he eats a family-sized chicken pot pie for lunch, he will fall asleep. If he eats a lot of sugar, he will have a manic sugar rush and then, sure enough, fall asleep. Stanley and Phyllis are the uncle and aunt, although Stanley in particular is uneasy in that role because he wants nothing to do with Michael’s development. In Michael’s mind, Stanley is a sassy, street-smart black mentor to him, not the grumpy white-collar worker that Stanley actually is. Michael treats Phyllis as if she is the office’s resident elderly woman, although, as Phyllis points out, they were in high school together. Whenever Phyllis behaves like an ordinary middle-aged woman with ordinary needs, Michael is squicked out. (There’s one moment early on where she does an expert dancer’s shimmy, and Michael practically runs out of the room; in her youth, Phyllis Smith was a burlesque performer.) Remember Phyllis’ wedding, where Michael behaved as though he were simultaneously her father and her son? Running around wanting attention, yet also presuming to take charge of proceedings? Dwight is the other-son, the disappointment to Michael, the one who actually gives Michael the loyalty and love Michael craves but which Michael in this instance doesn’t want, because it comes from Dwight. Michael is aware that Dwight is himself highly immature, as witnessed by Dwight’s extreme gullibility and his susceptibility to Jim’s pranks. Jim represents something Michael needs: Dwight, in the early seasons, represents something Michael wants to avoid. If Jim is the golden boy, Dwight is the Tin Man. He thinks he’s on a quest, which is to do awesome things in life, like be a karate expert, or a supervillain: actually, he just needs to grow a heart. Dwight’s estrangement from the world of society has something to do how he seems to belong to a different century. In season 5 ep 5, ‘Crime Aid’, he mentions that Angela has ‘introduced’ him to, among other things, pasteurised milk, sheets and monotheism. It’s as if the Schrutes are some weird, inbred, Lovecraftian clan, and Dwight has a mutant brother who dwells beneath the beets. Dwight’s immaturity rears its head in season 3’s ‘The Coup’, where he mistakes the story he is in for a political thriller, instead of a family drama. Angela encourages him to take over the office from Michael, so Dwight arranges a meeting in a diner with Jan where he lays out his idea that she should make him manager. I thought it was interesting that, in this meeting, Dwight is stuffing his face with waffles and sausage, whereas Jan confines herself to sipping coffee. This subtly emphasises how needy and appetite-driven Dwight is, and how cool and collected Jan is (at this point in the show, anyway.) Dwight mistakes himself for someone with the same status as Michael. He expects Jan to calculate that he would be a suitable replacement and behave accordingly. Jan, who knows that she is not in a political thriller, interprets Dwight’s demand not as a power move but as ordinary insubordination, and bluntly instructs Michael to get his office in order. And here’s where the family dynamic plays out. Michael treats Dwight’s professional betrayal of him as something intensely personal and familial. Dwight’s excuse for leaving the office to meet Jan was that he was at the dentist, so Michael, simmering with barely concealed rage, asks him the dentist’s name: Dwight, who is terrible at deception, can only come up with ‘Crentist’. Michael proceeds to closely inspect Dwight’s teeth (this scene is so weird) and eventually confronts him with the knowledge that he knows everything. A humbled Dwight grovels pathetically on the floor, sobbing. The emotion in this scene goes way beyond anything necessary for a boss reprimanding an employee. But a) it’s funny to see Dwight’s hubris go boing and rebound in his face, and b) it underlines Michael’s quasi-paternal relationship to Dwight. It’s an Oedipal situation, except Oedipus doesn’t kill Laius: he just unsuccessfully tries to take over the office from him. (Michael may also be unconsciously disturbed that Dwight went behind his back to Jan, who Michael regards—not very accurately—as a former lover.) When, in season 4’s ‘Did I Stutter?’, Stanley is publicly insubordinate to Michael in a less serious way, Michael is able to recognise that Stanley is not part of his line of succession, and is able to take Stanley aside, admit that he knows Stanley doesn’t respect him, and tell him that, nevertheless, Stanley can’t talk to him like that. Stanley, perhaps relieved to be recognised for once as who he is, agrees to be less snarky in future. Michael grows up, a little. The film crew is the mirror in which Michael sees himself as the man he would like to be. The film crew’s presence encourages Michael to perform, all the time: perform the role of world’s best boss, father to his people, office joker, cool guy, politically incorrect rebel, sensitive advocate for diversity—whatever his little mind feels like doing on any given day. We need to talk about Todd Packer. Packer is Michael’s evil twin, another irresponsible and self-centred manchild, except that Packer entirely lacks Michael’s need to be loved. Packer is solely interested in following his every last immediate impulse. It’s not that he’s anti-social: that would imply an intellectual attitude, which Packer is not capable of having. It’s that society means nothing to him. Again, not unlike an infant. Packer’s resemblance to an infant, and the threat he represents to Michael ever achieving maturity, is first shown in season 2’s ‘The Carpet’, where Michael discovers that something foul-smelling (it’s implied to be human faeces) has been left on his office carpet. He is disgusted by this and is plunged into depression as to who in the office would do something so horrible to him—until Packer gleefully informs him that he, Packer, did it, whereupon Michael declares it hilarious. Watching the scene where Michael realises it was Packer, I can never quite decide whether his prolonged laughter and applause is meant to seem rather forced—like he knows he ought to find it funny and is doing his best to perform amusement for Packer—or whether he is genuinely very relieved to learn that it was just Packer being Packer, and not someone who secretly dislikes him. A tribute to Steve Carell’s acting. Throughout the episode, Michael behaves like a mini-Packer, randomly thumping Creed on the arm and then getting Dwight to join him in a ‘raid’ on the accounting department. It’s Michael living up to the idea of cool that Packer represents to him, even though it amounts to no more than random assholism. Still, ‘The Carpet’ is the last time Michael wholeheartedly endorses Packer. When Packer took a dump on Michael’s carpet, he finally did the thing that made Michael begin to think of Packer as someone who had to be excused. And here we need to go back to Jan Levinson. I would insert a picture of Melora Hardin as Jan, here, but one of the interesting things about Jan, which makes her unlike Jim, or David Wallace, or Todd Packer, is that no one picture can be said to show what Jan looks like. This is because Jan’s role changes so much. In the first season and a half, Jan is basically the all-father, the ultimate authority figure, the person with the power to order Michael what to do, and reprimand him for doing things badly. Jan is the line beyond which no-one may cross. However, because The Office is a comedy and not an academic paper, this is disrupted from the very start by Michael finding her attractive. The tension between Jan’s unquestionable authority and her presence as a person gets stretched and snapped in the crucial season 2 episode ‘The Client’, where for the first time we see Michael Scott operating in the sphere of his competence. I’m sure you know the story, and skip the next bit if you do. ‘The Client’: skippable synopsis Jan has arranged for her and Michael to meet a client at the Radisson hotel for lunch, to broker a deal where Dunder Mifflin will supply paper to local government. The client, Christian, has to cut costs, and Dunder Mifflin are more expensive than their big chain competitors. Michael switches the meeting to his favourite local restaurant, Chili’s, without Jan’s permission. When they meet the client, Jan tries to talk business but Michael insists on making small talk and ordering food and drinks. What was supposed to be a lunch meeting goes on until late in the evening, and by the end of it, Christian has come to like Michael so much that he’s persuaded by Michael that Dunder Mifflin’s customer service justifies the extra cost. Jan is so impressed that she kisses Michael in the parking lot. This is only the beginning of Jan’s character development. Dunderpedia notes that her original name, Jan Levinson-Gould, seems to have the surnames of two of the psychologists most associated with the concept of the midlife crisis, Daniel Levinson and Roger Gould, although they add ‘this is probably just a coincidence’. I think not: Jan is, as they also say, ‘the epitome of a midlife crisis’. Jan’s turn from no-nonsense authority figure, to girlfriend from hell, to hospital administrator and single mother who’s recorded an entire album of cover versions of songs made famous by Doris Day, is one of the great joys of the show, thanks in part to Melora Hardin’s wilingness to play Jan as a complete nutjob. Jan’s most sympathetic moment and her least come very close to each other, in season 4, after she’s been fired from Dunder Mifflin for screwing up at work too often. By season 4 episodes 7/8, ‘Money’, she has moved into Michael’s condo. Michael, now the sole earner in their relationship, quickly runs into money problems, which he attempts to solve by declaring bankruptcy, except that he’s under the impression that you do that by walking into a public place and saying in a loud voice, ‘I… DECLARE… BANK-RUPT-CYYYYYY!’ Michael attempts to get rid of his money problems by literally climbing onto a freight train, but Jan comes to find him, and tells him that he is the one person who has stuck by her in difficult times, and they walk off holding hands. However, three episodes later, in ‘Survivor Man’, Michael becomes annoyed that Ryan did not invite him on a survival weekend. Convinced that he needs to undergo a wilderness ordeal, he decides to go on one by himself, getting Dwight to take him deep into the forest and leaving him there with only a knife and a roll of duct tape. Unknown to him, Dwight remains behind to keep an eye on him, using the scope on his hunting rifle as a telescope. (Dwight’s own paternal instincts finally kicking in.) Of course, Michael utterly fails to find food and shelter, succeeding only in destroying his suit, and only when he ingests some random mushrooms does Dwight come charging out of hiding and force him to spit them out (in a peculiar reversal of Michael’s inspection of Dwight’s teeth in ‘The Coup’). Cured of the need to prove himself in the wild, Michael returns to the office, where his newfound enthusiasm for the office and its comforts bucks him up, and he single-handedly rescues Jim’s lame attempt to organise a combined birthday. This plays directly into the next episode, ‘The Deposition’, in which Michael has to testify in Jan’s wrongful dismissal suit against the company. During the deposition, Michael realises that Jan has submitted his personal diary as evidence, with neither his knowledge nor permission. He further realises that she gave him a bad performance review after they had started dating. Finally, he learns that he was never seriously considered for a corporate position. Nevertheless, he defends the company against Jan, earning the gratitude of David Wallace, the CFO. Michael’s verdict is ‘You expect to get screwed by your company, but you never expect to get screwed by your girlfriend.’ The angry silence in which Michael and Jan drive home is the smouldering mound of garbage that ignites in the next episode, one of the show’s very greatest: ‘Dinner Party’. Jan in ‘Dinner Party’, becoming the devil. ‘Dinner Party’ is one of the ultimate examples of the family dynamic in the show, with Michael and Jan as warring parents, and Jim, Pam, Andy and Angela as their more or less mortified children witnessing the break-up. Andy, true to form, is so self-absorbed that he’s largely oblivious to the intensely radioactive cloud of passive-aggression that’s boiling between Michael and Jan, while Jim and Pam start out by finding it funny, and end up finding it excruciating. One touch which I cite in support of my theory: when the guests have already been there for some time, Pam is distressed to find out that Jan hasn’t even started cooking the osso buco yet. Jan will later shower love on her own daughter, but at this stage she can’t provide for her symbolic ‘children’, Jim, Pam, Andy and Angela. In ‘Dinner Party’ we learn that Jan has taken over an entire room of Michael’s condo for her experiments in candle-making, and forces Michael to sleep on a tiny bench at the foot of his own bed. (In, we may note for psychoanalytical reasons, the fetal position.) ‘Dinner Party’ is, among other things, a masterclass in tight-lipped smiling. It’s also, I would argue, the American show’s ultimate revenge on the British show, in terms of cringe comedy. The whole episode piles awkwardness upon hideous awkwardness, climaxing with Michael’s lament about the physical toll that multiple vasectomies have taken on his body. For once, the chief source of awkwardness is not Dwight, who crashes the party with his date, his former babysitter, and who seems relatively sane, compared to Michael with his comically tiny plasma screen television, and Jan compulsively dancing and crooning along to her former assistant Hunter’s awful CD. Dwight has also come prepared, bringing his own food in the form of turkey legs and beet salad, thereby underlining that he can survive in this god-awful house but Jim and Pam must go hungry. (In a nice touch, Jim steals Hunter’s CD, as a sort of punishment for the surrogate parents’ dreadful dinner party, and he and Pam enjoy it while contentedly munching burgers in their car, later that evening.) The entire stretch from ‘Money’ to ‘Dinner Party’ is the trauma that fatally cracks the Michael/Jan axis. In the immediate aftermath of it, Dwight rescues Michael from Jan. Michael regresses so far beyond helplessness that, when he’s riding in Dwight’s car to spend the night at Dwight’s house, he sticks his head out of the window like a dog. But although Jan does return, she is never again the force of nature that she is here. She is not, in the end, the paternal authority figure that Michael still needs to measure himself by. That figure is David Wallace. Who I’ve discussed separately. Which brings us, at long last, to Holly Flax. Holly is, quite possibly, the nicest person in the show. She was created to be possibly Michael’s love interest. Amy Ryan said on the Office Ladies podcast that she was initially booked for only one episode, and she understood that whether or not Holly would actually become his love interest depended in large part on how well she did in the role. She was meant to be the first character who simply liked Michael: an amiable, rather dorky woman who used bad jokes and funny voices and mild sarcasm as a way of negotiating awkwardness. In terms of the family dynamic that I describe in this show, it makes perfect sense that Holly is Toby’s replacement in HR. Michael hates HR. Or rather, he thinks he hates HR. Actually he just hates Toby. I think that the reason Michael loathes Toby so much is not just Toby’s low-key, mumbly, lukewarm personality (and let’s hear it for Paul Lieberstein’s self-effacing performance) but because Toby, as HR person, represents the accumulated wisdom of the universe about all the lessons Michael desperately needs to learn in life, but, because he’s Toby, Michael can’t bear to learn those lessons from him. Michael can’t stand to be schooled by someone so entirely unlike him: such a droopy, dreary, brown-suited killjoy. So, when Holly shows up in season 4’s ‘Goodbye Toby’, Michael is initially suspicious, but when he finally meets her, she succeeds in completely disarming him by distinguishing herself from Toby, in front of Toby: Michael: Hi. Yeah. Right. Okay, well, they hired a female Toby. Good for the world. Thank you, God, for creating two of you. Here's how things work here: my job is to make the office fun. Your job is to make the office lame. And we have an eternal struggle, you and I. And only one of us can be the winner. Spoiler alert: I'm gonna win. Holly: Man, someone doesn't like HR. Michael: Yeah. Holly: [to Toby] What did you do to him? Toby: Nothing. Michael: No. He tortured me... with his awfulness. Holly: [smiling] Yeah, I know what you mean. I nearly fell asleep when he gave me a tour of the files. Holly manages to say this without unduly offending Toby, almost as if she’s gently mocking Michael for having such a ridiculously low opinion of Toby. But it serves to flip Michael completely in her favour. Because, as everyone who’s watched this show knows, Holly is in many ways a female version of Michael. In fact, I’ll go further: she is, in terms of the spiritual epic that I maintain lies beneath this whole show, the missing half of Michael. Besides having similar verbal habits, such as doing impressions of people and then murmuring the name of the person she’s just done an impression of, she gets Michael, recognising all of his good qualities and noticing (at least at first) none of his bad ones. Holly brings human resources to Michael. Ryan’s acting convinces us that Holly is a genuinely warm person, such as the way she interacts with Kevin, who she has been told by Dwight is mentally handicapped. Because Kevin is Kevin, this is not all that hard to believe (even though Kevin is quite capable of displaying remarkable savvy when he wants to.) Of course, Holly’s beaming smile and general kindness only convinces Kevin that she’s super into him. Michael’s growth accelerates dramatically as soon as he’s met her. In season 5 episode 3’s ‘Business Ethics’, Holly attempts to conduct an ethics seminar in the office, after it’s revealed that Meredith has been sleeping with a supplier in return for discounts. The seminar collapses because the staff aren’t interested, and when Michael attempts to tell Holly that it doesn’t matter, it doesn’t work, because she is genuinely upset at Meredith’s breach of ethics. Then, he is present when Holly’s line manager brusquely chews her out over the phone, telling her to stop trying to do her job properly, and just get the staff to sign the papers saying that they’ve had the seminar, because never mind about the stupid ethics, the company needs the discount. Michael does not joke about this, nor is he triumphant that he’s been proved right. Instead, when he’s alone, he asks the camera one of the wisest questions he’s ever asked: How do you tell someone you care about deeply, ‘I told you so?’ He muses on various different ways of doing this, and being Michael he settles on the obviously wrong way—but then, crucially, he doesn’t do it. He lets it go. By the next episode, all is forgotten and the office likes Holly again. Holly is an element in Michael’s universe that is both subversive and healing. She uses her common sense and sympathy to expel him from the infantile world of fantasy that he lives in, and consoles him with her mere presence for that expulsion. When she is sent back to Nashua, this process is only half complete, and so he is sorely wounded. Remember that Holly was not some late-stage element in the show. She got introduced at the end of season 4, she’s whisked away only a few episodes later in season 5 ep 6 ‘Employee Transfer’, and does not properly return until ‘Classy Christmas’, halfway through season 7. For most of the intervening period, more than two whole seasons of the show, Michael is more or less secretly pining for her. At the end of season 5 ep 7’s ‘Business Trip’, his sudden question to David Wallace is as real and as honest and as authentically sorrowful as Michael ever gets: Michael: No, David, you listen to me. Why did you send her away? That—God. You knew I liked her and you just sent her away. And that… that was a sucky thing to do, man. David Wallace: Michael, sometimes— Michael: That was a really sucky thing to do. David Wallace: Sometimes, we— [Michael hangs up on him.] The childish word ‘sucky’ reminds us of the little boy Michael who we saw in a clip from an old TV show in season 2, telling a puppet that his dream was to get married and have one hundred kids, so I can have one hundred friends, and no one can say ‘no’ to being my friend. That is the yawning abyss of loneliness within Michael. That is what goes away when he’s around Holly. By season 6 ep 6 ‘Whistleblower’, Dunder Mifflin has been taken over by a larger company, Sabre, and David Wallace is out. The new boss, Jo Bennett, is an ambiguous figure with regard to Michael’s development: neither a father- nor a mother-figure. Michael struggles to adapt to her being the new boss, which involves him standing up to her; it doesn’t get the results he wants, but it does make him feel more grown-up. When it turns out that Sabre printers have a tendency to catch fire, Jo knows that the company has to make some sort of recognition of this, but she has very good reasons for not wanting to: Jo: When I was growing up, there was nothing better than being a big old business tycoon. And I thought I'd break that glass ceiling and be a hero to all those little girls out there... and they'd make a Barbie out of me. […] I, did I sell cheap printers? I do. But if I have to go out there in front of the press and make one of them public apology recalls, I mean, it's all I'll ever be remembered for. Nobody will want to play with my Barbie. Michael: You know, I would be willing, under the right circumstances, to do that for you. So Michael does do that, and at the end of the episode, Jo is appreciative: Jo: I hope your rough patch ends soon. Michael: Thanks. Today helped. Jo: Well, give me a shout if I can brighten your life. Michael: Okay. Hey, [jokingly] you could transfer Holly back from Nashua. Jo: Let me see what I can do. Michael looks… stunned. The very next episode of the show has, as its cold open, the lip dub, where almost the entire office dances and lip-syncs to the Human Beinz’ ‘Nobody But Me’. It’s there because that’s the only possible reaction the show can have to the idea that Holly may return. A goofy explosion of joy and good humour. Even Dwight gets in on it, although being Dwight he goes too far. Only Darryl and Angela remain on the outside, Angela because I said I didn’t want to be on the internet! and Darryl so that Angela can have someone to shut herself in a side office with. I think the ultimate example of Holly directly influencing Michael’s growth comes in season 7’s ‘Threat Level Midnight’. This is the completion of a stage that began in season 5 ep 11/12, ‘Stress Relief’, where Michael organised a roast of himself, and then found that he couldn’t handle people laughing at him. After going to the park and being by himself for a while, he comes back and quick-fire insults the entire staff, and an increasingly tense moment is defused when he tells Stanley You crush your wife during sex and your heart sucks, and Stanley finds this hilarious. Having got even with his ‘children’, Michael visibly relaxes, tells them he’s kidding, and sincerely adds, You guys are the reason I went into the paper business. He has at last learned the grade-school-level lesson of being able to take a joke. Two seasons later, in ‘Threat Level Midnight’, Michael has finally finished the terrible movie he’s been making for years, using the office staff as cast. He announces that he’ll screen it for everyone. Pam prepares them for it by reminding them that the last time he screened an unfinished version of it, they all laughed and he got mortally offended. She urges them not to laugh this time, and for most of the first half of the screening, the staff manage to keep a respectful silence. However, Pam herself shatters the strenuous politeness when she exclaims in horror at seeing her mom playing a sexy nurse, and then Jim can’t keep it in anymore when he sees the absurd dance sequence, ‘The Scarn’. Michael has a hissy fit and stops the screening. Outside the conference room, he goes to Holly for confirmation that his masterpiece isn’t just laughable nonsense, but she can’t give it to him. Look at the sheer economy of how B.J. Novak wrote this conversation: Michael: No, no. Holly, this isn't Ocean's Eleven, where you get together with all your friends and just have fun and don't care about how it turns out. What'd you really think, honestly. Holly: Um... Michael: Is it, is it because you're afraid of where this is gonna take me? See, because I need you... to keep me grounded. Holly: [deadpan] Not worried about that. (Holly’s sarcasm is nicely understated.) Michael: [angrily] It was eleven years, okay? This has been my dream for eleven years, and if you don't think it's great than you're basically saying that you don't believe in my dream. Holly: Wha- It's your dream and you never even mentioned it before! Michael is still clinging to the illusion that ‘Threat Level Midnight’ has a future outside of this office, and that it’s more than something where you get together with all your friends and just have fun and don’t care about how it turns out. Still, there’s an element of realism to his awareness that, if a manager of a paper office in Scranton, PA is going to make a film which he wants people to take seriously, it had better be more than just an Ocean’s Eleven-type of film. (And I’m thinking more the slack and self-indulgent 1960 Ocean’s 11, than the slick 2001 Ocean’s Eleven.) Michael: I talk about a lot of things, Holly! I was eventually gonna get around to my dream! Obviously! Eleven years I could've been working on the Scarn Nebulus. Holly: Well, why do you have to make a movie at all? Michael: Because, if I don't have this, what do I have? I have nothing. Holly: Really, you can't think of anything else that you might have? The armour-piercing question. Michael: I have my book on business, Somehow I Manage. I have my HBO comedy special, Here I Go Again… But you know what? When I think about it, when I really think about it, none of those things are as real to me as my movie. Holly: I'm real. Michael: Yeah, you're a real pain in the ass. And I'm gonna go watch the movie with people who think it's great! And I'm sorry I called you a pain in the ass, I'm angry, and I love you. Holly: I love you too. He couldn’t stand the idea that people were laughing at what it is, as opposed to what he wanted it to be. But she has got to him. Because, before, he would never have sincerely apologised to someone he was in the middle of a fight with. And he would never have been able to accurately assess his own motivations, and he would never have been able to remember, while still angry, that he loved that person. He and Jan do have a superficially similar I love you/I love you moment at the end of ‘The Deposition’ but in context, it’s cold and unconvincing. Here, it’s two lovers reassuring each other that their love is stronger than this fight, but yes, they’re still definitely having a fight. He asks the staff if they want to watch the rest of it. They say that they do. He puts it on again. And this time around, Michael is no longer in his bubble of comforting illusions. Holly is in the next room, more real to him than his movie is. He’s no longer seeing the movie that he wanted it to be: he’s seeing it through the eyes of everyone else in the room. That’s why he’s no longer watching in a tense silence. He’s remembering the shoot and how much fun it was. He starts laughing. Because it’s hilariously bad, and he can see that now. He gets up and goes out to her. Holly: Hey, I'm sorry. It is good. Michael: No it's not. [smiles, kisses her] It's not. But, they really seem to be enjoying it. It doesn’t matter that it’s terrible. That’s actually what’s good about it. This moment seems to me to be a version of one of those archetypal moments in stories—not necessarily American stories—where a character realises who they are, and humbly or bravely accepts a humdrum reality as opposed to a grandiose fantasy. I’d compare it to the great moment towards the end of Toy Story, when Woody brings it home to a dejected Buzz that he is not a Space Ranger, but a beloved children’s toy. Buzz becomes more himself, and finally learns his true value. It is one of the pivotal moments for Michael: a moment when he realises, and accepts, his true stature in his life. The next thing that has to happen is that he has to psychologically detach himself from Packer. It happens in the very next episode, which is named after Packer. Packer is back in the office, and spends the episode being his usual obnoxious self, and both Jim and Dwight loathe him, but Michael laughs dutifully as always, and is keen for Holly to like him. But after Holly’s observed Packer at length, she refuses to take the bait, and bluntly describes Packer as a ‘jerk’. Michael is confused, and tries to cling onto the image of Packer as a fun-loving master of misrule. When Jim and Dwight team up to prank Packer into going to Florida, pretending to him that he’s been offered a job there, Michael is outraged, and tells them he will tell Packer. But Packer tells Michael, I'm gonna tell you something that none of these people have the stones to tell you. It's your girlfriend, man. She's uptight. Michael freezes. Packer has insulted the person closest to his heart. He doesn’t tell Packer about the prank. Packer goes to Florida. Four episodes later, Michael leaves Dunder Mifflin, and the show, to live in Colorado with Holly. It’s symbolically interesting that Michael’s departure is so low-key and so understated. The attention-needing Michael of seasons 1–3 couldn’t possibly have left the show. But in ‘Goodbye Michael’, he leaves the office a day earlier than he told everyone he would, because all he wants is to be with Holly and he doesn’t want big goodbyes. Only Jim figures it out, and he and Michael say an emotional goodbye by discussing the goodbyes that they will never make, at the lunch they plan to have ‘tomorrow’, that they know they will never have. Michael’s departure is rather like the unexpected death of a family member: one minute they’re there and you’re making plans, then they’re gone. At the airport, a visibly more cheerful Michael takes off his radio mic, bids the film crew goodbye with a last That’s what she said gag, and casually ambles off, independent, free at last from the need to perform for the camera. He is intercepted by Pam, and they share a silent goodbye (this shot was Jenna Fischer and Steve Carell actually saying goodbye, on Carell’s last day.) Once Michael has left the show, and the symbolic death-of-the-father has happened, the remaining characters are free to grow up as they will. The symbolic death of Packer is part of this. He returns for the season 8 Florida sequences. In ‘Last Day in Florida’, a quiet hint from Robert California warns Jim that, if Dwight claims credit for the Sabre store, he will get fired because Robert was never interested in the store. Jim physically tackles Dwight to the ground, warning him not to make the presentation, and stalls Dwight for long enough that Nellie has Packer do it—whereupon Packer gets canned, which Dwight sees. A chastened Dwight silently extends his hand to Jim and helps him up off the floor. Jim and Dwight have become true brothers. Never again do they resume their former antagonism. In the last season of the show, Jim and Pam negotiate marital troubles, and Dwight finally, ruefully accepts that he has screwed up too many times to become manager. The latter is a crucial moment for him. He has stopped living his life like he is a broadsword-wielding knight errant, or (as on his bad days) like he’s a Bond villain. At long last, he behaves like a salesman in a paper company, the job he excels at. He even says that Jim should be manager instead of him. Jim, for his part, is content to be an underachieving paper salesman with a loving family, and has abandoned his plans to switch jobs to the now-thriving business he helped found. There’s just one thing he didn’t reckon on. Pam doesn’t find the office any more magical than Jim does, and she is upset to think that this, after all, is who they are, when she knows that they could do better. In the last moments of the show, she pulls the second-bravest stunt of her life: she sells their house, so that they can move to Austin and Jim can have his ideal job. But in the meantime, Jim becomes Dwight’s best man, and Dwight refers to Pam as his ‘best friend’. And it’s true that Dwight is one of the few male characters in the show who never professes any romantic or sexual interest in Pam—which makes sense if you think of them as, symbolically, brother and sister. (He does once talk with characteristically brutal frankness about how she’s not as attractive as she was before she had children, but he never seems to be attracted to her.) Still and all, when Jim has loyally discharged his Bestischmensch duties, he does the only thing he can possible do, which is step aside and bring back, from the symbolic dead, the spiritual father, Michael, to be the true Bestischmensch for Dwight. I think it’s significant that, in the Finale, Michael—who, for the first time, barely even acknowledges the camera—has only two lines: Dwight: [turns around] [amazed] Michael. I can't believe you came. Michael: That's what she said. And: Michael: [crying] I feel like all my kids grew up and then they married each other… It's every parent's dream. I rest my case. There are a lot of things I’ve left out of what’s already a very long answer. I didn’t talk about all the episodes which also support this theory—and also all the ones that undermine it. I didn’t talk about the show’s more dodgy episodes, such as season 3’s ‘A Benihana Christmas’, where one joke turns on Michael’s inability to tell his date from another woman (because they’re both Benihana waitresses, and all Asian people look alike, you see.) I didn’t talk about capitalism. And I could have. But I didn’t. Be grateful you were spared that. If my very long exposition of this theory has entertained you, that’s all it was meant to do. Do I really, honestly believe it? Sure, let’s go with that. I think, however, that this theory helps to explain why some people, like me, consider the US version of the show to be be superior to the UK version. I’ve heard the US version dismissed as a ‘soap opera’, or as somehow lacking the edge of the UK version. I disagree; the UK version never got anything like as intimately nasty as ‘Dinner Party’. I think the US version is a much more ambitious and much more successful piece of entertainment. It’s longer, and tougher, and has more twists and turns, and it’s more fleshed-out, but when you take the whole thing as it comes, it’s a great deal more satisfying. … That’s what she said. Question: In the movie “ An American Werewolf in London” why wasn’t the Warren Zevon song on this same subject used? It would seem to be the perfect fit.
Answer: Because it would have been a terrible fit. The movie is essentially a horror movie with some comic elements. The song is a comedy song with some light horror references. The songs in the movie are straightforward, non-comedy songs that refer to the moon: ‘Bad Moon Rising’, ‘Moondance’, ‘Blue Moon’. They preserve and underline the idea that the moon is an important thing in human affairs, and so they support the serious horror elements, but because they’re quite upbeat songs, they inevitably sound ironic. The songs have to not know, as it were, that they’re on the soundtrack of a horror movie about a werewolf. If they had used ‘Werewolves in London’, it would have sounded knowing. It would have kicked you right out of the horror, and would have made the whole thing seem campy and jokey. They were absolutely right to not use it.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What does Alex Johnston think of the band Soundgarden?
Answer: How nice to have a bespoke question. Normally, when I like a band, I like most of their stuff; some albums or phases more than others, but Soundgarden are unusual for me because, while I really love one of their albums—like, it’s possibly my favourite rock album of the 90s—I don’t care at all for the rest of their stuff. Why this should be, I don’t know. But I checked it recently, by having a quick listen to all the stuff I hadn’t listened to, or had listened to and not liked, and I felt the same: mild impatience (Soundgarden songs tend to take a while to get going), alternating with lack of interest. Which brings us to: Superunknown, from 1994. If Superunknown is simultaneously more focused and more stylistically diverse than other Soundgarden albums, I attribute some of this to its producer, Michael Beinhorn, who was active in this space up until a couple of years ago, and who I actually knew of before I listened to this album, because as a teenager I’d listened to Memory Serves by Material, the band Beinhorn had been in before he’d become a producer. I think Beinhorn was the perfect guy to guide Soundgarden towards making a masterpiece. Because I think Superunknown is a masterpiece, one of the great albums of the 90s. Confession: since we’re talking 90s bands, and grunge, I never really liked Nirvana. I disliked what I thought was the whiny tone of their songs. Or maybe it was just the sound of Cobain’s voice. Chris Cornell in Soundgarden also suffered from depression, and sadly it got him in the end, but Soundgarden never sound ‘whiny’, at least not on this album. This album delivered what I want from a hard rock album, because it’s all about power and confidence and swagger, without being boneheadedly phallic. (Heh heh: I said ‘bone’.) When Chris Cornell opens up his throat and gives those mighty yells, it’s exhilarating. He may be singing about despair and alienation, but he sounds to me like he’s defying them, rather than being crushed by them. Very rarely for me with an album that straddles genres such as hard rock and metal, there are almost no songs on this that I routinely skip. I’ve probably been involuntarily subjected to ‘Black Hole Sun’ too many times, but it is a brilliantly written song, and very effective. For me, the outstanding tracks are the ones that have more of a groove. ‘Let Me Drown’ is a great track 1; so what if I don’t exactly know what it’s about? (I just read the lyrics for the first time, and I’m still not much the wiser.) ‘My Wave’ has that guitar hook in the chorus, which always made me think of R.E.M. in a good way. ‘Fell On Black Days’ is a little on the nose, for me, and ‘Mailman’ is a bit of a plodder, but then we get into the title track, with that blistering jangly riff: a song which to me is about the experience of listening to the album of which it’s the title track. And the chorus is a real belter, with that cool minor-second riff. That’s why I love this album. Well, that and the deeply odd next track, Ben Shepherd’s ‘Head Down’, which sounds like a small acoustic band close by playing along with a far louder, heavily amplified rock monster in the distance. Dreamy, doomy, sly, trippy, magnificent. I saw the video for ‘Spoonman’ a lot back then, and Cornell was right when he remarked that the band was clever to keep out of it. Instead, it’s mostly the titular character doing his thing: the band appears only in pictures. This gave them a certain mystique, although when you did glimpse them, they were intriguingly ragbag: L to r: Kim Thayil, Ben Shepherd, Chris Cornell, Matt Cameron; or, the Beardy Indian One, Lyle Lovett, the Rock God and the Kid Brother of the Surfer. ‘Spoonman’, like ‘My Wave’ mixes up time signatures: the main riff is in 7/4, the chorus is in 4/4 and during Artis’ spoons solo it drops into 3/4. That keeps things lurching along in an interesting way. Then there’s the jaunty shanty of ‘Limo Wreck’, and we’re into another angsty ballad, ‘The Day I Tried to Live’. I admit to being very tempted to skip this one. After that, there’s a brief burst of pure punk rock with ‘Kickstand’ and then we’re into the majestic ‘Fresh Tendrils’, featuring the ominous clavinet of Natasha Shneider. I didn’t realise until a few years later that I had fallen briefly in crush with Natasha Shneider after seeing her in Peter Hyams’ 1984 movie 2010, where she played a young cosmonaut opposite Roy Scheider and Helen Mirren: Anyway: RIP, Ms Shneider. (She died of cancer in 2008, aged only 52.) Your hammering clavinet is a big part of why this song is so great. ‘Fresh Tendrils’ fulfils all my requirements for a great rock song: it sounds awesome, and it’s opaque enough that I can project my own interpretation onto it. And it’s written by the drummer. Then we’re onto ‘4th of July’, a more sardonic ballad than the other ones, which is maybe why I generally prefer it—even if I concede that it’s not, like ‘Black Hole Sun’ is, a song that could be covered by Frank Sinatra and still sound great. (Paul Anka did cover ‘Black Hole Sun’ on Rock Swings and the result is mostly as grisly as the rest of that sorry exercise in painfully heterosexual camp.) There’s another Shepherd song, the weird ‘Half’, and then the official final track, ‘Like Suicide’, which I always admired for its music but otherwise disliked for what I thought was its romanticisation of human damage—until very recently, when I realised it’s literally Chris Cornell writing about a bird that flew into a window of his house, whereupon my regard for it skyrocketed. An epic, slow-build hard rock song about a dead bird. Amazing. After being wrung out by ‘Like Suicide’, I seldom had the energy for the throwaway bonus track that appeared on my international CD, ‘She Likes Surprises’. I definitely liked Superunknown in part because I was the right kind of listener for it: about 23–24, young, dumb, frustrated and at least somewhat alienated. (I was, at the time, 2–3 years into the long stretch between my first girlfriend and my second one.) For all the nihilism and despair, it was crackling with energy and life. And it still bucks me up, with its odd, irregular metres and sexy riffs, and moments of lightness and dream. And what other great rock album has a.) a song about a dead bird, b.) a song you could imagine being arranged by Gordon Jenkins, and c.) a f***ing spoons solo? I faithfully bought Down on the Upside, but it was a headache. I was starting to move on from rock music. Still, if you can make one great album, that’s greatness enough. Ave atque vale, gentlemen. Edit: I’d like to dedicate this answer to the memory of another rock hero of mine, recently departed. RIP Steve Albini.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What was something a teacher or professor did that made you say "let’s drop this class immediately."?
Answer: Well, I didn’t actually drop the class, because I needed the credit, but I did stop trusting the teacher. I was in a Technology of Music tutorial. Our tutor was a physics lecturer who sang in a choir in his spare time. He was very good about things like the inverse square law and the Sabine equation, and I lapped all that stuff up. However, his grasp of music history was… less certain. He was talking about piano manufacture and construction, and he got onto the subject of John Cage’s music for prepared piano. Cage would ‘prepare’ pianos by placing objects on and between the strings, to make them sound different. I have the score of his Sonatas and Interludes for Prepared Piano and there’s a big table on p. 5 telling the performer what to put where on the strings, so as to get the effect Cage desired: However, our tutor told us about Cage preparing pianos, and then said with a combination of amazement and horror at human folly, And Cage used to drive nails into pianos, and screw bolts into them! He physically destroyed perfectly good pianos, doing this! Shocked murmurs from some of the other students. Well, I knew Cage’s career pretty well, and I was startled, too much so to raise my hand and say Uh, sorry, but that’s completely untrue. I actually wondered if he might be right. Once I was home I looked it up, and there is zero evidence of Cage ever damaging pianos with his preparations. But after that, while I listened to our tutor when he was talking about science, I never trusted him again when he was discussing music history.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Is modern art (1860–1970) and contemporary art really as bad as the general populace believes?
Answer: I’m not arrogant enough to presume that I know what the ‘general populace’ thinks of the art of the last 160 years. But art in that period did shift from being something that the average person probably found reasonably legible, to something that some supposedly intelligent people profess to find baffling and worthless. The progress of how that happened is beyond my ability to describe in detail, but I think it’s not a coincidence that the beginning of the shift in art away from immediately intelligible, realistic representations of the visible world, coincides with the increasing popularity of photography. In 1838, Louis Daguerre published the first photographic image to depict people. It wasn’t the first photograph ever, but because photographic images in those days required such long exposure times, moving people didn’t stay in one place for long enough to register on them. (Daguerre’s pictures took minutes to expose, but they were still a vast technical improvement on those of his late colleague Niépce, which had taken hours.) However, in the above picture, the guy on the lower left having his shoes shined stayed in one place for long enough for he and his shoeshine guy to appear in the image. I don’t think we can appreciate now what an earthshaking development the first photographs were. For centuries, the visual world had been represented by artists painting and drawing it, and sculptors sculpting it. But now it could be reproduced by a machine. The portrait had once been a luxury item for the rich and powerful, but now anyone could be photographed. This threw the most intelligent artists for a loop. Artistic practice changed. Visual art became an interrogation of representation itself, a process that we can see beginning in the work of e.g. Turner, but the Impressionists really went for it. The line from Impressionism to Cubism is pretty obvious. By WW1, you’ve got an artist like Duchamp rejecting his youthful Cubism and deciding that the point of art is not to please the eye, but to engage the mind. Which is how Duchamp goes from Nude Descending a Staircase, in 1912: —To Fountain, in 1917: Now, the reader may ask: Why? Why couldn’t artists go on painting nice pictures like they used to? Why did they have to start doing things like stick a urinal in a gallery and pretend it’s a sculpture? Why was that necessary? Photography had become the most efficient way of showing what things merely look like. The entire artistic tradition of the female nude, especially when painted by heterosexual male artists, has an element to it that seems to reach its ultimate expression in the far less labour-intensive and far more multiple pornographic photo. I mean, consider François Boucher (1703–1770). There are a lot of different ways to paint nudes, but it would not be controversial to say that Boucher’s female nudes are painted in such a way as to maximise the visual pleasure of the straight male viewer. In Kenneth Clark’s 1956 The Nude: A Study in Ideal Form, Clark talks about Boucher’s The Resting Odalisque in exactly these terms, discussing the painting entirely as if its point was to invite the viewer to ogle its subject, Marie-Louise O’Murphy, one of Louis XV’s mistresses: And Clark says this without any hint of censure. For him, this painting exists for us to ‘take pleasure’ in Miss O’Murphy’s body, and the fact that she’s not looking at us renders her delightfully unselfconscious, which for him is all part of the visual pleasure the picture offers. But there’s another way of looking at it. The picture was commissioned by the French court, and at the time it was painted, Miss O’Murphy was not yet Louis XV’s mistress, but a teenage model affiliated with the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture, where Boucher taught. The story goes that, when Louis XV saw the picture, he was sufficiently intrigued to want to meet O’Murphy and take her as his mistress. She duly became the youngest of his mistresses, and remained one for a couple of years until she unwisely tried to supplant Madame de Pompadour as the main mistress. She was expelled from court at the age of about 17 (yes, she was younger than that when this picture was painted) and was swiftly married off to a nobleman. She managed to survive three husbands, several pregnancies and the French Revolution, and died in 1814 aged 77. Rather than being an innocent picture of a nude girl, as Clark saw it, this picture can be seen as part of the politico-sexual negotiations of the French court of the Ancién regime: a juicy bauble commissioned and designed to advertise its subject to the monarch, so that he could enjoy her sexual services. The history of the nude in Western art is full of this kind of thing. And artists are, on the whole, no longer willing to play that game—not least because royal courts don’t exactly have in-house painters the way they used to. Artists continue to paint nudes, but the best of them don’t paint nudes the same way that the camera reproduces the appearance of them. I’m thinking of Egon Schiele, and Lucian Freud, and Jenny Saville, and Frank Auerbach, who make the viewer’s encounter with the image much more intimate and ambiguous and raw than it is with the creamy prettiness of Boucher. All along, I’ve been avoiding the question. The reason is that the development of visual art has been such that many people come to the art with an expectation that it’s going to offer them something it has no intention of offering, because the thing that those people want can be had more easily elsewhere. So they think that the art is ‘bad’. A painting like The Resting Odalisque might look, to a certain sort of viewer, simple and easy to enjoy. It’s a lot less simple when you consider the nature of the subject, and the circumstances in which it got made. If you just want to see nice pictures, there are plenty of them to look at. The best modern art is no longer about showing us the world, but about how the artist sees and reproduces it. And that requires a little more effort on the viewer’s part.

Question: If Blood Meridian was made into a film, do you think Vin Diesel would make a great Judge Holden?
Answer: Judge Holden in Blood Meridian is something more than human, a combination of almost infinite ability and endless rapaciousness: a giant, a pedophile, a polymath, and an unstoppable force for evil. A terrifying embodiment of American malignity. Vin Diesel is a pork chop in human form. So, no.
