Question: How does a average or casual movie watcher figure out what the overall theme, subject matter or different tropes of a movie without resorting to the internet for answers?
Answer: These are three different things, and in a way, the ‘average or casual movie watcher’ doesn’t need to know about two of them, while the third should, I think, be fairly self-evident. The theme of the movie is not always something easy to put into words. But sometimes it is. For example, the theme of Toy Story 3 could be phrased as The pain of leaving childhood behind. (Throughout this answer, I will use Toy Story 3 as my preferred text because my son’s been watching it, I know it well, and chances are, you do too.) The most moving scene in the movie is, I think, when Andy, who has owned the toys since the first movie, decides that he won’t store most of them in his attic and take his beloved Woody doll to college, but will in fact give them all to Bonnie, the little girl whose mother works at the hellish gulag that is Sunnyside Daycare (as Mr Pricklepants puts it with unforgettable gravitas: Sunnyside is a place of ruin and despair, ruled by an evil bear who smells of strawberries.) All the adventures that the toys have been on throughout the film have really been preparation for this moment: they have either been trying to negotiate the hell that is Sunnyside, or they’ve been trying to rejoin Andy, even though he has no desire to play with them anymore because he’s grown out of them. And so, the moment when Bonnie finds Woody at the bottom of the box of toys Andy’s giving to her, and happily exclaims My cowboy! because Woody has also strayed into her house and been played with by her, and Andy’s first reaction is to keep Woody, becomes the moment when Andy realises that if he’s really going to grow up, he has to hand Woody on, too. So he gives Woody to Bonnie, as well, but before doing so, he describes Woody to her: Now Woody… he's been my pal for as long as I can remember. He's brave, like a cowboy should be. And kind, and smart. But the thing that makes Woody special, is he'll never give up on you... ever. He'll be there for you, no matter what. The thing that really sells this moment, I think, and has the power to make even adults cry, is not just the brilliant writing that has got us to this point, but the fixed, wide-eyed smile on Woody’s face which he can’t not have, because he’s being handled by kids at that moment: Woody will never be, for Andy, the rather harassed, dorky, bossy-but-endearing leader of this group of toys, whose bad moods and mistakes and triumphs and follies we, the audience, have followed for three movies: he’ll always be the eternally brave and reliable friend who he had a million adventures with. The above is what Woody always looks like, to Andy. And so Andy hands Woody over, and in doing so, says goodbye to childhood. (It’s worth remembering that it’s Woody himself who prompts Andy to give his toys to Bonnie, by writing a note as if from Andy’s mother suggesting that he do so. So, although Woody has always been Andy’s favourite toy (well, nearly always: cf. Toy Story itself), there’s an element of heroic self-sacrifice involved when he manipulates Andy into giving him away.) The movie’s theme is the thing that has the power to grab us emotionally, when it’s the basis for a story and only when it is truly knitted into the story, which I think is the case with Toy Story 3. Just as Fear of the sea is knitted into the story of Jaws. Another movie can have the same theme, but if it’s badly done, it won’t work. It’s not themes that make movies great. It’s the art which which the story and the theme/s support each other. Well… that’s one of the things that make movies great, anyway. The subject matter of the movie is a bit different, I think. I would characterise the subject matter of the movie as simply the thing that the story is about, on a literal level: in this case, A boy going off to college decides to store most of his toys and take his favourite one with him, but owing to a series of minor mishaps, it all goes wrong, and the toys themselves must fix it. You could make a far less bittersweet movie than Toy Story 3 using that subject matter—one in which, for example, Andy decides to take all his toys with him, or else one in which all the toys spend the next several years in the attic until Andy himself has kids and decides to give his old toys to them. But it wouldn’t be this film. To put it another way, the subject matter of Toy Story 3 could be abstracted further to A teenage American boy and his relationship with his childhood toys, which lead a secret life when he’s not playing with them. Except that, if you take out the word ‘teenage’, this is also the subject matter of the previous two Toy Story movies. Anyway, to my mind, ‘subject matter’ is less deep-structure than ‘theme’. As far as the tropes are concerned, these are simply the storytelling/filmmaking devices that the movie uses. You don’t have to know what they are for them to work on you, but it’s fun to recognise them being used. The website TV Tropes is a wiki where users exhaustively provide tropes that they’ve identified in movies, TV and other media, and the more popular the thing being examined, the more tropes are likely to be found in it. Toy Story 3 is no exception: the main page is divided into eight sub-pages. Random examples: The thing about this is that identifying a trope is not a science, it’s more of a knack that you learn. Toy Story 3 is now 14 years old, and its TV Tropes page has probably settled into as good a shape as it’s going to get. If you really want to, you can find hundreds of tropes in a movie, and like I said, it’s not necessary to do so in order to appreciate the movie. I think my experience of the site was fairly representative: at first you’re so delighted that there are names for all these things you’ve noticed in movies and TV and books etc. that you become half-convinced that the movies and TV and books, etc. can be reduced to lists of the tropes that appear in them, but as you get a bit older and wiser, you realise that it’s not true, and that there will always be something that you can’t quite account for. There’s also the fact that some tropes have rather arcane names, such as ‘Wham Shot’, which is not a character hitting something hard, but a shot in a movie which takes the story in a dramatically new direction that we probably hadn’t anticipated. An example of a Wham Shot in Toy Story 3 is when the toys have escaped the shredder and are being carried along a conveyor belt, and Rex the dinosaur thinks he sees daylight ahead, only it turns out to be reflected light from the giant incinerator they’re all inexorably heading towards. Because of their odd names and the sheer number of them, tropes are probably the things in a movie which you can least easily learn about without consulting the internet. Unless you want to make up your own ones, it’s easier (and more fun) to browse TV Tropes and learn them that way. I can testify that, after 20 years of the site’s existence, it’s become so encyclopedic that it’s very difficult to think up a new trope that someone hasn’t already thought of, and that the site itself is so designed that it’s very easy to find a way to make an existing trope fit something you know, by means of the ‘Playing With’ tab, whereby a trope can be inverted, parodied, subverted, deconstructed etc. in a work. Here’s one of my favourites where you can see that in action: It goes on for another page. To sum up: Malcolm McDowell in Kubrick’s A Clockwork Orange, giving us the classic Kubrick Stare. Thanks for reading.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: With hip-hop and rap artists/ producers, how are they finding the old tunes that they sample? Are they just listening to old records until they find something they like, or do the producers already know tunes that are conducive to sampling?
Answer: It’s basically the former. Hip hop artists and producers tend to be bargain bin fiends, in both the physical sense of loving to riffle through stacks of obscure and deleted vinyl, and the figurative sense of having a deep knowledge of music. They love finding good, obscure stuff to sample, and the most creative of them are expert at transforming a sample into something else. I’m currently reading and watching everything I can find about the late hip-hop producer/rapper J Dilla, and in Jordan Ferguson’s fine little 2014 book about Dilla’s last album, Donuts, I found some unspoken rules about sampling that were codified by the ethnomusicologist Joseph G. Schloss, based on his interviews with producers and DJs. These rules (which are not necessarily a conscious code of rules, just indications of general practice within hip-hop at one point in time) are: (I would point out, here, that when contemporary rock bands consciously emulate early 70s rock, a certain kind of rock fan tends to have no problem with that, because they consider it a ‘homage’, or something, whereas more forward-thinking contemporary musicians have righteous contempt for that kind of thing. I don’t know any better example of this within rock than Faith No More singer Mike Patton, a truly creative musician, who in 2007 interrupted his own interview when he overheard the hopelessly retro Australian band Wolfmother doing their sub-Zeppelin schtick in the background.) Most of us with a basic knowledge of hip-hop are aware that there are some tracks that have been sampled many, many times: James Brown’s ‘Funky Drummer’, The Winstons’ ‘Amen Brother’, The Incredible Bongo Band’s ‘Apache’. And there are others. The above rules date from a time after people were just wildly sampling whatever the hell they thought they could get away with. However, even by the 90s, tracks like the aforementioned had been sampled to death. The most creative producers knew that, and have always sought out obscure recordings, and made something out of them that nobody could have predicted. How they did that is beyond the scope of this answer, but I’ll try to address it later. To sum up: hip-hop producers/DJs have historically prided themselves on having both an enormous knowledge of obscure music, but also, the skill to take that music and transform it into great beats. The real skill lies in the understanding that anything is ‘conducive to sampling’, as long as you know what to do with it once you’ve sampled it. Thanks for the A2A, Michael David Clasing.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Why are there no genius writers like Shakespeare, Balzac, Dostoevsky, and Dickens these days?
Answer: The kind of writers you want (brilliant writers with wide appeal) are still around. You’re just looking for them in the wrong places. I agree with Lee Ballentine that there are plenty of great living writers: he mentioned Thomas Pynchon and Margaret Atwood, among others, and I would concur. Thomas Pynchon, being reclusive on TV. However, novelists like them do not have the mass appeal that Shakespeare, Balzac and Dickens had back in their respective days. (I personally think that Balzac is overrated, mainly because Proust convinced me that he is.) In Shakespeare’s time, theatre was, with music, one of the most popular kinds of mass entertainment; now it isn’t. In Dickens’ time, the serial novel had the same kind of popularity. So where, you ask, are the genius writers to be found? Who are these brilliant writers with wide appeal, and why haven’t you heard of them, let alone read them? From top to bottom: You could make a longer list than this. (For example, I left off David Chase only because I’ve never watched The Sopranos.) And these are merely American ones. I could have made as long a list of British writers. But these are the brilliant writers who are making work that has broad appeal. They’re just doing it on television. In many cases, the concept of ‘writer’ has broadened to include a lot of things that people in TV have to do which don’t really involve putting words into Word files. (Or Final Draft files, as the case may be.) US TV shows are almost invariably written by writing teams, but one person is usually the head writer, which may or may not overlap with the role of ‘showrunner’, the top-level executive producer. In US TV, showrunners outrank everyone else, including the directors of episodes, and are usually writers themselves. But they work to give their shows a coherence and a thematic cohesiveness that we get from the best literature. Breaking Bad was, if nothing else, a virtuoso feat of storytelling, insofar as almost every one of its 62 episodes flowed chronologically from the preceding one: it had almost none of the time skips between episodes that most TV shows rely on. There’s no point in lamenting that huge readerships no longer devour 800-page novels by the greatest novelists of our era, or watch five-act dramas in blank verse. They just don’t. Instead, we watch TV, and some of the shows above are among the greatest writing I’ve ever known in any medium. If you were to ask me who’s my favourite, I’m more of a comedy fan, and I have to admit that Greg Daniels and Michael Schur are closer to my heart than Jenji Kohan or David Simon. But a show like The Good Place wasn’t just an unusually good sitcom: it had a narrative from the first episode to the last, and with all its weirdness and twists and turns, it was about a fundamental question: How can we be good people? (Just as Breaking Bad dealt with the question, Why not be a bad person?) So what if The Good Place treated that in a comic mode, rather than in Dostoyevsky’s favoured mode of somewhat overwrought tragedy? (The only novel by him that I actually enjoy is The Double, which also happens to be his funniest.) We can’t write Dostoyevsky again. The age of the writers you want to have is long gone. We are living through a great age for television. If you’re not bothering to watch, you’re missing out.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What are your thoughts on '80s King Crimson?
Answer: Ah. The New Wave King Crimson. With the pastel suits, and Robert Fripp’s mullet, and weirdly low-cut t-shirt. l to r: Robert Fripp, Bill Bruford, Adrian Belew, Tony Levin I first started listening to KC very shortly after Fripp had abruptly pulled the plug on this lineup, in 1984. As usual, I came late to the party. I was a teenage bass player, desperate to bust my listening habits out of predictable 60s blues-rock, when I got a copy of Starless and Bible Black, by the ‘73-’74-era band, with Fripp and Bruford and David Cross and John Wetton. It blew my freaking mind, and so for fairly obvious reasons I still regard that lineup as, more or less, apex King Crimson. When I listened to Red years later, my reaction was to wonder why I hadn’t listened to it earlier. (I seem to remember that it was out of print, which it was still possible for an album to be in those days.) But around the same time, I was discovering Talking Heads and Brian Eno. So, when I found a copy of the above lineup’s Discipline, I immediately thought Ah, right, so they formed a new version and went all Talking Heads-y. Discipline didn’t have the same attractions as Starless and Bible Black. Instead of being huge, heavy and brooding, it was jittery, clattery and ran on a strange sort of world-music groove, owing to Fripp deciding to spend much of his time avoiding big guitar solos and instead playing those relentless crosspicked arpeggios. Adrian Belew’s shrieky guitar was in the forefront, which was cool with me since I liked his shrieky guitar. It took me literally years to realise that Bruford hardly plays cymbals on this album (don’t judge, my ears were less trained back then). As a bass player, I was flummoxed because Tony Levin mostly plays Chapman Stick on this album, and there was no chance of me reproducing his lines on my crappy East German P-bass knock-off. Not that I could have hoped to play the lines of the genius Fripp refers to as ‘T. Baldy Levin’. But there was a spaciousness about the music that was very cool, and an openness to influences that was inspiring. ‘The Sheltering Sky’ sounds like an intricately written piece of music, yet it was almost completely improvised. ‘Matte Kudasai’ was like country & far-eastern. ‘Thela Hun Ginjeet’ had an intriguing Escher-esque quality: it seemed to be vaguely about urban unrest, and then in the middle it broke down into this long section with a recording of a jittery Adrian Belew recounting how he’d been walking around the neighbouring area (in London, where it was made) talking into a tape recorder, when he’d been confronted by some local hard lads who’d demanded to know why he was walking around talking into a tape recorder. All this was accompanied by some top-class shrieky guitar, which I know now to have been Belew playing his battered Strat, with a partially unwound pickup, through his MXR DynaComp. (This album made me want to own a compressor pedal. And also learn a whole bunch of new scales, which I did. The recording of Belew talking was made by Fripp, and it was a real incident that had happened during a break in recording.) Anyhoo, Discipline was probably the furthest-out thing I’d listened to at that point in my very sheltered life. I forget when I got a copy of Beat: probably not long after. I really liked it. I got all the Kerouac/Beat references (well, the first song is called ‘Neal and Jack and Me’) and despite a couple of dud songs—’Heartbeat’ is a bit perfunctory, and ‘The Howler’ is half-baked—some of it was really gorgeous. ‘Waiting Man’ is a truly lovely song, and there aren’t a ton of them in the KC catalogue. ‘Neurotica’ was an exhilarating, jazzy splurge. ‘Two Hands’ was another beautiful song. And then there was ‘Requiem’, the improvisation over some doomy Frippertronics which (I know now) they stuck on the album because they ran out of written material. Just… one of the great KC improvisations, what with Tony Levin’s lush descending bassline and Fripp and Belew having a raging guitar battle. I read somewhere that, in the middle of recording it, Levin’s bass was plugged into so many effects that, as an experiment, he unplugged it from them, and it made no difference. Beat was apparently a difficult album to record: the band had lost its initial burst of inspiration, and Fripp was concerned that it was drifting away from the original vision and was becoming more of a vehicle for Belew’s songwriting, although, being Fripp, he was too passive-aggressive to actually say so. Belew later called it ‘the most awful record-making experience of my life’. Beat remains a favourite album of mine, with the combination of beautiful chimy songs and hellish improvised noise (‘Requiem’); it got me through a Tough Period In My Teens. And then they finally got around to making Three of a Perfect Pair. This is perhaps my least favourite of the 80s KC albums, not that I dislike it, so much that it seems to have less inspiration. I mean, you could probably play ‘Industry’ and ‘No Warning’ at the same time as each other and it would sound like the one track. I like the mood of those tracks, but I don’t really need ten minutes of it spread over two tracks. And ‘Larks Tongues in Aspic Part III’ has that dazzling opening guitar thing by Fripp, one of the most remarkable guitar performances I’ve ever heard, but then turns into a plod. I used to play the opening bit to guitarist friends of mine on my Walkman, whenever they thought they were getting pretty hotshot because they could play an entire Dire Straits song. I have a special memory of finding a cassette of this in a Fnac store on my first ever trip to Paris with my family; I hadn’t known that it existed. I think that this album shows the split that had opened up in the band: it was basically divided into abstract sound sculptures that involved everybody, and pop songs by Belew. I get why Fripp broke the band up on the morning after the last show of the tour. This particular incarnation of KC had run its course. But what a cool little monster of a band it was. I recently got the DVD Neal and Jack and Me, containing live performances from 1984 and 1982 (the latter previously released on VHS as The Noise). Once you get past the annoying mid-80s video effects added in post, it’s a document of a band that could really rock. Some of the live versions make the studio versions seem relatively pedestrian, and even though Fripp spends the entire gig sitting down, as he has done since 1969, he gets positively animated during his solos. It’s hard to believe that a band like this existed, yet they did. Perhaps my very favourite KC lineups are the ones I actually saw live, decades later: the Fripp-Jakszyk-Collins-Levin-Mastelotto-Rieflin-Harrison one, and the subsequent one where Rieflin moved to keyboards and Jeremy Stacey replaced him on drums. Because I saw them live, and so finally got the full KC experience. (Fripp: A King Crimson record is a love letter; King Crimson live are a hot date.) King Crimson, Usher Hall, Edinburgh, 17 Sep 2015. l to r: Mel Collins, Pat Mastelotto, Tony Levin, Bill Rieflin (RIP), Jakko Jakszyk, Gavin Harrison, Robert Fripp. Photo by me. But the 80s version will always have a place in my heart, in that they taught me a lot about music, and fused the heart with the head and the hips and the nerves in a very satisfying way. They were also enormously influential. For a while in the mid-80s, guitarists in sooo many new wave-ish bands were trying to sound like Belew, playing shrieky angular solos with loads of reverb, but without his taste and soul. Probably a good thing that that’s died down, eh.

Question: Are there any girl drummers that are just as good as a male drummer?
Answer: All good answers, although I question the use of the word ‘girl’. I think you meant ‘women drummers’. One answer mentioned Dame Evelyn Glennie. She’s an outstanding percussionist, one of the greatest in her field and the subject of a fine documentary, Touch the Sound. Off the top of my head, I’d also name Cindy Blackman and Janet Weiss as excellent drummers, and Ikue Mori and Susie Ibarra as virtuosi. One drummer who I’d never heard of is Jess Bowen, of the pop-rock band The Summer Set. That’s her on the right. I am not a big fan of pop-rock. The YouTube channel Drumeo has a series of videos where they invite a drummer to listen to a song they haven’t heard before, with the drums mixed out, and come up with a drum part on the spot. Jess Bowen took this challenge, and confessed in advance that she wasn’t the kind of drummer who could play a song after hearing it only once. She was given ‘Bulls on Parade’ by Rage Against the Machine, a song she was completely unfamiliar with. She proceeded to play the living shit out of it. Afterwards, on hearing the original song complete, she was mostly critical of herself for playing too much. Still, it’s a pleasure to watch a good drummer in action.

Question: How did Adam Smith and Karl Marx know so much about capitalism when they wrote their works in a agrarian society that didn't become industrialized until the late 1800s after they both died?
Answer: Karl Marx didn’t write his work in an agrarian society which etc. etc. From 1849 to his death in 1883 he lived in London, the capital of the most industrially advanced country in the world at the time. If you read Capital, you soon notice that among Marx’s primary sources are countless UK government reports on working conditions in British factories, which he devoured in endless hours of research. His buddy and colleague Friedrich Engels managed a factory. So, I don’t know where you think Marx was living, but Britain was the cutting edge of industrial capitalism when Marx was writing, and he lived there.

Question: Let's say it was just proven that life begins at conception, would you still be pro-choice?
Answer: Life doesn’t ‘begin at conception’, it was going on before then. The sperm and the egg are both alive. It’s not about when life begins. I am pro-choice because it’s only the mother’s choice that matters. The blastocyst/embryo/foetus can’t make a choice, and I don’t believe that anyone else has the right to make a choice about the situation. I have nothing but contempt for anyone who thinks that their moral sentiments are more important than the bodily integrity of the mother. They aren’t. I believe that mothers should have a choice on whether or not they have an abortion. And, I frankly don’t care if they decide to have it in the final month, just because they want to—not that anyone does do that, and not that any reputable doctor would perform the procedure. But my reason for saying so is that I see no reason why any woman should be deprived of this choice on the grounds of her supposed moral depravity, if only because I don’t trust the people who want to deprive her of that choice to be capable judges of who’s ‘deserving’ and who isn’t. In my view, once you start dictating why women shouldn’t have the right to make this choice, you forfeit your own right to a place in the debate. You become morally unfit to take part in it. Because you assumed that you get to tell women what they may do with their bodies. For me, the entire issue is about women having the right and the power to dictate what they do with their bodies. It’s not about anything else.

Question: What is the last television show you have watched?
Answer: Barry, the HBO show created by Alec Berg and Bill Hader, starring Hader as a depressed hitman who takes up acting in an effort to find more meaning in life. Sarah Goldberg, Bill Hader and Anthony Carrigan in Barry. I reviewed the first season when I watched it four years ago, but I didn’t get around to watching the remaining three seasons until the last few weeks, when I binge-watched them on a nightly basis. Spoiler alert. I won’t give away major spoilers, but I refuse to not talk about what the show was about. This was my reaction to season 1: Well… let’s just say that that answer didn’t age as well as I hoped it would. Season two was still pretty funny, but it got increasingly darker as Barry’s crimes (specifically, a couple of major crimes he committed towards the end of season 1) began to catch up with him. I wrote a couple of answers touching on it, but then got so swept up in seasons 3 and 4 that I’m still, as they say, ‘processing’ them. Season 3 added a new layer of Hollywood satire, as Sarah Goldberg’s character, the self-absorbed actor Sally Reed, got a deal to create a TV series based on her own life—and the show was funnily and brutally unsparing about the ways in which ‘based on her own life’ was both true and not true. It turned out that one of the themes of Barry was ‘fictionalisation’, and the ways people choose to tell stories about themselves. Sally and Barry’s acting class have a project to come up with a piece of drama about their own lives. Sally chooses to fictionalise her walking out on her abusive ex-husband, but she does so by writing the scene so that she comes across as more courageous and defiant, and the event itself as more dramatic, than was actually the case. She initially feels really bad about having done this. The trouble is, though, that people don’t want to hear how it really happened, and part of Sally herself doesn’t want to think about how it really happened—so although she genuinely wants to tell the truth, when she does the heroic/untruthful version, it makes people thank her and be genuinely grateful to her, because stories about a battered woman standing up to her ex-husband are more inspiring than a story about a battered woman who just walked out without any confrontation. So she ends up convincing herself that she was right to do the heroic version. And in subsequent retellings, she makes herself sound more heroic. This goes back to a scene in season 2 episode 1, where Barry, desperate to keep the acting classes going, tells a story about the first person that he killed. We see him telling the story, but we also see his actual memory of the occasion. At the time, he was a Marine sniper in Afghanistan. He was on his first tour. None of his colleagues considered him to be much of a soldier. But Barry is an incredibly good shot, and he snipes three Afghan guerrillas from 700 yards away—which (it so happens that I know) is some seriously good sniping. His fellow Marines are jubilant that he pulled this off, and he is pleased by their approval. But, in the present, Gene instructs other students to act out what they imagine were Barry’s reactions to his shooting. And they decide that he must have been traumatised by killing Afghan people. Barry, who wants the approval of his fellow students, timidly agrees that the false re-enactment of his sniping triumph is the truth. This sets the tone for the acting class: that it’s better to tell an inspiring fiction, than to tell an unwelcome truth. Anyway, a combination of factors mean that Sally is catapulted into a position where she’s running her own TV show based on her now heavily fictionalised life story, but then it all falls apart, and long before Barry itself ends, she reaches her level of ultimate minor celebrity: after screaming at a former assistant in an elevator and being caught on video doing it, she becomes resigned to the fact that she is known to the world at large as ‘Entitled Cunt Girl’. Meanwhile, Barry has problems of his own, most of them stemming from his relationship with his deeply untrustworthy mentor, Monroe Fuches. After trying for all season 2 to restrain his impulses towards violence, Barry at the end of the season goes on an absolutely savage killing spree, which pretty much sets the tone for him in season 3. Season 3 itself has a finale that topped this, in terms of violence, by having a.) two characters mauled to death by a panther (thankfully offscreen) and b.) having a previously non-violent character snap and beat another to death with a baseball bat—not offscreen, in this instance. And yet season 3 also had one of the most hilarious bike chases ever put on film, a glorious succession of bad decisions by characters, with superb stunt work and filming. Season 4 simply has to be seen to be believed. I thought it was great. By then, my eyes had become accustomed to the darkness. Barry became a strange pleasure to watch: all day I would think Oh god, I really don’t want to watch another episode, it’s too dark, and then night would fall and I would turn it on and watch three in a row. It was an absolute feat of writing and directing, especially by Bill Hader, who wrote and directed much of it, but everyone in it was remarkable. I read that, when Hader was initially showing the cast the scripts in season 1, he asked them if they had any feedback, which is unusual for a show creator. Sarah Goldberg told him that she hoped Sally wouldn’t always be like she is in season 1, a funny if sharp portrayal of a rather vapidly selfish actress, and that if possible she’d like to go into ‘Gena Rowlands territory’ and make Sally rather more dimensional and dark. They did this. Sally’s journey in the show is extraordinary, and much of the credit has to go to Goldberg for her incredible ability to make Sally kind of awful, and comic, and also tragic. At one point, she finds out that Barry has an audition for a (terrible) movie with its director, while she doesn’t. In response, she delivers a two-page, almost three-minute monologue, in one breathless take, in which she manages to express both her pride in his achievement, her resentment of his success, her frustration that her career isn’t happening nearly as well as his, and her deeper frustrations about life and her art and society, while also being excited about her own writing and its possibilities, and also being comically deluded about those possibilities. Apparently Goldberg did four takes of this shot, and after each one, the crew gave her a round of applause. And don’t even start me on Henry Winkler, who played a tour de force as the egotistical acting coach, Gene Cousineau, who gets caught up in the whole story and becomes central to it. Or Stephen Root as Barry’s mentor Fuches, who goes from shabby joke to terrifying gang lord, or Anthony Carrigan as the perpetually cheery Chechen gangster NoHo Hank, whose cheeriness wears off somewhat after he gets to hear the aforementioned death-by-panther from an adjoining cell. In the end, Barry felt a bit like a four-season meditation on the lines from Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar: The evil that men do lives after them; the good is oft interred with their bones. The show didn’t dramatise this notion—it explored it, questioned it, held it up to the light and left it hanging. Can a person who does very bad things stop doing them, and become a ‘good person’? What matters more: who you are, or who you are remembered as being? It was a great, great show. One of the best I’ve seen in years.

Question: In what ways do creationist beliefs intersect with theories of musical development and innovation?
Answer: My understanding of creationist beliefs regarding musical development and innovation are mostly derived from two articles. This one: And this one, which is more up to date: From these articles, I gather that the basic creationist take on music can be summed up in a few bullet points: If we look here: We find such sentiments as: ‘God created the physical universe and the human ear and mind to make music possible.’ ‘God created music to benefit our minds and bodies and our social interactions.’ ‘With all of these amazing things about music in mind, let’s use the mnemonic device M-U-S-I-C to represent five aspects of music—aspects we can enjoy and appreciate and thank God for.’ Yeah, let’s not, although if you’re curious, the letters stand for Magnificent, Unifying, Shareable, Inspirational and Creative. I have a problem with statements such as the ones quoted above. My problem with them is derived from my lifelong interest in music, which was sharpened and deepened a good deal when I studied it at university and came to a better understanding of how music is made in different societies and time periods. My problem is simply this: This stuff is bollocks. Creationism is utter garbage, but it also seems to severely damage the mental faculties of those who subscribe to it. They lose the ability to assess evidence, and reason backwards from the answers they want, so that they end up talking counterfactual drivel like There is simply no evidence that the striving for art and music has anything to do with the pragmatic requirements of survival and reproduction. There is a mountain of evidence to suggest that art and music have something to do with the requirements of survival and reproduction, beginning with the fact that countless millions of young people take up music in the hope that, further down the line, it will get them laid. That said, countless musicians across the centuries have turned to music as a means of trying to appeal to, or praise, or get close to, their god/s. And some of the resulting music is among the greatest music out there. From Bach to the Mahavishnu Orchestra, and from William Byrd to Ravi Shankar, and from Mahalia Jackson to Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, devotional music can be extraordinarily powerful and moving, even if you don’t believe in any sort of supreme being. But here’s the thing: That music came from people. Not from god. It is an expression of human desires and fears and longings, using musical languages that humans created, not something that ‘originat[es] from a source much greater than ourselves’. The creationists in the above quotes write about music the way that people who have never left their home town write about foreign countries. Or the way people who have never had sex talk about sex. Music has many functions and many roles in society. It is not all a happy-clappy whitebread song circle, in which we praise a blue-eyed, blonde-haired Jesus by means of the CAGED system. Music does not always bring people together with hugs and prayers. The CIA used loud popular music as a torture device in Guantanamo Bay. Among the songs they used were ‘Born in the USA’, ‘Raspberry Beret’ and the theme song from Barney & Friends. When US special forces wanted to arrest Panamanian unelected dictator Manuel Noriega, they did so by continuously blasting AC/DC’s ‘You Shook Me All Night Long’ at the building he was sheltering in, and it worked: after ten days he came out. Musical innovations are driven by human needs. The programmable drum machine was invented so that musicians who were poor drummers could use it to make demos, but J Dilla worked out how to tweak it so that it sounded human, because he didn’t want it to sound like a machine. The solid-body electric guitar was invented because country guitarists didn’t want their guitars to feed back. The Marshall 1962 combo amp was invented because English blues guitarists did want their guitars to feed back, or at least wanted the tone to break up. Bigger amplifier-speaker setups were invented because a generation of young men wished to project their masculinity across large music venues. As a result, the electric guitar became—at least for a while—what Frank Zappa called ‘the single most blasphemous device on the face of the earth.’ To sum up: Creationists think that the Christian god gave us music and that music is simple. He did not. It is not. Creationism has nothing credible to say about development and innovation in music.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Is Jim Halpert a sociopath?
Answer: Not even slightly. Jim Halpert, non-sociopath I don’t trust dictionary definitions much, but as I understand sociopathy, it involves a lack of concern for society and ideas of right and wrong, and a lack of respect for the feelings of others. Jim has neither of these things. Yes, he likes to prank some people, but look at who he pranks: the two most annoying and overbearing people in his vicinity, Dwight and Andy. He pranks Dwight both to relieve his own boredom with his job (which job he does very well, even though he doesn’t work very hard) but mainly to puncture Dwight’s absurd pomposity. When he first pranks Andy, Andy explodes in a violent rage, and Jim—clearly aware that pranking Andy will have potentially worse consequences than pranking Dwight—doesn’t prank him again until much later, when Andy is being peak annoying. I’ve skimmed a couple of ‘Jim is a jerk/Jim is objectively a scumbag’ articles, and they are unconvincing. One article claimed in a subheading that Jim cheats on Pam, but then dialled it down in the text to observing that Jim has the opportunity to cheat on Pam: very shoddy journalism. This is of course a reference to Cathy, who blatantly attempts to seduce Jim in Florida by showing up in his room in her pyjamas, and then goes further by taking a shower and lying on his bed in nothing but a bathrobe—and then has the nerve to act offended when Jim points out that he’s married. Jim takes numerous measures to get rid of her, and ultimately spends the night in Dwight’s room, eating desserts and watching sports with his usual rival. (In a deleted scene, Jim talks to Pam on the phone and flat-out tells her about the whole Cathy situation, which she finds both amusing and ‘pathetic’.) The producers actually wanted Jim to cheat on Pam with Cathy, but John Krasinski firmly refused. Jim and Pam’s marital problems were deferred until season 9, and his attempt to help start up the sports marketing company in Philadelphia: eventually he chooses to stop working for the startup, because it’s damaging his marriage. That is not the action of a sociopath. One common criticism of Jim is for the rather blunt way he breaks up with his girlfriend Katy in season 2’s ‘Booze Cruise’. Roy has just publicly announced a date for he and Pam to get married: Katy: Do you think that'll ever be us? Jim: No. Katy: What is wrong with you? Why did you even bring me here tonight? Jim: I don't know. Let's break up. Katy: Whoa. What? This happens at the very moment Jim realises that his love for Pam—which he came very close to confessing to her in the previous episode, ‘Christmas Party’—is doomed, because she’s finally going to get married. Under the circumstances, breaking up with the girlfriend he doesn't love is a highly honourable thing to do, even if he could have been more gentle about it (but this is funnier.) I mean, compare Andy, who in season 8 travels to Florida to win back Erin, and only on the trip home with her does he get around to breaking up with his existing girlfriend, Jessica. Another article observed that Jim pranks Dwight, but when Dwight pranks him back, in season 7’s ‘Classy Christmas’, he can’t handle it. This fails to note that Dwight’s prank is characteristically Dwight-ish in that Dwight goes way too far, relentlessly ambushing Jim with snowballs, and throwing them with such force that Jim gets a bloody nose. It goes on beyond the point where anyone except Dwight finds it funny. Jim’s pranks are never actually brutal. Who’s the sociopath now, entertainment news content providers? In season 4’s ‘Money’, Angela has broken off her relationship with Dwight because he euthanised her beloved cat without her permission (and rather clumsily, at that). Dwight is so heartbroken that he takes to sitting in the stairwell, moaning. Jim, who at this stage in the show still doesn’t really like Dwight, sits down next to him and says this: Did I ever tell you why I left Scranton? Yeah, I didn't think I had. Well, it was all about Pam. Yeah, I mean, she was with Roy... and I just couldn't take it. I mean, I lost it, Dwight. I couldn't sleep, I couldn't concentrate on anything. And then weird stuff, like, food had no taste. So my solution was to move away. It was awful. And it is something that I wouldn't wish on my worst enemy. And that includes you. Again, not the act of someone who lacks regard for other people’s feelings. Five seasons later, Jim and Dwight have buried the hatchet. One reason why is that Jim saved Dwight from getting fired. Dwight was going to take credit for the Sabre store, but Jim, alerted by Robert California, physically prevents Dwight from doing so, wrestling with him outside the conference room. Todd Packer steps in to do it, and duly gets canned. A stunned Dwight witnesses this, and wordlessly holds out his hand to Jim so he can get up from the floor. Their rivalry is effectively over, as of that point. In the penultimate episode of the final season, Dwight is regional manager, and Jim is not assistant regional manager but assistant to the regional manager. Dwight asks Jim for advice. Jim has been happily pranking Dwight all episode, by subtly manipulating Dwight into appointing himself as Jim’s assistant (prompting Dwight to remark with satisfaction From now on, anyone who needs to speak to me has got to go through me first). He first tries to palm Dwight off to his assistant (Dwight himself) but Dwight is serious: he plans to marry Esther, who is beautiful and young, plus ‘Her family admires me, my family tolerates hers’, and her dowry includes a walk-in freezer full of frozen premium cattle sperm. But the problem, Dwight admits, is Angela, who has a baby that Dwight thought his own, but the DNA test says otherwise. Jim’s advice is wise and heartfelt: Jim: I don't know what you want me to tell you, man. All I know is that every time I've been faced with a tough decision, there's only one thing that outweighs every other concern. One thing that will make you give up on everything you thought you knew, every instinct, every rational calculation. Dwight: Some sort of virus? Jim: Love. Dwight: Oh. Jim: Dwight, listen: no matter what happens, you gotta forget about all the other stuff. You gotta forget about logic and fear and doubt. You just gotta do everything you can to get to the one woman who's gonna make all this worth it. At the end of the day, you gotta jump. You love Angela, Dwight. I think you always have. Dwight: You're a good assistant, Jim. Jim: Not as good as you. Dwight: That's very true. Get the hell outta here. That’s not someone who doesn’t care for other people’s feelings. In the same episode, Pam has been worrying that Jim will always regret not pursuing the other job in Philadelphia. She confesses this to Jim, and he requests the documentary crew to cut together a DVD of scenes of Jim and Pam having moments of love. Pam watches this, much moved, whereupon Jim gives her the Christmas card he almost gave her in ‘Christmas Party’, in which card he first confessed his love to her. Back then, he’d decided not to give it to her, because she was engaged to Roy: he gives it to her now, seven years later, because it’s what she needs to hear from him. Jim understands right and wrong, and is willing to do small, relatively harmless wrongs, but he understands people enough and sympathises with them enough to do right by them when it matters. The ‘Jim is actually a jerk’ articles ignore all that. Jim Halpert is not a saint or a role model, just a happily married sports marketing exec and former paper salesman, living in Austin. And not a sociopath.

Question: What exactly is studied in musicology, and how does it differ from music history?
Answer: Music history is simply the history of music—although nothing is simple, and how we tell the history depends a lot on our assumptions about how history works. Older styles of music history tend to tell it as a history of great composers, but more modern approaches (for example, the volumes in the Cambridge History series) take a more thematic or genre-based approach. It’s difficult to say ‘exactly’ what is studied in musicology, because the nature of the subject itself changes over time, and so do definitions of it. The late Joe Kerman was one of the 20th century’s greatest musicologists, and someone whose work I have the greatest admiration for. Joseph Kerman, 1924–2014 Kerman noted in his 1985 book Musicology that: the word was originally understood (as Musikwissenschaft still is) to cover thinking about, research into, and knowledge of all possible aspects of music. However, Kerman added: But in academic practice, and in broad general usage, musicology has come to have a much more constricted meaning. It has come to mean the study of the history of Western music in the high-art tradition. […] Musicology is perceived as dealing essentially with the factual, the documentary, the verifiable, the analysable, the positivistic. Musicologists are respected for the facts they know about music. They are not admired for their insight into music as aesthetic experience. He went on to say: Which is the subject of this book—musicology in the ideal, comprehensive, original definition, or musicology in the restricted, more mundane, current one? The broad or the narrow? The answer lies somewhere in between. Kerman goes on to discuss the overlaps between musicology, theory and ethnomusicology—all of which disciplines were a bit more separate from each other forty years ago, when he wrote the book, than they are now. I would say that one effect of the revolution in musicology brought about by Kerman and younger colleagues of his, such as Philip Brett, Susan McClary and Lawrence Kramer, is that the original, broader definition of musicology has become much more accepted in practice than the narrower one. The influence of the narrower one still lingers, especially in the tendency many people have to place ‘Western music in the high-art tradition’ at the top of a sort of pyramid of ‘musical quality’. But the new musicology, which got going in the 1980s, is much more willing to pay attention to other forms of music and take them seriously, and is also more ready to talk about the aesthetic experience of music, than the kind that focused on musical analyses of works of Western classical music, as if no other kind of music deserved such close attention. (I would add a link to the Wikipedia article on the new musicology, but as is the way with so many Wikipedia articles about subjects one actually knows a little bit about, I can’t honestly recommend it.) (I would separate the musicology of popular music from a cultural studies approach to popular music. The former tends to pay more close attention to the music itself, the latter to its context and its relationship to the culture. I’m currently reading a book-length study of the music of Kate Bush, Ron Moy’s Kate Bush and Hounds of Love, which is written from a cultural studies perspective rather than a musicological one, and which suffers accordingly, IMO. Hopefully the next book on my reading list, Dan Charnas’ Dilla Time, about the life, music and cultural afterlife of Detroit hip-hop producer J Dilla, will delve a bit deeper into Dilla’s music than Moy does into Bush’s. Edit: It does. It’s shaping up to be one of the most remarkable books about popular music I’ve ever read.) So, musicology is not solely concerned with music history, or musical analysis, but it can encompass those things while taking a broader look at music in general, and trying to promote an understanding of it.

Question: Is there something like a guide that translates 18th century English literature into modern English the phrasing used in the book The Vicar Of Wakefield by Oliver Goldsmith?
Answer: The bad news is that The Vicar of Wakefield is already in modern English. The even worse news is that, compared to other 18th century writers, Goldsmith is noted for the exceptional clarity and simplicity of his style. Here’s the opening of chapter 1: I was ever of opinion, that the honest man who married and brought up a large family, did more service than he who continued single, and only talked of population. From this motive, I had scarce taken orders a year before I began to think seriously of matrimony, and chose my wife as she did her wedding gown, not for a fine glossy surface, but such qualities as would wear well. To do her justice, she was a good-natured notable woman; and as for breeding, there were few country ladies who could shew more. She could read any English book without much spelling, but for pickling, preserving, and cookery, none could excel her. The only phrases in this which I think require any gloss are ‘talked of population’, which is about how the single man doesn’t want to add more people in the world, and ‘taken orders’, which given the novel’s title is fairly self-explanatory: it refers to the narrator taking holy orders as a vicar. The Vicar of Wakefield should only present difficulties for a reader with very limited skills in modern standard English. If you were to turn it into contemporary 21st century English, the language would necessarily reflect contemporary attitudes and it would cease to make any sense, because it’s a story that only makes sense in an 18th century setting. (If it makes sense at all, which is a separate matter.) Note in the above that one of the things the narrator values about his wife is not just that she’s good at cooking, but she’s expert at ‘pickling and preserving’, which was an essential household skill in the era before the invention of the refrigerator and freezer, but now is basically a hobby. Just get a decent edition of it with annotations. This book shouldn’t require ‘translation’.

Question: Has any genre of music gone extinct in the way that languages go extinct?
Answer: This is a very interesting question which I’ve been thinking about ever since I got the A2A from Seth Bjornsson. (Thanks, Seth.) My first instinct is to answer Maybe, but how would we know? If we have evidence of a genre of music, we can probably reconstruct how it sounded, or probably sounded. And if we can do that, is it really ‘extinct’? Musical scholarship in the 20th century has produced editions of music by countless Western composers whose music had gone un-listened to for centuries. People in the 18th century really didn’t pay much attention to 16th century music; only in the 19th and early 20th century did working composers start going back into music history and become antiquarians. Brahms was a pioneer, in this: he studied the music of Palestrina and Gabrieli, among others. In the 20th century, Anton Webern’s doctoral thesis was about the Choralis Constantinus of Heinrich Isaac (c. 1450–1517), and even today, when Renaissance music is far more widely listened to, Isaac is a very deep cut. If a genre of music can still be studied, someone will almost certainly revive it, at some point, if only to play it, not compose in it. People don’t still write masses and motets in the style of Guillaume de Machaut, although the French avant-garde guitarist Noël Akchoté has recorded albums of his arrangements of Machaut for electric guitar, which is a drastic, almost heroic way of keeping that music alive. Another way of thinking about this is the question of styles, and how performance styles change, and what it means that they change. The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein came from a very musical family. Brahms and Mahler both gave recitals in the Wittgenstein family home, which Wittgenstein could have attended as a boy. Wittgenstein himself was extremely musical and could whistle entire classical works from memory: he even took up the clarinet at the age of 30, and became pretty good at it. In his cultural preferences, Wittgenstein was extremely conservative. He once remarked that music ‘came to a stop’ with Brahms, and added ‘even in Brahms I can hear the sound of machinery.’ Another time, he was listening to a recording of classical music with a friend, and commented that it was ironic that, in an age where the technology of recording was getting better and better, ‘fewer and fewer people know how the music should be played.’ I’ve often thought about this. What about difference performance styles disturbed Wittgenstein so much? Would he have listened to a contemporary recording of, say, a Beethoven piano sonata by Daniel Barenboim, and considered it to be so lacking in the proper spirit of Beethoven-ness, as to be ‘not-Beethoven’? Or would he have simply considered it not to his taste? (And what would he have made of Artur Schnabel’s recordings, given that Schnabel was seven years older than him?) I could compare Wittgenstein’s reactions to modern performances of classical music to my own reactions to certain kinds of blues performance. I grew up listening to blues of the 1930s-60s: Robert Johnson, Skip James, Howlin’ Wolf, Jimmy Reed. I deliberately avoided contemporary blues players of my own time, because I wanted a grounding in the classics. I learned to play blues guitar from listening to players like Hubert Sumlin, Otis Rush, Albert Collins. And also Eric Clapton, who I stopped listening to once I could get my hands on recordings by the musicians who’d inspired him. (And, now I think about it, Jimi Hendrix, who was a lot of other things besides a great blues guitarist, which he was.) When, years later, I first listened to blues-rock guitarists like Joe Bonamassa, my initial reaction was that this wasn’t blues, but something else. I’m sure Bonamassa is more steeped in the blues than I am, but I don’t hear in his playing what I hear in Otis Rush, or Albert Collins. I hear some of their distant influence, but it’s heavily filtered through the playing of white rock guitar players who had listened to them, people like Jeff Beck and Rory Gallagher. Whose playing I don’t like. It’s muscular and athletic and all those things, but it doesn’t move me. But do I think that blues is ‘extinct’? No. Gary Clark Jr strikes me as continuing directly from the guys I mention, bringing in reggae and soul and even punk. His music may be less technically flashy than Bonamassa’s, but to my ears, it’s a lot more soulful, emotional and involving. In his hands, the blues are still alive. And I’m sure there are others like him. In the end, I don’t think that the analogy between music and spoken language really works. Languages die when they have no more native speakers and stop developing. Latin is a dead language because nobody is doing cool new things with Latin. Irish is not a dead language, because Irish people are still doing cool new things with Irish. Blues is not a dead genre as long as people are still doing cool new things with blues. If rock seems dead, it’s because we can no longer think of cool new things to do with it. Actually, I can think of a number of things that could be done with it, but not a lot of rock musicians seem to want to do them. They prefer to sound like previous rock musicians. Musical genres don’t rely on native speakers, because nobody can innately play music, the way we can innately speak our mother tongue (unless there’s something wrong with us.) Music is like a second language: it must always be learned. And since it must always be learned, it’s always possible to learn to play new music, no matter how old or neglected it is—if you can only figure out how it worked.

Question: Which bones make the best bone broth for soup, stews, and gravies?
Answer: I really think it varies. If you want a basic, flavourful, all-purpose stock, I recommend using a roasted chicken carcass where you’ve already cut off the good bits (legs, wings, breasts) for some other purpose. If you make stock with it, and then boil it down with a bottle of red wine, you’ve got demi-glace, which you can then freeze and use as a great flavour enhancer. But chicken stock is in general a very useful thing to have around. If you want to make tonkotsu, the legendary Japanese bone broth for a particularly sumptuous ramen dish, you’ve got to use pork bones, but I have never succeeded in making it myself. I think I wasn’t boiling the bones for long enough at a high enough temperature. Pork trotters are great because they have a lot of gelatin, but the disadvantage with them, as I see it, as that they’re pretty good to eat, too, but not after you’ve extracted all their gelatin. If you’re going on full-on French cuisine you should use veal bones, but who can be bothered, to be honest? Veal isn’t all that flavourful, and chicken does yield similar results, at least in terms of flavour. Veal has the edge when it comes to gelatin, I think. But we’ll get to that in a minute. I do like veal bones for their delicious marrow, but that’s another story. Beef bones also have delicious marrow because it’s the same animal, just older. For intense beefiness, you can’t beat beef bones, but beef has a pronounced flavour which is not the case with chicken and veal. One of my favourite things to make is a steak with bone marrow on top: I roast the bone with the marrow before I start cooking the steak, and when they become ready at the same time, I scoop out the marrow and dollop it onto the cooked steak like a topping. However, if you really want a stock that is loaded with gelatin, and has plenty of flavour but not a pronounced flavour profile like beef, I recommend chicken feet. Possibly in tandem with chicken carcass. You can get them in Chinese supermarkets. Chicken feet are basically bone and skin held together with collagen. There’s little enough to eat on a pork trotter, but there’s even less on a chicken foot, and when that collagen melts and turns to gelatin, you’ve got some of the best stock you’ll ever have. The disadvantage is that, when you’re preparing chicken feet, you have to individually snip off the talons, otherwise you’ll have to strain them out of the stock when it’s all over. Which is a bit of a faff. But seriously: chicken feet make incredible stock.

Question: How do some people get their ramen to taste so good?
Answer: I like some instant ramen as much as anyone else. However, this is not my guide to how to make instant ramen taste better. I think instant ramen tastes fine as it is. At least, I’ve gone the rounds with that stuff, and I have nothing to add to other people’s instant-ramen-hacks answers. This is how I made the ramen I made two nights ago. Which was awesome. First off, I agree that the foundation of any good ramen is the broth. However, I’m not going to boil pork bones for 24 hours or whatever, because life is too short. I also happen to think that the foundation is all very well, but if you don’t build a nice building on top of the foundation, what you’ve got is the equivalent of a 70s local government office building: you can do things in it but it’s not a place you’d want to live in. To me, the excuse for making ramen in the first place are those luscious slices of roast pork perching on the top, crisp on the edges yet succulent. That’s why I fell in love with ramen all those years ago. The pork isn’t enough on its own: it must be in harmony with the other ingredients (noodles, broth, egg, nearly-raw vegetables.) And only last night did I succeed in approximating my ideal. This recipe for making the roast pork comes from RamenLord, by way of the excellent YouTuber Way of Ramen. The next day, you have a humongous lump of chilled, soy-braised/roasted pork in a bag full of liquid and bits of solidified fat. Good for you. Unless you are cooking ramen for many people, you’re going to want to freeze some of that. Hoik out your pork and cut into big hunks, enough for one dinner each. I ended up with three. Transfer the un-needed hunks into freezer bags with some of the liquid, and freeze. Congratulations! Now you can can have roast pork at 12 hours’ defrosting’s notice. Frozen chashu pork. In the meantime, you have a rather unappetising looking hunk of meat, brown on the outside and white in the middle, rippled with fat. Don’t worry, you’re not going to eat it like that. The way to make good broth, if you can’t be bothered to make broth from scratch, and maybe even if you can, is to make tare. Tare is the concentrated flavour essence that gives a boring-ass broth richness and savour. You make it in advance, and then add your boring-ass broth to it at the point of serving. To make tare, you begin with the remainder of the cooking liquid that your cooked pork has been steeping in overnight. I put this in a saucepan and added some more soy sauce, sake and mirin, and for good measure, some unsmoked pancetta I had in the fridge. Don’t use smoked bacon, as it’ll make your tare taste of bacon. You then boil this until it reduces from a liquid to a syrupy consistency, and reserve it, straining out the pancetta. I threw the pancetta away because you can have too much of a good thing. (I used a Kallo chicken stock cube to make the boring-ass broth because the tare was going to transform it anyway.) Tare should be too intensely salty/sweet/umami-ish for you to want to have it on its own. It’s like Coca-Cola syrup: it will do its magic later. Next, the egg. These are a pain in the ass because, to be the right consistency for ramen, they should be soft-boiled, and I don’t know about you, but to my mind, peeling a soft-boiled egg is very annoying. Still, I use J. Kenji Lopez-Alt’s method: boil water, add egg/s, cover, take off heat and leave for four minutes. Actually I gave them four minutes and 30 seconds because I was using large eggs and his recipe was for mediums. Then, peel the egg/s, trying to not break that wobbly white in half so that liquid yolk spills everywhere. Reserve your peeled egg. If you’d done this last night you could have made tea-soaked eggs, but that’s a whole other recipe and I liked the simplicity of plain egg. Why egg? It adds a richness to the broth, once that liquid yolk seeps into it. If you’re scared of soft-boiled eggs because of low food safety standards in your area, take it up with the government, Poindexter. Next, cook your noodles. Noodles, boiling water, five minutes, drain, run under cold water till cold, reserve. Easy. Next, vegetable prep. I went with enoki mushrooms (tear off as many as you want, cut the root part off, rinse) and sweetheart cabbage, cut into thin slivers, for bite and freshness. Chop some spring onions. Next, finishing the pork. I put foil over my grill tray (broiler in the US), to save on cleaning up later, and a rack over the foil. Slice your pork and lay the slices on the rack. Place under hot grill/broiler until the slices of pork are golden and sizzling. Flip them over and do the other side. Now, they are ready to eat. Bring broth to a simmer. Add your vegetables to it and cook for no more than three minutes. You want those vegetables fresh-tasting, and you also want your broth really hot because you’re adding room temperature ingredients to it. Place a tablespoonful of tare in the serving bowl, and place your cooked noodles on top. Ladle in hot broth, and stir so that the tare gets nice and mixed up in it. You should see the broth turn dark brown as it does so. Add vegetables. Add egg. Don’t worry if it breaks, it’s supposed to. Add pork slices, fresh from the grill. Sprinkle chopped spring onion on top. Behold. A bowl of ramen. Enjoy.

Question: I was once told by a student of classical music that 'all music has been written before'. Does this make any sense?
Answer: Yeah, that’s the kind of thing classical music students tend to say. Usually, the less brilliant ones. On a trivial level it’s not all true, because not all music is ‘written’ in the first place. I write this in the reception area of a public swimming pool. A few feet away, some girls are playing a clapping game that involves chanting a song. Did some composer with a wig in the 18th century ‘write’ that song? Or was it made up by some kid, at some point, somewhere? And then did it evolve from generation to generation, passed down by word of mouth? Or did it only do so occasionally, because some parent passed it down to their own kid? Or maybe the kid got it off the internet? Who knows, exactly? But on a larger and more important level, a wider level than mere Western classical music, it doesn’t make much sense, either. When Irish traditional musicians play a tune, they never play it exactly the same way as it’s been played before. Irish traditional music changes slightly, from player to player and performance to performance; with some players, as with the late great fiddle player Tommy Potts, it changed dramatically when he played it. And Irish traditional musicians are hardly unique that way: how about blues musicians? With Hindustani classical musicians, the music isn’t written out in the first place. The musicians take the rāg and use it as the seed from which to grow an improvisation. With jazz—actually, when jazz is uninspired, it really does sound like it was written before. With post-WW2 Western popular music, yes, there’s a lot of recapitulation of existing music, and re-contextualisation of existing music. Whenever I give out my opinion that much of mainstream rock music is basically a dead language, I get people telling me No, rock’s not dead, check out this band and this band and this band. And they always sound like music I’ve already listened to. It’s just that, instead of being four guys from late 60s UK, the band is four-to-six guys from 2020s Michigan, or Melbourne, or London, or whatever. Doesn’t mean that rock music is utterly spent. It just means that what too many people in 2024 think of as ‘rock music’, has been done to death, and there are a lot of abandoned side-roads in rock music which could be explored further. Even a note-for-note performance of a previously written work is not the same as any previous performance, because it’s in that place, with those musicians, to that audience. Doesn’t mean it has to be, or alternatively can’t be, numbingly predictable. Classical music students tend to only know about classical music. It’s like ballet: you gotta start early and do nothing else, if you want to be really good at it. But there is always new music to be made. It’s just that there is no formula for making it. And that should be an encouraging thought.

Question: How do children's stunts work in movies?
Answer: Royce Allen Dudley, who knows a thing or two, says in his answer ‘They are performed by small adults, or CGI.’ …Yeaaahhh, not always. In the HBO show Barry, which I enjoyed the first season of but am still watching, an entire episode, ‘ronny/lily’, was basically written because the show’s creators were told about a child stunt performer who happened to be available. Bill Hader in ‘ronny/lily’. Barry, which ran for four seasons to great acclaim, was co-created by Bill Hader, and is the story about a depressed hitman, Barry Berkman, played by Hader, who finds himself in L.A. and joins an acting class in an attempt to find more meaning in his life. I won’t give away any spoilers about the show in general (I know how it ends), but one episode, in season 2, made spectacular use of a then-13-year-old stunt performer, Jessie Giacomazzi. Jessie Giacomazzi in ‘ronny/lily’. The episode came about in part because the show’s stunt choreographer, Wade Allen, was told about Giacomazzi by a mutual friend: Hey, if you ever need a kid who can do stunts, I know one… The episode then became a prolonged exercise in finding a good narrative excuse for Barry to get into a fight with a little girl. In the previous episode, Barry has been blackmailed by a corrupt cop into killing the cop’s ex-wife’s lover, Ronny. Ronny comes home to his house and finds Barry waiting for him. Barry, at his most reasonable, owns up to why he’s there, and tells Ronny that he has no intention of killing him, but instead is offering him the chance to escape to Chicago, ‘for about a year’. As Ronny assembles a bag of his things, Barry realises, with some concern, that Ronny is a master of Taekwondo. Sure enough, just when Barry is off his guard, Ronny attacks him, and gives him a vicious beating. However, Barry is not an ex-Marine hitman for nothing, and succeeds in wounding Ronny in the windpipe, such that Ronny collapses, apparently dead. Barry goes downstairs, where he meets Lily, Ronny’s daughter, played by Giacomazzi (above), who on seeing the bloodstained hitman before her, exclaims ‘Dad?!’ and runs upstairs. Barry follows her, hoping to pacify her, or subdue her, or do whatever he has to do to neutralise her, but he finally tracks Lily to the kitchen, where she is crouched, making unnerving growling noises. Lily proceeds to jump on Barry and beat the living shit out of him, while in her turn being flung here and there by him, which culminates in her stabbing him in the back hard enough that he can’t fight anymore. Giacomazzi did most of her own stunts, apart from one stunt where Lily is thrown off Barry, bounces off a table and falls to the floor, where they used another stunt performer. Her parents are veteran stunt performers, she’s a trained gymnast, and she was climbing trees and climbing up houses and doing flips on trampolines and learning karate from an early age. At one point, Lily escapes from the house and vaults over a fence, and then does a forward flip over a hedge into the next garden. For another stunt, her character climbs rapidly up a tree and jumps from the tree onto the roof of an adjoining house. The tree didn’t actually exist: the crew built a green-screen tree next to the house, for her to climb up, which she did (with a safety wire which was then digitally removed, and a CGI tree replaced the green-screen one.) Bill Hader, who directed the episode, was apparently in a car watching on a monitor while she did this, and praying that she wouldn’t have an accident. But she didn’t. Giacomazzi’s most elegant stunt was when she slides off the roof of Barry and his mentor Fuches’ car and in through one of the rear windows, without them noticing, whereupon she bites into Fuches’ face, clings there for a long time while Barry and Fuches bicker about what to do with her (Barry is too wounded to intervene and Fuches has accidentally superglued his hands to the steering wheel), then she finally rips a chunk out of Fuches’ cheek before fleeing, but not before giving them a last defiant roar: Hader said later that the peculiar, comically-nightmarish tone of the episode came in part from watching rehearsals, and seeing what Allen and Giacomazzi could do, which prodded him to turn Lily from a merely angry young girl into someone who justifies Fuches’ remark, She ain’t human. Lily really does comes across like some unstoppable demon of daughterly vengeance. It’s a great standalone episode of a show. It got and deserved Emmy nominations for writing and directing. Sources: Wikipedia will lead you to most of them, but I did listen to this: Incredibly boring host, but still informative.

Question: How did the 1990s go from raw and real soul searching grungy rock and roll music to plastic boy bands and 'La Vida Loca'?
Answer: It didn’t. The boy bands were there all along. Ricky Martin got started in the 80s, as a member of Menudo. Grunge became briefly popular, that’s all. A few good songs got written by talented songwriters who happened to be working in that idiom. From the perspective of someone who, in the 1980s, was listening to grunge’s precursor, alternative rock, the distinctive thing about grunge was not its musical quality or its supposed emotional authenticity, but the fact that the media went nuts about it, in a way that they hadn’t gone nuts for the Meat Puppets or Hüsker Dü or the Pixies. I worked for a freesheet in Dublin in the early 90s, and I remember that on the one occasion I was invited to a party by the editor, I was standing in the kitchen having a beer and overhearing a conversation between the editor and one of the music journos, in which, without any irony whatever, they agreed that Kurt Cobain was ‘the voice of his generation’. I thought, Kurt Cobain? He’s a journalist’s idea of the ‘voice of a generation’. Dinosaur Jr’s ‘Freak Scene’ is the voice of my generation. Michael Stipe would be the voice of my generation, if I could understand a fucking word of what he’s singing. —Oh wait, nowadays, I can understand what he’s singing, and it turns out to be not very interesting. I knew better than to say that to them. I was not cut out to be a journalist. We know now, of course, that Cobain was tormented by the fact of his own fame, and couldn’t handle it. He suffered badly from the delusion that anything that’s widely popular can’t be all that good. Your question implies that there is some sort of decline from ‘raw and real soul searching’ blah blah blah to pop music, when really, these were two different musics for two different audiences. It’s just that grunge briefly had mainstream popularity, before the pop audience got sick of the strenuous emotionality of it all and went back to fun music. And, like all musical forms sooner or later, grunge declined into mannerism. Soundgarden (who I always preferred to Nirvana) peaked with the magnificent Superunknown before making Down On the Upside, which by contrast was merely a headache. In the meantime, I salute Ricky Martin for having the courage to come out. I’m not a fan of his music, but that took some cojones back in 2010.

Question: If someone really loves music should they at least once in life try to play an instrument or create some music? Let's say loving music doesn't include just a few pop hits, but entire range like pagan folk, classical music, blues, jazz, metal …
Answer: Put it this way: I play guitar, bass, mandolin, a bit of keyboard and blues harmonica, ukulele, a bit of drums. At one point I knew how to use a MIDI editor: I’m sure it would come back if I tried one. And I don’t like the ‘should’ in the question. I don’t think any music lover should ever be made to feel bad or inadequate for not playing an instrument, or not being able to sing. Some people just love listening to it. And that’s fine. I think people ought to have every opportunity to try making music, but if they don’t want to take the opportunity, whether they’re shy or worried of looking foolish or they simply aren’t interested, their decision should be respected.

Question: In the current political climate, is it worse to be an Islamophobe or an anti-Semite?
Answer: The political climate has nothing to do with it. It’s bad to be a bigot. And Islamophobia and anti-Semitism are not rational analyses of the political situation, but forms of bigotry. If the Taliban ‘makes’ Alfie hate all Muslims, that’s Alfie generalising from a small sample: being a bigot, in other words. If the IDF ‘makes’ Serena hate all Jews, Serena is no better. The truth is, people choose to hate, or at least they fail to choose not to. I have a close relative who displays one of these tendencies. I have no idea why she’s like that. It’s got nothing to do with being treated badly by members of a particular group: she’s had practically no contact with either of them. She merely finds it very easy to hate all members of the group, in an abstract and impersonal kind of way. It’s irrational. But some people are like that.

Question: Can you recommend a book or three on the subject of "Musicology"? I understand the 25 word or less version of what it is, but I want to be able to 'follow the conversation' as it were, when a piece of music, or composer, is being discussed/analyzed.
Answer: I certainly can. Thanks for the A2A, John Iannone. In the first place you’ll need to get a grounding in what musicology is, and for that I can’t think of a better book than the one that made me want to study the subject itself: Joseph Kerman’s 1985 book Musicology, published in the USA as Contemplating Music. Kerman was a great musicologist with a long career. He started by causing a stir with his book Opera as Drama, in which he made it clear that he didn’t think much of Puccini. He followed this with classic monographs on the Elizabethan madrigal and Beethoven’s string quartets, then he did musicology a real service by editing an edition of one of Beethoven’s notebooks. (Beethoven remained one of his touchstones.) He followed that up with a magisterial book on William Byrd’s masses and motets. It was meant to be part of a three-author, three-volume survey of all Byrd’s music, but one of the other authors died. In Musicology, he didn’t so much provide a neutral introduction to the subject as describe the revolution in musicology that he himself had been a main mover of. Musicology in the early 20th century had become a rather scientistic discipline, primly avoiding critical judgments and confining itself narrowly to harmonic analysis. Kerman wanted musicologists to have the kind of freedom that literary critics took for granted, and which he practised. Once you’ve got a sense of what musicology is, it would be a good idea to learn about what musical analysis is like. A good introduction is Nicholas Cook’s A Guide to Musical Analysis, which describes different types of analysis (because there’s more than one way to break down a sonata or a hip-hop track) and the various advantages and limitations of the different approaches: e.g., Schenkerian analysis is useful when applied to music like the kind it was invented for, Western baroque, classical-era or romantic music, but almost useless when applied to post-WW2 popular music. Cook won’t teach you how to do the analysis; you only learn to do it by doing it. But he is a handy guide to how people do it. Musical analysis is not all musicology is, or even most of what it is, but it’s as well to learn about it. Finally, get a book where people apply musicological ideas to a piece of music. The Cambridge Music Handbooks are really good, here: I have quite a few. But I think a good one to start with is Allan F. Moore’s one on the Beatles’ Sgt Pepper, because chances are the music will be more familiar than Haydn’s Creation or Beethoven’s Eroica. Hopefully that’s enough to be going on with.
