Question: Does unsalted butter taste good/as good on toast as salted butter or should I stick to salted butter, as far flavor? Want to know your opinions about it before I buy.
Answer: Salted butter tastes buttery, whereas unsalted butter doesn’t taste of much. I come from Ireland, which has (no, I’m not biased) the greatest butter in the world—so good that I can’t afford it at post-Brexit prices. If you’re buttering toast, the idea is to put enough butter on the toast that the toast soaks up plenty of butter without turning into a completely sodden mess. For that purpose, salted butter is The Man. However, unsalted butter is far more useful for cooking, because it doesn’t add salt the more butter you add. Unsalted butter helps to convey flavour without adding much flavour, although it also adds loads of silky mouthfeel, so there’s that. If you’re pan-frying a steak, presumably you salted it well beforehand, preferably the previous night. So you really don’t need to be adding any more salt to that. For popcorn, unsalted butter is preferable. Why? Because although it’s perfectly easy to spread enough butter on a slice of toast so that the whole slice tastes good, in order to season the popcorn properly you need to salt it properly, and if you add a lot of salted butter after you’ve salted the popcorn, it will be unbearably salty. And you don’t need tons and tons of butter to make the popcorn taste buttery: a little goes a long way. If you attempt to coat every last popped kernel with butter, it will be unacceptably greasy. Incidentally, my daughter’s method for buttering popcorn is to melt the butter in the hot pan that the popcorn was cooked in. I disapprove of this, because the pan is likely to be so hot that the butter will foam and cook. I melt my butter separately and take it off the heat once it’s melted but before it foams, so that it remains fresh-tasting but liquid. In the end, salted butter is good for a.) toast and b.) certain kinds of sandwich. And possibly corn on the cob, if it’s not already been seasoned. And it is the only thing I permit inside a baked potato. Unsalted butter is a lot more versatile.

Question: How can the author of a book review have a judgment on the book being reviewed without being biased or prejudiced? Why is this important?
Answer: I don’t think that this question works. In order to make a judgement of a book’s quality, which is what book reviews are for, the reviewer has to have some sort of standards according to which they judge it. In other words, the reviewer has to have opinions. Someone who disagrees with those opinions is likely to consider them biases and prejudices. How is a reviewer supposed to make a non-biased judgement of a book? With reference to what standard? Do you think that there’s some objective standard of literary excellence out there, a sort of Official Novel, impervious to fashion and opinion and human subjectivity, according to which other novels are judged? Because there isn’t one. Reviewers use their own judgement and their own experience to make judgements of a book. They can’t ban these from their mind before they start reading, because a) it’s impossible, b) even if it weren’t, it would render them incapable of making judgements, c) it’s unreasonable to expect them to. That said, some ‘biases and prejudices’ are more likely than others to make a reviewer write a shitty review. A reviewer who is a chauvinist for their own nation is probably more likely to dislike foreign literature, simply because it’s foreign. A literary snob is more likely to have a low opinion of science fiction, fantasy or romance, because they’re science fiction, fantasy or romance. An inverted snob who distrusts ‘literature’ is more likely to have little patience with anything that seems ‘literary’. Book reviewing is an art. A minor art, perhaps, but still something that requires, like all good writing, a modicum of knowledge, empathy, openness and style. I’m sure I’m not the only person who thinks that the late John Updike’s book reviews were better art than many if not most of his rather pedestrian novels. But it’s not a science: it’s not something from which the reviewer should seek to banish their personal inclinations, and pretend to an objectivity which is unachievable. That’s pretentious and arrogant. Better for the reviewer to own up to all their feelings about the book, than to hide them behind a mask of spurious impartiality.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Who is the most annoying character in the Office?
Answer: Interesting question, but I think I have a solid answer. It’s not Angela. Apologies to anyone who saw Angela’s picture in the preview, and assumed that this answer would be about her. Angela’s great vice is not that she’s judgemental, or hypocritical, or prissy, although she is all those things, at various times. Her great vice, which in season 9 she abjectly owns up to, is pride, which encompasses all those things. Angela thinks she’s ‘virtuous’, but we see from almost her earliest appearances that she isn’t. She’s carrying on a secret thing with Dwight, and apparently she’s rather good at sex. (Which is, of course, not a vice, but from the way Angela talks about other people, you’d think she thinks it is. Dwight describes her as ‘energetic’ and ‘flexible’.) So, from the get-go, Angela is someone whose desire is at odds with her sense of herself—and that’s not annoying, that’s pitiable. Angela’s subconscious longing for a fulfilled life with a good partner is perfectly fine; what’s not fine is her mean-minded sniping about other people who actually have that, because she only snipes about them because she doesn’t have it. Angela’s fortunes slowly decline until, late in season 9, she is genuinely pathetic. Watch her in the scene when her marriage ends, as her gay husband Senator Lipton comes out in a press conference: her reactions are priceless, going from smiling, loyal wife, through disgruntlement, then a look of pure Oh you have to be f***ing kidding me, and finally, when Lipton confesses that he’s really in love with his chief of staff, Angela gasps with disbelief and appears to be about to throw up. (Angela Kinsey, her actor, was wonderful in the role: apparently she’s basically the complete opposite of her character.) A couple of episodes later, she’s dishevelled and dejected, she’s being evicted from her apartment and her beloved cats are being taken away, and she’s sneaking vodka into her giant soft-drink cup. That’s when Oscar, the former lover of her former husband, invites her to stay in his place until she gets her life sorted out. Angela accepts help, almost immediately breaks down and, for the first time in the show, is completely honest with someone else, tearfully confessing to Oscar that she loves Dwight. In the basically humane and compassionate environment of The Office, this is enough to redeem her. From then on, Angela’s fortunes improve. It’s not Dwight, either. Dwight is only superficially annoying. Dwight does not exactly occupy the same moral universe as the rest of us. Dwight lives in a world where he’s the hero of an epic adventure story, in which his least decisions are crucially important. However, to everyone else, including us, Dwight is a paper salesman who also runs a beet farm. So we can’t exactly take Dwight at his word; but, on the other hand, because Dwight adheres so faithfully to his peculiarly archaic and harsh code of ethics (most of the time), there is something oddly noble about him, even at his most idiotic. When things don’t go the way he wants them to, we may well be pleased that some of his more petty and idiotic schemes get defeated; but we might also feel sorry for him, because he is, so often, the architect of his own humiliation. Dwight sets up his own quite stringent standards of failure and success, and at his best, he at least tries to live by them. Which is perhaps why Jim and Pam end up liking him, and consider him a friend. And why, in the end, he considers them as friends—and gives up a dowry that includes a walk-in freezer’s worth of bull semen, because the one he really loves is Angela. Nor is it Jim and/or Pam. They’re relatively normal, funny and sympathetic, unless you’re a dick. So that’s them out. Arguments could be made for a number of other characters. And I might agree with such arguments, as applied to Todd Packer, or Nellie Bertram, or Deangelo Vickers. But I believe I can make a far stronger case for someone else. In my view, the most annoying character in The Office, by far, is Andy Bernard. The enduring feature of Andy’s character, in my view, the one that persists through all his character development and un-development, is his sense of entitlement. It underwrites every aspect of him. Andy tends to coast through life on his first impressions of people, because his smug self-confidence tells him that they’re correct. On Jim’s first day in Stamford, Jim has a tuna sandwich for lunch, so Andy assumes that tuna is Jim’s favourite food, and immediately nicknames him ‘Big Tuna’, although tuna is not Jim’s favourite food. Later on, he assumes that Pam, too, must be sick of eating tuna because, in his mind, Jim wants to eat nothing else. Pam, for her part, is merely baffled. When Jim attempts to prank Andy the way he pranked Dwight, by embedding Andy’s stapler in Jello, it backfires horribly. Dwight got haughty and pompous and made comically unreasonable demands that Jim be fired, which amused Jim no end and which is exactly the kind of thing he expects Andy to do. Instead, Andy epically loses his shit, starts yelling, and kicks a wastebin across the office. And nobody except Jim even raises an eyebrow, because they’re all used to Andy’s explosions of rage when his sense of propriety is violated. When the two branches merge, and Andy comes to Scranton in season 3’s ‘The Merger’, he blithely tells the camera how he plans to gain power: Andy: I'll be the Number Two guy here in Scranton in six weeks. How? Name repetition, personality mirroring, and never breaking off a handshake. I'm always thinking one step ahead. Like a carpenter that makes stairs. Sure enough, this is what Andy does—and it works on Michael, but it doesn’t work on Pam, who sees him doing it to Michael. Check out her silent reactions in the background of the scene where Andy and Michael first meet. We can see that she gets Andy’s number within seconds: Andy: [cautiously] Hello. Michael: Ah! You must be Andy Bernard. Michael: Aloha and welcome! Andy: And you must be Michael Scott. Aloha and... hello. Michael: A-ha-ha-ho. Very good! Welcome to our little kingdom. Ah, we have a bag of nifty gifties for you. Andy: Michael, thank you for welcoming me to your little kingdom, Mike. Michael: Oh. Andy: [looking into the bag] Nifty! Michael: They are nifty! They're nifty gifties. [Cut to Michael in a talking head segment] Michael: You know who I really like, is this guy Andy Bernard. He has got this… very likable way about him. You can watch the whole exchange here. If you’re an obsessive nerd. Andy correctly identifies Dwight as his main ‘rival’ for Number Two Guy in Scranton, and spends the next few episodes not very subtly trying to undermine him, and equally unsubtly trying to get Michael to be his best buddy. Unfortunately for Andy, he does not naturally project warmth, the way Michael does—and indeed, the rather weird way Dwight does. (In Dwight’s case it’s more like ‘fervent heat’.) Andy, when he’s being manipulative, is chilly, and so his attempts to be friendly come across as calculating, and his snide jokes about Dwight come across as bitchy. It doesn’t help that, a few episodes before ‘The Merger’, Dwight had tried and abjectly failed to wrest the management job from Michael, but Michael has already conditionally forgiven him—so he doesn’t need to hear Andy hinting that Dwight can be less than loyal, because he already knows that, but he also wants to think the best of Dwight, and not have some new guy stirring bad blood. In ‘The Return’, a combination of Andy’s last-ditch effort to ingratiate himself with Michael, and Jim’s exasperation with Andy’s mannerisms (such as loudly singing the Cranberries’ ‘Zombie’ at his desk), creates a situation which pushes Andy over the edge. Dwight has been fired (long story), and now works at Staples. Michael notices that Dwight did a lot of little things around the office that made it a nicer place, and is already missing him. Pam points out that Dwight not only watered the plants but arranged the toys on Michael’s desk. Michael: Really? That was very nice of him. We need more attitude like that around the office. Andy: [coming up to them] Feel ya, dawg. Michael: [turning to him] Yeah, do you? Andy: Absolutely. Michael: [hard stare] What did I say? Andy: [who has no idea what Michael was talking about] … You said... [makes gibberish noises] Michael: Huh. Andy: Which is like, "Right on." And Pam was like "blah blah blah" and you were like "Yeah, psht." [smugly] Nailed it. Michael: Oh, no. Andy: [trying and failing to mirror Michael] Oh, no. And now, Michael complains to us that Andy likes him ‘too much’ and is ‘always up in my bidnis.’ The stage is set. Andy has put a ringtone on his phone of himself singing ‘Rockin’ Robin’ in four-part harmony, which he can’t resist showing off. Jim decides to prank him. Pam helps Jim to steal Andy’s phone and hide it in the ceiling above Andy’s desk, and then Pam and Jim take turns to ring it. This, predictably, drives Andy up the wall. Eventually, Michael realises that he has been unjust to Dwight, and that he wants Dwight back. Unfortunately, at this point, an already jittery Andy makes his last attempt to be Michael’s best buddy. It does not go well: Michael: [preparing to go to get Dwight back] Pam, I have a mission to accomplish. Make sure this party gets rolling and I will be back shortly. Andy: Wait up. Where are you going? Do you want me to come with? Michael: Um. Andy: Just listen, I forgot to tell you the plan for this Saturday. You, me, bars, beers, buzzed. Wings. Shots. Drunk. Waitresses, hot. Football: Cornell/Hofstra. Slaughter. Then a quick nap at my place and we'll hit the tiz-own. Michael: [annoyed] No. I don't want to do any of that. Andy: [smarmy] Duh. Which is why I was just joking about doing that. Michael: [snapping] No, just stop. Stop. Stop doing it. You're going to drive me crazy. Andy: [seething] Fine. I'll just sit at my desk and be quiet. Sorry I annoyed you with my friendship. [Andy's phone rings] Excuse me. [to the rest of the office] And I'm also sorry that a lot of people here for some reason think it's funny to steal someone's personal property and hide it from them. Here's a little newsflash! It's not funny! In fact, it's pretty freakin' unfunny! Oh, my GOD! And he punches a hole in the wall. Andy goes off to anger management classes, which he claims he’ll be able to finish in less than the allotted time, and when he comes back he is indeed less angry. However, Andy on his best behaviour is Andy out of focus. He veers between being Michael Lite, Mediocre Jim, or The Guy Angela Got With To Make Dwight Jealous. When he’s not being subjected to routine indignities (like in season 3’s ‘Beach Games’, where he falls into the lake in his sumo suit and spends the rest of the episode drifting helplessly on his back, with everyone ignoring his cries for help), he’s completely failing to see that Angela doesn’t love him. When that’s ended he’s courting Erin, which he does without ever telling Erin that he used to be engaged to Angela. When Erin’s no longer with him and is with Gabe, he drives himself and others nuts trying to win her back—like in season 7’s ‘Viewing Party’, where he ingests large quantities of Gabe’s powdered seahorse in attempt to give himself ‘virility’, and then spends much of the rest of the episode throwing up. Andy only comes back into focus in season 8, where he becomes office manager. Here, he becomes a little more sympathetic because of the trials he’s put through. The best example is ‘The Incentive’, in which he introduces a scheme whereby if the office makes enough sales, he’ll reward them. The top reward is that he’ll let them tattoo whatever they want on his butt. Because Andy isn’t as smart as he thinks he is, he fails to prevent them from pooling their sales, and they quickly make enough sales to meet the target. Andy ruefully but pluckily agrees to go ahead with the butt-tattooing, although I personally think that that the writing team was being soft on his character because it was his turn to be sympathetic—but never mind. He insists on having the tattoo, even though Jim assures him that nobody expects him to, and at the last minute, the office staff take pity on him and switch the tattoo from an insulting one to a picture of a dog with ‘Nard’ written on it, so it’s his old Cornell nickname, ‘Nard Dog’. Andy ends up feeling accepted. But this is one of the few times that Andy lets himself be the butt (!) of the joke. Oh yeah. About the Cornell thing. Andy went to Cornell, one of the Ivy League colleges, and he seldom lets people forget this. Nothing wrong with that. My dad went to Harvard, and even me saying that feels like me ‘doing an Andy’. What matters, though, is not what college you went to, but what you got out of the experience. What Andy got out of it was the sense that he’s better than other people because he went to Cornell. In season 8, Andy decides that he simply has to get back together with Erin, even though he’s engaged to the lovely Jessica. Being Andy, he drives down to Florida to get Erin back, and then breaks up with Jessica on the way home, during her bridal shower. Once he’s got Erin back, the next thing that happens is that his family loses its money and has to sell the family yacht, which he’s never been allowed to captain. Being Andy, he drives with Erin to the harbour, personally commandeers the yacht and sails it to its buyer in the Bahamas, leaving Erin behind. It doesn’t even occur to him to ask her if she’d like to go along, which she admits she would have. He then stays in the Bahamas for three months but doesn’t tell his employers that he’s doing so, leaving the office to run itself (which it does with extreme success). While he’s gone, he tweets continually but only emails his girlfriend twice. On returning, he calmly asks for and accepts all his paychecks and the bonus cheque he hasn’t earned, and then causes Jan to cancel an important sale made in his absence when he annoys her about a minor technical point—the sales team had given her a price they technically weren’t entitled to give her without first clearing it with him, which they couldn’t do, because he was in the Bahamas. Eventually, in season 9, Andy’s love of showbiz trumps his mediocre interest in his job, and, against everyone’s advice, he decides to quit Dunder Mifflin and audition for a reality show. None of the other employees think this a good idea, but the truest and most withering verdict comes from Phyllis: Phyllis: Andy sings beautifully. And he's really good at dancing. He's a good speaker. But there's just something there you don't want to look at. Sure enough, after pointlessly taking a dump on David Wallace’s car (so as to ‘burn my bridges’), Andy barges into a young girl’s audition and starts belting out the ‘Cornell Fight Song’ before finally collapsing before the pitiless unenthusiasm of the judges, and bursting into self-pitying tears. In the end, unable to function in the regular world, Andy gets to retreat to his beloved Cornell. Which he probably should never have left. Andy is annoying partly because privileged people shouldn’t be so f***ing clueless. He should know better. With his preppy background and his Ivy League education, you’d think Andy would at least have more manners, but his sense of manners is confined to pointless instructions about how to eat food at his disastrous garden party (which the others have to rescue for him: when the gang are all relaxing at the end, and Darryl is cooking on the grill which Andy specifically told him not to bring, Darryl offers Andy a cheeseburger, and Andy finally relaxes, instead of yearning after the approval of his asshole father). When he was making an effort to be a better man, he did become more genuinely friendly and helpful. But there’s something queasily inauthentic about him: some part of him that is always pretending. Michael Scott needs to be liked. Dwight doesn’t care whether he’s liked. Angela just doesn’t like people. Kevin rather endearingly assumes that he is liked. Jim and Pam and Darryl are naturally likeable. But Andy thinks he deserves to be liked, and that if people refuse to like him, he can make them like him by tricks and hacks, and when they fail, by plain old sucking up. When he is thwarted, he typically reacts by either exploding with rage or bursting into tears. In the end, once he had the job he wanted, the real Andy had to re-emerge. Privilege let him be his truest self: convinced he had the right to be the boss, but only barely competent as one, and fatally too uninterested be a good one. It also has something to do with Ed Helms’ tight smirk and narrow, wary eyes, and Andy’s slightly too-loud voice, and irritating hamminess, such as his fondness for fake Cockney accents. I know, I know, it’s subjective. Some people probably find Andy endearing. An unloved child, fretting in the shadow of his handsomer, more talented brother (who is after all Josh Groban.) But to me, Andy is the character you most enjoy getting punched. Like Phyllis said: there’s just something there you don’t want to look at.

Question: Why do (white) men always complain about diversity in movies?
Answer: Speaking as a white man, we white men have grown up for decades with movies that usually featured a white man as the protagonist, and white men as most of the supporting characters. Women were featured mostly as wives and girlfriends, less frequently as mothers and sisters, but mostly there not to do anything themselves, but to represent to us what we regard as valuable. (Movies where women were the main characters were relegated to the sub-genre of ‘women’s movies’.) Black people were usually supporting cast: perhaps the protagonist’s work partner, or a minor authority figure (the black police captain who chews out but basically respects the white maverick cop.) Brown people were frequently there as stock villains (if Arabic) or comic characters (if South Asian). East Asian characters tended to be either entirely absent, or villainous: if the latter, typically WW2 Japanese soldiers. LGBTQ characters were either absent, or cartoon villains, or campy stereotypes. Or, very infrequently, butch stereotypes, if women. Or, if bisexual, probably sociopaths (Basic Instinct). If they were the main characters and weren’t any of these things, the movie belonged to the sub-genre of ‘gay/lesbian movies’. The lesson we learned was that ‘real’ movies were about white (straight) men who did stuff, and it was largely unthinkable that we could watch a movie in which we were obliged to follow the fortunes of a protagonist who wasn’t one. Then came diversity. One of the results of diversity has been that many white men simply cannot accept that it’s even possible for us to have sufficient empathy with a protagonist who isn’t a white man, to watch a whole movie about that character. The entire structure of ‘Western’ society has, for years, encouraged us white men to think of ourselves as the baseline of ‘normal’, and everyone else as a departure from the norm. It has to be admitted that movies, at their best, have long since identified the fissures and difficulties and rips in this sense of the basic solidity and security of (white, straight) male identity. Great movies have long since portrayed white male protagonists who broke down into despair, and failed to be heroes, inasmuch as they couldn’t get to the end of their story through their own efforts: James Stewart as George Bailey in It’s a Wonderful Life. They have long since portrayed white male protagonists who were deeply flawed, and whose flaws are dramatised within the movie, and not excused, and who recognised how flawed they themselves are: John Wayne as Ethan Edwards in The Searchers. Robert Ryan as Jim Wilson in On Dangerous Ground. But alongside that, there was a parallel tendency to treat flawed white male characters as infinitely deserving of our indulgence, because they ‘get results’, or something: Clint Eastwood in Dirty Harry. Mel Gibson in Lethal Weapon. And since it’s more flattering to be told that it’s okay if you’re violent, or bigoted, or lacking control, as long as you ‘get results’, we tended to forget about George Bailey, and Ethan Edwards, or Jim Wilson—or romanticise them, which is also a kind of forgetting. The first step that many white men can’t or won’t take, is to step down from the top of that podium of cultural and societal self-importance, and accept that not all good stories are about us. Or that, if we’re in them, we’re secondary characters. Or maybe even the bad guys. We were okay with films where the bad guys were white men, as long as they were defeated by good white men—because the latter made us feel good about being ‘good guys’. (The slasher film is an exception to the general rule that movies had to have male protagonists, but that’s a whole other answer. I sometimes think that the Alien franchise is also given a special pass: Ellen Ripley is, for some male film fans, the Token Woman Protagonist who they’re willing to watch as proof that they don’t need protagonists to be avatars of themselves.) Diversity in film demands that white men—if we are to go on enjoying films in general—greatly extend our historically-evolved sense of who deserves to get their story told, and whose stories we might actually enjoy. Question: How do you accurately write a character who is grieving?
Answer: That’s the wrong question. The right question is How do I write how this character grieves? If you’re thinking that grief expresses itself the same way in everyone, so that there are hints and tips and hacks you can use to write any character, in such a way that the reader will go Ah, the character is grieving, then you might as well give up writing, because you’re not going to write characters who seem like real people. How you write them depends on what you know about grief. Have you ever known anyone who is grieving? What did they do? How did it affect them? If you’ve never known anyone who has experienced grief, why are you writing the character? Probably best not to, eh? Grief is not a question of the writer accumulating enough technical knowlege to make a character seem realistic. It’s a deeply personal thing and it affects everyone differently. So, if you have to ask this question, because you have no idea what grief looks like in different people, sounds like you probably shouldn’t try to do this.

Gold and lead were still gold and lead in ancient Greece, but ‘drama’ is not the same thing in 2024 as it was in classical Athens. In my own lifetime, film-watching habits have changed dramatically. Question: Could two violins play together and sound amazing?
Answer: Yes. Actually, one of the greatest works of orchestral music in the Western classical tradition culminates—and ends—with just two violins playing together. Nothing else. And there’s a good reason why. Story time! In Western classical music, the great codifier of the symphony was Joseph Haydn. Joseph Haydn. Genius. Wore a wig. The original wiggy genius. In Haydn’s time, as for centuries before him, composers were not freelance musicians but were employees of the church or the nobility, whose job was to provide the church or nobility with bespoke music for all their music-listening needs. For most of his life, Haydn was employed by the Esterházy family, immensely rich landowners in the Kingdom of Hungary. Haydn lived in their houses, hired and conducted their musicians, and supplied the family with an endless stream of music. His original boss, Prince Paul Anton Esterházy, died and was replaced by his son Nikolaus, a decent musician who favoured an obscure instrument called the baryton, a very distant and fretted cousin of the cello (via the viola da gamba), with a sprinkling of guitar DNA. As a result, Haydn wrote a number of baryton trios for his boss to play. No other composer of Haydn’s stature wrote so much music for such an obscure instrument. Anyway, as the main head of music for the family, Haydn was rather isolated from the main centres of musical development at the period. As he put it, ‘I was obliged to become original’, and he turned himself into one of the main centres of musical development, which involved, among other things, developing the symphony from a rather obscure musical form into one of the forms that later composers had to show they could write. Haydn wrote 104 symphonies, and I’ve never heard one that wasn’t worth listening to. What concerns us here is Symphony No. 45. Every summer, the Esterházy family would travel, with its staff, including its orchestra, to their summer residence, Eszterháza, instead of their usual residence in Eisenstadt. Eszterháza. Nice little summer house. Nowadays, the journey is about an hour by car, but back in the 1770s it took a day. Meanwhile, the wives and families of the orchestra were not invited to Eszterháza. In the summer of 1772, the noble family lingered on at Eszterháza for longer than usual. The orchestra got increasingly pissed off at being separated from their families for so long, and they asked Haydn to ask Prince Nikolaus if they could get back to Eisenstadt. Instead of flat-out asking the prince to cut short the family holiday, Haydn wrote Symphony No. 45. And the orchestra played it one evening, for the family’s entertainment. It’s in the highly unusual key of F# minor. The first movement is in Haydn’s best Sturm und Drang style of the period. Then there’s a slow movement, a dignified minuet, and then the gutsy final movement kicks in. However, only a few minutes in, the movement slams to a halt, and then changes character entirely. It goes from a fairly hectic 2/2 to a much more wistful 3/8, with a lilting melody. And one by one, in little groups, the players stop playing and leave the stand. Some of them have a little solo before they go. But, bit by bit, the orchestra gets smaller and smaller. First one of the oboes and one of the horns say goodbye, then the bassoon, then the other oboe and the other horn, then the double bass, then the cello, then half the violins (the two first violins don’t play this bit), then the viola. At the end, just the two first violins are left onstage, duetting with each other in this happy-sad little melody, and then they become quieter and quieter, and then they stop. And that’s the end of Haydn’s Symphony No. 45. The end of Symphony No. 45, showing how the music runs out. Even in those days, people expected symphonies to have big dramatic endings. The ending of Haydn’s 45th is still one of the most avant-garde gestures in music history. It’s still startling to hear a symphony that fades out. The day after the first performance of Symphony No. 45 at Eszterháza, Prince Nikolaus took the household back to Eisenstadt.

Question: What sound is 1,000 dB?
Answer: The thing about decibels is that they’re logarithmic, and they measure sound pressure levels. This means that they don’t increase arithmetically, but in a non-intuitive way, and as you increase the level of decibels by 10, the sound pressure levels don’t get 10% louder, but considerably louder. I found my notebook from my university days (music technology, in this case), in which I noted the relationship of decibels to amplitude ratios. From here, it’s maybe best if we move to examples of phenomena that can create sound pressure levels. It should be obvious, from this, that there is no sound on Earth that has a sound pressure level of 1,000 decibels, which is inconceivably loud. Like, you can’t even begin to imagine how loud. I don’t know for sure, but I suppose events like supernovae could be assumed to create sound pressure levels of ginormous magnitude, were they to occur in a medium in which sound can travel. But since sound doesn’t travel in a vacuum… we’ll never be able to ‘hear’ them. Physicists, chime in. This is about the limit of my scientific knowledge (although I can also calculate the reverb time of a room, given enough information about it…) Edit: Cathal Murphy has pointed out that when sound pressure levels get high enough, which is about 194 dB, they cease to be sound at all and become a blast wave. To remind ourselves of what a blast wave can do, here is the video of the horrendous 2020 Beirut port explosion.

Question: What makes playing guitars enjoyable? Is there a hidden aspect of guitars that contributes to their fun factor?
Answer: For me, it’s not this. I’m not interested in that. Or in this: The acoustic guitar, whether it’s steel-string or nylon-string, has very little interest for me, as a player. I have owned both, at various times, and I don’t regret owning and playing them, but they’re not for me. This is what I find enjoyable: On a brief tangent: my son is on the autistic spectrum. However, one reason I suspect I’m not on it myself is remarks like this, from another answerer of this question: Yeah. See, I actually like random noise. I appreciate where the other guy is coming from, but there is something about a guitar turned up to the point where it begins to feed back, and starts making all sorts of odd squeaks and scratches and shrieks and hums, which I find exhilaratingly unpredictable. I admit that I want to be able to turn that on and off—but I still want to be able to turn it on. For me, part of the fun of the electric guitar is the dance you have with the instrument, where you know mostly what it’s going to do but you don’t know exactly what it’s going to do. What I like about the electric guitar is its capacity for making lots of different kinds of sound. The only pole that I navigate by, in the strange world of electric guitar tone, is not some vague idea of the ‘best’ sound I can get, which will then be set in stone. It’s more like an unclear notion in my mind of the tone that will make the instrument sound like I want it to sound, in that room, in the mood I happen to be in, in whatever moment happens to be passing. I don’t particularly enjoy the sound of a guitar played cleanly, in itself. This is why I’ve never been interested in Chet Atkins, or Tal Farlow, or Tommy Emmanuel. I prefer players who have a more orchestral approach to the instrument. What I don’t like about the acoustic guitar is the sound that it makes. You hit a note and it goes twaaannnggggg and dies away. And that’s pretty much all you can do with it. (I can think of more experimental players, but you probably won’t have heard of them.) Whenever I hear people who are touted as virtuosi on the acoustic guitar, they’re usually playing very intricate, complex fingerpicking-y things that sound really impressive, but do nothing for me as music. But some people regard that as ‘real’ guitar playing, and think of electric players who like to use effects as ‘cheating’. To me, that’s a lot of crap. It takes skill and experience to learn to use effects in a way that they will be musically effective. That’s why I don’t regard more acoustic-oriented players (or, for that matter, classical guitarists) as more ‘real’ or ‘authentic’ guitar players than people like me, who prefer electrics. I mean, good for them, but I have no interest in their music, so I’ll pay them due respect but I’m not going to pretend that I think they’re better than me because of the kind of instrument that they play. I want the guitar to sound good played clean, but I need it to sound good when it’s going through a load of overdrive and really singing. Or howling. Or roaring. Or chiming. Or tinkling. Or squeaking. And the guitars I have, and the gear I have (see the pedalboard on the sofa), is the stuff that best helps me to find the sound I want that’s more in area. It would be fair to say that I don’t love the guitar, as an instrument. Not the basic idea of a six-string plucked chordophone. I don’t even own a regular acoustic. That Casino up there is the closest I want to get to one. I feel like, if I really loved the guitar qua guitar, maybe I’d be content to play on it nothing but folk songs and Bach arrangements, and other such things that respect the fundamental sonorities of the acoustic instrument. But the fact is, what I really love is what happens when you bolt pickups onto a guitar that will generate a signal, and can pass that signal into a device that can mess with and transform that signal, in lots of different ways. That’s why I think that the electric guitar is a fundamentally different instrument from the acoustic, and—as regards my needs as a player—a much more interesting and useful one. Question: Is it bad that I don’t really know a lot of classical music? I’ve only been listening it to it for a year, and there’s a lot of songs I’ve never heard of before
Answer: I’ve been listening to classical music for well over 30 years, at this point, and before then, it was being played at me but I wasn’t exactly listening to it. By ‘listening to’ I mean ‘listening to it with a serious effort at comprehending and appreciating it’. I started with Bach and have expanded from there. I now listen to a lot of Western classical music, from the 11th century or so to the present. There are a few composers I really have no time for (mostly the hardcore romantics and about half of the Russians: Chopin, Liszt, Tchaikovsky, Rachmaninov) but basically, I’ll give anyone else a listen. Let me tell you something. The feeling that there’s a lot of it that you haven’t heard before, is the default feeling that anyone has who loves this music. There is always stuff that you haven’t heard before. I consider myself a lover of Haydn’s music, but have I listened to all his 104 symphonies? Hell, no. I love Bach: have I listened to all his cantatas? Nope. I have a great love for Beethoven: have I listened to all the quartets and piano sonatas? I haven’t even listened to Fidelio or the Missa Solemnis. I love Webern’s music: have I listened to all of it? Well, yeah, actually I have, because you can fit all of it onto about six CDs. But Webern is an exception. Do not feel that you have to listen to everything, because you can’t, and you won’t. The Western classical composers tended to be so insanely prolific that the idea that you should, or indeed can, listen to everything they wrote, is an absurd fantasy, unless you happen to be someone who has an academic or professional specialism in their work. It’s better to know a dozen pieces really well, or two or three dozen, than to have a vague and skimpy acquaintance with as many as you can find the time to listen to. So, don’t worry about it.

Question: What is the thinking (or what apparently passes for it) behind the claim that the NSDAP were socialists?
Answer: The ‘thinking’ behind it is that, if a political party or movement or nation has a term in its name, then that party is ideologically aligned with every other party, etc. that also has that term in its name. In other words, that labels are always truthful and always refer to the same thing. It follows, from this, that the Democratic Republic of Korea—North Korea—is a democracy, which it obviously isn’t; that the Jamaica Labour Party is socialist, when actually it’s very socially and fiscally conservative; and that the National Socialist German Workers Party—the NSDAP—was socialist, like the UK Socialist Workers Party, which has a very similar name but which is Trotskyite, and which in 1977 founded the Anti-Nazi League, to combat the rise of the far right in the UK. Strategically, the claim that the Nazis were socialist serves, of course, to blacken socialism by associating it with totalitarianism and genocide. At least, it does so in the minds of those who are willing to ignore the Nazis’ ruthless persecution of actual socialists. It does, however, force those who claim it into a number of inconsistencies. For example, those who like to claim that the Nazis were socialists can point to the fact that Hitler more than once claimed that Nazism was ‘real’ socialism—as opposed to that weird, fake socialism practiced by Marxists, etc. (i.e., actual socialists.) So it’s not like we have Hitler on record going Bwahaha, of course we’re not real socialists, what fools these people are! (The Hitler Wikiquote page is crammed full of claims by Hitler that Nazism is real socialism, and yet is relatively unmarred by his far more frequent and wholly repellent comments about Jews; I suspect it’s been edited to be like that by right-wing Americans.) However, if you want to smear socialism by saying that Nazis were socialists, that does assume that you disapprove of Nazism. And if you disapprove of Nazism, then presumably you disagree with many of the claims that Nazis made for Nazism—that it was a movement of national renewal, that it transcended ordinary politics, that there exists a malign global Jewish conspiracy which must be ended with the utmost ruthlessness, et cetera. There are plenty of other things Nazis said which presumably one disagrees with. Curious, then, that they still agree with Hitler’s claim that Nazism was socialism, and don’t dismiss it as just another self-seeking lie by a power-hungry maniac. We can all agree that Hitler was a morally repellent war criminal (albeit an unconvicted one) and a racist fantasist—and yet, on this one subject, we are somehow obliged to take him at his word? Then there is the question of guilt by association. Even if we were to accept that the Nazis did have elements of socialism in their political program, and such elements did exist from 1920 to— most historians would agree—1934 or so, the existence of these elements do not damn socialist movements that do not feature the things that we find objectionable about the Nazis, such as the invading Europe and the mass murder. To the objection that socialist governments inevitably tend towards those things, we can respond that that is a classic ‘slippery slope’ fallacy: the UK had a socialist government between 1945 and 1951 and yet it did not become a totalitarian state. It also obliges them to overlook the fact that Hitler explicitly disassociated the Nazis from existing socialist parties and movements, characterising them as, in effect, ‘Socialist In Name Only’, which is a remarkable move considering socialism is a lot older than Nazism. Nazism was born in the 1920s, but socialism was being theorised as early as the beginning of the 19th century. Older forms of socialism would therefore seem to have a far stronger claim than Nazism to dictate what socialism is and what it isn’t. So, those that claim that the Nazis were socialists first have to ignore that the Nazis were violently opposed to existing socialists. When some attempt is made to address this, it usually takes the form of ‘It was a fight between rival factions’, which is unconvincing. Then they have to take Hitler’s word for it, which they don’t about most other subjects. Then, they have to explain what about Nazism resembled socialism, which is not easy to do for anyone with any knowledge of the Nazi economy. If they resort to the claim that socialism inevitably leads to tyranny, they have to explain why it demonstrably hasn’t, in many cases. This, I have not seen them even attempt to do. Finally, they have to pretend that there are no such things as branding and marketing, and that politicians always tell the truth. This, they don’t even believe themselves, except when it comes to this one issue. Basically, it’s a lie which is made easy by the fact that the Nazi party had the word ‘socialist’ in its name.

Question: Are any of the very first Les Pauls off the production line still in use or even exist outside of a museum?
Answer: 1952 Les Pauls still occasionally come on the market, but after doing a reasonable amount of research, I can’t find anyone very notable who actually plays one. A reason for this is that the earliest Les Pauls, 1952–1956, are not really the most sought-after Les Pauls, because of their design: This is an actual 1952 Les Paul which I found on eBay. Someone wants thirty grand for it (that’s in UK pounds; in US dollars, about $37k.) The thing is, that’s not what most people who want a Les Paul, want in a Les Paul. They don’t want the P90 pickups and the weird tailpiece. They want the regular tailpiece and Tune-O-Matic bridge that came later, and the PAF pickups that weren’t standard until 1957. Like this: This is a 1957 Les Paul which is, at the time of writing, on sale in a guitar shop in London’s Denmark Street for a cool £139,000. It’s the 1957–60 Les Pauls that are the Holy Grails. Not the awkward first draft that we see in the top photo. I don’t know who’s willing to spend just over 1/7 of a million quid for a guitar, but I doubt it’s someone who’s going to start using it as their regular instrument. Videos of 1952 Les Pauls can demonstrate that, in the hands of a decent player, they can have a fabulous tone. But they’re not the Les Paul that most people want who want a vintage Les Paul. I personally would be uneasy about carting even a £30k guitar around. But then, I’ve never spent as much as four figures on a guitar.

Question: How effective is the chord progression III-vi-V-IV, and what key would it sound best in?
Answer: It’s neither effective nor ineffective. It isn’t anything. Chord progressions as such are rather like ideas for novels. People who aren’t novelists have ‘ideas for a novel’ all the time, and some of them come on this site and ask if some writer is willing to ‘work with me’ on turning the idea of the novel into a finished novel. What they don’t realise that ideas for novels are, basically, worthless. Novels gain their power and reach from the quality of work put into the realisation of them. And so it is with chord progressions. They’re worth nothing in themselves: they only gain meaning by the musical context of the song that they end up in. I’m sure there are songs out there that go III-vi-V-IV, but I can’t be bothered to look for them at the moment. However, this is only four chords. It’s not really a ‘progression’. There are a million songs out there which have the form of a 12-bar blues. However, not all of them are equally great, and none of them are great because they have that form. One very common sequence of chords is a minor 7 followed by a descending line cliché, so that the root note drops by a semitone with each chord, e.g Am7-Am7/G#-Am7/G-Am7/F#. You can hear this type of the thing at the beginning of two very different songs: ‘Michelle’ by the Beatles and ‘’Round Midnight’ by Thelonious Monk. In a rather different form, it forms part of the beginning of ‘Stairway to Heaven’ (not identical, but it has a similar rather wistful feel.) In itself, it’s not interesting because it gets used so often. In those contexts, it’s perfect. And so it is with III-vi-V-IV. It’s nothing in itself. However, put it in a good song and it might be effective. Put it in a bad song, and it won’t be.

Question: Who is the most normal character in The Office?
Answer: Easy. David Wallace. David Wallace starts the show as the Chief Financial Officer of Dunder Mufflin. The reason why David Wallace is there, in terms of the show’s development, is I think that the show needed to have an authority figure. Somebody who stood for the corporate world. The original authority figure in the show was, of course, Jan Levinson, Melora Hardin’s character—but, almost from the off, Jan’s authority is being undermined by the fact that Michael Scott obviously fancies her. To begin with, Jan effortlessly brushes this off. She gets through season 1 and much of season 2 without this seriously threatening her authority, but in season 2’s ‘The Client’, she is a.) getting over a divorce, b.) forced to have many drinks by Michael’s sales tactic and c.) deeply impressed that Michael’s tactic works, and that they gain a valuable client. So she kisses Michael in the Chili’s parking lot. From there, Michael and Jan enter an increasingly excruciating, mutually-destructive gavotte which came to an ungodly climax in season 4’s classic ‘Dinner Party’. But that’s for another answer. Let’s just say that, whereas in the UK version of The Office, there was never a chance that Jennifer Taylor-Clarke would get together with David Brent, in the US version, with its less clenched and less jaundiced view of the world, there was at least the possibility that Jan Levinson-Gould might get together with Michael Scott. In the meantime, once Jan could no longer be the impersonal authority figure, because she had become a character that others had intense personal relationships with, somebody else had to assume that role. And that character was David Wallace. How that came to happen is, I think, involved with the casting of the character. (My source for much of this is an episode of the excellent podcast Office Ladies, in which two of the show’s stars, Jenna Fischer and Angela Kinsey, bring their wealth of inside knowledge to discussing the show itself. And invite old friends back to be interviewed.) David Wallace’s actor, Andy Buckley, had been scuffling away for years trying to make it, doing sketch comedy with the Groundlings in L.A. But he wasn’t earning a living. Eventually, like so many actors, the need to make a living and support his family made him recognise the need for a day job. He followed the example of a friend, and his degree in political science helped him to get a day job as a stockbroker with Merrill Lynch. To his surprise, he enjoyed the work. But he still had the yearning to act. One day, he was approached by casting director Allison Jones, who had seen him in his Groundling days and remembered him. She asked him what he was up to, and he explained that he was working in finance. Jones told him that she might be getting in touch with him about something. What she got in touch with him about was playing David Wallace in The Office. When Buckley told this story in Office Ladies, Fischer’s opinion was that the Office’s producer Michael Schur would have been fascinated by the fact that Buckley was, like, a real live businessman, as well as being a capable actor. I think that this ‘real life’ quality is what underpins Buckley’s performance. David Wallace is the least quirky character in the show: almost his only quirk is that he is almost invariably referred to not as ‘David’ or as ‘Wallace’ but as ‘David Wallace’. Buckley, as Wallace, gives in my view the most dialled-down performance in the show. Of all the characters, he is the one who seems most like an ordinary person in a documentary. Somebody once described The Office as a comedy where characters give each other looks across rooms while something else is going on, and Andy Buckley is a master of underplaying. In season 4’s ‘The Deposition’, when his own testimony that Michael is a ‘nice guy’ but unsuited to a corporate job is read aloud before both him and Michael, he looks genuinely pained that Michael has had to hear that. In season 9’s ‘Livin’ the Dream’, he consults Jim about hiring Dwight as office manager, and all our doubts about this are put into his performance. David Wallace: And I'm looking for a new manager. And with his performance this year, I have been considering Dwight. Am I crazy? Jim: Not at all. It should be Dwight. David Wallace: You sure? Jim: You're gonna want to invest in a lot more liability insurance, but, uh— David Wallace: Yeah. Jim: Hey, if there is someone out there who loves paper more than Dwight, I definitely don't want to meet that person. Other bosses in the show tend to be larger than life. Jan is of course an example, but so is Kathy Bates’ Jo Bennett, eternally trying to prove herself, and James Spader’s hyper-sleazy Robert California, with his perpetual air of wanting to have sex with literally any of his employees. Of Will Ferrell, as Deangelo Vickers, let us not speak. I am not one of the people who sees the point of Will Ferrell. Somebody in Dunder Mifflin has to seem generally competent and not… odd. Jan becomes fabulously odd, with her transformation from competent line manager to crooning, candle-making nutjob (although she seemed to end up pretty happy, so good luck to her), but David Wallace remains a rock of calm ordinariness throughout the entire run of the show. Except once. That once is a minor story arc that begins in season 6’s ‘Sabre’, when the failing Dunder Mifflin has been bought out by Kathy Bates’ Sabre, and David Wallace has been fired, along with the rest of the company’s senior management. Michael is not pleased at the way Sabre’s policies clash with the way he’s used to doing things, so he drives to David Wallace’s house to seek his advice. And there, he has one of the frights of his life. He finds his former boss has morphed into a rudderless, de-energised, unshaven shadow of himself in an ugly grey zip-neck jumper. Michael and David’s reunion has a soundtrack provided by David’s son, who is enthusiastically playing his drums in the living room: the bashing of his drums proceeds through David and Michael’s entire conversation, rather like the nightmarish drug deal scene in Boogie Nights with its perpetual soundtrack of thrown firecrackers. David is delighted to see him—which he’s never been before, and which almost instantly puts Michael on his guard—and invites him in. David’s wife Rachel passes through and seems rather concerned that her husband hasn’t gone anywhere or done anything all day. Over beers in the Wallace’s hot tub, Michael confides his problem and asks David for advice. David admits that he has none, and then immediately changes the subject to his new business idea, ‘Suck It’, a vacuum cleaner designed to pick up children’s toys. At this point, Michael gives the camera the kind of mildly anxious aside glance that other characters normally give when they witness his behaviour. When Michael Scott does that kind of look to the camera, it is a World Turned Upside Down. Michael declines to invest in Suck It and confesses his disappointment to the camera, before getting into his car and reversing away from the Wallace house. David Wallace follows him down the driveway, visible through the windshield, smiling and waving for just a bit too long. That is not David Wallace, Michael tells us. That is some weird creature that lives in David Wallace’s house. He’s right. David Wallace without power is simply not David Wallace. In David’s next few appearances, he’s still trying to shill his ridiculous vacuum cleaner idea, even unto wearing a ridiculous hoodie with the name on it: This situation does not resolve itself until season 8’s ‘Fundraiser’, in which Andy Bernard, newly fired from the office and looking to start his own company, meets David Wallace at a fundraiser and learns that David sold his vacuum cleaner patent to the military and now has $20m which he wants to invest. Sure enough, Wallace ends up buying Dunder Mifflin and becoming its CEO, and his previous normality is restored. David Wallace is not a wonderful boss. But neither is he an absurdly bad one, like Deangelo Vickers. He’s exactly the sort of boss you’d expect a second-string paper company to have. Calm, reasonably competent, makes the occasional bad decision (seriously, hiring Charles, of all people, to manage Scranton, of all places, was a bad call) but he gets there in the end. That’s why, in a show that was about, as Pam put it, ‘the beauty in ordinary things’, David Wallace was… … the ordinary in ordinary things. Which is, I think, why he seems so ‘normal’.

Question: I play cello. Would it be easier for me to learn the bass guitar since I can read bass clef and I have the strength and stamina to pluck?
Answer: Very good question. It so happens that I have had cellist friends, and I play the bass guitar. Well, sometimes. First question: easier than what? You don’t specify. Bass guitar does require some core strength—you got to strap that baby on and move your fretting hand around quite a bit, and I find that my plucking hand also gets quite a workout. I would say that, for the sake of timbral variation, and if you’re playing a bass that has more than one pickup, a good player needs to be able to pluck with equal power and precision in at least three places: nearer the neck; between the neck and the bridge; and nearer the bridge. And plucking near the bridge is hard, because the strings are harder to get going there. Other answerers have observed that the cello is tuned in fifths, CGDA, whereas the bass guitar is tuned like the double bass, EADG. This is something that you’ll have to get used to. Except: Wait, Alex—is there by any chance a precedent for a cellist taking up the bass guitar and tuning it like a cello? Why, yes there is! That rather grainy photo is of Georgina Born, an English cellist who joined the radical prog-rock band Henry Cow in 1976. She joined as their bass player, and tuned her bass guitar down to cello tuning. If you want to know about Henry Cow, I wrote about them here: Here she is rather more visibly, with her Ampeg bass: Anyway, Georgina Born tuned her bass like a cello, and played some great basslines with it. However, it might be easier in the long run to tune the bass normally. In any case, I see no reason why you shouldn’t take to the bass with ease. And if you want something to practice bass with which you may be familiar, I have this book and I recommend it: Enjoy!

Question: What could I do to try to get a deeper sound on my jazz bass like the precision? Would changing the capacitor help?
Answer: A Bass EQ. I’ve tried out a Jazz Bass, and while they look cool, and I like the flexibility of having two pickups rather than one, the sound is indeed a little less bass-y than a Precision-type bass. This can easily be remedied if you get a Bass EQ pedal. There’s no need to go mucking about with the electronics of the bass itself. An EQ pedal helps you to raise certain frequency bands and lower others, and the results can be very striking indeed. It gives you far more control over the general frequency response of your instrument, and it can significantly boost bass frequencies and cut higher ones—or lower them, depending on what you want to do. It is the ultimate expansion kit for your bass’s tone knob. It’s not going to fundamentally alter the timbre of your instrument beyond recognition, but it can certainly help you to sound ‘deeper’, without permanently altering your instrument.

Question: The show "Brooklyn 99" was a pretty awesome show but was canceled because of a police brutality protest done by BLM. Do you think it was right to cancel a show that did well and was only shutdown by BLM to appease BLM's narrative?
Answer: Brooklyn Nine Nine wasn’t ‘shutdown by BLM to appease BLM’s narrative’. BLM does not have the power to cancel TV shows, and you don’t ‘appease a narrative’: that’s gibberish. Only people can be appeased. Brooklyn Nine Nine has the distinction of having been shut down twice. First by Fox, which cancelled it after five seasons, when it was at the peak of its powers, and then by NBC, who picked it up, gave it three more seasons and then cancelled it. B99 was a show that found its moment. Unfortunately, the moment ended before the show did. The premise was a police procedural comedy. It skilfully played TV stereotypes against a sense of real life: Andy Samberg’s character Jake Peralta was basically a Generation Xer (on the young end of the scale) who was a police detective, and who fantasised about being a more maverick, rule-breaking, old-school detective than he actually was. He kind of wanted to be Andy Sipowicz from NYPD Blue, but when it came to the crunch, he couldn’t be: he was too sensitive and empathetic, and he wasn’t a grouchy, alcoholic Vietnam veteran but a perky, thirty-something Taylor Swift fan. (Peralta: She makes me feel things. Terry: She makes ALL OF US feel things!) Peralta’s boss, Ray Holt, was a gruff, stern, black police captain, who was also gay, and married to a history professor at Columbia, and had an unusual knowledge of things like Hungarian fencing terms, and was a stickler for correct grammar. Peralta’s partner, Charles Boyle, was not a brilliant detective but a hard-working, methodical one who was also a huge dork, as well as a food nerd whose idea of comfort eating was takoyaki: octopus dumplings. Peralta’s colleague, rival and eventual girlfriend and wife, Amy Santiago, was a Hispanic woman detective, and an even bigger nerd, with an almost sexual attraction to binders, who devised her own ludicrously complex mnemonic for memorising the moons of Jupiter (Every Individual Gets Crayons, After Telling His Aggressive Little Mongoose Painter Called Ernest Some Lies About Tiny Panda Head, Period…). And as if to defy the stereotype that a cop show could only have one Latina detective, there was a second one, Rosa Diaz, who was insanely aggressive (although deep down a solid friend) and owned several leather jackets, including a ‘formal’ one (It’s the one without any blood on it.) And finally, the sergeant, Terry Jeffords, was in spite of his huge build a massive softy, who doted on his daughters Cagney and Lacey and took yoghurt very, very seriously. I’ll resist the temptation to do a full breakdown of the whole show, but will only observe that these characters seemed hilarious as long as the police itself, which was the background to the show’s comedy, didn’t seem to be a problem. However, over the course of the show, there was a steady rise in anger about police brutality, culminating with the 2020 murder of George Floyd by Officer Derek Chauvin. There was widespread indignation and rage about this incident, except among people who didn’t think it was important, either because they thought that Chauvin hadn’t done anything wrong, or else that Floyd deserved to get killed, or else that it didn’t matter because Floyd was black. Not sure where you fall in those categories, Mollgrave, but from your profile it’s clear that you’re not here to spread wisdom and enlightenment, but to attempt, in your childish way, to be annoying: Anyway, who cares about you. The makers of B99 felt the need to rejig the show in the wake of the George Floyd murder, and the eighth season featured considerable changes. It wasn’t that the writing was bad, exactly; it’s just that the goodwill no longer existed in which Jake’s shenanigans seemed like good fun. Because the writing staff were exceptionally talented, they managed to round it off in a satisfying way. There were some good individual episodes, like ‘The Lake House’, but too much of the necessary storyline was about Jake dialling down his craziness so that the finale would make sense. But I doubt that I’m the only person who found season eight less fun. In fact, I know I wasn’t. A glance at the viewing figures show that B99 steadily shed viewers from season one onwards, with a brief blip in season 6. Season 1 averaged 4.8m viewers; by season 7 it was 2.69m, the lowest in the show’s history. Brooklyn Nine Nine didn’t get cancelled to appease Black Lives Matter. It got cancelled because not enough people wanted to watch it anymore.

Question: Is 'cultural Marxism real? Or is it right wing paranoia/propaganda?
Answer: It’s both real and unreal. There absolutely is such a thing as a Marxist analysis of culture. However, the thing that right-wingers call ‘cultural Marxism’ isn’t it. In this answer, I’ll refer to the Marxist analysis of culture as cultural Marxism, without quotes, and the thing right-wingers are talking about as ‘cultural Marxism’, within quotes. The late French philosopher Jacques Derrida, who we’ll come back to later, referred to this practice as placing something ‘under erasure’ (sous rature), which means that you can’t do without the notion and you have to call it something, so for the sake of convenience you’re calling it this, but this is a really bad name for it. Jacques Derrida. Philosopher. Very handsome. Not a Marxist. ‘Cultural Marxism’ is really a kind of bizarre philosophical/cultural chimera, a weird and indigestible burgoo of different ideas, thinkers, theories, movements and received ideas about same, which often lumps together people who not only had little or nothing to do with each other but who violently disagreed with each other. Whenever I read people ranting about ‘cultural Marxism’, it’s clear that although they don’t really know what they’re talking about, they sure as heckfire know that they’re agin it. (Dagnabbit.) At different times, ‘cultural Marxism’ has been said to include such diverse phenomena as: … And I could go on. One of the notable things about ‘cultural Marxism’ is that it tends to contain very little actual Marxism. In fact, many of the things in the above list are things that have a problem with Marxism, or which Marxism itself has a problem with, or in the case of things like kneeling before the flag, vaccination and the Democratic party, have nothing whatever to with Marxism. There is also the Frankfurt School, which we’ll come back to in a minute. Take postmodernism, for instance. Postmodernism is, to people who understand it, something that everyone is affected by, whether we realise it or not, and which we can choose to more or less embrace or more or less reject, insofar as it’s not like knitting—something that you can take up or drop in your spare time—but more like neoliberalism: something that is all around us and which affects us whether or not we want it to. One of the classic works about postmodernism is Frederic Jameson’s hefty 1991 book Postmodernism, or, the Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism, in which Jameson examines manifestations of postmodernism in culture, and seeks to analyse it, from a Marxist perspective. Jameson does provide a coherent account of postmodernism (which he refers to in the book’s famous opening sentence as ‘an attempt to think the present historically in an age which has forgotten how to think historically in the first place’) but it would be a disservice to his great book to say that he is simply for or against it. In general, he comes across as less than celebratory, which makes sense given that Jameson is a Marxist, and postmodernist theory tends to be impatient with what it sees as Marxist pretensions to providing a coherent conceptual structure within which postmodern society can be analysed. Anyway, however you slice it, postmodernism is not a form of Marxism. Neither is the work of Foucault, or Derrida, and deconstruction isn’t a kind of Marxism either, and neither is diversity casting in Hollywood, and neither is anything else on the above list. I’ve read a lot of answers by right-wing people associating ‘cultural Marxism’ with the Frankfurt School, which was a grouping of German thinkers in the 20th century, who sought to analyse contemporary culture and society using a variety of methodologies. Some of them were influenced by Marxism, some of them not. So there is a grain of truth to referring to the Frankfurt School as ‘cultural Marxism’ The Frankfurt School included people like the philosopher Theodor W. Adorno, the philosopher and sociologist Max Horkheimer, the political scientist Franz Neumann, the sociologist Leo Löwenthal, and several others. The literary critic Walter Benjamin was loosely associated with them, but he died from his own hand in 1940 while in fear of being arrested by the Gestapo (he was Jewish) so he was at best a peripheral associate. The spirit of the Frankfurt School lives on in the still-living German philosopher and social theorist Jürgen Habermas: he’s 94 but he published his most recent book last year. However, I think the influence of the Frankfurt School can be, and has been, greatly exaggerated, not least by anti-Semitic elements on the right, who like to make much of the fact that many of its members were Jewish (including all of the above except Habermas), even though most of them came from assimilated families. Basically, the Frankfurt School has been characterised by the American far-right as a branch of the Global Jewish Conspiracy, undermining the American Way of Life. This is certainly related to the fact that some of its members lived in and wrote about America during and after WW2, on account of being exiled from Nazi Germany. Adorno co-wrote the monumental sociological study of how fascism was related to elements of human psychology, The Authoritarian Personality, which was based on interviews with American subjects. Löwenthal co-wrote a much more concise and brilliant study of far-right-wing agitators in post-war USA, Prophets of Deceit, a book which is still highly relevant today. If the works of the Frankfurt School are damned by today’s American far-right as ‘cultural Marxism’, it’s partly because there is an element of truth to that, but also, to repurpose a quote from Oscar Wilde, it’s the rage of Caliban at seeing his face in the mirror. However, I’ve seen right-wingers calling the Frankfurt School ‘postmodernists’, which is so off-base it’s funny. If anything, Adorno in particular was horrified by the incipient phenomenon of postmodernism (he died in 1969) and much of his work can be read as a cry of despair about the emerging postmodernity. Jameson is mostly respectful of Adorno in Postmodernism, but he does sardonically remark: … any sophisticated theory of the postmodern ought to bear something of the same relationship to Horkheimer and Adorno’s old “Culture Industry” concept as MTV or fractal ads bear to fifties television series. In the era of the internet, that passage now reads to me as painfully early 90s. So given that ‘cultural Marxism’ includes some things that have a definite Marxist tinge, and an awful lot more things that have nothing to do with Marxism, why is it called that? In the USA, a very good job has been done by the government, the media and business to make socialism and communism seem malevolent and evil. ‘Marxism’ is a handy codeword for what in previous centuries would have been called ‘Satan’. (Saul Alinsky was called a Satanist by right-wingers because he dedicated a book to the character of Lucifer, the villain in Paradise Lost, a poem by a Christian poet, John Milton. Milton’s Lucifer has been repeatedly thought of as a rather sympathetic character by various people, including another poet, William Blake, also a Christian, albeit an unorthodox one.) So, ‘cultural Marxism’ is really a catch-all term for any cultural phenomenon that some people perceive as ‘undermining’ or ‘subverting’ what they consider to be the natural and organic order of American culture, which—if you look up what they claim to consider natural and organic—is usually a grotesque, heavily censored parody of the American culture of the 1950s, with the social unrest and despair taken out, where white heterosexual men are safely in charge, people of colour know their place, LGBTQ folk are invisible, property rights are protected, and good stories are about men like them being heroes. To my mind, the version of the American 50s peddled by the contemporary American far-right is grossly unfair and dishonest about the real complexities and intellectual and cultural currents of that period. It’s a version of 50s American culture that completely lacks the moral ambiguity of film noir, the anger and anti-establishment passion of the Beat movement, and the increasing politicisation of jazz: Charles Mingus in 1957 released ‘Fables of Faubus’, his scathing jab at the Governor of Arkansas, who refused to allow the integration of Little Rock Central High School, although the version with lyrics didn’t come out until 1960. The 50s were the decade when one of the most innovative American comic strips first appeared: Charles M. Schulz’s Peanuts, which in that decade was marked by its eerie silences, and its willingness to portray small children as malevolent and unsympathetic. The 50s and early 60s were the time of Willam H. Whyte’s scathing critique of corporate culture, The Organization Man; of David Riesman’s The Lonely Crowd; of Daniel Boorstin’s prescient analysis of the news media, The Image, which theorised the idea of ‘celebrity’. America in the 50s was critiquing the heck out of itself, is what I’m saying: the idea that it was some prelapsarian condition of blissful content is nostalgic moonshine. Anyone who’s spent time on the more racist spaces on this site will have noticed how American white supremacists often have a special fondness for the mid-20th century paintings of Norman Rockwell. Freedom of Speech and Freedom from Want, in particular, tend to make regular appearances in ‘It’s OK to be White’. Rockwell himself would have been highly unimpressed by this, given that he spent the last ten years of his career devoting himself to three of his favourite subjects: the civil rights struggle in the USA, poverty and space exploration. Rockwell’s famous 1964 painting The Problem We All Live With depicts Ruby Bridges, a young African-American girl, being escorted to school by US marshals: the wall behind her has been daubed with the n-word and the letters ‘KKK’, and a thrown tomato has splattered against the wall and slid to the ground. One of the subtler touches in this painting is that we don’t see Bridges from the perspective of the escorting marshals (I notice that the one on the left in the cream suit appears to be black, or at any rate, not white), or from Bridges’ own perspective, but from the perspective of the protesters screaming abuse at her. Perhaps that’s partly why Rockwell received a ton of racist hate mail about it, some of which called him a ‘race traitor’. Why do I go on about Norman Rockwell? Because the reception of his work by the racists on this site is an example of the postmodernist disdain for context and authorship that they profess to deplore. It’s only possible to claim (some of) Rockwell’s paintings for white supremacism if you ignore the entire context of his work, including his fervent anti-racism. In Freedom of Speech, which I’ve seen more than once being used as an icon for white supremacists, Rockwell’s model, Carl Hess, was the son of German immigrants (this for a painting from 1943), and the series that the painting came from was inspired by a 1941 speech by Franklin Roosevelt, a hate figure for right-wingers because of his commitment to large federal social programs, so much so that they feel compelled to tell lies about his historical stature. Here’s an answer to the question Why is Franklin Roosevelt considered the best president?: (For the record, almost all attempts by historians to rank the US presidents have placed Roosevelt in either the top 3, or at the top of the list. But in terms of intellectual honesty, this answer is fairly typical of this user.) To get back to Rockwell: the idea that you can completely ignore the statements and context of an artist, and decide that the work means whatever you want it to mean, is really a right-wing caricature of postmodernist theories about the reception of works of art, yet that’s exactly what white supremacists do when they appropriate the art of the anti-racist Norman Rockwell for their own racist purposes. See what I mean about postmodernism getting in everywhere? So, if ‘cultural Marxism’ is something which even people who hate ‘cultural Marxism’ appear to be afflicted by, what is cultural Marxism? On the most basic level, it’s both the analysis of culture from a Marxist perspective, and cultural artefacts made by Marxists, the former being a subset of the latter. There are volumes of this stuff, some of which you’ll find in here: Marxist literary theory varies enormously in power, range and sophistication, from the crude Stalinism of Soviet critics who damned anything that wasn’t dreary socialist realism as ‘bourgeois formalism’, to… well, other Soviet critics, such as V.N. Voloshinov, whose 1929 book Marxism and the Philosophy of Language developed a remarkably powerful and convincing theory of language, which related the relationship of the linguistic concept of signified and signifier to the Marxist concept of base and superstructure. Then there was the Hungarian Georg Lukács, who began in his apolitical youth with highly precocious and brilliant books like Soul and Form and The Theory of the Novel, and then became a communist after the Russian Revolution and wrote the classic History and Class Consciousness, which made him hugely unpopular in Moscow because he dared to question the eminence of Friedrich Engels on philosophical matters. Lukács’ later career is marked by drearily orthodox Marxist-Leninist literary criticsm like The Meaning of Contemporary Realism and the rather pedestrian but still interesting The Historical Novel. In Britain, the 50s and 60s produced John Berger, the great art critic, novelist, poet, activist and writer of unclassifiable books about migrant workers, photography, time and colour. In an academic context, there was the remarkable Raymond Williams, a former WW2 tank captain turned Cambridge professor, who was highly influential in the 60s and 70s, and is still so to this day through the work of his most brilliant students, such as the literary critic Terry Eagleton and the sociologist and cultural theorist Stuart Hall. I wrote about Hall in another answer; he was an eclectic thinker who took what he needed from Marx but declined to regard himself as a disciple of anyone. In the USA, there are figures as illustrious as Angela Davis and Marshall Berman. Harvard University published a monumental four-volume edition of Walter Benjamin’s Selected Writings. Trinidad had C.L.R. James, who acutely analysed sport from a Marxist perspective. We could list a lot of names of important Marxist thinkers about culture and society, from lots of other countries, but let’s not do that. The main thing is that these people, who are or were outstanding in the field of Marxist analysis of culture, are hardly aligned shoulder-to-shoulder with people like Foucault, or Derrida. For the record, I happen to think that Foucault and Derrida highly interesting figures who are both well worth reading, and widely and drastically misunderstood. (Derrida, who did tend to get disciples, was usually a far more rigorous and serious thinker than some of the people who cite him as an influence.) So, ‘cultural Marxism’ could be characterised as ‘the current label for the demonology of the right-wing’. It is a heterogeneous collection of people, phenomena, myths, misunderstandings, lies, distortions, ideas and ideologies, which are only given the appearance of unity by the fact that right-wing people disapprove of them. Cultural Marxism, by contrast, is relatively unpopular. Society just doesn't make Marxists like it used to. Yet Marxism does give us some useful tools for understanding culture and society. Thanks for reading.
