Question: Should a person study the concept of computer programming before learning a particular computer language? What books and resources are recommended?
Answer: I am not someone who writes code, or is involved in computer programming, for a living. So I have no professional credentials, on this matter. There are others who will write you much better answers than this one. I did take a college course in introductory computer science, using a very simple, visual-based coding language based on Scratch, a language that is normally taught to grade school kids. I had already tried to learn something about programming, via the languages C and Python. But I hadn’t got that far, because I hadn’t begun to understand why people learn those languages in the first place. (My college course, and some independent reading of works by great programmers, helped me to understand what programs are and why they get written.) I have been very interested in programming, for about… 23 years, at this point. In a fumbling, amateurish, not very coherent way. So feel free to dismiss my opinion on those grounds. I am in no way a professional authority. It could be said that the only thing I know about this subject is how much I don’t know about it. That said. Everything I have learned from every expert I have attended to, has taught me that it is far more important to learn the fundamentals of programming—the issues of why you are writing a program in the first place, what programs are, how they work, and how you turn a real-life task into a program—than to focus on learning the vocabulary and syntax of a particular language. The paradox, of course, is that you can only learn how to create a working program by rendering it in one language or another. Because the specifics are very important. I think that the misleading thing, here, is the word ‘language’. As someone from a humanities background, I’m used to thinking of language as having many different functions. It’s not all there to do the same thing. Language can have many different roles and purposes. Poetry is not like prose. But some of it is. And some prose is like poetry. However, computer languages only have one role: to tell the computer to do something. They are a more or less convenient way for humans to interact with machines. (Edit: And also, to tell subsequent programmers what the computer is being told to do. Thanks to those who brought this up in the comments.) Once you know how this works, it becomes possible to make aesthetic judgements about one person’s use of the language as opposed to another’s. There are clean ways to write code, and clunky ways to write it. But in order to write good code, the most important thing to understand is how able the machine is to interpret what instructions you choose to give it. And so, on that level, the particular language that you use to instruct it is less important than the fundamental intelligibility, to the machine, of the way you have broken the task down into instructions that it can handle. Because, if you are able to abstract the primary task into creating the basic kind of instructions that the machine can handle, then the question of translating those instructions into the grammar and syntax of specific programming languages becomes a relatively simpler matter of learning the grammar and syntax of those languages—and let’s not kid ourselves that programming languages are as complex as spoken languages. I also found that once I had tried and succeeded in solving the basic problem, it was an awful lot easier to render that problem in whatever language I happened to be using. So, from my very limited experience, and from my very limited knowledge, which is confirmed by the statements of basically every expert I’ve read on this subject, the hard and important part is not learning this or that programming language. The hard and important part could be phrased as ‘learning how to turn a task into something that is computable’.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: Why do atheists believe in morality? Why does it even matter to them? I do not understand why somebody would be moral in a world where everything is decided by a genetic roll of dice.
Answer: This is a very interesting question. Not because of what it suggests about atheists, but because of what it suggests about the person who asked it. It should be possible to break down the underlying assumptions in the question in such a way that the person who asked it would probably agree on what those assumptions are. Something like this: One. The world is constituted in such a way that humans are capable of making moral choices that are meaningful and intelligible. This is fairly uncontroversial, and amounts to saying It is possible to make moral choices. Two. It is constituted this way because of the existence of a divine being, which created it and handed down a system of morality by means of religion. This is a lot more controversial, and involves the acceptance of the truth of a religion that contains a code of moral law imposed by a divine being. The existence of such a being is at least arguable, which in turns puts the moral legitimacy of a religion based on the existence of such a being at least into question. I might notice in passing that at least some schools of Christian theology have gained adherents, while basically kicking into touch the entire question of the literal existence of a divine being. Three. Morality is a system of laws that dictate how humans must behave. This is arguably true about morality. However, ‘morality’ is not the only way of thinking about ethics, or about ethical behaviour. Morality tends to have very little to say about the individual, and tends to rule out things like personal feelings and personal interests in favour of universal laws. So we end up with ethical problems like the one where you have a choice between saving two people from a house fire: the universally beloved sage and philanthropist Professor Goodbody, or your own infant child. Many systems of morality dictate that it’s in the wider interests of humanity that you save the professor and let your child die, but is this really a rock-solid ethical argument? Why do we have to automatically rule out our own interests as a parent? If we are not bothered by questions like that when thinking about such a dilemma, I suggest that we are leaving out important considerations in our thinking about ethics. Four. Since these laws have ultimate and binding authority over all humans, they must not derive that authority from mere human whim (because humans are fallible), but must come from some superior power—which must be the aforementioned divine being. Quite a lot to unpack here. First it seems to assume that a system of morality which consists of a set of authoritative laws that dictate how humans must behave, is the only way humans have of talking or thinking about ethics. This is far from being the case, as I’ve hinted above. Then, it assumes that humans are incapable of constructing moral laws which have such authority, or of answering difficult ethical questions (because our answers are only ever ‘mere’ opinion), and it goes on to ascribe that authority to the aforementioned divine being whose existence is assumed in assumption #2. However, it is not self-evident that humans are incapable of ethical behaviour without moral laws which they believe have supra-human origins. Five. However, atheists don’t believe in a divine being. This is, or should be, uncontroversially true, in that attempts by some theists to assert that atheists ‘actually’ believe in some sort of divine being in spite of themselves, have not been convincing. Six. Therefore, they have no such supreme authority to prove morality for them. This assumes that they require such a thing, which is what’s asserted in #4, and which is not self-evident. Seven. Atheists believe in a world where everything is decided by chance (‘a genetic roll of the dice’). This is absolutely not true, in that not all atheists think that everything is decided by chance. If we’re right to think that this is a veiled allusion to/snipe at the theory of evolution by natural selection, as I believe it to be, anyone who understands that theory knows that it does not say that chance governs everything: only that chance is one factor among many in the evolution of life. So this very skimpy account of that theory lacks credibility. But, also, what the theory of evolution by natural selection has to do with arguments about morality, is not at all clear. Morality is part of human culture, whereas the theory of evolution by natural selection is a feature of nature. Another answer to this question held up a quote from Richard Dawkins as ‘evidence’ that atheists cannot be moral: Assuming for the moment that the quote is authentic, here’s a definitely authentic quote from Dawkins’ The Selfish Gene: Dawkins emphasises that ethics are something that can be taught, not something that we simply ‘read off’ from nature, or accept as natural. Our ‘ambassador for Christ’ thinks that the universe is intrinsically moral, by divine design, and that atheists wilfully ignore this. But trying to make moral arguments from nature is to gamble on one’s understanding of nature, and the house always wins. If arguments from nature had moral force, than it would be e.g. immoral to travel at speeds faster than humans can travel under their own power, without the assistance of technology: i.e., about 23.35 mph. I don’t think it’s unreasonable to assume that the ambassador for Christ occasionally rides in a car. Eight. Therefore, it is impossible for atheists to talk about ‘morality’ since their intellectual framework precludes the possibility of any such thing. It makes no sense to talk about moral choices if no laws exist against which those choices can be judged. If assumption #7 were true, then this would be a fair comment, but there is no evidence that assumption #7 is true, not least because it betrays a basic misunderstanding of a scientific theory, and a whole raft of extra assumptions about the applicability of that misunderstanding to arguments about ethics. So, this really compounds misunderstanding upon misunderstanding. Nine. If no existing code of laws exist against which supposedly moral choices can be judged, then such ‘choices’ become a purely subjective matter of one preference against another. This amounts to a blanket dismissal of ethical arguments that question the validity of deontology, which is rule-based ethical theory. Since no attempt is made to engage with criticisms of deontology, this is at least lazy and at worst avoiding the central point. Ten. Therefore, there is nothing to stop atheists from behaving with immorality or even amorality, and it’s maybe even inconsistent of them to not behave with immorality or amorality. This is, perhaps, the most fundamental and the weirdest assumption behind the question. Why? Because it appears to assume that the only thing that stops people from behaving immorally is the existence of a strict code of divinely-imposed moral law. And that, if such a code did not exist, people would inevitably behave with maximum selfishness and amorality. This is, to say the least, arguable. By way of evidence, it’s easy to point to atheists who do not compulsively behave in immoral ways, and also to self-styled religious people who do, such as religious leaders who practice child sexual abuse. To return to the original question: I do not understand why somebody would be moral in a world where everything is decided by a genetic roll of dice. Not understanding why someone would be moral in a world without an religiously-ordained moral code, implies that the querent is plagued by the desire to behave in ways that that code regards as immoral or amoral, and only doesn’t do so because of fear of, or respect for, the code. I don’t think most people live with the constant temptation to be immoral in serious ways. Of course, we can infer whatever we like about what the querent considers to be ‘immoral’. Maybe it’s wanting to sneak candy bars off the supermarket shelf and into one’s pocket; maybe it’s something much more serious by any standard, such as the desire to commit a major crime. Maybe it’s something which their church frowns upon but secular society regards as normal and unobjectionable, like same-sex desire: we just don’t know. The user account in question is long defunct. But to bring this answer to a close, I think the question is much more about the querent’s fears and lack of education in moral philosophy, and their own unspoken desires, than about the moral failings of atheists, of which it has little to say, and none of that well-informed. Sources: Richard Dawkins, The Selfish Gene, OUP, 1989 Bernard Williams, Morality: An Introduction to Ethics, Pelican, 1973

Question: What's the creepiest old folk song you've ever heard?
Answer: Possibly ‘The Bonny Hind’. It’s about a guy who meets a girl and they fancy each other: It’s May she comes and May she goes Down by the Holland green, And it’s here she spied a brisk young squire, As brisk as ev’r she seen. “Come give to me your green mantle, Give me your maidenhead; If you won’t give me your green mantle, Give me your maidenhead.” He’s taken her by the milk-white hand And gently laid her down; And it’s when he raised her up again Given her a silver comb. After they’ve had sex, they introduce themselves to each other, and that’s where it all goes wrong: “Perhaps there may be bairns, kind sir, Perhaps there may be none, But if you be a courtier Pray tell to me your name.” […] They call me Jack when I’m abroad, Sometimes they call me John; But when I’m in my father’s bower, Oh, Jock Randall is my name.” “You lie, you lie, you bonny lad, So loud I hear you lie. For I am Lord Randall’s only daughter, He has no more than me.” “You lie, you lie, you bonny lass, So loud I hear you lie. For I am Lord Randall’s very own son That new come from the sea.” Well, she’s not best pleased to hear that she’s just had sex with her brother, so she takes drastic action: She’s put her hand down by her side And out she’s taken a knife; And she’s put it in her own heart’s blood And taken away her life. And he’s taken his young sister With a big tear in his eye, And he’s buried his only sister Beneath the Holland tree. It’s soon he’s hired him o’er the dales, His father dear to see, “It’s oh and oh for my bonny hind Beneath the Holland tree.” His father, finding him noticeably, well, mopey, tries to cheer him up by offering him deer: “What care you for your bonny hind, For it you need not care. There’s eight score hinds in yon green park And five score is to spare. “What care you for your bonny hind, For it you need not care. Take you the best and give me the worst, Since plenty is to spare.” But he remains inconsolable: “I care not for your hinds, kind sir, And I care not for your fee. But it’s oh and oh for my bonny hind Beneath the Holland tree.” Whereupon the father makes a spectacularly inappropriate comment: “Oh were you at your sister’s bower, Your sister fair to see; Oh, you’ll think no more on your bonny hind Beneath the Holland tree.” In other words, You’d soon stop thinking so much about your dead deer if you saw how smokin’ hot your sister is. Question: Why is Marc Lawrence so passionate about trans women?
Answer: Marc Lawrence has exactly one thing to say about trans people in general, which is his claim that they do not exist. In his opinion, there are men and there are women, and gender and sex are the same thing. It follows from this that people who experience their gender as being different from the sex assigned to them at birth are merely mentally ill, and can presumably be prescribed anti-psychotic drugs to rid them of their delusions. Why he believes this is unclear. What is clear is that he is very confident and very ready to explain other people’s experiences to themselves. He thinks he knows exactly what other people are like, and he thinks he knows why they are wrong about what they’re like, and he behaves as if he can set them right about themselves. However, there is a problem with this. The problem is that trans people do not, apparently, recognise themselves in Mr Lawrence’s descriptions of what they are like. Let me use an analogy. I write with my left hand. However, I do a lot of other things with my right hand: I play guitar right-handed, I chop food with a knife in my right hand, I use right-handed corkscrews, etc. Therefore, I might think that this whole left-handed/right-handed thing is not simple: maybe it’s that I do some things with my left hand and other things with my right hand. I don’t ‘think’ that I write more easily with my left hand; it’s not something that I could be wrong about. Suppose that, instead of thinking the way he does about gender and sex, Marc Lawrence were obsessed with handedness, which is, rather like gender identity, a complex phenomenon where biology and the environment intersect. Suppose he thought that any kind of left-handedness were simply a form of mental illness: that nobody is ‘really’ left-handed in any way, they just ‘think’ they are, and it’s a delusion on my part that it’s far more natural and easy for me to write with my left hand, than to try to do so with my right. Suppose he were to turn his attention upon me, and say: You only think you write more easily with your left hand. You do most things with your right hand. If you only accepted that you find it easier to write with your right hand, then the problem would go away. To which I can only reply: No, I really find it more natural to write with my left hand. To which I think our handedness-oriented Marc Lawrence would confidently reply: No you don’t. You only think that you do. This is the way that Marc Lawrence behaves, with respect to gender. He thinks that he knows what other people’s experiences are. We know he thinks this, because he tells them what their experiences are. From the response he gets from trans people, the evidence is that he actually does not know what their experiences are. However, any hint of self-doubt he may have on this matter is not visible. Perhaps his religious convictions assure him that he is right. As far as he is concerned, other people’s experiences are unreal, and a symptom of their mental illness. That’s why he writes about other people’s experiences, over and over and over again, with his trademark combination of imperturbable self-satisfaction and rock-solid ignorance.

Question: It seems most questions are about Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. Are people not interested in composers of the Renaissance or the Baroque period?
Answer: An awful lot of questions about classical music are about those three composers, yes, which is a pity, because they don’t have a huge amount in common with each other, and the people who link them together generally show no evidence of having listened to them much or knowing much about them. Incidentally, Bach was a composer of what we now refer to as the ‘baroque period’, so it could be that you don’t know much about them either, Francine Sicard. Or maybe you were just having an off moment. To complicate things further, Bach died in 1750, only six years before Mozart was born, and at a time when Mozart’s great friend and sometime mentor Joseph Haydn was already 18. Haydn and Bach never met (Bach spent almost his whole life in Saxony, whereas Haydn at 18 had never left Austria) but whereas Haydn is considered a founding figure of classical-era music, he was clearly born in the ‘baroque period’. A far more natural grouping of composers is Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven, because they actually knew each other. But people treat Bach, Mozart and Beethoven as a sort of informal triumvirate of Great Composers, usually to ask inane questions comparing the music of the 21st century with the music of Olden Tymes, generally in order to make the present look bad. This is thankfully not that sort of question. But it’s worth bearing in mind that Renaissance music fell out of the repertoire for a long time, and didn’t re-enter it until the early 20th century, so composers like Ockeghem, Dufay, Byrd and Gibbons aren’t the household names that they deserve to be. Even Bach basically stands in for almost all baroque music, at least in the minds of casual listeners. Handel is known to casual listeners for the Messiah, Vivaldi for the Four Seasons and Pachelbel for his Canon in D, but most baroque composers are only listened to by more dedicated fans of that music. Handel’s many Italian operas are highly regarded by those of us that know them, but are almost invisible to the general public compared to the warhorse that is the Messiah, just as Bach’s church cantatas aren’t nearly as widely popular as his instrumental music; yet, not only by volume but by quality, the cantatas form the keystone of his achievement. So, yes: people are generally less interested in Renaissance and baroque music—bar the Greatest Hits of a handful of big names—than they are in Mozart and Beethoven. It may not be irrelevant that Bach’s cantatas and Handel’s Italian operas feature copious amounts of singing in, respectively, German and Italian, which might put some casual listeners off them, just as there are probably more people who prefer Schubert’s chamber music to his songs.

Name: Alex Johnston
Question: What are the reasons why people choose to learn how to play the guitar over other instruments?
Answer: When I was 13-14, growing up in Dublin in the 80s, I was entranced by the playing of three musicians. Charlie Parker, alto saxophone player: Bud Powell, pianist: The young Eric Clapton, specifically his music from 1965–1970. After 1970, whatever I liked about his music went out of his playing. I had already tried to learn jazz piano, but my piano teacher had disliked jazz, and hadn’t taught me anything useful except some basic music theory, so I’d got nowhere. It was, therefore, a choice between saxophone or guitar. I made a mental list of pros and cons. (This answer is very much about my teenage mindset as a wannabe musician, so bear that in mind.) Saxophone pros: Saxophone cons: Guitar pros: Guitar cons: In the end, it was something else that clinched it: It really was as simple as that. I wanted to play a popular instrument, not a more specialised one. To this day, while I still find the guitar in many ways inadequate, and ineloquent when played badly, I’m really glad I went with guitar. The guitar is a more universal instrument, not confined to any one form or style of music. But the instant people hear a sax, they think ‘Jazz.’ And I love jazz. But I don’t want to be a jazz musician (any more). But that’s not the whole story. There was a last decision I took which ended up serving me well, based on this: Furthermore: But, I had reservations. I had a little debate with myself, which went like this: —Hold on. You’re not that interested in the bass. You’ve never wanted to be a bass player. Nobody hears the bass. Bass players are dorks. You could end up as one of those ‘disappointed bass players’. —True, very true, but I will get a guitar later on, okay? I will. Also, guitars have six strings, basses have four, only got five fingers on each hand. So basses are probably easier. —Well, maybe, but maybe not. Are you going to take this seriously? —Yes. —Well, you’d better get interested in bass guitar pretty damn sharpish, then. —Okay. —What bass players can you think of? —Um. That guy who played on those boring Clapton records from the 70s. Carl Radle. —Yeah, he’s not cool. —The guy in Status Quo. —We don’t like Status Quo anymore. —True. Your man from ZZ Top. —Haven’t really listened to them. —The guy in Level 42. —They’re so lame. We need to think of a cool bass player whose music we already like. —Wait, I got one. —Who? —Philo! —Philoooo! —PHILOOOOOOO!!! —Okay, okay, you’re right. Philo is cool. We’re gonna play bass. —PLAY BASS! Yes, my first bass hero was Phil Lynott of Thin Lizzy. Before I even owned a bass, I was plucking out his bass lines on a stretched rubber band with one end held to the tragus of my ear. Question: Why does the song “the world looks red” from ultrakill (https://youtu.be/In3SLsHpCSg?si=00n9P4RbxdmJW-Aj) make me want to cry so much especially at 3:30. My main question is what is the physiological reasoning for this?
Answer: There isn’t a ‘physiological reason’. If there were, it would make me cry too, whereas I am entirely unmoved by it. However, at about 3:32, there’s a passage where the guitars play a slightly different harmony from the rest of the song, which I would briefly describe as minor tonic C followed by a major dominant with a passing note of a diminished ninth, followed by Eb7, F, Fm, and back to Cm. This sort of progression (i-Vb9-V-III7-IV-iv-i) is a very common thing in common practice harmony. I personally would describe it as ‘schmaltzy’, or else as the sort of thing that would underscore an aria in a low-grade Italian popular opera where the hero gets a letter telling him that his beloved mamma back in Napoli is morta, and now he feels bad that he left her for this low-grade floozy on Mulberry Street. (Ahimè, perché mai sono venuto a Nuova York?!) But it worked on you, because… it worked on you. On a more abstract level, it’s got to do with things like suspensions in the voice leading (the way certain notes in the upper harmonies are carried over from one harmonic region to the next before resolving). It creates a vaguely yearning quality, which is admittedly very effective in the right context. The related IV-iv-I change was very popular with the Beatles, at one point, and you can hear it under a line like All my li-i-i-ife, though some have changed in ‘In My Life’. Anyway, tl;dr, it’s not a universal thing, it’s a music theory thing. As to why you personally find it so sad, that is a matter for you, which music theory cannot answer. To me, it’s more like By golly, they’re really strumming the ol’ heartstrings there. Pass the Kleenex.

Question: Is it me or do Gibson guitars just sound more real, fuller, and clearer than any other brand, and are the best electric guitars in the world?
Answer: It’s you. ‘More real’ isn’t a thing. All guitars are real, except for ones that we dream about. So that doesn’t mean anything. ‘Fuller’? Maybe. Gibsons tend to have humbuckers, and humbuckers tend to have more bass and more mid-range than single coil pickups. But lots of other guitars have humbuckers too; it’s not like only Gibsons do. ‘Clearer’: this is subjective, but I don’t experience humbuckers as being ‘clear’ so much as ‘rich’ or ‘creamy’: the analogue is between a glass of water, or a glass of Coke, and a cup of coffee or tea with milk. Single-coil pickup guitars are the former, humbucker-equipped guitars are the latter, at least to my ears. But that in itself is complicated by the fact that plenty of guitars have both kinds of pickup installed. And then there are P-90s, which Les Pauls were originally equipped with: they sound like neither regular single-coils nor humbuckers. ‘Best electric guitars in the world’. Subjective. I would like a Gibson Les Paul Classic, but I am far from wealthy, so it would take me several years to save up for one, and by the time I could afford one, I might not want one anymore. In the meantime, given my socioeconomic situation, whereas someone with a lot more spare cash than me might feel fine about spending close to three grand on a Les Paul Standard, while I might enjoy owning one, I would be so aware of all the things I could have spent that money on (like my kids, for example) that the instrument would be a permanent source of guilt for me, not a thing of enjoyment. So, for me, a Gibson is very much not one of the ‘best electric guitars in the world’, because use-value is a lot more complicated than that. For me, a Gibson would be little more than a reminder that I was spending money in a selfish way. tl;dr: It’s you.

Question: Harrison wrote the "Aah, look at all the lonely people" part in Eleanor Rigby, but did he write only the lyrics or also the melody? Is the melody entirely McCartneys?
Answer: I know of no evidence that Harrison wrote the ‘Ah, look at all the lonely people’ refrain in ‘Eleanor Rigby’. McCartney’s The Lyrics doesn’t support this claim, and neither does the Miles/McCartney Many Years From Now. Ian MacDonald’s Revolution in the Head only says that the refrain ‘seems to have been designed by committee, possibly later in the studio’. Lennon would later claim in the 1980 Playboy interview to have written most of the words apart from the first verse, but his friend Pete Shotton, who was present while much of the song was being put together, would say in his memoir In My Life that Lennon’s contribution was ‘virtually nil’. McCartney also denies Lennon any important role in the composition. Shotton also said that he himself was the one who found the name ‘McKenzie’ in a phone book: originally the priest was called ‘Father McCartney’ but it was pointed out that that made him sound like he was Paul McCartney’s dad. Shotton’s other contribution was to suggest that Eleanor Rigby die in the end of the song, and that Father McKenzie should preside over her funeral. Lennon shot this suggestion down with I don’t think you understand what we’re trying to get at, Pete. This irritated Shotton a good deal, but he was very pleased later on when he heard the song on the radio and realised that his suggestion had been taken on board after all. (Later, in the early 70s, McCartney would meet Shotton and observe that there was one song in particular that Shotton helped him write, presumably ‘Eleanor Rigby’.) Ringo Starr contributed the detail that Father McKenzie was ‘darning his socks in the night’. McCartney mentions in The Lyrics that he particularly remembered his mother’s Nivea cold cream, which is the source of the image of Eleanor’s face being kept ‘in a jar by the door’. Other than that, none of the research I have done has in any way supported the idea that Harrison wrote either the melody or any significant portion of the words for ‘Eleanor Rigby’. The available evidence suggests that McCartney wrote the entire melody, and the lyrics were written later, mostly by him and the others working as a committee. Thanks for the A2A, Emil Tolonen. Sources: Walter Everett: The Beatles as Musicians: Revolver through the Anthology, OUP, 1999 Mark Lewisohn, The Beatles Recording Sessions, Harmony Books, 1988 Ian MacDonald, Revolution in the Head: The Beatles’ Records and the Sixties, Vintage Books, 2008 Paul McCartney, The Lyrics, Penguin, 2023 Barry Miles, Paul McCartney: Many Years From Now, Vintage Books, 1998 David Sheff & G. Barry Golson: The Playboy Interviews with John Lennon & Yoko Ono, New English Library, 1981 Pete Shotton: John Lennon In My Life, Coronet, 1983

Question: Who is your favorite character from The Office?
Answer: My favourite character from The Office, the one whose behaviour I enjoy the most, is Pam. Season 1 Pam. Season 9 Pam. One of the things that I like about Pam is that, of almost all the main characters, she is the one who projects the least ease about being in a television show. It’s not that her actor, Jenna Fischer, is a naturally self-effacing performer. In the highly successful Office Ladies podcast that she’s been doing with her best buddy from the show, Angela Kinsey, she is enthusiastic, warm and a fluent and relaxed talker. The characteristics of Pam as a character are about how she’s written, and about Fischer’s decisions as an actor. Michael Scott loves the camera. He spends most of his storyline revelling in being covered by a camera crew. Only in his final appearance, in the finale, does he seem cheerfully indifferent about whether or not he’s on camera. Because by then, he has a new life. Jim Halpert is totally at ease with the camera. He treats the talking heads rather like a vlog: a way for him to explain himself, and tell the audience what he’s thinking. Jim’s confidence and general cheerfulness make him very easy to watch. —Whereas his English counterpart, Tim Canterbury, sometimes seemed like a man who, whenever he talked to the camera, was staring at the failure of his life. Jim, by contrast, seems like someone who feels like, even if his life is going badly, he’s not too downhearted, because at least he’s got the camera to confide in. Dwight Schrute treats the camera in talking heads sequences rather like he’s testifying at his own trial. He’s always justifying himself, or boasting about himself—often hilariously, like when he claims to have shot a werewolf except ‘by the time I found it, it had turned back into my neighbour’s dog’. Most of the other characters are pretty okay with the camera. Kelly Kapoor adores it, because she is under the delusion that she’s appearing in a Kardashians-like TV show in which we’re interested in her private life. Angela resents it, but then Angela resents pretty much everything, until she doesn’t. But when Pam does a talking head, it takes her a very long time before she entirely loses that faint air of rabbit-in-headlights—maybe four or five seasons. Her eyes dart from here to there, and she measures her words carefully, and gets distracted when she overhears herself. In one cold open, Michael Scott came in to the office, tossed his overcoat onto Pam’s head, went into his office and spent the rest of the day roaring things like ‘WHERE’S MY STEAK?’ Pam explained to the camera that Michael had just got Netflix, and was watching The Devil Wears Prada. The next day, Michael came in, very apologetic, and explained to Pam that he hadn’t realised that ‘Meryl Streep is the bad guy.’ Pam accepted the apology, and Michel affectionately called her ‘Manushka’ before going to his office. Cut to Pam, in a talking head: ‘Manushka’? [Pause, beams as she gets it] ‘Macushla’! He’s watching Million Dollar Baby. [Pause, smile fades] He’s going to kill me. When Fischer auditioned for the role, the casting director Allison Jones gave her the advice, ‘Dare to bore me.’ Fischer decided that Pam didn’t have an interview persona, and didn’t particularly want to have one. So, when she was in character and was asked by one of the producers ‘Do you like being a receptionist?’ she gave the flat reply ‘No,’ and then waited for the next question. This amused the producers so much that she got the part, incidentally fulfilling her lifetime ambition to have a leading role in a major sitcom. I think some viewers mistake Pam’s lack of complete ease with the camera as a feeling on her part that she thinks she’s better than all this. And there is something to that. At the beginning of the show, Pam and Jim are the only two characters who seem badly unfulfilled by working in the office. As time goes by, this air of discontent never quite wears off, but the office comes to seem like a more friendly place, because of the way the show’s tone changes over time. So I think that’s why some of the audience came to dislike them: the office started out like a dull, claustrophobic shithole with an annoying boss, but it turned into a more fantastic, absurd place with a lovable-but-annoying boss, and so Pam and Jim—who always wanted more out of life than this—came to seem ungrateful for not appreciating it more. Pam tries to make the best of things, with an initiative like her ‘Finer Things Club’, which she forms with Toby and Oscar, the other two people in the office with the biggest cultural ambitions. They get together and drink wine and eat nibbles and discuss literature, and on the one hand it’s kind of comically pretentious, but on the other hand, it’s a genuine attempt to recognise that the office really is not—at least, not for everyone—the city of dreams that Michael imagines it as being. (I have a theory as to why Michael adores the office so much until he doesn’t, and this answer is a spin-off from that theory.) Anyway, let’s just say that I sympathise with Pam’s artistic ambitions, and her dissatisfaction with being an office worker. A more valid charge against Pam, if we’re going to be drawing up charges, is that her girl-next-door charm and lovable vulnerability are belied by her tendencies towards bitchiness. … Yyyyeeaahhh, but I don’t really buy that, either. I don’t think that Pam was ever portrayed as someone who was supposed to be uncomplicatedly lovable. As the receptionist, Pam starts out as the person in the office who’s at the bottom of the heap. This is underlined in the pilot when Michael introduces her to the camera. Michael: This is our receptionist, Pam. Pam! Pam-Pam! Pam Beesly. Pam has been with us for... forever. Right, Pam? Pam: Well. I don't know. Michael: If you think she's cute now, you should have seen her a couple of years ago. [growls] Pam: What? And yet, from very early on—the first episode of season 2, to be precise, ‘The Dundies’, it becomes clear that Pam has a side that will not be held down. In that episode, she defies her boring-ass boyfriend Roy, who wants to go to a bar, and goes back to the Dundies so that she can hang out with Jim, and after a couple of enormous drinks, she casually takes a two-thirds-full pitcher of margaritas from a neighbouring table (Hey you guys can I finish that?), and then rescues the entire event with her booze-fuelled sympathy for Michael, her sheer enthusiasm for being out with the guy she likes most, and then her Halle-Berry-winning-the-Oscar-for-Monster’s-Ball-type speech on winning the ‘Whitest Sneakers’ award. A scene which beautifully ended with a completely rat-arsed Pam sliding off her barstool and laughing her ass off. (Fischer was not actually supposed to fall off her barstool, but kudos to Rainn Wilson for immediately leaping into amateur-paramedic action on that. Just as the reason why Pam steals other people’s drinks is that the scene is shot in an actual Chili’s restaurant, and the Chili’s chain wasn’t happy with her ordering more than two, as they have a strict ‘two drinks per customer’ rule.) From early on, Pam, in spite of her low status, has a lethal way with a put-down. Especially when the target is Ryan, the person she hates the most. Ryan: [seeing Pam behind the reception desk} Nice. Right back where I like you. Can you make ten copies of this for me? Pam: No. Ryan: Why not, what are you doing? Pam: Ah, buying lottery tickets online. Ryan: [chuckles] Everybody wants to be rich, but nobody wants to work for it. Pam: You came in at 10:30 today, right? Andy: [having just returned from an unscheduled three-month boat trip, seeing Pam leave the office early] Where are you going? Pam: … Uh, not on a three-month boat trip. Dwight: [when Pam, as office administrator, has threatened to move Dunder Mifflin out of the building that Dwight now owns, because of his ridiculous cost-cutting measures] Moving is one of the most stressful things you can do in life. You’ll probably just take it out on your kid. Jim will turn to the drink. Your family will fall apart. And twenty-five years from now, Cece will become world-famous… for stripping. Pam: That’s a sad story. I have another one. We move. The other tenants follow. The bank takes your building, takes your farm, takes your car, and beats the crap out of you. Penniless, you die, and my daughter Cece dances on your grave… fully clothed. And then there’s the bit where she complains about the filthiness of the office microwave. Ryan, very Ryan-ishly, tells her he’s totally on her side about that but that, after all, someone’s going to have to clean it, so… Pam turns her steeliest glare on him and murmurs ‘Yeah, I guess there’s a reason we have a temp, huh.’ But, for me, Pam’s most glorious moment of snark was wordless. In ‘Niagara Part 1’, Pam, who is pregnant and suffering heavily from morning sickness, politely requests the others to not eat very pungent food or wear strong perfume around her, because it makes her vomit. They are not impressed by this (Meredith refuses to give up her ‘afternoon cigar’) and Dwight in particular is delighted that strong smells can cause the foetus inside Pam to make her throw up, which he considers ‘badass’ of it. So Pam decides to step up her retaliation. I note that, of all of them (except Creed, who goes on cheerfully eating his lunch), Pam has the coolness to maintain eye contact with Dwight while throwing up, and then gives him an I warned you… look after she’s daintily wiped her mouth. The Office was always a show heavily centred on growth and development, and I have another answer on the back burner about that. But whereas Michael grew from a self-absorbed but nevertheless high-spirited baby to a mature man, Pam grew more naturalistically, from a glum doormat to a calm and confident woman. In a show full of larger than life characters, Jenna Fischer played Pam with the subtlety and nuance you’d expect of a character in Jane Austen. (Pam does rather resemble Anne Elliot in Persuasion.) She fully earned her place in sitcom history.

Question: Why did young Vito Corleone seem like such a slow-witted kid compared to the sharp, deliberate mobster he grew into?
Answer: Vito’s best quality is patience. He had it as a kid. When he knew that Don Ciccio wanted him dead, he learned to be quiet and not be discovered as he was being taken out of the town. When he was diagnosed with TB and put in a room on Ellis Island, he didn’t kick up a fuss. He sat on the bed and sang a song from home, to cheer himself up. He never jumps to conclusions. He gathers evidence and gives himself time to decide what to do. When Clemenza throws him a blanket full of stolen guns, he stares at the contents in perplexity, but he doesn’t freak out. When Clemenza offers to repay him by giving him a rug, he tags along and, baffled rather than scared, observes as Clemenza calmly sets about stealing the rug and then preparing to shoot a cop, should the cop attempt to interfere. It’s as if Vito starts out with the question What must I, Vito Corleone, do and not do, in order to succeed and build a life for my family? And, slowly and patiently, he goes about researching the answer: learning from others’ mistakes (Don Fanucci, who has no loyal friends); remaining grateful and friendly to Abbandando even when Abbandando has to fire him; building his own network of friends who are loyal to him because of his loyalty to them, his hospitality, and his willingness to take care of business (Fanucci again.) Vito never speeds up, never gets greedy, never makes assumptions. His deliberation as a man is just the experienced, grown-up version of his apparent slow-wittedness as a kid. He was never interested in seeming to be smarter, more important or more intelligent than he really was—unlike Clemenza, whose man-of-the-world bullshit got Vito involved in the theft of a rug. Vito likes that about Clemenza (and the Corleones got a nice rug out of it) but it’s not his style at all. By the time he has his own business, he doesn’t even need to threaten the hapless landlord Roberto, who wants to evict the woman that came to him for help. Instead, he offers the guy six months’ rent in advance, and when the guy blows his top and threatens to ‘kick your Sicilian ass right out in the street’, Vito remains calm and affable, presses the money into his hand ad advises him to ask around about him, then shakes his hand and strides off. When the landlord shows up at the Genco office, a mouse-sized shadow of himself, Vito’s reputation alone leads the landlord to first let the widow stay in the apartment, then Vito’s silence and imperturbable calm makes him knock $10 off the rent. Only at that point does Vito smile and offer him coffee, whereupon the landlord fumbles his way out of the office, babbling excuses. Look at when Sonny interrupts during the meeting involving Vito, himself and Sollozzo: Vito silences him with a gesture and a look and a curt Wait a minute, and then turns back to Sollozzo and says mildly that he has a sentimental weakness for his children. Only after Sollozzo’s gone does he express his annoyance to Sonny: Never tell anyone outside the family what you’re thinking again. Patience. It looks like stupidity, but it doesn’t have to be.

Question: Can you write a whole novel with Stream of consciousness?
Answer: Hardly anyone ever has, because it’s not a very good way of telling a story. The earliest examples I know of are Édouard Dujardin in his 1887 novel Les lauriers sont coupés and Dorothy Richardson in her brave but rather boring novel cycle, Pilgrimage, published between 1915 and 1967. I’ve tried more than once to plough through Richardson’s first volume, Pointed Roofs, but her relentless focus on her heroine’s every last thought wore me down. Edit: More examples in the comments, including Faulkner, who I should’ve remembered. Franklin Veaux, in his answer, said that James Joyce did it in Ulysses and that the result is ‘impenetrable’. He is entirely wrong on both counts. Ulysses has 19 episodes, and only the first six and the last one of them could be regarded as containing examples of this technique. Beginning at episode 7, Joyce introduces different techniques and by episode 13 he’s all but abandoned the stream of consciousness. And even before then, he doesn’t use it in a systematic way. It could even be argued that only the last episode in the book, Molly Bloom’s, is a pure example of the stream of consciousness, because it’s supposed to be a representation of the thoughts passing through the character’s head, but in every other episode, Joyce describes what people are doing and generally narrates the action; only in the last one are we entirely inside Molly’s head. (Also, it’s not ‘impenetrable’, although quite a few people lined up to confess their substandard reading skills in his comments section.) The problem with using this technique for a whole novel is that, when every event is screened through the prism of the character’s consciousness, it’s difficult to render action and drama. It’s much easier to avoid the strict stream of consciousness style and place the reader sort of behind the character’s shoulder, observing what they’re doing and able to tell what they’re thinking, but not hearing every last thing that goes through their brain. This is what Joyce and most good writers do with the technique. Stream of consciousness works for Molly in Ulysses, because her episode is in the middle of the night and she’s not doing much besides thinking. But when a character needs to go to the toilet or buy something in a shop, or, for that matter, engage in an exciting battle with an adversary, we’re better off leaving their head so that we can get a clear picture of what’s happening.

Question: What is the reason for the male 'gay' accent? It isn't regional, it isn't communal, it is just annoying. Why is it that I know tons of gay guys who just talk like people?
Answer: I assume you mean something like the accent of Buddy Cole, the ‘alpha queen’ character created and performed by Scott Thompson, on the great Canadian sketch comedy show The Kids in the Hall. Buddy is of course a parodic character, but he’s also an exuberant celebration of a particular kind of performative sexuality. (Thompson is himself gay, but he doesn’t talk like this in everyday life.) Look, some people like to perform their sexuality in a certain way. Others don’t. If you were to meet me in real life, I doubt that my queerness would be apparent to you. A lifetime of being quiet and reserved has made me quiet and reserved. Get me started on something I’m enthusiastic about, however, and I light(en) up. Most gay men I know (and I don’t know any other openly bisexual men, except online) don’t talk like Buddy, either. … Well, actually hardly anyone talks like Buddy. Few have the balls to. To perform your sexuality in this way can be very risky, if you don’t know the company you’re in. But people who do, do so because they want to, and they’re not seeking your approval. I wouldn’t say they do it because it feels ‘natural’: even the idea of that causes the shade of Oscar Wilde to loom over me and smirk at my naivety. What I mean by that is that Buddy’s lisp and his little sighs of satisfaction are no less of a performance than the one given by straight men who have no indoor voice, and who can’t give a handshake that isn’t bone-crushing. So, my advice is: live and let live, okay? We all perform. Just sit back and enjoy it.

Question: Why is there so much angst(?) about "reading" music? To those of us who are serious musicians, it is not a bane - it is more of a blessing that allows us to easily, efficiently, and quickly exchange musical ideas.
Answer: It’s all about people’s insecurities and anxieties regarding skill and professionalism in musical performance. Personally, I blame the invention of recording technology. Dog: [thinks] The bass response on this thing is for shit. Why? Well, before we had recorded music, there were two ways of hearing music: People like hearing music, so there was much more demand for live music in everyday situations, since there was no way to hear it other than hear someone playing it live. People were more likely to learn basic instrumental or singing skills, because they were more likely to be called upon to use them. Musicianship in society was, as a result, more widely distributed. People were more likely to be able to read sheet music for simple popular songs. And then recording technology was invented. And it became possible to hear truly expert musicians without having to go and see them. In rural County Sligo in Ireland in the first decades of the 20th century, there was a proliferation of local styles of traditional fiddle playing. One of the best local fiddlers, Michael Coleman, emigrated to the USA in 1914, settling in New York City. After establishing himself in the US, Coleman in the 20s and 30s recorded a series of sides for several record companies, notably Columbia. His records sold well and were exported abroad, including to Ireland. When Coleman’s records showed up in Sligo, such was his prestige that people organising dances started using them to supply the music, and local fiddlers who couldn’t imitate his style were turned away in favour of record players. Coleman’s style became the dominant style of fiddle playing. The different varieties of Sligo style gradually died out. When post-WW2 popular music took off in the Fifties, people took up playing it but they learned it by ear, because it wasn’t difficult to learn by ear. In the Sixties, popular music was transformed by a combination of factors: This became further complicated later in the 60s, when young middle-class musicians with more musical education turned to rock music as an outlet, rather than jazz or classical music. Result: prog and its descendants. So what happens then is that the popular music begins to fragment into innumerable sub-styles, some more difficult than others, some reliant on playing by ear, some not. And these styles create subcultures which differ from each other: some styles of popular music prize technical difficulty and display, others prize simplicity and directness, others even prize a kind of defiant amateurism. And even then, the prestige of recorded music is such that many people will consider a band of self-confessed non-readers which has a recording contract to be more respectable or more admirable than a less successful band of higher-skilled musicians, because one is more ‘professional’ than the other. It used to be easier to distinguish professional musicians from non-professional ones than it is now: the professionals made a living playing music and the other ones didn’t. But in the streaming era, the financial rewards of playing music have catastrophically shrunk. Many musicians in popular bands have to work at other jobs in order to earn enough money to go on the road and play to paying audiences. Professional/amateur is not a binary thing anymore, if it ever was: it’s a spectrum. It doesn’t really help that arguably the most influential of bands, the Beatles, were a.) highly creative and musical, generating a body of songs that go on inspiring people and that continue to be re-interpreted, and also b.) defiantly amateurish in their refusal to learn to read music or formally study it. (And c.) enormously financially successful, at that.) When most of the music we listen to is recorded music, made in professional circumstances, unless we deliberately only listen to cheap punk rock or similar genres which are self-consciously shambolic, the chances are that our baseline expectations of musical proficiency will be quite high. This makes us less tolerant of lower standards of musicianship. We may not be relaxed enough to appreciate the informal sing-song. We become skill snobs. (Think of Andy Bernard in The Office, incapable of even singing along to a car radio without putting a finger to one ear and turning it into an audition for America’s Next A Cappella Sensation.) Music can only ever be an extraordinary event, not a casual conversation. And so, our anxieties about performance and skill and expertise become so great that some people go through the looking glass and come to think that being able to read will ‘stifle their creativity’, because that’s the excuse given by the Beatles and bands like them for not bothering to learn to read. Others perhaps genuinely fear that it will do so, or that learning to read will destroy their confidence because it’ll reveal to them the limits of their skill. The problem with this is that, of course, not everyone is as musical and as creative as great non-reading musicians like the Beatles, or Wes Montgomery, or Erroll Garner. Even a non-reading musician such as Jimi Hendrix realised, towards the end of his life, that if he wanted to develop further as a musician, he’d probably have to buckle down and do some studying, which he unfortunately never lived to do. Since learning to read is also time-consuming and occasionally frustrating, it feels too much like work to some people for whom music should be all play, and rather than confess to this, they make out like it’s not a skill worth having. When really, it’s just a normal skill which is worth having, if you want to play music, and don’t want to be confined to styles of music where it’s unnecessary. Or even considered vaguely suspect. For me, as for any musician with some reading skills, it’s the awareness that I’m really not as good as the Beatles or Wes Montgomery or Jimi Hendrix that makes me keep up my reading skills. Like most guitar players, I need all the help I can get.

Question: What are the best songs by R.E.M.?
Answer: Well, these are my favourites, anyway, so I think they’re the best. The boys in 1991, kings of the world: Bill Berry, Peter Buck, Mike Mills in ‘suddenly handsome’ mode, Michael Stipe. R.E.M. were, I think, inseparable from their time and place, for a lot of us who were/are fans of them. Their early songs was self-consciously incomprehensible. Their very earliest songs, as captured on bootlegs and rehearsal tapes, were simple boy-girl garage rock ditties, but at some point they decided that if they were ever going to get anywhere, they needed some extra ingredient, and that extra ingredient was contributed largely by singer/lyricist Michael Stipe: mystery. Stipe went from coherently bawling simple lyrics to mumbling enigmatic lyrics, or stretching out vowels and swallowing consonants so that even when he could be heard, you had little idea what he was singing. Large stretches of their debut album are, as a result, impossible to decipher. When you’re a confused adolescent, as so many of us were in the 80s, this meant that you could project whatever meaning you wanted onto their songs, and pesky things like clear interpretations wouldn’t get in the way. Eddie Vedder of Pearl Jam put this superbly well when he inducted them into the RRHOF in 2007: And, how do you explain the dialogue between Michael and the listener—a dialogue that grew up and we grew up with it? Uh, such wisdom in the feelings in these songs that, I think, they helped us find things that we knew were inside us, and I think they helped us find things that we didn’t know we had inside us. And I can say, there are things that I hold and feel [hand on heart] very deeply about inside here, that Michael Stipe put in there himself. What’s really incredible about this is, is that while this is happening… this all happens without ever being able to understand a fucking word he is saying. And while the songs were incomprehensible, the music of those songs was always direct, appealing, and a strange combination of 60s nostalgia and 70s new wave: energetic enough to be stirring, but familiar enough to feel comforting. Back in the day, they used to get endless comparisons to the Byrds, but there was always as much Soft Boys and Television and Patti Smith in the mix. This is what made them so appealing, when you’re young. But as we grew older, they maybe started to seem less like something that we needed. Stipe couldn’t go on singing like that forever. He had opinions—righteous ones, to be sure—and he wanted to share them. In song form. Which wasn’t always 100% effective. Their music became less elusive and more direct. They became huge with a song like ‘Everybody Hurts’, which I thought was so on-the-nose that it was silly, but some people loved it. Then they took stylistic turns which sometimes thrilled me, but which displeased many of the fans they’d gained by becoming world-famous. I thought Monster was a sleazy, sardonic, noisy, surprisingly tender masterpiece, but it turned off the people who wanted more ‘Everybody Hurts’. By the time I was in my late 20s, they were still going, and getting new audiences, but I was no longer in love with them. (And, believe me, I had a serious and very confusing Stipe crush when I was 16 or so, and too lacking in self-knowledge to realise that I had one.) And then Bill Berry left, and they kept going. I bought Up out of loyalty, but it made me sad, and I couldn’t tell if it made me sad because the songs were sad, or because the band made me sad by no longer being what they had once been to me. (I suspect now it was both.) And after that, I lost touch with them. I didn’t even listen to their last three albums until after they’d broken up, years later. But I have at least listened to all their stuff. And I salute them, on behalf of all of us who were helped through difficult adolescences by their music. In no particular order, then:

Question: What would world reaction have been if the UK had tried to defeat the IRA by flattening Dublin, Cork and half of Belfast?
Answer: It would have been regarded as a completely insane decision. For one thing, support for the IRA was far from universal in the Irish population. I grew up in Dublin, and I was an adult before I met people who were actual IRA supporters, as opposed to people whose position was something like ‘I see where they’re coming from but I entirely disagree that physical force was the way to go about it’, or else vaguely sentimental about the ‘Ra but certainly not inclined to funnel money their way, or harbour escaped prisoners, or otherwise lift a finger and risk imprisonment. When I met people in Dublin who actually were hardcore republicans, it was clear to me that a.) they weren’t f***ing around, and b.) there weren’t very many of them. So, flattening an entire city of a million people because of the acts of maybe a few hundred of them, would be regarded as a horrific crime. Especially as the victims wouldn’t have been safely ‘Middle Eastern’, or whatever, and therefore easier to dehumanise. Also, the Catholic half of Belfast is still technically part of the UK. I fancy that even the unionists would have been pretty pissed about it. (The novelist George A. Birmingham’s 1912 novel The Red Hand of Ulster is an alternative history novel in which loyalists in the north of Ireland take up arms against the British forces because, in the course of suppressing an uprising, a stray British shell has destroyed a statue of Queen Victoria.) So, not entirely sure why this rather silly question got asked, because even Thatcher at her most militantly stupid wouldn’t have sanctioned carpet-bombing the capital city of one of the UK’s major trading partners at the time. … On the other hand, if they had flattened Cork, I think most of the rest of Ireland would have been like, Well, makes sense. Question: How and what did Plato do to live to the age of 80 in the classical era?
Answer: This is a question about statistics. You’ve heard that the average life expectancy in Plato’s time was 40, or whatever it was, and you’re wondering how in the world he managed to live to twice that age. What you don’t realise is that ‘average life expectancy is 40’ does not mean ‘people in those days usually died at the age of around 40’. It means ‘if you average how long people in that era tended to live, you get the number 40’. Actually, people in Plato’s time quite regularly lived into old age. Sophocles was over 90 when he died. Aeschylus was about 67. Euripides was about 74. The reason the life expectancy figure is so low is not because everyone lived shorter lives back then: it’s because so many people died in infancy. If you have 10 people who died at the ages of (for example) 67, 70, 75, 35, 78, 80, 87, 54, 73 and 86, their average life expectancy is (67+70+75+35+78+80+87+54+73+86)/10=70 years old, rounded down to the last birthday. However, if they died at the ages of 67, 65, 1, 1, 2, 4, 87, 54, 73 and 86, their average life expectancy is 44 years old, even though, as you can see, most of them made it well past that age. Because that’s how averages work. So, Plato didn’t have some special secret for living so long in an age where most people died younger than they do today. He just survived infancy in an age where many didn’t.

Question: What are some classic rock songs to introduce to someone that's never heard it and have the person instantly love the genre?
Answer: There are none. You can’t ‘have’ people ‘instantly love’ an entire genre of music. And no music, by anyone, anywhere, ever, is so instantly and universally appealing as to have the power to make people love all other music in that genre. Besides which, there is a problem with the whole idea of ‘classic rock’, as we can see from the extraordinary variety of music that other answerers have decided is ‘classic rock’. It’s that ‘classic rock’ doesn’t exist. Any ‘genre’ that includes musicians as diverse as Chuck Berry, Pink Floyd, ZZ Top, The Eagles, Led Zeppelin, The Bee Gees, The Knack, Iggy Pop, Wings, Guns ’n’ Roses, Queen and the B-52s, is not a ‘genre’. It’s a demographic. ‘To Love Somebody’ and ‘Black Dog’ are both fine songs, but playing one of them to someone isn’t going to make them like the other one. Similarly, just because a person likes Zappa’s ‘Apostrophe’ is no guarantee that they will also like Kiss. That’s why this ridiculous question and these ridiculous answers don’t work. ‘Classic rock’ is not a kind of music, but a kind of music fan. That’s why it’s so incoherent as a musical category. Everyone who likes to think that they love classic rock—and I myself am not one of those people—will have their own personal playlist of what constitutes it, and, as we have seen, they are not linked by common stylistic features of the music in them. ‘Classic rock’ is merely whatever a person who likes classic rock, calls classic rock. I mean, if ‘To Love Somebody’ is classic rock, is ‘Stayin’ Alive’ also classic rock? Because it’s by the same band. Is it possible that the Bee Gees were only classic rock some of the time? If so, when? And why? ‘Classic rock’ was, as we know, originally a name for a radio format. It has since been reified to the point that people now think of it as if were a musical form. But it isn’t one. Classic rock fans are often of a certain age, and they have a tendency to have certain habits of thought, such as (for example) thinking that the music they like is ‘good’ or ‘real’ music, whereas music that came later—typically hip hop—is not real music. This is of course nonsense, and plenty of people (me included) enjoy some of the rock music of the 60s and 70s and also have a healthy love of hip hop. But we probably need to stop talking about classic rock the way this question does. Because it’s nonsense to think that it refers to a kind of music that you could play to someone, and which would have the effect of making that person ‘instantly love’ all other kinds of that music. Classic rock is a lot of different, stylistically diverse kinds of music, from different times and places, that have only one thing in common: Somebody, somewhere, calls them ‘classic rock’.

Question: How can someone who doesn't know how to read/write/understand sheet notation/music still improvise/solo on their instrument effectively?
Answer: You do realise that being able to read/write/understand sheet music has absolutely nothing to do with the ability to improvise? Nothing. Nada. Níl aon rud. I’m an improvising musician, and I’ve met professional classical musicians who were far better at sight reading than I am, and I’ve invited them to improvise, and they’ve said no because they didn’t know how to and were too scared to try. Improvisation is the most primordial musical gesture. We were improvising long before we had notation. We know this because the oldest surviving instruments are far older than the oldest surviving music notation. Most rock guitarists can’t read music, and yet there are few of them who would never, ever improvise even a little bit. Now, I grant that being able to read may make you a better musician, because it gives you easier access to more music. But I very much doubt that it makes you a better improviser. If it did, all classical musicians would be good improvisers, yet as we’ve seen, many if not most of them don’t play improvised music at all, ever. Improvisation is not about knowing how to read notes. It’s about knowing how to make up music on the spot, and having the nerve to do it, instead of playing music from sheet music or from memory.

Question: What would be a good war story that should be a film but hasn’t?
Answer: All the people in this picture were almost certainly killed, shortly after it was taken. This is a bit of a cheat, because there actually are a couple of movies very loosely based on this story, but they’re not very good and certainly not popular. I think the full story, properly made with a decent budget and a good script and some good effects, would make a great movie. WW2 buffs will already have guessed that I’m talking about the St Nazaire raid. The St Nazaire raid, which took place on 28 March 1942, was so audacious that its story reads like a treatment for a movie. It happened because the port of St Nazaire in northwestern France had one of the largest dry docks in the world: the Louis Joubert dry dock, big enough to hold an ocean liner, and also, if necessary, a German battleship. The Bismarck had been sunk while it was trying to make for St Nazaire for repairs in that self-same dock. When its sister ship the Tirpitz was declared operational, the Royal Navy had already begun planning to attack the dry dock. If the dry dock were out of action, no German battleship in the Atlantic could be assured of adequate repair facilities on the French coast. The Tirpitz could never risk sailing too far from Germany or German-occupied territory. Various plans were discussed. The lock gates were too big for SOE agents to blow them up by hand. The port was five miles up the Loire estuary, making a straight naval attack too risky. So the plan was conceived to take an old destroyer, fill it with explosives, stick a bunch of commandos on it, sail it up the estuary and have it ram the dry dock and then deploy the commandos, who would personally demolish some docking facilities. The destroyer would be accompanied by motor boats that could be used to evacuate the crew and commandos, and then, once everyone had got away, the destroyer would blow up, wrecking the dry dock. You’re probably already envisaging the cinematic possibilities. The mission commander was Commander Robert Ryder of the Royal Navy, who would use the motor gunboat MGB 314 as his command vessel. The destroyer was an old WW1 destroyer which had begun life as the USS Buchanan before being donated to the Royal Navy, whereupon it became HMS Campbeltown. It would be commanded by Lt Cdr Stephen Beattie, a Welshman, 33 years old, known to his colleagues for some unknown reason as ‘Sam’. The commandos would be led by Lt Col Augustus Newman. The Campbeltown was heavily modified for the mission, receiving extra armour and a lighter, faster-firing deck gun. Two of its funnels were removed and the other two were modified to make it look more like a German destroyer. Four and a half tons of high explosives were packed into its bow and equipped with time fuses, then the explosives were cemented into place to make them impossible to remove. The fuses were set to detonate at 4.30 in the morning, by which time the raiding crew would be assumed to have long gone. Sixteen motor boats would carry the bulk of the commandos and also defend the raiding party from surface vessels. Two other destroyers, Tynedale and Atherstone, would accompany the Campbeltown and its flotilla of motor boats to French coast, and await the raiding team’s return. In all, the raiding party comprised about 346 sailors and 265 commandos. St Nazaire was defended by about 5,000 German troops, with dozens of coastal and anti-aircraft guns. There were also three German navy vessels in the Loire estuary: a destroyer, an armed trawler and a minesweeper. The raiding team left Falmouth in Cornwall at 2pm on 26 March. The journey to the French coast was mostly uneventful, although they did encounter two French trawlers. The trawler crews were captured and the trawlers were sunk to prevent anyone from telling tales. On 27 March, RAF bombers attacked the port. Due to bad weather, only four aircraft managed to hit targets in the town. The bombers had been ordered to drop only one bomb at a time: the bombing raid’s real purpose was to divert German attention away from the sea. It didn’t really work. Karl-Konrad Mecke in command of the 22nd Naval Flak Brigade smelled a rat. At midnight on the 28th, he issued a warning that there might be an impending parachute attack. At 1am, he ordered the guns to stop firing and the searchlights to be turned off. By then, the raiding convoy had entered the Loire estuary half an hour earlier. The Campbeltown, flying the German naval ensign, barely scraped over the sandbars. At 1.22am on the 28th March, the entire convoy, steaming towards the harbour, was suddenly illuminated by German searchlights and ordered to identify itself. MGB 314 replied with a phrase captured from a German trawler. A shore battery began firing at them, and MGB 314 and Campbeltown radioed the Germans that they were shooting at their own ships. The ensuing doubt in the minds of the Germans bought them a few more minutes. At 1.28, with the convoy one mile from the dock gates, Beattie on Campbeltown lowered the German flag and hoisted the White Ensign. The shooting from the shore batteries became more intense. Several of the motor launches carrying commandos were unarmoured, and quickly destroyed. Campbeltown herself was hit over and over again. It didn’t matter, as long as she kept going: this was always going to have been her final voyage. The helmsman of the Campbeltown was killed. Another helmsman replaced him, was wounded and in turn replaced by a third one. All the ships and boats in the convoy were now firing back at the gun emplacements and searchlights. Weathering a hail of machine gun and artillery fire, Campbeltown sped up to 19 knots, cut through the anti-torpedo netting slung across the harbour and, at 1.34am, rammed the gates of the Louis Joubert dry dock so hard that it wedged itself 33 feet into them and crushed 36 feet of its own bow. The commandos in the surviving motor launches disembarked and set about suppressing the German defenders and demolishing various targets. The Campbeltown’s crew opened her seacocks, flooding her and making it harder to remove her. Lt Col Newman coordinated the commando attack, using mortar fire to destroy a German machine gun position and generally buying time for the commando demolition teams. Cmdr Ryder went aboard the Campbeltown to ensure that she was firmly stuck, then returned to MGB 314. Some of the Campbeltown’s wounded crew were being taken aboard launches for evacuation. Ryder noted that the Germans had already recaptured much of the harbour era and that it would not be possible to evacuate the surviving commandos, so he ordered MGB 314 to head back to sea. When Lt Col Newman realised that he and his men weren’t going to be evacuated, they decided to do their best to get back to England by themselves. The commandos fought their way through the town, but eventually their ammunition ran out and they surrendered. 4.30am came around, the time when the fuses in Campbeltown’s explosives were set to go off. Nothing happened. At 6.30, the destroyers Tynedale and Atherstone saw MGB 314 and two launches coming towards them. They scooped up the survivors, including Ryder, and sailed for home. Three more launches made it to the rendezvous point some time later, but the destroyers had long gone. The launches made it back to England under their own power. 169 members of the raiding team were dead. 215 were taken prisoner, including the Campbeltown’s captain, Stephen Beattie. The sun rose on an estuary full of charred wrecks, with the Campbeltown still wedged in the dock gates. German soldiers and sailors searched the ship. They didn’t find the explosives. They didn’t realise that the explosives were there. Shortly before noon, a party of senior German officers and civilians were taking a tour of the wrecked but still intact Campbeltown. Meanwhile, Stephen Beattie was being interrogated by a German naval officer. The officer told Beattie that the raid had been rather foolish, and that it wouldn’t take long to fix the damage. At that moment, the Campbeltown exploded. I leave it to the reader to imagine the effect on the immediate environment of four and a half tons of high explosives going off inside the already weakened hull of a 1,280 ton destroyer. According to legend, Beattie waited for the noise to die down and then told his interrogator, We’re not quite as foolish as you think. About 360 people were killed by the blast, which rendered the dry dock inoperative for the rest of the war. It wouldn’t be repaired until 1948. 89 decorations were awarded to members of the St Nazaire raiding party, including five Victoria Crosses, three of which went to Ryder, Beattie and Newman. Newman died in 1972; Beattie in 1975; Ryder in 1986. The Tirpitz never entered the Atlantic. It remained in Norway, obliging the Royal Navy to keep ships in the area to prevent her from having a free hand in the North Sea, before being sunk by RAF bombers in 1944. Tell me this isn’t a potentially awesome movie.

Question: What is the absolute worst album by a successful band?
Answer: I’m not saying that this is the worst album by any successful band, but it is the worst by this particular one. Around the Sun by R.E.M., 2004. An album so utterly forgettable that it’s almost as if they hadn’t made it at all. Most of the songs have very similar arrangements, tempi, moods, chord progressions and general feel: bland alternative folk-rock where you really can’t be bothered to pay attention because there’s just nothing there. The sound of a band with nothing worth saying but a determination to say it anyway. To their credit, they realised that it sucked and they did their best to get it together on the next album. Peter Buck called it ‘not listenable’, and I fully agree. I once loved this band, and I still enjoy a lot of their music, but I’d prefer to sit in silence than listen to Around the Sun.

Question: I've seen movie stunt doubles look exactly like the main actors. Why don't the stunt person do the acting themselves AND do their own stunts? Wouldn't this be cheaper than paying the actor and stunt person?
Answer: I answered an almost identical question before. You haven’t thought this through. Actors are paid what they are paid because their presence in a movie can guarantee an audience, which guarantees box office revenue. People don’t usually know who stunt performers are, so the presence of a stunt performer does not guarantee an audience; also, this means that actors can have different stunt performers doing their stunts because the stunt performer is not required to be recognised by the audience, and indeed shouldn’t be. They should be mistaken for the actor. If the stunt performer is also doing all the acting, they become famous as actors and so their value goes up, and all of a sudden they aren’t cheap anymore. So that’s why stunt performers a.) don’t do all the acting and b.) are cheaper than actors. As long as they’re passing for the actor in the stunt, they don’t bring people to the movie the way actors do. If they became visible as actors they would become more expensive. It would also be a great deal more expensive to insure them.
